name: El Presidio Real de San Francisco
summary: Founded 17 Sep 1776 by José Joaquín Moraga. A 1792 inventory found just one 3-pounder brass cannon; guns were concentrated at the Castillo, not the quadrangle.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I; NPS Golden Gate NRA
notes: Vancouver (1792) saw a brass 3-pdr lashed to a log at Fort Point and one on a rotten carriage here.

name: Provisional earthwork, Punta del Cantil Blanco
summary: Six mounted guns on a barbette platform Vancouver saw natives erecting in 1793, on Anza's 1776 cross site; superseded that August by the permanent Castillo.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I

name: Castillo de San Joaquín
summary: The flagship Spanish work, on the Fort Point bluff. Armed 1794 with eleven brass 9-pounders landed from the Aránzazu; rebuilt to a horseshoe c.1815; embrasures for 16 guns. Built by mission Native laborers. ⭐ The SF presidio company's monthly artillery relaciones give the post-rebuild armament: by 1 Apr 1816 the battery mounted 3 iron 24-pdrs, 1 iron 12-pdr (+1 burst), and 8 bronze half-culverins (8-pdr), with 2 bronze pedreros at the presidio; three iron 8-pdrs were added by May 1817 (a dozen+ serviceable guns at its Spanish-era peak). A standing 2-man 'vigía en la costa' coastal watch appears by Jan 1820 (post-Bouchard); the fort guard was 1 corporal + 4 soldiers. ⭐ The 1 Feb 1820 estado records a major post-Bouchard reconfiguration: a new iron 32-pounder, the bronze half-culverins cut from 8 to 6, three iron 4-pounders redistributed to Mission Santa Clara, and a second (new) royal flag. Into the Mexican era, the 7 Jan 1837 San Francisco artillery-park inventory (Comandante General M. G. Vallejo handing the parque to Capt. Francisco Sánchez) lists iron cannon of 24/12/8/4-lb and bronze of 10/8/2½-lb with garrison gun-carriages; by 1839 the SF, Sonoma, Monterey and Santa Bárbara detachments each held only small ordnance stocks and chronically short cartridges.
result: Demolished 1853; cliff cut down for Fort Point
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I; Thompson, Seacoast Fortifications SF Harbor (HRS 1979) | Vallejo Documentos, BANC MSS C-B 15 (SF presidio artillery relación, 1 Apr 1816); C-B 16 (monthly relaciones 1817; estado 1 Feb 1820, the 32-pdr reconfiguration); C-B 24 (SF artillery-park inventory, 7 Jan 1837, Vallejo→Sánchez); C-B 25 (1839 presidio detachment ordnance states)
notes: Six 17th-c. Peruvian bronze cannon survive on the Presidio. Bancroft V: Frémont spiked four guns, 1 July 1846 (not five, per some sources).

name: Batería de San José / de Yerba Buena
summary: Built under Gov. Borica on Point San José (Black Point) to cover the Yerba Buena anchorage; brushwood fascines, eight embrasures, five bronze 8-pounders sent over from the Castillo. No permanent garrison.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (Prov. St. Pap. xvi.55, xvii.148–9)
notes: Second-oldest Spanish battery on the bay; derelict by 1806.

name: Castillo de San Joaquín (Mexican era)
summary: Inherited and left to decay by Mexico. An 1843 sketch shows a horseshoe adobe of 16 embrasures with just five guns still mounted: three obsolete, plus a pair of sound Manila-cast bronzes; by 1835 essentially one artilleryman.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. V

name: Presidio of San Francisco (Mexican era)
summary: Garrison shrank to 15–20 men (1824–25) and was largely relocated to El Cuartel de Sonoma (1835, Vallejo); by the 1840s the presidio was 'entirely dismantled.'
sources: Bancroft, History of California; NPS

name: Batería de Yerba Buena (Mexican era)
summary: Already ruinous 'Black Point' under Mexico; no documented refurbishment.
sources: Bancroft, History of California, vol. I

name: Fort Point (Fort Winfield Scott)
summary: Brick-and-granite casemated fort, four tiers, designed for 126 guns; the only Third System fort west of the Mississippi. Held 40 ten-inch Rodmans in its casemates by 1867.
result: Preserved; Fort Point National Historic Site (NPS)
sources: NPS Fort Point NHS; Martini, Fort Point (2016); Thompson HRS 1979
notes: Never fired a shot in anger; the Golden Gate Bridge arch was redesigned to span it.

name: Fort Alcatraz

result: GGNRA/NPS; works buried under the later prison
sources: Martini, Fortress Alcatraz (1991); Thompson HRS 1979
notes: No post in the harbor carried heavier armament; became a military prison from 1907.

name: Mare Island AA defenses (WWII)
summary: Mare Island Navy Yard was defended in WWII by MOBILE 90 mm AA guns and .50-cal machine guns (211th Coast Artillery, on station a week after Pearl Harbor) plus barrage balloons (309th CA Balloon Bn), in positions spread across the south end, Hwy 37, and North Vallejo. The yard never had a FIXED coastal-defense gun battery; San Pablo Bay was screened by the Golden Gate forts ~20 mi downstream.
result: ⚠ Mobile AA only; no fixed seacoast battery; air-raid siren tower & shelter booths survive
sources: North American Forts (ca-central); Calif. State Military Museum (Mare Island / HDSF)
notes: Civil War: a garrison (soldiers on USS Independence, then Marines), no mounted gun battery. Endicott era: explicitly excluded from the Harbor Defenses of San Francisco. FortWiki lists Mare Island as a Navy yard, not a coast-defense fort. Position approximate (south-end AA site). The pin sat at 38.065,-122.253, which is open water in Carquinez Strait rather than the yard the guns defended. The 211th Coast Artillery's 90 mm guns were MOBILE, so no fixed emplacement exists to pin; the marker is placed on the Navy Yard at the south end of Mare Island and stays CONJECTURAL, which is what it is.

result: Spain depends on visiting vessels to cross its own frontier
sources: C-A 14 p. 113. Arrillaga.

name: Viceroy Orders Bodega · "Whether or Not English Are There"
summary: Revilla Gigedo orders Bodega occupied. Full fortification plan for Bodega + SF + Monterey + SD. Never executed. Supplies eventually repurposed (June 10, 1794).
sources: C-A 22, ii.144–148; bodega-failure-1793.

name: English at Bodega "con los cañones en tierra"
summary: Arrillaga reports an English vessel anchored at Bodega with "cannons on land." Identity uncertain; Colnett traces? New vessel? Rumor? Same year as Spanish Bodega failure.
result: Foreign military presence in territory Spain cannot reach

name: Zúñiga Shows Bodega Plans to British · No Concealment
summary: San Diego commandant Zúñiga freely shows Bodega harbor plans to British officers. No concealment at all; contradicts the tight security at SF. The policy was inconsistent.
result: Concealment policy fails at San Diego
sources: Menzies 1924:335.

name: RAC Fur-Collecting Begins at Bodega
summary: 130 Aleut hunters aboard Kodiak. First Russian representative: Tarakanov. 40+ Russians + 150 Indians by 1809 (Argüello report). Moraga protests; ignored.
result: Permanent Russian presence established; Spain protests but cannot act
sources: Milliken 2009:22–25; C-A 12.

name: 130 Bidarkas in San Francisco Bay
summary: 130 Aleut bidarkas (kayaks) hunting sea otter inside San Francisco Bay. The Russians are inside Spain's premier port and Spain cannot stop them.
result: Russian hunting inside the Bay; sovereignty violated
sources: C-A 12 (Prov. St. Pap. XIX).

name: Farallon Islands · Russian Sealing Station
summary: Russian sealing station on the Farallones; 18 miles off the coast of San Francisco. Aleut hunters camped seasonally. Spain/Mexico never contested it.
result: Russian territory visible from SF; unchallenged
sources: Bancroft II; Fort Ross sources.

name: Hagemeister Treaty with Kashaya Pomo
summary: Russia negotiates land cession with Kashaya Pomo chiefs; not Spanish authorities. "Allies of Russia" medals distributed 1819. Russians treat indigenous peoples as sovereign landowners because, north of the Bay, they are.
result: Russia treats Pomo as sovereign; Spain does not exist here
sources: Protocol of the meeting at Colony Ross between the Indian tribal chiefs and Captain-Lieutenant Hagemeister, 22 September 1817. Archives of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire, published by the Fort Ross Conservancy Digital Library in the 2012 bicentennial collection of sixteen documents.

name: Kuskov's RAC Letters to the SF Commandant
summary: Ivan Kuskov, RAC commercial councillor at Ross, writes directly to the SF commandant "in the name of the Honorable Russian-American Company under special protection of His Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias," sending agent Slobodchikov to settle accounts and pressing for the return of captured Kodiak Aleuts.
result: Ross corresponds with SF as one sovereign to another

name: Spanish Missions Supply Kuskov at Fort Ross
summary: The Spanish missions supplying Kuskov's Russian colony; Spain's own establishments provisioning the foreign outpost on the ground it claimed. The open coast as routine economic fact, running in Spain's disfavor.
result: Spain provisions the colony it was ordered to uproot

name: Fort Ross Abandonment Resolved
summary: The RAC Main Board resolves to abandon Ross and "sell or barter for wheat to the inhabitants of San Francisco." The otter gone, Ross is liquidated; the economic close of the arc that opened with the resource.
result: Russia leaves; Ross sold to Sutter, a promoter of the US invasion
sources: Fort Ross AVPRI, 1841 abandonment resolution (via Gibson & Istomin).

name: RAC Parlamentario · Podushkin on the Chirikoff at Monterey
summary: Baranov, from Novo-Arkhangelsk, protests the "insults to the Russian Flag and the capture and keeping in cruel bondage of Russians… in the waters and the coasts of California," invokes the 1812 treaty, and sends Lt. Podushkin as a parlamentario aboard the Chirikoff to Monterey. Russia negotiating as a commercial sovereign on Spain's claimed coast.
result: Russia treats with Spain as an equal power on the California coast
sources: C-A 13 Docs 263–264 (Podushkin's request, 22 Apr 1817; Baranov's protest, 2 Feb 1817). Formerly cited as survey entry 20.

name: Yanovsky's RAC Trade Overture
summary: RAC chief manager Semyon Yanovsky proposes a joint, equal-shares otter-hunt and open commerce (via Khlebnikov and the Madrid embassy; the Ilmena to supply Ross). Solá replies he cannot grant otter-hunting; only the Viceroy can. The third volume of one continuous Russo-Spanish negotiation.
result: Russia again negotiates as a commercial sovereign; Spain defers to Mexico City
sources: C-A 55 Docs 333–334 (Yanovsky / Solá, ~1820).

name: The Suvorov at SF + the RAC Proclamation to California
summary: The RAC ship Suvorov (Lazarev) calls at San Francisco carrying a formal RAC directors' overture "to the noble and honoured Spanish inhabitants of California," invoking Russo-Spanish friendship, the 1812 treaty, and Rezanov's 1806 visit; the institutional Russian demand for the California provision trade, arriving by ship.
result: The RAC's formal trade-opening request, delivered to SF
sources: C-A 12 C478 + C479 (Suvorov 1815; passport-proclamation St. Petersburg, 12 Jul 1811).

name: Rezanov Arrives on Juno
summary: Nikolai Rezanov; Imperial Chamberlain, RAC shareholder, diplomat. Arrives at SF. Concepción Argüello courtship. Intelligence gathering on Spanish defenses. First Russian official at SF.
sources: Bancroft II; Gibson & Istomin 2014.

name: Coast Miwok Intelligence to Sal
summary: Coast Miwok informant tells Commandant Sal two ships at Bodega; soldiers "dressed like ours turned inside out." Earliest warning of foreign presence, 3 weeks before diplomatic intelligence through official channels.
result: Indigenous networks faster than imperial intelligence

name: Coast Miwok Deceive Goycoechea
summary: Coast Miwok tell Goycoechea the eastern shores are "impassable"; he takes the harder western route via Marin headlands. Later admitted he was "deceived." Information control: indigenous peoples directing Spanish military movements.

name: Coast Miwok Calibrated Diplomacy at Bodega
summary: Coast Miwok "prepared to give us battle"; choose instead to present pinole and fruit. Not submission; calibrated response. They evaluated the Spanish party and chose diplomacy.
result: Military capability held in reserve; diplomacy chosen

name: Coast Miwok Bilingual Intermediaries at Tomales
summary: Coast Miwok calling "Amico," speaking Spanish, pointing up lagoon repeating "Spaniard." Bilingual intermediaries positioning between British and Spanish empires. They know both powers and broker between them.
sources: Menzies 1924:302.

name: Guirmenes Intel on Bodega · "Keep This Indian Happy"
summary: Indigenous informant (Guirmenes) reports no foreign ship at Bodega for 2 years. Governor orders: "previene se tenga á ese indio contento" (keep this Indian happy). Indigenous surveillance network sustained across years; Spain depends on it.

name: Chief Vallí-éla Requests Russian Flag
summary: Chief Vallí-éla of Bodega Miwok requests Russian protection and asks Golovnin for a Russian flag. "Very glad to have Russian neighbors." Three independent accounts (Golovnin, Matiushkin, Lütke). The indigenous chief chooses his empire.
result: Indigenous imperial choice; requests Russian protection
sources: Golovnin 1979:165 via Farris 1998:6; AVPRI deep read lines 176–190.

name: Menzies Lands at Tomales Bay
summary: Menzies lands from Vancouver's ship. Finds cross made from cask stave, horse tracks from Goycoechea's expedition. Coast Miwok calling "Amico," speaking Spanish, pointing up lagoon repeating "Spaniard." British find Spanish traces in territory Spain couldn't hold.
result: British find evidence of failed Spanish expedition

name: HMS Raccoon at San Francisco
summary: British warship from Columbia River. HMS Raccoon had seized Fort Astoria Dec 1813. Needed gunpowder. Crew deserting to Spanish protection as "Roman Catholics." Written in English in the archive.
result: British warship uses SF as supply port; War of 1812 reaches Pacific
sources: C-A 12; ca12-russian-california-documents.

name: Kotzebue Visits on Rurik
summary: Otto von Kotzebue arrives at SF on scientific circumnavigation. Spain demands Ross abandonment. Diplomatic failure; Russia ignores the demand.
result: Spanish diplomatic protest; Russia ignores it
sources: James R. Gibson and Alexei A. Istomin (eds.), Russian California, 1806-1860: A History in Documents (Hakluyt Society), Doc. 32.

name: Colnett's Argonaut at Bodega
summary: British ship takes refuge during storm; cuts spars, makes repairs. Later misidentified by Spanish as active English threat. Ghost presence that haunted Spanish intelligence for years.

name: Solá to Viceroy: San Rafael + Russian Threat
summary: Same letter contains Mission San Rafael founding AND Russian threat warning. Dual purpose: health + strategic. Proves mission expansion was explicitly about territorial defense against Russia.
sources: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. pp. 583-604 / scan n429-n449, Doc 756: Sola's report to the Viceroy, Monterey, 3 April 1818, on the Russian establishments at Ross and Bodega.

name: Colony Ross (Russian benchmark)
summary: The measuring stick. A single Russian-American Company outpost, founded September 1812 with about 95 Russians and 80 Alaska Native hunters. A 1813 Spanish intelligence report credited it with about 13 mounted cannon; Moraga's 1814 eyewitness reconnaissance counted 8 cannon in two corner towers with embrasures for far more. Either figure matches or exceeds the serviceable artillery of the entire San Francisco defense in the same decade.
result: One Russian fort ≈ the principal Spanish fort, in guns and in men
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault), section 0
notes: Both the Ross figure (a Spanish estimate) and the SF figure (a Spanish self-inventory) are Spanish-sourced, so the comparison is internally consistent. The defensible claim is order-of-magnitude parity, not a precise gun-for-gun ratio.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: 1776. Northernmost military post. $1,400 total investment by 1793. Garrison: ~35 men.

name: Fort San Joaquín (Castillo de SF)
summary: 1794. Battery guarding the Golden Gate narrows. 1 cannon (burst 1792), 8 by 1793, 6 functional by 1820. Unmanned by 1800.

name: Mission San Rafael
summary: 1817. Anti-Russian buffer. 83 days after Hagemeister treaty. Founded without a boat.

name: Bodega y Quadra discovers and charts the port
summary: The schooner Sonora under Bodega y Quadra and pilot Francisco Mourelle charts the port on the return leg of the 1775 voyage. Their manuscript plano, with keyed points and soundings, is the founding document of the Spanish claim. The chart is in this site's gallery.
sources: Plano del Puerto del Capitan Bodega (LOC, gallery item loc-bq05); resurveyed 1793 (Cartas esfericas sheet 8) | Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms: El Puerto de la Bodega and Bodega Bay' (1964) · identifies the 1775 anchorage as Tomales Bay | Wagner, Sir Francis Drake's Voyage Around the World (1926), 158–59 · reads the chart as Bodega Harbor
notes: Which water the Sonora actually entered is disputed: Edwards (1964) and Beals identify Tomales Bay, Wagner (1926) Bodega Harbor; see the hollow companion point for the Tomales reading.

name: The 1793 occupation attempt fails
summary: The year Spain finally moved to occupy Bodega: Matute's establishment attempt, mounted amid the Nootka crisis, was abandoned. The port Spain had claimed in 1775 stayed empty, and the re-survey of the same year became its monument. The full argument is the subject of the companion article.
result: Spain never occupied the port it discovered
sources: C-A 55 (Matute dossier); the 1793 re-survey, Cartas esfericas sheet 8 (gallery)
notes: Deliberately summary-level here; the article carries the argument and the full citations.

name: The 1811 Aleut otter fleet in San Francisco Bay
summary: Russian-American Company hunting reaches inside the bay itself. On 30 May 1811 Argüello reported Aleut baidarkas working the port, up to fifty together, and some 130 counted between Punta Bonita and Punta San Antonio; six neophytes sent across to fish sea lions for their padres were held for some hours as suspected spies before being released. Spain's inner waters were a Russian hunting ground a year before Ross was founded.
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 381 · Argüello, San Francisco, 30 May 1811: the otter-fishing canoes still working inside the port, up to 50 seen together, and ~130 counted between Puntas de Boneta and San Antonio. | Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 12) Doc 334 · the same hunt a year earlier: ~20 canoes heading into the San José esteros, and gentiles reporting a large ship at Bodega.

name: Vallejo's reconnaissance of Ross (informe reservado)
summary: M. G. Vallejo's confidential report on Ross: about 300 people, a wooden stockade, cannon in the towers, and Russian-American Company intelligence gathered through Wrangel's circle. The fullest Mexican-era picture of the colony, twenty years in.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53), Doc 45 (n97–n111)

name: Ross sold to Sutter; the Russians withdraw
summary: The Russian-American Company sells the Ross establishment to John Sutter and withdraws from California, ending the colony the Spanish had watched for thirty years without ever dislodging.
result: The Russian era ends by sale, not by force
sources: Duflot de Mofras (1844) records the post-sale coast; cf. the borderlands map's abandonment-resolved pin

name: Port Rumiantsev (Bodega Bay)
summary: ~1807. RAC fur-collecting base. First representative: Tarakanov. Permanent.
notes: Anchorage in Bodega Harbor; the precise landing/port site is approximate.

name: Kostromitinov Ranch
summary: 1833. Russian River near Willow Creek. ~100 acres wheat by 1841.
notes: Exact ranch site debated (Osborn); descriptions place it on the south side of the Russian River near its mouth.

name: Khlebnikov Ranch
summary: 1833. Upper Salmon Creek valley, ~5 mi E of Bodega. Largest ranch; bakery, forge, tobacco shed.

name: Chernykh Ranch
summary: ~1833. Near Graton (Purrington Creek). First vineyard in Sonoma County.

name: Matute on the Sutil · the Occupation Refused
summary: Naval lieutenant Juan Bautista Matute arrives on the Sutil to plant the Bodega settlement, finds no English, and refuses to carry out the occupation: the harbor too shallow for the mission, no timber, no building material. He takes his artisans and troops back to San Blas in October; the quiet end of Spain's last northward move. If Edwards is right about the 1775 name, Matute was also surveying a different water than the one Bodega had praised.
sources: Matute's resultas of the Bodega commission (AGN, Historia 71) | Matute's 1793 plan of Bodega (AHN, Estado, MPD. 33) | Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964) · the wrong-harbor argument

name: The 1775 Anchorage · the Tomales Reading
summary: Edwards's reconstruction: the water the Sonora entered on October 3, 1775; the original 'Puerto de la Bodega'; was Tomales Bay. Beals's edition of Bodega's journal reaches the same identification. Everything on the modern map called Bodega carries a migrated name.
sources: Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964) | Beals (ed.), For Honor and Country: the diary of Bodega y Quadra (Hakluyt, 2007), editorial note
notes: Drawn hollow: a scholarly reconstruction, not a documented position.

name: San Rafael Attacked · the Piña Expedition
summary: Mission San Rafael, its founding padre Amorós just dead and its population collapsing, is attacked by gentiles; an expedition goes out under Lázaro Piña. Word of the rising carries through fugitive mission Indians to the Ross-area rancherías; the likely referent of the Russians' report of a 'spring 1832 San Rafael revolt'.
sources: Bancroft, History of California III, 716 (citing Vallejo, Documentos, MS, i.307) | Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6 (the Russian report)

name: Kashaya Resistance at Ross
summary: With the otter gone and Ross living off its grain, manager Kostromitinov's parties seize Kashaya laborers by force; Wrangell records up to 150 gathered, families 'driven to the settlement like cattle to work'. Kashaya and Miwok answer with five years of attacks on company property, culminating in an 1838 raid that kills about a hundred Ross cattle. Indian resistance becomes one cause of the colony's unprofitability and sale.
result: Resistance presses on the colony's economics
sources: Wrangell and Kostromitonov, ethnographic reports (Stross trans., 1974) | Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6

name: RAC Possession Plate No. 14 · Malaya Bodega
summary: Kuskov's expedition buries numbered metal claiming plate No. 14 at 'Malaya Bodega,' the inner harbor; one of a chain of iron plates with brass crosses by which the company staked New Albion years before Ross was built (No. 1 at Trinidad, 1808).
sources: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12) | Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

name: RAC Possession Plate No. 20 · Drake's Estero
summary: A second numbered claiming plate buried at the mouth of Drake's Estero; the company quietly marking the shore of New Albion down to 38°.
sources: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12) | Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

name: The Buried Eagle · a Plate in San Pablo Bay
summary: The company later reported placing 'plate No. 1000 and one coat of arms'; a double-headed eagle; at 'Malaya Bodega, in the northern arm of San Francisco, where the fort and mission of the Spaniards were built': a possession marker buried inside the Spanish bay itself, in the waters of San Pablo Bay. Its spot has never been found.
result: A claim buried inside Spanish waters
sources: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12) | Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)
notes: Position conjectural; drawn hollow; the RAC report's geography is ambiguous.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: October 3, 1810. Governor orders Moraga to investigate Russian fur-hunting at Bodega Bay. 10-day reconnaissance.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, fn. 52: 'Gabriel Moraga's Diary of his Expedition to the Port of Bodega, Oct. 3, 1810, Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.' Diary survives in the Archives of California.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay from the Presidio to the Marin shore. Method uncertain — possibly native balsas or a borrowed vessel.
sources: SF Presidio had limited boat access. See boat-problem article.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Passed through future site of Mission San Rafael. Bancroft: 'The site was probably selected on the advice of Moraga, who had several times passed it on his way to and from Bodega.'
sources: Bancroft, II, p. 330.

name: Novato / Olompali Area
summary: Route north through Marin. Approximate — following the natural corridor through the Novato gap toward Petaluma Creek and the coast.
sources: Exact route not specified in diary abstract.

name: Petaluma Creek / Estuary
summary: Likely crossed or followed Petaluma Creek toward the coast. Natural route from interior Marin to Bodega Bay.
sources: Route reconstruction based on geography.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Arrived at Bodega Bay. Found an American ship and Alaskan Indians (Aleut hunters working for the Russian-American Company). 10-day reconnaissance of the area. Wrote a diary of the expedition.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: 'finds an American ship and Alaskan Indians.' Diary: Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns after 10 days. Report confirms Russian presence and fur-hunting operations at Bodega.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: July 1812. Argüello sends Moraga with 4 men to investigate construction of a small Russian fort on the Sonoma coast. Fort Ross had been dedicated Sept. 10, 1812 — but Kuskov had been building since spring.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay to the Marin shore.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Through future Mission San Rafael site. Moraga's repeated passage through here informed his later recommendation of the site.

name: Petaluma Creek Area
summary: North through Marin toward the coast. Approximate route.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Passed through or near Bodega Bay en route to Fort Ross.

name: Fort Ross
summary: Moraga identifies the Russian settlement: a brigantine-anchored base with a 150-yard-square stockade and cannon. Notes the Russians' friendly manner. Fort Ross had been dedicated by Kuskov with 95 Russians and ~80 Aleut hunters.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: '150-yard-square stockade and cannon; notes the Russians' friendly manner.'

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to SF. Report filed with Argüello.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: January 1813. Moraga drives 20 cattle and 3 horses to Fort Ross — practical diplomacy. Returns again in 1814 with Cadet Gervasio Argüello.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed bay to Marin shore with livestock.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Through future mission site, driving cattle north.

name: Bodega Bay Area
summary: Through Bodega country toward Fort Ross.

name: Fort Ross
summary: Jan. 1813: Delivered 20 cattle, 3 horses as goodwill gesture. 1814 return: accompanied by Cadet Gervasio Argüello. Wrote a report describing 40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon, glass windows in the commandant's house. Also carried official demands for Russian withdrawal.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: '40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon guarding the place, and glass windows in the commandant's house.'

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to SF Presidio.

name: Golden Gate Crossing · Borrowed Launches
summary: 32 horses ferried across the Golden Gate using launches borrowed from visiting San Blas frigates Princesa and Aranzazu. Spain cannot cross its own bay without foreign ships.
result: Spain depends on visiting vessels to cross its own frontier
sources: C-A 14 p. 113. Arrillaga.

name: Goycoechea's Overland Expedition to Bodega
summary: 10 soldiers + sergeant march overland from SF via Bolinas and Tomales Bay to Bodega. Coast Miwok direct them to harder western route; later admitted "deceived." Territory 45 miles north of SF is "tierra incognita."
result: "Tierra incognita"; Spain's own governor admits unknown territory

name: Moraga's 1st Interior Expedition
summary: First major Central Valley expedition. Named the Sacramento River. 30+ stops, 17 villages contacted. No permanent occupation.
sources: Cook 1960; gabriel-moraga-military-campaigns.

name: Moraga's 2nd Expedition · Sacramento Valley
summary: Second interior campaign. Again, a round trip.
sources: Cutter 1957.

name: Battle of Suisun
summary: 17 men cross Carquinez Strait by boat to attack Suisun ranchería. Suisun had killed 16 Christians over prior 3 years. Hard fight; survivors in huts preferred to "perish in the flames" rather than surrender. Moraga received royal commendations.
result: Spanish tactical victory at the frontier chokepoint
sources: C-A 12; C-A 25; Bancroft II:91 fn.24. | Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales tocante a la Alta California, Tomo 1, ch. 10, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 151, recounting Alférez José Sánchez's narration. Vallejo's footnote records that the phrase stands in English in the original manuscript.
notes: Malaca's words come from Vallejo's memoir of the 1870s reporting what Alférez Sánchez told him, not from a contemporary record, and Vallejo wrote the phrase in English. Earlier versions of this map rendered it into Spanish and presented that rendering as the source wording. Bancroft flags the provenance problem directly: Vallejo places this fight with Jose Sanchez in 1817 rather than Moraga in 1810, Alvarado dates it 1817 but puts Moraga in command, and Bancroft concludes 'It is possible that the author has confounded two different battles' (History of California II, n. 29). Malaca's words reach us only through that account.

name: Moraga Investigates Russian Bodega
summary: Moraga goes by boat to Bodega. Finds 40+ Aleut hunting canoes, Russian supply ships at anchor. Reconnaissance, no confrontation. Protests to commandant.
sources: C-A 12; gabriel-moraga-military-campaigns.

name: Moraga Discovers Fort Ross
summary: Moraga with 4 soldiers investigates grounded vessel. Discovers Fort Ross: ~80 men, Kuskov commanding, all from Unalaska/Kamchatka. Vessel 8 leagues above Bodega. No opposition.
sources: C-A 12; gabriel-moraga-military-campaigns.

name: Moraga's Fort Ross Defense Assessment
summary: 40 Russians, 80 Aleuts, 12 guns (4-pounder), 3 falconets. Spanish troops: "no shirts, no pants, no hats." The most damning comparison in the archive.
result: Russians armed and supplied; Spanish naked
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), orig. pp. 1215-17 / scan n371, Doc 439: Gabriel Moraga's reconnaissance and defence assessment of the Russian establishment at Ross, 1814.

name: Argüello's Northern Expedition
summary: 55 men; one of the largest Spanish/Mexican expeditions in CA history. Two full days spent ferrying horses across Carquinez Strait with 4 assembled boats. A power that needs a weekend to cross a channel does not control the territory beyond it.
result: Two days to cross the Strait; not an empire moving through its own territory
sources: Ordaz, Diario, 1821, MS. Bancroft II:444–446.

name: Colnett's Argonaut at Bodega
summary: British ship takes refuge during storm; cuts spars, makes repairs. Later misidentified by Spanish as active English threat. Ghost presence that haunted Spanish intelligence for years.

name: Vancouver's 1st Visit to San Francisco
summary: HMS Discovery and Chatham anchor at SF. Warm reception from Commandant Sal. Menzies walks to Fort Point; finds one cannon "lash'd to a log of Wood." British see the weakness firsthand.
result: British assess SF defenses; one burst cannon

name: English at Bodega "con los cañones en tierra"
summary: Arrillaga reports an English vessel anchored at Bodega with "cannons on land." Identity uncertain; Colnett traces? New vessel? Rumor? Same year as Spanish Bodega failure.
result: Foreign military presence in territory Spain cannot reach

name: Menzies Lands at Tomales Bay
summary: Menzies lands from Vancouver's ship. Finds cross made from cask stave, horse tracks from Goycoechea's expedition. Coast Miwok calling "Amico," speaking Spanish, pointing up lagoon repeating "Spaniard." British find Spanish traces in territory Spain couldn't hold.
result: British find evidence of failed Spanish expedition

name: Vancouver's 2nd Visit · Concealment Policy
summary: Dramatic change from 1st visit. Armed guards, 2-mile limit, refused access to mission. But 8 new brass 4-pounders visible on beach, workers building battery. Spain scrambles to hide weakness and show strength simultaneously.
result: Concealment policy; Spain hides its defenses from the one power that matters

name: Zúñiga Shows Bodega Plans to British · No Concealment
summary: San Diego commandant Zúñiga freely shows Bodega harbor plans to British officers. No concealment at all; contradicts the tight security at SF. The policy was inconsistent.
result: Concealment policy fails at San Diego
sources: Menzies 1924:335.

name: English Launches at Santa Cruz
summary: English launches spotted off Santa Cruz coast, withdrew. Sgt. Pedro Amador sent as reinforcement. Soldier Mesa punished for misreporting.

name: English Shipwreck at Point Reyes / Farallones
summary: Ship sinks near Farallones. Indigenous informants report two uniformed Englishmen at Point Reyes. English naval presence at the Bay entrance during wartime. The report comes through indigenous intelligence networks.
result: English at the Bay entrance; indigenous networks provide the warning
sources: C-A 8; ca8-prov-state-papers-xiv-xv-survey, Find #3.

name: English Vessel at Santa Cruz
summary: English ship arrives at Santa Cruz port, 60 miles from SF Bay. Vallejo coordinates with alcalde; no military officer available. Thin defense exposed.
sources: C-A 8; ca8-prov-state-papers-xiv-xv-survey, Find #4.

name: English Corsair Campaign · Gulf of California
summary: 4 English frigates (22–24 guns each) raided Gulf of California shipping. Ransomed ships, captured brigs. Governor Arrillaga: "sin ningunos elementos de defensa." Maritime reinforcement route to California contested.
result: English naval dominance; supply route threatened
sources: C-A 14; english-corsair-campaign-1799.

name: HMS Raccoon at San Francisco
summary: British warship from Columbia River. HMS Raccoon had seized Fort Astoria Dec 1813. Needed gunpowder. Crew deserting to Spanish protection as "Roman Catholics." Written in English in the archive.
result: British warship uses SF as supply port; War of 1812 reaches Pacific
sources: C-A 12; ca12-russian-california-documents.

name: Eliza's Activo at Bodega · Spain's Last Pacific Exploration
summary: Eliza arrives in Activo after near-starvation NW Coast voyage. Spain's last Pacific exploration. The exhausted vessel barely makes it to Bodega; the empire's reach is collapsing.
result: Last Spanish Pacific exploration; barely survived
sources: Wagner 1931; C-A 14.

name: Rezanov Arrives on Juno
summary: Nikolai Rezanov; Imperial Chamberlain, RAC shareholder, diplomat. Arrives at SF. Concepción Argüello courtship. Intelligence gathering on Spanish defenses. First Russian official at SF.
sources: Bancroft II; Gibson & Istomin 2014.

name: RAC Fur-Collecting Begins at Bodega
summary: 130 Aleut hunters aboard Kodiak. First Russian representative: Tarakanov. 40+ Russians + 150 Indians by 1809 (Argüello report). Moraga protests; ignored.
result: Permanent Russian presence established; Spain protests but cannot act
sources: Milliken 2009:22–25; C-A 12.

name: 130 Bidarkas in San Francisco Bay
summary: 130 Aleut bidarkas (kayaks) hunting sea otter inside San Francisco Bay. The Russians are inside Spain's premier port and Spain cannot stop them.
result: Russian hunting inside the Bay; sovereignty violated
sources: C-A 12 (Prov. St. Pap. XIX).

name: Farallon Islands · Russian Sealing Station
summary: Russian sealing station on the Farallones; 18 miles off the coast of San Francisco. Aleut hunters camped seasonally. Spain/Mexico never contested it.
result: Russian territory visible from SF; unchallenged
sources: Bancroft II; Fort Ross sources.

name: Kotzebue Visits on Rurik
summary: Otto von Kotzebue arrives at SF on scientific circumnavigation. Spain demands Ross abandonment. Diplomatic failure; Russia ignores the demand.
result: Spanish diplomatic protest; Russia ignores it
sources: James R. Gibson and Alexei A. Istomin (eds.), Russian California, 1806-1860: A History in Documents (Hakluyt Society), Doc. 32.

name: Golovnin on Kamchatka at SF
summary: Captain Golovnin arrives at SF on world circumnavigation aboard Kamchatka. Same season as Russian Kutuzov and American Ontario. Three-power naval convergence in one month.
result: Three-power convergence: Russia + Russia + America in SF at once
sources: ca25-tomo-ix-gap-read; Golovnin 1979.

name: Russian Kutuzov at SF
summary: RAC vessel Kutuzov at SF alongside Golovnin's warship and American Ontario. Spanish garrison watches foreign warships parade through their port.
sources: ca25-tomo-ix-gap-read.

name: Vasiliev Corvettes at SF
summary: Two Russian warships anchor at SF; sailing past the fortress that had 6 functional cannons and no grapeshot. Argüello follows orders to receive them "cordially and hospitably."
result: Russian warships pass indefensible fortress; received as guests
sources: C-A 13; ca13-prov-state-papers-xx-documents, Doc. 10.

name: Hagemeister Treaty with Kashaya Pomo
summary: Russia negotiates land cession with Kashaya Pomo chiefs; not Spanish authorities. "Allies of Russia" medals distributed 1819. Russians treat indigenous peoples as sovereign landowners because, north of the Bay, they are.
result: Russia treats Pomo as sovereign; Spain does not exist here
sources: Protocol of the meeting at Colony Ross between the Indian tribal chiefs and Captain-Lieutenant Hagemeister, 22 September 1817. Archives of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire, published by the Fort Ross Conservancy Digital Library in the 2012 bicentennial collection of sixteen documents.

name: Battle of Punta de Guijarros · Lelia Byrd
summary: First naval engagement between a Spanish battery and foreign vessel. American smuggling + armed rescue + artillery duel. Shaler's crew put pistols to Spanish guards' chests. Ship escaped under grapeshot fire. Spanish soldiers were complicit in the otter skin trade.
result: First foreign attack on California; American smugglers
sources: C-A 11; lelia-byrd-punta-guijarros-1803.

name: American Frigate at SF · Troop Crisis
summary: Damaged American frigate anchors in SF port. Argüello forced to pull invalidos (retired soldiers) from San José to augment escorts. Chronic troop shortage: presidio can't staff itself when a foreign ship appears.
result: One foreign ship exposes garrison collapse
sources: PP 0389; pueblo-papers-project.

name: USS Ontario at San Francisco
summary: American warship Ontario at SF; same month as Golovnin's Kamchatka and RAC Kutuzov. Three nations' vessels in the Bay simultaneously. Spain watches.
sources: ca25-tomo-ix-gap-read.

name: Mercury Trial · Capt. Eyres
summary: Boston captain, 8 years trading with Russians and NW Coast Indians. Testimony at Santa Barbara. American commercial penetration of the coast; trading network connecting Boston, Russian Alaska, and California.
sources: C-A 12, scan n360.

name: Anglo-American Vessel Blockades Guaymas
summary: Brig "Cesak," Captain "Clarick," raised American flag, fired 3 cannon shots, blockaded Guaymas. American aggression on Pacific coast in same period as Bouchard.
result: American naval aggression on Pacific coast
sources: C-A 13; ca13-prov-state-papers-xx-documents, Doc. 13.

name: Bouchard's Attack on Monterey
summary: Argentine privateer: Argentina (38 guns) + Santa Rosa (26 guns), ~285 crew. 400 men landed. Presidio burned. Only time a California capital fell to a foreign enemy. Solá retreated to Salinas with archives + 6,000 cartridges.
result: MONTEREY FALLS; only foreign capture of a California capital
sources: bouchard-raid-1818; Bancroft II:227–243.

name: Bouchard at Refugio
summary: Bouchard lands, plunders Ortega's rancho, kills cattle. 3 insurgents captured in ambush: Lt. William Taylor (Boston), Martin Romero (Paraguay), Mateo José Pascual.
result: Ranch plundered; 3 captured by Spanish ambush
sources: bouchard-raid-1818; Bancroft II:236–237.

name: Bouchard at Santa Barbara · Guerra's Bluff
summary: Bouchard anchors. Guerra bluffs with marching troops trick; soldiers march around a hill repeatedly to look like a large army. Prisoner exchange. No fighting.
sources: bouchard-raid-1818; Bancroft II:237–239.

name: Bouchard at San Juan Capistrano
summary: Bouchard lands. Minor damage; straw houses burned, wine spilled. 4 insurgent deserters surrender.
sources: bouchard-raid-1818; Bancroft II:240–241.

name: La Pérouse at Monterey
summary: First foreign account of Spanish military capacity. Governor Fages tells La Pérouse "North California has no northern boundary at all; it extends to Mount Saint Elias." Reality: 282 soldiers for 800+ leagues of coast, 25 missions, ~50,000 Indians, only 10,000 Christian. Continental claim vs. actual control; 7 years before Nootka.
result: France sees through the fiction; 282 soldiers for 800 leagues
sources: Milet-Mureau (ed.), Voyage de La Perouse autour du monde (Paris, 1797); English translation, London, 1799.

name: Coast Miwok Intelligence to Sal
summary: Coast Miwok informant tells Commandant Sal two ships at Bodega; soldiers "dressed like ours turned inside out." Earliest warning of foreign presence, 3 weeks before diplomatic intelligence through official channels.
result: Indigenous networks faster than imperial intelligence

name: Coast Miwok Deceive Goycoechea
summary: Coast Miwok tell Goycoechea the eastern shores are "impassable"; he takes the harder western route via Marin headlands. Later admitted he was "deceived." Information control: indigenous peoples directing Spanish military movements.

name: Coast Miwok Calibrated Diplomacy at Bodega
summary: Coast Miwok "prepared to give us battle"; choose instead to present pinole and fruit. Not submission; calibrated response. They evaluated the Spanish party and chose diplomacy.
result: Military capability held in reserve; diplomacy chosen

name: Coast Miwok Bilingual Intermediaries at Tomales
summary: Coast Miwok calling "Amico," speaking Spanish, pointing up lagoon repeating "Spaniard." Bilingual intermediaries positioning between British and Spanish empires. They know both powers and broker between them.
sources: Menzies 1924:302.

name: Guirmenes Intel on Bodega · "Keep This Indian Happy"
summary: Indigenous informant (Guirmenes) reports no foreign ship at Bodega for 2 years. Governor orders: "previene se tenga á ese indio contento" (keep this Indian happy). Indigenous surveillance network sustained across years; Spain depends on it.

name: Suisun Resist Moraga at Carquinez
summary: Suisun warriors fight Moraga at the Strait. Had killed 16 Christians over prior 3 years. This is a military frontier; Spain fights across it, does not govern beyond it.
result: Indigenous military control of the Strait frontier
sources: Bancroft, History of California II, 91 and n. 24, citing Arrillaga's report at Prov. Rec. ix. 122-23 (C-A 25); Vallejo, Recuerdos, Tomo 1 ch. 10, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 151-52.

name: Suispaques Evade Cabo Ortega
summary: Cabo Ortega dispatched to capture Suispaques/Guispaques; returned without success. Indigenous captain later offered to return fugitives himself; on his own terms.
result: Indigenous autonomy; Spanish military cannot operate here
sources: C-A 26; ca26-prov-rec-xi-xii-survey.

name: Chief Vallí-éla Requests Russian Flag
summary: Chief Vallí-éla of Bodega Miwok requests Russian protection and asks Golovnin for a Russian flag. "Very glad to have Russian neighbors." Three independent accounts (Golovnin, Matiushkin, Lütke). The indigenous chief chooses his empire.
result: Indigenous imperial choice; requests Russian protection
sources: Golovnin 1979:165 via Farris 1998:6; AVPRI deep read lines 176–190.

name: Gualinela's Armed Resistance · 200 Men
summary: Chief Gualinela of Tiutume ranchería (Bodega), 43 people. 200 armed men; heathen + Christian neophytes from Mission San Rafael; band together to resist Mexican troops. Cross-mission alliance.
result: Armed indigenous coalition; 40 years of continuity at Bodega
sources: Farris 1998:7 (Vallejo report).

name: Sal's Boundary Letter · "English Want SF Bay for a Boundary"
summary: Sal to Arrillaga: "Segun sus opiniones, quieren los ingleses la boca de este puerto por línea divisoria." Also reports one burst cannon, two English frigates at Bodega. Intelligence from Bodega y Quadra at Nootka.
result: THESIS-CRITICAL; the boundary claim stated explicitly
sources: C-A 54, MS p. 119; bodega-failure-1793.

name: SF Cannon Burst · Sole Weapon Destroyed
summary: Cannon exploded during saint's day firing. 10 pieces, fragments reached church 125 varas. Fired by Soldado Arriola. San Francisco's sole defensive weapon destroyed before the Nootka crisis peaked.

name: Arrillaga: "Presidios Are Indefensible · English Said So"
summary: "Los Presidios de Alta Cal. están indefensos, cuya circunstancia ha sido notada por los mismos ingleses... no pueden resistir contra una invasion." The governor's own admission to his viceroy.
result: THESIS-CRITICAL; Spain admits its own weakness
sources: C-A 14; ca14-prov-state-papers-xxi-xxii-survey, Find #1.

name: Arrillaga: "Tierra Incognita"
summary: "El grande rodeo y tierra incognita." Territory 45 miles north of SF is literally unknown to the Spanish governor after 24 years in California.
result: THESIS-CRITICAL; Spain does not know its own territory
sources: Prov. St. Pap., MS., tomo xxi, p. 113.

name: Viceroy Orders Bodega · "Whether or Not English Are There"
summary: Revilla Gigedo orders Bodega occupied. Full fortification plan for Bodega + SF + Monterey + SD. Never executed. Supplies eventually repurposed (June 10, 1794).
sources: C-A 22, ii.144–148; bodega-failure-1793.

name: Fiscal: "Fortifications Would Not Prevent a Landing"
summary: Crown fiscal officer declares defense should be naval; land fortifications useless. Devastating assessment from within the imperial bureaucracy itself.
result: Spain's own bureaucracy declares California indefensible
sources: C-A 8; ca8-prov-state-papers-xiv-xv-survey, Find #5.

name: Yerba Buena Battery Abandoned
summary: Argüello reports Yerba Buena Battery unmanned; only a daily visit by the vigía. SF garrison: 1 cabo, 4 artilleros, 3 cabos, 10 soldados. Barely sufficient for Presidio + fort. The key battery controlling the narrows has no one in it.
sources: C-A 11; ca11-prov-state-papers-xviii-survey.

name: Pedro de Nava: Isolation Was Deliberate Policy
summary: Comandante General of the Provincias Internas explicitly rejects overland California–New Mexico road. Cites 1786 prohibition. California's territories "useless." Indigenous nations form impassable barrier. The only route is the Sea of Cortez.
result: THESIS-CRITICAL; isolation was policy, not accident
sources: C-A 11, orig. pp. 101–3; ca11-prov-state-papers-xviii-survey.

name: Fortress San Joaquín in Collapse
summary: Only 8 cannons (2 non-functional), no grapeshot, no forge, no hot-shot furnace, wadding falling apart, cartridges irreplaceable. Two years after Bouchard proved the vulnerability; still not repaired.
sources: C-A 13; ca13-prov-state-papers-xx-documents, Doc. 7.

name: Solá to Viceroy: San Rafael + Russian Threat
summary: Same letter contains Mission San Rafael founding AND Russian threat warning. Dual purpose: health + strategic. Proves mission expansion was explicitly about territorial defense against Russia.
sources: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. pp. 583-604 / scan n429-n449, Doc 756: Sola's report to the Viceroy, Monterey, 3 April 1818, on the Russian establishments at Ross and Bodega.

name: The 1793 Bodega Occupation Attempt · Matute / Aránzazu
summary: The occupation the whole story turns on. On the Viceroy's order to "reconocer y ocupar dicho Puerto, quitando á extranjeros ese abrigo inmediato á los Presidios," an expedition under Lt. Juan Bautista Matute aboard the Aránzazu was to plant a Spanish establishment at Bodega. Matute reported he "no verificaría aquel año el establecimiento"; the attempt collapsed for want of imperial capacity, not suitable ground.
result: The establishment that did not happen; Spain's claim north of SF never occupied
sources: C-A 55 Doc 335 (Matute/Aránzazu, 25 Jul 1793). | Occupation order: C-A 6 Doc 192 (Revillagigedo, 6 Jul 1793). | C-A 15 Doc 515 (presidios & Bodega, 16 Jul 1793).

name: Bodega Establishment Abandoned
summary: Sal reports that "no se efectuará el establecimiento del puerto de Bodega," and that the articles destined for Bodega have been reassigned to the San Francisco presidio. The closing bracket on the 1793 order-and-attempt.
result: The Bodega plan formally dead; supplies redirected to SF
sources: C-A 15 Doc 520 (Sal → Arrillaga, 25 Jul 1794).

name: Wilcocks Calls at Russian Bodega · and the Annexation Plot
summary: The American trader James Smith Wilcocks calls at "un establecimiento ruso llamado Bodega"; "los rusos no quisieron comprar nada"; then sells Gov. Solá $700 of blankets for the four presidios. In 1817 he is accused of plotting to "levantarme con las Californias para integrarlas a los anglo-americanos"; the earliest dated articulation of the U.S.-annexation fear the open coast invited.
result: Bodega as a (failed) commercial port in the US–Russian–Spanish triangle
sources: C-A 13 Docs 193–206 (the Wilcocks affair; the Bodega call & blanket sale in his voyage account, Doc 206, orig. i.716–726; the annexation accusation denounced in Doc 203). Formerly cited as survey entry 19.

name: Elliot de Castro / Ilmena Seized at Refugio
summary: The Russian brig Ilmena's shore party; John Elliot de Castro, an American, an Aleut and others; is seized at Ortega's Refugio rancho, the coast's otter-smuggling rendezvous. A $2,000 ransom is offered and refused. Spain/Mexico can catch the people but not stop the trade.
result: The Mexican-era sequel; Refugio as a second Bodega-style keyhole

name: RAC Parlamentario · Podushkin on the Chirikoff at Monterey
summary: Baranov, from Novo-Arkhangelsk, protests the "insults to the Russian Flag and the capture and keeping in cruel bondage of Russians… in the waters and the coasts of California," invokes the 1812 treaty, and sends Lt. Podushkin as a parlamentario aboard the Chirikoff to Monterey. Russia negotiating as a commercial sovereign on Spain's claimed coast.
result: Russia treats with Spain as an equal power on the California coast
sources: C-A 13 Docs 263–264 (Podushkin's request, 22 Apr 1817; Baranov's protest, 2 Feb 1817). Formerly cited as survey entry 20.

name: Kuskov's RAC Letters to the SF Commandant
summary: Ivan Kuskov, RAC commercial councillor at Ross, writes directly to the SF commandant "in the name of the Honorable Russian-American Company under special protection of His Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias," sending agent Slobodchikov to settle accounts and pressing for the return of captured Kodiak Aleuts.
result: Ross corresponds with SF as one sovereign to another

name: Spanish Missions Supply Kuskov at Fort Ross
summary: The Spanish missions supplying Kuskov's Russian colony; Spain's own establishments provisioning the foreign outpost on the ground it claimed. The open coast as routine economic fact, running in Spain's disfavor.
result: Spain provisions the colony it was ordered to uproot

name: Fort Ross Abandonment Resolved
summary: The RAC Main Board resolves to abandon Ross and "sell or barter for wheat to the inhabitants of San Francisco." The otter gone, Ross is liquidated; the economic close of the arc that opened with the resource.
result: Russia leaves; Ross sold to Sutter, a promoter of the US invasion
sources: Fort Ross AVPRI, 1841 abandonment resolution (via Gibson & Istomin).

name: Yanovsky's RAC Trade Overture
summary: RAC chief manager Semyon Yanovsky proposes a joint, equal-shares otter-hunt and open commerce (via Khlebnikov and the Madrid embassy; the Ilmena to supply Ross). Solá replies he cannot grant otter-hunting; only the Viceroy can. The third volume of one continuous Russo-Spanish negotiation.
result: Russia again negotiates as a commercial sovereign; Spain defers to Mexico City
sources: C-A 55 Docs 333–334 (Yanovsky / Solá, ~1820).

name: The Suvorov at SF + the RAC Proclamation to California
summary: The RAC ship Suvorov (Lazarev) calls at San Francisco carrying a formal RAC directors' overture "to the noble and honoured Spanish inhabitants of California," invoking Russo-Spanish friendship, the 1812 treaty, and Rezanov's 1806 visit; the institutional Russian demand for the California provision trade, arriving by ship.
result: The RAC's formal trade-opening request, delivered to SF
sources: C-A 12 C478 + C479 (Suvorov 1815; passport-proclamation St. Petersburg, 12 Jul 1811).

name: British Squadron Sounds San Diego Harbor
summary: A sworn 1799 deposition: a British naval squadron awaiting the Manila galleon, with 22 Peru prizes, states a plan to winter at San Diego; whose harbour they had already secretly sounded c.1797, "entered in their boats one moonlit night, sounded the whole harbour," "instruidos por los planos de Nutka." The open coast as an actual reconnaissance ground.
result: San Diego's harbor already mapped by the enemy; the threat the 1793 order feared
sources: C-A 15 Doc 392 (Loreto deposition, 28 Jun 1799).

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: 1776. Northernmost military post. $1,400 total investment by 1793. Garrison: ~35 men.

name: Fort San Joaquín (Castillo de SF)
summary: 1794. Battery guarding the Golden Gate narrows. 1 cannon (burst 1792), 8 by 1793, 6 functional by 1820. Unmanned by 1800.

name: Presidio of Monterey
summary: 1770. Capital of Alta California. Burned by Bouchard 1818.

name: Presidio of San Diego
summary: 1769. First presidio. Punta de Guijarros battery.

name: Mission San José
summary: 1797. Staging base for Central Valley expeditions.

name: Mission San Rafael
summary: 1817. Anti-Russian buffer. 83 days after Hagemeister treaty. Founded without a boat.

name: Mission San Francisco Solano (Sonoma)
summary: 1823. Northernmost mission. Altimira: "you will all be Russians."

name: Pueblo de San José
summary: 1777. First civilian settlement in Alta California.

name: Villa de Branciforte (Santa Cruz)
summary: 1797. Third and last pueblo. Named for Viceroy Branciforte. Planned as strategic settlement near Santa Cruz mission.

name: Santa Eulalia (Cordelia)
summary: ~1824. Mission Solano farming outpost; house for padre, corral, neophyte in charge. Suisun Valley.

name: Port Rumiantsev (Bodega Bay)
summary: ~1807. RAC fur-collecting base. First representative: Tarakanov. Permanent.
notes: Anchorage in Bodega Harbor; the precise landing/port site is approximate.

name: Fort Ross (Metini)
summary: 1812. Ivan Kuskov. 95 Russians, ~80 Aleut. 12 guns, 3 falconets. No Spanish opposition.

name: Farallon Islands Sealing Station
summary: ~1812. 18 mi off SF coast. Seasonal Aleut camps. Unchallenged.

name: Kostromitinov Ranch
summary: 1833. Russian River near Willow Creek. ~100 acres wheat by 1841.
notes: Exact ranch site debated (Osborn); descriptions place it on the south side of the Russian River near its mouth.

name: Khlebnikov Ranch
summary: 1833. Upper Salmon Creek valley, ~5 mi E of Bodega. Largest ranch; bakery, forge, tobacco shed.

name: Chernykh Ranch
summary: ~1833. Near Graton (Purrington Creek). First vineyard in Sonoma County.

name: The Sonora Names Puerto de la Bodega
summary: Returning from the north, Bodega y Quadra's 36-foot schooner Sonora anchors and names the Puerto de la Bodega, charting it with keyed points and soundings; the founding document of the Spanish claim to this coast. Which water he actually anchored in is a live scholarly dispute: Edwards (1964) demonstrates the 1775 anchorage was Tomales Bay and the name later migrated north; Wagner (1926) read the chart as Bodega Harbor.
sources: Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms: El Puerto de la Bodega and Bodega Bay', Pacific Historical Review 33 (1964) | Plano del Puerto de la Bodega (1775), Savage copy in C-A 15 | Wagner, Sir Francis Drake's Voyage Around the World (1926), 158–59 (the Bodega-Harbor reading)
notes: Drawn at Bodega Harbor for continuity with the migrated name; see the companion conjectural point for the Tomales reading.

name: The 1775 Anchorage · the Tomales Reading
summary: Edwards's reconstruction: the water the Sonora entered on October 3, 1775; the original 'Puerto de la Bodega'; was Tomales Bay. Beals's edition of Bodega's journal reaches the same identification. Everything on the modern map called Bodega carries a migrated name.
sources: Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964) | Beals (ed.), For Honor and Country: the diary of Bodega y Quadra (Hakluyt, 2007), editorial note
notes: Drawn hollow: a scholarly reconstruction, not a documented position.

name: Matute on the Sutil · the Occupation Refused
summary: Naval lieutenant Juan Bautista Matute arrives on the Sutil to plant the Bodega settlement, finds no English, and refuses to carry out the occupation: the harbor too shallow for the mission, no timber, no building material. He takes his artisans and troops back to San Blas in October; the quiet end of Spain's last northward move. If Edwards is right about the 1775 name, Matute was also surveying a different water than the one Bodega had praised.
sources: Matute's resultas of the Bodega commission (AGN, Historia 71) | Matute's 1793 plan of Bodega (AHN, Estado, MPD. 33) | Edwards, 'Wandering Toponyms' (1964) · the wrong-harbor argument

name: San Francisco · 'the Last Point We Can Hold'
summary: A long fiscal report on the Californias defines New California as running from San Diego to San Francisco inclusive; the last point Spain can hold in full and independent dominion on this coast under the Nootka convention. The empire's own paperwork drew its ceiling at the Golden Gate before the Russians ever landed.
sources: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 54), doc 216

name: Vancouver's Open-Door Claim
summary: In the Nootka negotiation Vancouver claims for Britain free access to Spanish establishments made or to be made; 'que se hayan hecho, ó se hagan'; as far south as San Francisco. The claim, delivered in a Spanish translation Bodega y Quadra could read unaided, declared this coast's door open two decades before Ross was built.
sources: Vancouver–Bodega correspondence, Nootka 1792 (AHN, Estado, leg. 4290, exp. 1)
notes: Anchored at San Francisco, the claim's named southern limit.

name: Calleja's Precautions · the Russians at Bodega
summary: Viceroy Calleja writes the governor on the Russian establishment at Bodega, ordering precautions against Americans and against privateers; Mexico City registering, mid-insurgency, that the coast north of the Gate now belonged to someone else's initiative. A parallel despatch went to the governor of Baja California.
sources: Provincial State Papers (C-A 12), doc 491 · Calleja to the Gov. of California, 9 Jul 1813 | Provincial State Papers (C-A 14), doc 455 · the Baja California parallel

name: San Rafael Attacked · the Piña Expedition
summary: Mission San Rafael, its founding padre Amorós just dead and its population collapsing, is attacked by gentiles; an expedition goes out under Lázaro Piña. Word of the rising carries through fugitive mission Indians to the Ross-area rancherías; the likely referent of the Russians' report of a 'spring 1832 San Rafael revolt'.
sources: Bancroft, History of California III, 716 (citing Vallejo, Documentos, MS, i.307) | Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6 (the Russian report)

name: The Mercado Affair
summary: Padre Mercado of San Rafael sends an armed party of neophytes against the gentile rancherías; some twenty-one are killed and prisoners taken. Figueroa suspends the padre; the violent peak of the 1832–33 North Bay crisis, with the mission itself now the aggressor.
sources: Bancroft, History of California III, 716–17 (the Mercado affair)

name: Kashaya Resistance at Ross
summary: With the otter gone and Ross living off its grain, manager Kostromitinov's parties seize Kashaya laborers by force; Wrangell records up to 150 gathered, families 'driven to the settlement like cattle to work'. Kashaya and Miwok answer with five years of attacks on company property, culminating in an 1838 raid that kills about a hundred Ross cattle. Indian resistance becomes one cause of the colony's unprofitability and sale.
result: Resistance presses on the colony's economics
sources: Wrangell and Kostromitonov, ethnographic reports (Stross trans., 1974) | Bolkhovitinov & Istomin, Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki III, ch. 6

name: RAC Possession Plate No. 14 · Malaya Bodega
summary: Kuskov's expedition buries numbered metal claiming plate No. 14 at 'Malaya Bodega,' the inner harbor; one of a chain of iron plates with brass crosses by which the company staked New Albion years before Ross was built (No. 1 at Trinidad, 1808).
sources: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12) | Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

name: RAC Possession Plate No. 20 · Drake's Estero
summary: A second numbered claiming plate buried at the mouth of Drake's Estero; the company quietly marking the shore of New Albion down to 38°.
sources: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12) | Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)

name: The Buried Eagle · a Plate in San Pablo Bay
summary: The company later reported placing 'plate No. 1000 and one coat of arms'; a double-headed eagle; at 'Malaya Bodega, in the northern arm of San Francisco, where the fort and mission of the Spaniards were built': a possession marker buried inside the Spanish bay itself, in the waters of San Pablo Bay. Its spot has never been found.
result: A claim buried inside Spanish waters
sources: Bolkhovitinov (ed.), Istoriia Russkoi Ameriki II, 210, 214 (RAC file, OR RGB F.204, K.32, D.12) | Istomin, the Kuskov reconnaissance reports, 1809–11 (cited ibid.)
notes: Position conjectural; drawn hollow; the RAC report's geography is ambiguous.

name: St. George Reef Light Station
summary: Long described in the lighthouse literature as the most expensive American lighthouse ever built, St. George Reef took eight working seasons (1883-1891) to raise on a wave-swept rock six miles off Point St. George, using 1,339 dressed granite blocks quarried near the Mad River. Its first-order flashing lens went into service in 1892 and warned shipping off the reef that had claimed the Brother Jonathan in 1865. The Coast Guard disestablished the station in May 1975 in favor of a buoy; the tower still stands and again shows a private light.
sources: [P] NRHP nomination, St. George Reef Light Station, ref 93001373 (listed 1993), incl. quoted 1892 Annual Report of the Light-House Board | [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI, 2025, COMDTPUB P16502.6, LLNR 561 | [S] USCG Historian's Office, Historic Light Station Information & Photography: California (page last modified 2016-09-15), Wayback capture | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
notes: Establishment sequence firmly documented from nomination + AR-1892 quote. Day-level first-lit (Oct 20) not confirmed in a located primary source. USCG table's "Station Established: 1867" reflects early reservation of the site, not construction. Also known as: Northwest Seal Rock Lighthouse, Saint George Reef Light.

name: Battery Point Light (Crescent City)
summary: Battery Point is one of the survivors of California's first generation of lighthouses: a brick tower rising through a granite Cape Cod dwelling on a tidal islet at Crescent City, first exhibited 10 December 1856. Automated in 1953 and dark from 1965, it was relit as a private aid on 10 December 1982 and now operates as a county museum still showing a light.
sources: [P] USC&GS, Pacific Coast. Coast Pilot of California, Oregon, and Washington, 4th ed. (GPO, 1889), Crescent City section | [P] NRHP nomination, Cresent City Lighthouse, ref 83001177 (listed 1983) | [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI, 2025, LLNR 555 | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California light stations page (2016, Wayback) | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
notes: The famous 1964 tsunami keeper eyewitness story is well known but was not verified in a located source for this survey; omitted. The 1860 dark period noted in the 1889 Coast Pilot deserves follow-up in Lighthouse Board records. Also known as: Crescent City Lighthouse, 'Cresent City Lighthouse' (sic, NRIS spelling).

name: Trinidad Head Light Station
summary: A squat brick tower of 1871 whose modest height; 18 feet from ground line to focal plane, in the Board's own figure; is multiplied by Trinidad Head's 196-foot cliff, this light covered the crowded lumber-schooner harbor at Trinidad. It keeps its original station arrangement minus the razed Victorian dwelling, and its 1871 lens survives in a replica tower in town. It remains an active Coast Guard aid, automated in 1974.

name: Table Bluff Light Station
summary: Table Bluff took over Humboldt Bay's seacoast light in 1892 from the failing North Spit station, placing a Stick-style dwelling-tower on the high bluff south of the bay. The Navy added a radio station in 1906 and the site swelled with beach-patrol and radio-compass functions in WWII, after which most of the original complex was demolished. Automated in 1953, the light was discontinued in the 1970s and the property sold.

name: Humboldt Harbor Light (1856)
summary: Lit on 20 December 1856, the Humboldt Harbor light was a brick Cape Cod dwelling-tower planted on the low, unstable North Spit of Humboldt Bay. Sited too low and plagued by fog and settling ground, it was criticized for decades; the Coast Survey was already reporting a proposal to move the light to Table Bluff in 1889, and the 1892 Table Bluff station superseded it.

name: Cape Mendocino Light Station
summary: Lit on 1 December 1868, Cape Mendocino's prefabricated cast-iron tower stood 422 feet above the Pacific on the state's westernmost cape, its first-order flash marking the great turn of the coast. Automated in 1951 and abandoned by the 1970s, the little tower was dismantled in 1998 and rebuilt at Shelter Cove, while its lens has sat in Ferndale since 1948.

name: Punta Gorda Light Station
summary: The 'Alcatraz of lighthouses' on the Lost Coast was built after the Columbia disaster of 1907 capped a dozen years of wrecks below Cape Mendocino; its fog sirens sounded from June 1911 and the fourth-order light first shone on 15 January 1912. Nearly roadless its whole working life, the station was extinguished on 15 February 1951, and only the small concrete lighthouse and oil house survived the BLM's burn of the abandoned quarters.

name: Point Cabrillo Light Station
summary: Point Cabrillo, first lit on 10 June 1909, is a wooden light-and-fog-signal building of the Lighthouse Service's late frame idiom, built for the redwood doghole trade out of Mendocino and Fort Bragg. Its original third-order lens survived automation in 1973, and the station complex, nearly complete, is now a California state historic park.

name: Point Arena Light Station
summary: Point Arena's first-order light of 1 May 1870 stood only 36 years before the 1906 San Andreas rupture, whose trace passes just offshore, shattered the brick tower. Its 1908 replacement, a slim reinforced-concrete shaft raised by a San Francisco chimney firm, was the first reinforced-concrete lighthouse in California, per its National Register nomination. Automated in 1977, it is now run by a local nonprofit.

name: Point Reyes Light Station
summary: Set into the cliff-face 294 feet above the surf because fog smothers the 600-foot headland above, Point Reyes first showed its first-order flash on 1 December 1870. Its iron-plate tower and clockwork lens served through a century of gales before automation in 1975, and the station now anchors the maritime story of Point Reyes National Seashore.

summary: The Farallones light, raised in 1855 on the granite peak of Southeast Farallon, was among the first cohort of Pacific lights and among the hardest built, with every brick packed uphill by hand. Its first-order lens covered the fog-bound outer approach to San Francisco for over a century; the tower, automated in 1972 and stripped of its lantern, still flashes over a national wildlife refuge.

name: Point Montara Light Station
summary: Montara began in February 1875 as a fog-signal station answering the wrecks on the ledges south of San Francisco, and only grew a light by stages: a small beacon around 1900, a fourth-order lens on a wooden tower in 1912, and the present little cast-iron tower in 1928. Automated in 1970, the station now doubles as a hostel above its still-active light.

name: Pigeon Point Light Station
summary: Pigeon Point's 115-foot brick tower of 1872, a New England profile transplanted to a low San Mateo terrace, carried a first-order lens marking the southern approach to San Francisco and memorializing the clipper Carrier Pigeon lost on the point. Automated in 1974, it stands within a state historic park.

name: Año Nuevo Island Light Station
summary: Año Nuevo was a fog station first and a lighthouse second: the government set a steam whistle on the islet in 1872 and added a five-story tower only in 1890. A buoy replaced the whole apparatus in 1948, and the island's keeper buildings have been decaying amid elephant seals and cormorants inside a state park ever since.

name: Santa Cruz Light Station
summary: Santa Cruz's little wooden harbor light of 1869-70 spent seven decades marking the wharves of Monterey Bay's north shore under just three keepers, most famously Laura Hecox. Discontinued in 1941 and razed in 1948, it was succeeded in spirit and function by the Mark Abbott Memorial Lighthouse, a 1960s brick memorial that now carries the official Santa Cruz Light and a surfing museum.

name: Point Pinos Light Station
summary: Point Pinos, lit in 1855, is the oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the Pacific coast of the United States, still showing its original French third-order lens from the original granite Cape Cod building. Its early keepers included two notable women, Charlotte Layton and Emily Fish. Automated in 1975, it now belongs to the City of Pacific Grove.

name: Point Sur Light Station
summary: Raised in 1889 from sandstone quarried on its own rock, Point Sur put a first-order light on the wild Big Sur coast after a decade of petitioning. Its complete hilltop station - tower, fog signal and dwellings - survived isolation, automation in 1972, and transfer to California State Parks, making it one of the most intact light stations in the state.

name: Piedras Blancas Light Station
summary: Piedras Blancas raised a tall first-order brick tower on the white guano rocks north of San Simeon in 1875, closing one of the longest unlit reaches of the coast. Earthquake damage cost it its lantern room, giving the tower its distinctive flat top, but its light never stopped; it was automated in 1975 and now anchors a protected coastal research station.

name: San Luis Obispo Light Station (Port Harford)
summary: The Port Harford light of 30 June 1890 answered the Queen of the Pacific's 1888 sinking and the long dark gap of the south-central coast, planting a gingerbread Stick-style dwelling-tower on Point San Luis. It is the only one of its three identical 1890 sisters still standing, its fourth-order lens now in county museum hands and its buildings restored for visitors.

name: Point Arguello Light Station
summary: Point Arguello, where the Yankee Blade went down in 1854 and seven Navy destroyers piled up at Honda Point in 1923, got its light station only in 1901. The original lighthouse gave way in the 1930s to a rotating aerobeacon, and today a simple post light on the Vandenberg coast carries on the station's warning at the west door of the Santa Barbara Channel.

name: Point Conception Light Station
summary: One of the original eight Pacific lighthouses, Point Conception first showed its French first-order light on 1 February 1856 at the hinge of the California coast. The station moved partway down its bluff in 1881-82 to escape the high fog, and the 1882 tower still turns the 1856 lens - among the longest-serving optics in the country. It was automated in 1973 and remains active.

name: Point Hueneme Light Station
summary: Hueneme's fanciful 1874 Eastlake lighthouse, sister to Point Fermin's, marked the grain wharves at the east entrance of the Santa Barbara Channel. In 1941 it gave way to the crisp Art Moderne tower that still works the harbor entrance, one of the last true lighthouse structures built on the coast.

Automated in 1968 and handed to the National Park Service in 2008, its third-order lens survives on the island it served.

name: Point Vicente Light Station
summary: Point Vicente's 1926 concrete tower, dressed in the Spanish Revival style of its decade, turned a Paris-made third-order lens 185 feet above the sea to funnel shipping toward the booming Los Angeles harbor. Manned for 45 years, it went to remote operation in 1971 and still flashes twice every twenty seconds over Palos Verdes.

Blacked out days after Pearl Harbor and stripped of its lantern for a lookout shack, it regained a rebuilt lantern room in 1974 and presides over a city park, while a plain pile light does its old job.

Its green flash and foghorns - Moaning Maggie, then Blatting Betty - defined the harbor entrance of Los Angeles; the keepers left on 1 February 1973 when the light was automated.

Its green-shaded fifth-order lens was the Pacific coast's last fixed classical light; when the failing tower came down around 1960 the optic went to Cabrillo National Monument and a utilitarian light took over the point.

name: Old Point Loma Lighthouse
summary: The 1855 Old Point Loma light crowned its headland so high that fog regularly blotted it out, an elegant failure of the first Pacific cohort. Extinguished on 23 March 1891 in favor of the new tower at the point's tip, it was saved by its inclusion in Cabrillo National Monument and a 1930s restoration, and is now among the most-visited lighthouses in the country.

Five vessels held the station over 73 years - LV-70, LV-83, WLV-612 and LV-100 among them - until a lighted horn buoy replaced the last ship in 1971.

name: Blunts Reef Lightship Station
summary: The Blunts Reef lightship tossed off Cape Mendocino from 1905, holding coastwise traffic clear of the reef that the cape's high light could not adequately cover in fog. LV-83's rescue of 155 souls from the steamer Bear in 1916 made it famous; buoys replaced the ships in 1971, and one veteran of the station, WLV-605 RELIEF, survives on the National Register at Oakland.

name: Alcatraz Island Light
summary: Alcatraz carried what the standard accounts call the Pacific coast's first lighthouse: a Gibbons & Kelly contract dwelling finished in 1853 that finally showed its third-order light on June 1, 1854, once the lens arrived. After the 1906 earthquake cracked the old building and the new cell house crowded it, the Lighthouse Service transferred the light on December 1, 1909 to the present 84-foot octagonal concrete tower, a move documented in the printed Notice to Mariners of December 2, 1909. Automated in 1963 during the island's federal-prison era, the tower still operates inside Golden Gate NRA.

USCG Historian's tower height (84 ft) vs lighthousefriends (90 ft) differ; Light List focal plane 214 ft above water per the 1909 notice. Also known as: Alcatraz Lighthouse, Alcatraces Island Light (period spelling). ⚠ The "first on the Pacific coast" claim belongs to the secondary literature, not to the Light-House Board. The Board's own printed Light List in its 1858 report (pp. 482-483, "When built") gives BOTH Alcatraz and Point Pinos as 1854 and does not rank them; what the Board does state (1857, p. 229) is that before it took charge in 1852 there were no aids of any kind on this coast.

name: Fort Point Light
summary: Fort Point ran through three lighthouses in eleven years: the 1853 contract tower was torn down unlit to make way for the brick fort, its 1855 wooden replacement was lit in March 1855 as the third light on the coast, and an iron nine-sided tower rose over the fort's stairwell in 1863-64 when the seawall forced another demolition. The Golden Gate Bridge finally made the station redundant, and the light was extinguished on September 1, 1934. The little iron tower survives on the fort, now a National Historic Site.

notes: Iron tower's exact first-lit date (1863 vs 1864) unresolved between USCG Historian and lighthousefriends; March 21, 1855 day for tower two not verified in a primary. Keeper roster from USCG Historian page (Chesapeake Chapter USLHS research). Also known as: Fort Winfield Scott Light.

name: Point Bonita Light
summary: Point Bonita's 1855 lighthouse was built too high: at 306 feet its second-order light sat above the fog it was meant to pierce, so in 1877 the Service tunneled through the headland and re-erected the lantern on the wave-cut outer point, where it was relit on February 1, 1877. The station pioneered west coast fog signaling with an army cannon fired from 1855. Automated in 1980 and last staffed in 1981, it remains an active light within Golden Gate NRA, reached by its 1954 suspension bridge.
sources: [P] USCG Light List, Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 4220 | [P] Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses FY1915 (Point Bonita cannon = first Pacific coast fog signal, used 1855-1857) | [P] The Fogs and Fog Signals of the Pacific Coast of the United States (pub. for the Light-House Board, 1888) - Bonita siren service table | [S] NPS, Point Bonita Lighthouse (GOGA) | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Point Bonita (archived 2010) | lighthousefriends.com, Point Bonita Lighthouse; Wikipedia, Point Bonita Light (NRHP #91001099) | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
