Also known as: Point Bonito Light (19th-c. variant).

name: Lime Point Light (Fog Signal Station)
date_display: Established as a steam fog-signal station September 10, 1883
summary: Lime Point began in September 1883 as a pure fog-signal station, its twin steam whistles answering Fort Point across the narrowest reach of the Golden Gate. A modest lens-lantern hung on the signal building's gallery from November 1900 gave it a light, but it was always a keeper-run fog station first. De-staffed and automated in 1961, when its dwellings were razed, the brick signal house still carries an active light at the foot of the bridge's north tower.
sources: [P] The Fogs and Fog Signals of the Pacific Coast (LHB, 1888) - Lime Point signal '4 yrs 10 mo' as of July 1888 | [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 4270 | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Lime Point Light (archived 2010) | lighthousefriends.com, Lime Point Lighthouse (cites LHB annual reports, Sausalito News, SF Call)
notes: Exact 1883 and 1900 dates are tertiary-quoting-primary; 1883 season independently supported by the 1888 fog study's service table. Also known as: Lime Point Fog Signal Station.

name: Mile Rocks Light
summary: The loss of the City of Rio de Janeiro in the fog off Fort Point in February 1901 pushed Congress to fund a lighthouse on Mile Rocks, a pair of wave-washed rocks a mile off Lands End. Crews working from a schooner bolted a steel-cased caisson to the larger rock and stacked a three-tier steel tower above it, lighting it on February 15, 1906. In 1965-66 the Coast Guard decapitated the tower for a helipad and automated the light, which still flashes from the surviving base.
sources: [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 4245 | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Mile Rocks Light (archived 2010) | lighthousefriends.com, Mile Rocks Lighthouse | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
notes: First-lit day is tertiary-quoting-primary; no primary notice pulled this session. USCG page's 'Feb 2, 1901' wreck date is an error against the standard Feb. 22, 1901 (used by lighthousefriends and the historical literature). Also known as: Mile Rock Lighthouse.

name: Point Diablo Light
summary: Point Diablo, the dark mid-point of the Golden Gate's northern shore, received a minor light and electric fog siren in 1923, installed in a small white signal house rather than a full station. It was an early experiment in remote operation: the keepers at Lime Point monitored it over wire and rowed or drove over weekly to service it. The automated light still shows an isophase white flash below the Marin headlands.
sources: [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 4250 | lighthousefriends.com, Point Diablo Lighthouse (drawing on Nelson & Nelson 1993) | [P] GNIS gaz_id 230851 (Point Diablo)
notes: Establishment year 1923 rests on secondary sources only; the Bureau of Lighthouses FY1923 annual report would confirm and should be checked when accessible. Station never on the USCG Historian California page.

name: Yerba Buena Island Light (and 12th District Lighthouse Depot)
summary: Lit on October 1, 1875, the small octagonal tower on Yerba Buena (then Goat) Island marked the crossroads of bay traffic, and shared its island with the 12th Lighthouse District's depot, moved there in 1873, from which tenders supplied every light and buoy on this coast. Its borrowed fifth-order Sautter lens gave way to a fourth-order in 1912; keepers left at automation in 1958. Light and dwelling survive inside the Coast Guard base beneath the Bay Bridge.
sources: [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 4595 | [P] Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses FY1915 - station listed as 'Goat Island, Cal.' | lighthousefriends.com, Yerba Buena Lighthouse (cites LHB annual reports) | [P] NRHP nomination, East Brother Island Light Station (1971) - notes planned central control of bay aids from Yerba Buena Island | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
notes: Depot's 1873 establishment and 'relocated from Mare Island' rest on lighthousefriends; the depot deserves confirmation in LHB reports (a documented depot existed at YBI into the 20th c. - the 1971 NRHP text corroborates its console/ops role). The USCG Historian California page has no YBI entry. Also known as: Goat Island Light (official listing name while the island was 'Goat Island,' to 1931).

name: Oakland Harbor Light
summary: Oakland's harbor entrance got its first lighthouse in January 1890, a wooden pile-borne dwelling whose foundations teredo worms ruined within a decade; a sturdier successor on steel cylinders took over on July 11, 1903. Deactivated in 1966, the second lighthouse lost its lantern to Santa Cruz's surfing-museum lighthouse and was floated up the estuary, reopening in 1984 as Quinn's Lighthouse Restaurant in Embarcadero Cove.
sources: [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Oakland Harbor Light (archived 2010) | lighthousefriends.com, Oakland Harbor Lighthouse (cites LHB reports, Lighthouse Service Bulletin, Shanks 1990, Nelsons 1993) | Wikipedia, Oakland Harbor Light (deactivated 1966; Quinn's 1984) | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
notes: Position NOT ESTABLISHED. No published latitude and longitude for either the 1890 or the 1903 structure was found; the 1889 Coast Pilot predates the station and the 1943 edition gives none. What the record does say is that the station stood on eleven piles off the end of the northern training wall, the two walls spaced 750 feet apart and running some two miles into the bay. This pin marks that approach, and should be read as an area with an uncertainty of about 1.5 km; an earlier version of this map cited a modern channel buoy as its anchor, which does not in fact produce this position. The 1903 building survives, moved about six miles to Embarcadero Cove. Also known as: Quinn's Lighthouse (relocated 1903 building).

name: Southampton Shoal Light
summary: Southampton Shoal received a cottage-style lighthouse on iron cylinders in December 1905, guarding the shoal on the run from the central bay toward San Pablo Bay. The 1906 earthquake racked its legs; braces and rock held it for another half-century of keepers until Point Blunt assumed its fog signal in 1960. In 1966 the wooden dwelling was barged to Tinsley Island in the delta as a yacht-club outstation, and an automated tower on the old site still marks the shoal.

Also known as: Southampton Shoals Light (USCG spelling).

name: East Brother Island Light Station
date_display: March 1, 1874; fog signal in operation May 1, 1874
summary: Built in 1873-74 on a dynamited islet off Point San Pablo, East Brother lighted the strait between San Francisco and San Pablo Bays from March 1, 1874, its steam whistle following that May. The Victorian tower-dwelling, cistern, and fog-signal building survived earthquake, automation in 1969, and a demolition plan, becoming one of the first West Coast light stations rescued by NRHP listing. A nonprofit has operated it as an inn since 1980, with the light still flashing.
sources: [P] NRHP Inventory-Nomination, East Brother Island Light Station (#71000138), 1971, citing USCG 12th District station file and LHB Annual Reports 1873-1874 | [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 5865 | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: East Brother Island Light (archived 2010, incl. full keeper roster) | Wikipedia, East Brother Island Light (NRHP ref/date; Pelz; inn operation); Frank Perry, 'East Brother: History of an Island Light Station' (steward-published history, lead) | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
notes: Strongest-documented station in the bay: nomination text, Light List, USCG Historian, and steward records all align. Pelz attribution is secondary. Also known as: East Brother Light, the San Pablo Strait light (functional designation).

name: Mare Island Light
summary: Lighted on September 1, 1873 at the southeastern tip of the Navy Yard island, Mare Island Light was East Brother's near-twin, a Victorian tower-dwelling with a fourth-order fixed white light and a fog bell moved up from Point Bonita. It is remembered for Kate McDougal, appointed in December 1881 months after her husband, the district's lighthouse inspector, drowned at Cape Mendocino, and keeper here for some 35 years until the light's discontinuation on July 1, 1917, by which time the new Carquinez Strait Light half a mile off had taken its work. The Navy razed the empty buildings in the 1930s; only the site remains, on the former shipyard.

McDougal, Lighthouse Inspector, drowned off Cape Mendocino light, March 28, 1881, from tender Manzanita) | [P] Notice to Mariners printed in San Francisco Call, 1910-01-19, p.15 (Carquinez Strait Light established Jan. 15, 1910, bearing/distance FROM Mare Island lighthouse - fixes the two stations' relation while both stood) | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Mare Island Light (archived 2010) - structure, bell, 'Kate McDougal (1881-1916)', deactivated 1917, razed 1930s, 4 photo files incl. c.1879 print | [S] USCG Historian's Office, 'Breaking the Barrier: Women Lighthouse Keepers' (archived 2008) - Kate C. That volume also settles where the station stood, describing it in its words: "a Light-house has been established on the extreme southeastern part of Mare Island"; which reconciles the Light-House Board's own inconsistency between the "southern end" it ordered in 1872 and the "extreme eastern end" its 1874 list printed. An earlier version of this map estimated the position and placed it about 300 m away; the published fix supersedes that estimate. Also known as: Mare Island Lighthouse. ⚠ Corrected here from the Board itself: the fog bell was not new and did not come from Cape Mendocino. The Annual Report for 1874 (p. 682) states: "The fog-bell and machinery formerly in use at Point Bonita light-station has been removed to this station, where a suitable house has been built for it."

name: Carquinez Strait Light
summary: Established January 15, 1910 on piles at the mouth of Mare Island Strait, the Carquinez Strait Light packed tower, fog signal, and a 28-room dwelling into one enormous wooden building at the end of a long dike - the inland gatepost for river-bound shipping, replacing the little Mare Island light half a mile away. The Coast Guard abandoned the building for automatic aids in 1951, and in 1955 the whole structure was barged to Glen Cove, where it still stands, de-towered, as a marina office. The station function itself was automated in 1963.

December 1966 USCG press release (1951 abandonment, Aug. 6, 1955 barge move to Elliott Cove, June 3, 1963 automation) | lighthousefriends.com, Carquinez Strait Lighthouse (appropriation March 4, 1907; keepers Czarnecke, Kaneen; Glen Cove Marina present use) | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page

Expect ±400 m, with a further ±140 m because the notice does not say whether its miles are statute or nautical. The building itself survives, moved: barged to Glen Cove in 1955, where it serves as a marina office. Also known as: Carquinez Straits Lighthouse, Glen Cove lighthouse (relocated building).

name: Roe Island Light
date_display: February 16, 1891, first keeper Richard A. Weiss
summary: The only staffed light station east of Carquinez Strait, Roe Island Light went into service on February 16, 1891, a low cottage lantern on pilings marking the Suisun Bay channel to the upriver ports. It survived half a century of fog and grain traffic only to be wrecked from within the bay: the Port Chicago explosion of July 17, 1944 tore its bell house loose from 3,000 yards away. Discontinued in 1945 and sold, the buildings later burned; only channel range lights carry the name today.
sources: [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Roe Island Light (archived 2010), incl. quoted 11 Aug. 1944 USCG station report and 1924 station photos C88/C94 | lighthousefriends.com, Roe Island Lighthouse (first lit Feb. 16, 1891; keepers Weiss, Nilsson, Scott; sale to Pittsburg 1946) | [P] US Coast Pilot, Pacific Coast (1943) - Roe Island Light 'northward of the channel opposite Bay Point'; GNIS 231813 | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page

name: Angel Island Light Station (Point Knox)
summary: Angel Island's light station began as a fog-bell post at Point Knox in November 1886, a bell house and cottage bolted to the island's fog-blind western bluff, gaining a small fixed-red light in 1900. Keeper Juliet Fish Nichols made it famous in July 1906 when the striking machinery shattered in dense fog and she beat the bell by hand through the night and the next day. After 1915 its keepers also ran the island's Point Stuart and Point Blunt minor lights; the station closed October 31, 1960 and was burned in 1963, leaving the bell standing in the state park.
sources: [S] USCG Historian's Office, 'Breaking the Barrier: Women Lighthouse Keepers' (archived 2008) - Juliet Nichols, Angel Island, 1902-1914 | lighthousefriends.com, Point Knox Lighthouse (cites LHB annual reports; George Worthylake, 'Point Knox,' The Keeper's Log, Fall 1996; Shanks 1990; Nelsons 1993) | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Point Blunt entry July 1970 press release (Point Knox station role and 1960-61 consolidation) | [P] GNIS gaz_id 254857 (Point Knox); Light List, Pacific Coast (1988) - Point Knox Lighted Gong Buoy 2 | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page

Nichols' death date not included (unverified). Also known as: Point Knox Light, Angel Island Fog-Bell Station.

name: Point Stuart Light
summary: Point Stuart got its light and electric fog siren in fiscal 1915 as one of a pair of unwatched aids added to Angel Island and run by wire from the Point Knox keepers. A white frame signal house on the island's western nose, it marked the mouth of Raccoon Strait for seventy-odd years, latterly under the name Raccoon Strait Light, before being supplanted by a buoy. Its establishment is documented directly in the Commissioner of Lighthouses' FY1915 annual report.
sources: [P] Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses, FY1915, p.8 (fog signals and minor lights established at Point Stuart and Point Blunt) | [P] US Coast Pilot, Pacific Coast (1943) - Point Stuart Light description; Light List, Pacific Coast (1988) | lighthousefriends.com, Point Knox Lighthouse page (1915 Angel Island minor lights detail) | [P] GNIS gaz_id 235615 (Point Stuart) | [P] Annual Report of the Light-House Board · the passages quoted in this popup, cited per passage to report year and page
