name: Point Blunt Light
date_display: Minor light and electric fog siren established fiscal year 1915
summary: Point Blunt began in fiscal 1915 as the third of Angel Island's remotely run minor lights, but after WWII the Coast Guard reversed the automation tide here, building a full manned station between about 1957 and 1961 - the last lighthouse station built and staffed in California - whose watch room controlled its own light, Raccoon Strait's, and Southampton Shoal's. It was automated on June 28, 1976 and still shows a green flash over the anchorage approaches.
sources: [P] Annual Report of the Commissioner of Lighthouses, FY1915, p.8 | [P] USCG Light List Vol. VI (2025), LLNR 4335 | [S] USCG Historian's Office, California page: Point Blunt Light (archived 2010), incl. July 1970 press release | lighthousefriends.com, Point Blunt Lighthouse (Shanks 1990; automation June 28, 1976; keeper roster 1957-76)
notes: The '1956' founding year sometimes quoted for the manned station is not directly evidenced in the sources consulted (roster from 1957; buildings 1960-61); USCG's own 1970 press release reaches back to the 1915 establishment. Treat 1956/57 with care.

name: Needle Rock Landing
summary: The northernmost Mendocino doghole port, about 2 miles up the coast from Bear Harbor (Davidson 1889 places it 6¾ miles from Point Delgada, Bear Harbor 8⅔). A wire-chute pier reputedly the highest and longest on the Mendocino coast shipped railroad ties, tanbark, and Whitethorn Valley shingles from the 1890s; a 3-mile railway (1890, Stetson) linked mill and landing. Chute operated until about 1930, making it one of the longest-lived Lost Coast landings.
sources: Northern California Doghole Ports MPDF (draft), inventory entry 'Needle Rock Landing (active circa 1873-1930)' - read directly | [P] Davidson, Pacific Coast Pilot (1889), p. 300 (Needle Rock geography) - read directly | Bear Harbor NR nomination (Mendocino Beacon 12 Dec 1896 on Olsen shingle mill shipments at Needle Rock)
notes: MPDF entry is the anchor; its 1873 start date is 'circa.' Davidson 1889 describes Needle Rock itself but records no chute at that date on the page read - the chute likely postdates 1889 or Davidson omitted it; flagged. Coordinate source: GNIS 229443 (Needle Rock, Bear Harbor quad, Mendocino Co.)

name: Bear Harbor Landing
summary: The definitive Lost Coast doghole port: split-products (above all tanbark) exported by schooner from 1874 and by steam schooner from 1890 over two successive pier-and-chute systems, fed after 1893 by the Bear Harbor & Eel River Railroad with its 2,000-ft gravity incline over the coastal ridge. The Southern Humboldt Lumber Co.'s half-million-dollar Andersonia sawmill was finished in 1905 but destroyed by the 18 April 1906 earthquake before ever cutting lumber; the port shipped its last products in 1907. 46+ vessels carried cargoes to 14 California ports over 33 years.
sources: Bear Harbor Landing Historical and Archaeological District, National Register of Historic Places Registration Form (Doghole Ports MPS), California OHP, listed c.2022-23 - Sections 7-8 read in full | [P] George Davidson, Pacific Coast Pilot, 4th ed. (Washington: GPO, 1889), pp. 299-300 (Bear Harbor Landing, wharf of 1885, apron, moorings, hydrography) - read directly | Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape MPDF (draft), NPS/OHP, inventory entry 'Bear Harbor Landing (active circa 1884-1909)' | 'The Bear Harbor Railroad, 1892-1905,' North Coast Journal, Nov. 2018 | [P] Thomas H. Peterson, Bear Harbor survey map, Sept. 1885 (Huntington Library) - cited via NR nomination; not directly viewed
notes: Exceptionally well documented (2022-23 NR nomination with newspaper-level citations). Discrepancies flagged: incline length 1,900 vs 2,000 ft; 3 vs 4 rails at incline midpoint; railway gauge (standard vs narrow) unresolved; MPDF gives McCornack sale as 1893 but the fuller NR nomination documents Nov 1889 sale to Weller & Stewart. Davidson 1889 says wharf built 1885, NR gives open-for-business 4 July 1885. Coordinate source: GNIS 221267 (Cluster Cone Rocks); NRHP nomination on disk (bear-harbor-landing-nrhp-nomination.pdf); Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot p.299-300

name: Northport Landing (Anderson's Landing)
summary: Robert Anderson built a wire chute here in 1872, on Mistake Point where Little Jackass Creek reaches the shore; a very early example of the type; abandoned 1883. Most business was tanbark, loaded by a cage lowered from the cliff landing stage.
sources: Davidson 1889:289; California State Parks 2019, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: GNIS 228860 Mistake Point (prim 39.860428,-123.9039126); GNIS 227283 Little Jackass Creek mouth (39.860428,-123.9016903)

name: Rockport Landing (Cottoneva Cove, Miller's Chute)
summary: William R. Miller landed mill machinery from the schooner David and Edward in October 1876 and built the first sawmill; the wharf-and-chute complex of 1876 cost $14,000 and was called the finest on the Mendocino coast (Palmer: 275-ft suspension span with seven cables a side). The 1889 Coast Pilot describes the mature system: a 175-yard wire suspension bridge from the north point to a 50-ft rock, a tramway across the rock, and a 45-yard chute over 15 ft of water; four principal mooring buoys; mill (25,000 ft/day) 1/3 mi up Cottoneva Creek, lumber brought by tramway, logs by steam railway; ~24 cargoes/yr; landing unused about four months after 1 December. Ownership: Miller to Cottoneva Lumber Co. 1886 (mill burned 1900); New York & Pennsylvania (Redwood) Co. c.1907 built a new mill (also burned); Cottoneva Lumber Co. reincorporated 1910 (nothing built); Finkbine-Guild Lumber Co. 1924-27 (financial disaster); Southern Redwood Co. 1928-29; Rockport Redwood Co. (from 1938, per the MPDF) chartered under Dusenbury interests in the 1930s (trucking era).
sources: Palmer 1880, Cotineva/Rockport (1876 wharf & chute, $14,000, 275-ft span) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Cottaneva Cove or Rockport | Guide to the Rockport Redwood Company Records (OAC) | CoastView, 'Cottoneva Creek, Rockport Bay' (ownership sequence) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Sequence 1900-1933 from CoastView/Hough-derived summaries; company names New York & Pennsylvania Lumber vs. Redwood Co. vary across sources. Coordinate source: GNIS 254782 Cottaneva Creek (prim/mouth 39.7359882,-123.829187); GNIS 231753 Rockport Bay (39.7340439,-123.8286314) Audit 2026-09-13: the David-and-Edward machinery-landing anecdote and the 'Southern Redwood 1928-29' span are re-sourcing tasks; Rockport Redwood Co. from 1938 (MPDF; the Dusenbury attribution is unsourced).

name: Hardy Creek Landing
summary: Mill settlement just around the point from Rockport; the mill belonged to Rockport's Cottoneva Lumber Co. and was run by part-owner E.T. Dusenbury. A wharf and a rail line served the mill, and the town supported a large hotel; fire took the mill, which was never replaced. The 1889 Coast Pilot already names Hardy's Rock on this shore; the mill era therefore falls in the Cottoneva Lumber Co. period (c.1886-1900s) but exact years are unverified.
sources: MCMRHS, Hardy Creek page | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot (Hardy's Rock) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Single-source (MCMRHS) entry; corroborate via Hough's Rockport articles in the Mendocino Beacon (CDNC). Coordinate source: GNIS 224927 Hardy Creek (prim/mouth 39.7107116,-123.8075196); derived-from-verbal for the landing itself

name: Union Landing (McFaul's Landing)
summary: Busy shipping point without a mill of its own, serving many small mills nearby (incl. the Juan Creek timber). W.P. McFaul built the first wharf, sending six-foot ties down to the Los Angeles Railway by way of San Pedro. After W.P. Frick acquired the Big Juan Creek timber in 1920, he had a new wharf built in 1926; no wharf was built on the Mendocino coast after it, and the Depression left it nearly idle. A large hotel/boarding house served the wharf hands.
sources: MCMRHS, Union Landing page | MCMRHS, Juan Creek page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Juan Creek (Alviso Creek) mills nearby; several small mills, the last burned 1944; their shipping route (Union Landing vs. Westport/Hardy Creek) is not documented; flagged as gap. Coordinate source: GNIS 226363 Juan Creek (prim/mouth 39.7029342,-123.8036305); derived-from-verbal (landing just S of mouth)

name: Westport Landing (Switzer's Chute, Beall's)
summary: First settled by Samuel Beal(l) (hence Beal's Landing); Fred Helmke's unfranchised 1875 chute soon washed away; James T. Rodgers built the wharf and chute in 1877 and renamed the town (Palmer 1880 says for Eastport, Maine; Wikipedia says Westport, Connecticut; unresolved). Palmer: a 375-ft wharf, 20 ft wide, with a ~200-ft suspension span, its outer end on a large rock, carrying two chutes. A new 610-ft chute with 75-ft apron (1882) let the loaded car haul the empty back. Two chutes (N and S) served three mills on Wages Creek plus DeHaven, Howard Creek and other feeders; ~65 vessels/yr, up to 85,000 ft loaded in a day; shipping suspended four months each winter, moorings lifted and overhauled. The south wharf was abandoned by 1900 and the port faded after WWI with the tie market.
sources: Palmer 1880, Westport and Ten-Mile ports (wharf specs; 1875/1877 chutes) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Westport Landing | MCMRHS, Westport page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Rodgers hometown discrepancy flagged above. 'Decline after WWI' from Kelley House/secondary summaries. Coordinate source: GNIS 1660154 Westport (populated place 39.6357148,-123.7830734)

name: Kibesilah Landing (Ackermann's Landing)
summary: Settled in the 1860s (first business, a blacksmith shop, 1867), Kibesillah grew to 'a dozen or twenty buildings... two hotels, one store, one livery stable, and two saloons' (Palmer 1880), shipping posts, cordwood and tanbark (not lumber, per Palmer) over its chute. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a very substantial 90-yard wharf continued by an apron over 20 ft of water; but by 1885 no moorings were laid and the landing was 'practically abandoned,' vessels having no demand for ties there. When Stewart, Hunter and Johnson moved the mill to Fort Bragg in 1885 the town followed; hence 'the Mother of Fort Bragg.'
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Kibesillah or Ackermann's Landing | Palmer 1880, Ten-Mile Township | MCMRHS, Kibesillah page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: School continuity to 1928 shows residual hamlet after the port died. Coordinate source: GNIS 234108 Kibesillah Creek (prim/mouth 39.59155,-123.7825171); GNIS 252713 Kibesillah PP 39.5901611,-123.7777947; Wikipedia Kibesillah, California 39.59028,-123.77778 (agrees)

name: Newport Landing
summary: 'One of the most contracted anchorages on the coast'; a cove 150 by 60 yards. The Field Brothers' mill (2 mi east on Mill Creek, Ten Mile drainage) burned 1877; brothers-in-law Calvin Stewart and James Hunter rebuilt it in 1878 (25,000 ft/day) and hauled lumber by six-horse jerk-line teams to a 260-ft gravity chute reaching 18 ft of water; a 200-ton vessel could load amid an elaborate web of six-plus moorings; Davidson called it 'one of the most contracted anchorages' on the coast. ~50 vessels/yr. C.R. Johnson bought in 1882, concluded the port could never grow, and moved the mill to Fort Bragg in 1885; by 1887 only posts and ties were loaded, and the landing died.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Newport Landing (1887 status) | Palmer 1880, Ten-Mile Township ports (Stewart & Hunter chute) | MCMRHS, Newport page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: The 'Mother of Fort Bragg' narrative (mill moved 1885) is consistent across Palmer-era and MCMRHS accounts. Coordinate source: Davidson, Pacific Coast Pilot 1889 (local OCR): 'The station inside the cliff at Newport (Brushy Point) is in latitude 39-34-25, longitude 123-46-34' - period government position; cross-check GNIS 1659222 Newport PP (39.5773839,-123.7747388) 450 m NE

name: Laguna Landing (Cleone Landing)
summary: The Dwelly brothers took timber on Laguna Creek early in 1883, built a water-powered mill and Cleone Point's first chute and wharf, getting a first cargo of lumber away by July 1883; the Little Valley Lumber Co. (Barto, Jarvis, Nichols, Salsig, inc. 23 May 1885) combined this with the Mill Creek mill near Inglenook. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a ~160-yard wharf with attached apron chute (vessel under it in 12 ft; 100-ton vessels; five moorings; mill 3 mi east at 18,000 ft/day), reported washed away in 1886 with business transferring to Fort Bragg; but an 1888 grant authorized rebuilding of wharf and chute, the wharf grew from 332 to ~500 ft (35 ft above the breakers; 300 ft collapsed to teredo worms Nov 1885, rebuilt), with loading wires extending to steam schooners ~200 ft offshore. A 2.5-mile wooden-strap-rail tramway ran gravity-down/horses-up through town; Union Lumber acquired all in 1901 and relaid light steel; the Laguna mill closed November 1904; the landing itself saw residual use to c.1920 (MPDF; Borden gives 1923).
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Laguna Point/Laguna Landing | Louis Hough via MCMRHS Cleone page (tramway, wharf, 1904 closure) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: 1885/1886 washout vs. 1888 rebuild chronology mixes the Beacon (Hough) and CP accounts; both retained with dates as given. Coordinate source: GNIS 226779 Laguna Point (39.4896098,-123.803627)

name: Fort Bragg Landing (Soldiers Harbor)
summary: The military post (est. 1857 to watch the reservation; abandoned by the mid-1860s; 'many years ago' per 1889 CP) gave its name to the cove C.R. Johnson chose after judging Newport hopeless: with Calvin Stewart and James Hunter he formed the Fort Bragg Redwood Co. (1885), moved the Kibesillah mill down, incorporated the Fort Bragg Railroad 30 April 1885 (rails up Pudding Creek; Glen Blair 1887), and built the wharf in Soldiers Harbor; incomplete July 1885, a working shipping landing in 1886, where 'steam schooners only load' (1889 CP). Union Lumber Co. formed 1891 (merging Noyo River Lumber Co.); National Steamship Co. 1901; California Western RR & Navigation Co. 1905, over the hill to Willits 1911; after which Fort Bragg was the only Mendocino coast mill with a rail connection over the coast range (the CWR to Willits). The pier grew to ~700 ft with three tracks and cranes; the Mendocino coast's final seaborne lumber cargo departed this pier in 1938. Mill (later Boise Cascade/Georgia-Pacific) ran until 21 June 2002.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Fort Bragg or Soldiers Harbor (wharf 1885-86; steam schooners only) | Wikipedia, 'Union Lumber Company' | MCMRHS, Fort Bragg / CWR / Ten Mile / piers / shipping pages (last sea cargo 1938; mill closed 2002) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: MCMRHS gives the fort's active years as 1857-59; standard accounts run to 1864; flag the discrepancy. ULC merger details (Stewart/Hunter buyout vs. merger) vary between sources. Coordinate source: GNIS 234869 Soldier Point (39.4393344,-123.8194605)

name: Noyo Landing (Noyo Anchorage)
summary: Capt. William Richardson had a mill built 3 mi up the Noyo in 1852-53 (washed out January 1854); A.W. Macpherson (& Weatherby) opened the lasting Noyo mill in 1858 (40,000 ft/day by 1880, ~120 million ft cut). No chute served the schooner era (a wire chute was added on the north point c.1900, active to the 1920s - MPDF): lumber was lightered from a wharf inside the river mouth to vessels at two mooring buoys in the cove, small schooners filling holds in the river; ships drawing 23 ft loaded direct for foreign ports (one cargo to Valparaiso), a tug shared with Albion towing vessels out; five vessels a month in ordinary seasons and the coasting steamer every trip (1889 Coast Pilot). One of the coast's earliest railroads was the mill's log line from Pudding Creek, on the alignment of today's Harrison Street; the company merged into Union Lumber in 1891.
sources: Palmer 1880 ('There are no chutes or wharfs at Noyo...on lighters'; mills history) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Noyo Anchorage/River | MCMRHS, Noyo page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: 1889 CP notes the sawmill closed in 1887(?) 'on account of litigation' (OCR year uncertain). Coordinate source: GNIS 229807 Noyo Bay (39.4273906,-123.8139048); GNIS 229808 Noyo River mouth (39.4276684,-123.8091824)

name: Pallas Bay Landing (Palace Bay Harbor)
summary: One trough chute from the north shore at the mouth of Hare Creek, built c.1880 for Blumberg & Hardy's railroad-tie operation. Mooring buoys removed by 1885; the 1884 railroad from Hare Creek to Caspar's mill probably diverted the traffic (MPDF); last shipment 1887.
sources: Davidson 1889:287; Mendocino Beacon July 20, 2006; Carranco & Labbe 1975, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: GNIS 224932 Hare Creek (prim/mouth 39.4171134,-123.8125158)

name: Bromley Gulch Landing
summary: NEVER ACTIVE: a trough chute was built in 1884 on the south side of the tiny cove at the mouth of Bromley's Gulch (Jug Handle State Natural Reserve), but no shelter and no mooring anchors were ever placed, so no vessel ever used it. The coast's built-but-unused exemplar.
sources: Davidson 1889:286; Jackson 1977, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal: Davidson 1889:286 'Bromley Gulch is at the mouth of a small creek one and one-quarter miles north of Caspar Point... chute built (1884) from the south side of the very small cove at the mouth of the creek'; latitude = GNIS 220679 Caspar Point (39.3696157,-123.8255714) + 1.25 mi N; longitude interpolated along the coast between GNIS Caspar Point and GNIS Hare Creek mouth

name: Caspar Landing (Caspar Anchorage)
summary: William H. Kelley & Randall built the sawmill at Caspar Creek mouth in 1861; Jacob Green Jackson bought it in 1864, incorporated the Caspar Lumber Co. in 1880, and his son-in-law Henry Krebs ran it from 1901 until closure 18 November 1955; the longest-lived family firm on the coast. The 1889 Coast Pilot: two lumber chutes on the north bluff (11 and 18 ft of water), excellent moorings overhauled each winter, four vessels loading at once, flag signals, ~50 vessels/yr, 150 million ft shipped to date. Its railroad began 1874 as a 1.5-mi wooden-railed horse/mule tram to Jughandle Creek, got a locomotive in 1875, crossed Jughandle trestle 1884 (Caspar & Hare Creek RR), and was incorporated 1903 as the standard-gauge Caspar, South Fork & Eastern (tunnel 1904; 30 mi by 1924; Mallets from 1910; rail to 1945). Company steamships (e.g. the 1888-built Caspar) carried the cut until trucking began 1939.
sources: Palmer 1880, Caspar (mill 1861, Jackson 1864) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Caspar Anchorage | Wikipedia, 'Caspar, South Fork and Eastern Railroad' (standard gauge; 1874-1945) | MCMRHS, Caspar Lumber Co. page (schooners Cora, Elvenia, Abbie, Maxim; steamship ops end 1939) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Jackson Demonstration State Forest is the ex-company land. 'First locomotive 1875' was second-hand from the SF Embarcadero seawall works. Coordinate source: GNIS 220676 Caspar Anchorage (39.3615606,-123.8200157) Audit: the Krebs succession and the 'longest-lived family firm' superlative are not in the located sources; treat as local tradition pending a Kelley House citation.

name: Russian Gulch Landing (Mendocino)
summary: Small two-pocket cove 1.5 mi south of Point Cabrillo; the 1889 Coast Pilot notes a chute built, in its words, 'from the top of the cliff on the south side of the north-east pocket' of the cove. Shingle mills came and went: L.E. Ballister & Co. 1867; Prince Grey 1878-88; Eugene Brown from 1888; Gray & Johnson Lumber & Shingle Mill 1918-1920s. High-line/wire rings remain in the headland rocks (now Russian Gulch State Park). A wire chute here in the 1890s is credited by the Kelley House with pressuring Mendocino to modernize.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Russian Gulch (Mendocino) | MCMRHS, Russian Gulch page (mill sequence) | Kelley House Museum, 'Wire Chute at the Shipping Point' (wire chutes at Little River and Russian Gulch before 1902) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Do not confuse with Russian Gulch, Sonoma County. Coordinate source: GNIS 232050 Russian Gulch, Mendocino Co. (prim/mouth 39.3289031,-123.8048157)

name: Mendocino Landing (Big River Landing)
summary: Founded on the Frolic: the Baltimore-built opium brig wrecked at Point Cabrillo 25 July 1850; Henry Meiggs's salvage agent Jerome Ford found no cargo but reported the redwood, and Meiggs's brig Ontario landed mill machinery in July 1852 (California Lumber Co.; first mill on the point 1852, second on the river flats 1853-54; reorganized after Meiggs's 1854 failure, eventually the Mendocino Lumber Co.; mill burned 17 Oct 1863, rebuilt 1864, 55,000 ft/day both sides); the origin story verified against Thomas Layton's Frolic research. Loading: initially lighters; then three trough chutes on the north headland (17-ft-draft vessels at the outer; 600-800-ton vessels in summer, 200-ton in winter; deeper ships loaded by lighter); a big wharf toward the river mouth washed entirely away; the famous wire chute at the Point was first used 28 March 1902. A railroad with a 64-ft stationary-engine incline linked mill to chutes. Production halted 1937; the last ship, steamer Noyo, took a deckload 24 November 1938.
sources: Palmer 1880, Big River Township (Ontario 1852; mill history; 3 chutes) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Mendocino Bay | Thomas N. Layton, The Voyage of the Frolic (Stanford UP, 1997) | Kelley House Museum, 'Wire Chute at the Shipping Point' (2022) and 'Last Days of Mendocino's Mill' | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Palmer misremembers the Frolic as 'winter 1851-2 at the Noyo'; Layton (1997) and Point Cabrillo sources fix 25 July 1850 at Point Cabrillo. Mill-closure dates vary (idle from c.1931; final logs 1938). Coordinate source: GNIS 219234 Big River (prim/mouth 39.3021191,-123.7947367); GNIS 228497 Mendocino Bay (39.2960083,-123.8019591)

name: Little River Landing (Bell's Landing, Kents Cove)
summary: Mill town built 1864 by Silas Coombs, Ruel Stickney and Tapping Reeves on land bought from W.H. Kent (1862); first whistle 15 October 1864, 38 schooners loaded the first year; mill burned 20 March 1874 and was rebuilt across the river by 4 July 1874 (30,000 ft/day); closed 1893. The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a 110-yard wharf (10 ft at its end) and two chutes (NW chute over 16 ft of water; SE chute 12 ft), four vessels able to ride out storms at the moorings; a noted harbor of refuge. Its shipyard made it famous: Capt. Thomas H. Peterson launched roughly three dozen wooden ships here and nearby (Palmer lists Phil Sheridan, Little River, Napa City, Alice Kimball, Silas Coombs, Emma and Louisa, Johanna Brock, Electra, Galatea, Hannah Madison, Barbara, Mary D. Pomeroy, etc.).
sources: Palmer 1880, Little River mill and shipbuilding lists | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Little River Harbor | MCMRHS, Little River page; Kelley House Museum (Hough) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: '~Three dozen vessels' is Hough's figure from Petersen's memoirs; Palmer (1880) already lists ~15. Coordinate source: GNIS 227343 Little River stream (prim/mouth 39.2740651,-123.791403)

name: Big Gulch Landing (Pullen's Landing)
summary: Single trough chute at the mouth of Dark Gulch, under a mile north of Albion. Two schooners loaded in 1882, none in 1883; marked out of repair 1883 and dead by 1885. Newspaper cargoes were railroad ties only.
sources: Davidson 1889:281, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: GNIS 222022 Dark Gulch, Albion quad (prim/mouth 39.2397877,-123.7740297)

name: Albion Landing (Albion Harbor)
summary: One of the oldest mill sites on the coast: a water mill upriver c.1851 for Capt. William Richardson (claimant of the unconfirmed Albion grant), then the Albion steam mill of 1853 (Dallas, Davidson & Macpherson), burned and rebuilt 1867, run by Macpherson & Weatherby in 1880 (35,000 ft/day, 27,000 acres). The 1889 Coast Pilot: schooners entered past Mooring Rock to 6-7 buoys; large schooners loaded by lighters, 90-ton schooners towed to the mill wharf; vessels drawing 18 ft 'loaded at the moorings direct for foreign ports' (Davidson 1889); ~70 vessels/yr; Henley's chute on the south side shipped ties and posts. Albion Lumber Co. reorganized 1891; the Albion & Southeastern RR (1902) became the Fort Bragg & Southeastern (1903, standard gauge, ultimately 25.65 mi to Christine); Southern Pacific bought the company in 1907 and the NWP-owned 'big mill' cut mostly redwood ties (much for SP of Mexico) until the last log 19 May 1928; the railroad closed 16 January 1930 and was scrapped 1937.
sources: Palmer 1880, Albion mill history | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Albion River | Wikipedia, 'Fort Bragg and Southeastern Railroad' (dates, standard gauge, 1928/1930/1937) | MCMRHS, Albion page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: 1851 water mill per MCMRHS; Palmer starts with the 1853 steam mill; treat 1851 as reported, not confirmed. Coordinate source: GNIS 218073 Albion Cove (39.2274004,-123.7741808)

name: Henley's Landing (Handley's Chute)
summary: Chute on the south side of Albion Cove built by settler William Handley (arrived 1865); on the 1872 and 1886 maps and in the 1889 Coast Pilot. One mooring anchor and four shore fasteners; loaded railroad ties and posts from surrounding mills.
sources: Munro-Fraser 1880a; Davidson 1889:280; Peterson 1886, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal: Davidson 1889:280 trig station 'on the southwest point of the cove' = 39-13-32 N, 123-46-25 W (period government position); chute 'on the south side of the cove one hundred and eighty yards from the Mooring Rock'

name: Whitesboro Landing (Salmon Creek)
summary: Renamed for L.E. White. The Salmon Creek Mill Co. built its mill in August 1876 (20,000 ft/day); the Salmon Creek Railroad Co. (L.E. White, James Townsend et al.) laid 8 miles of narrow-gauge from the wharf up the creek by January 1878; Gray & White added a 90,000/day shingle mill in 1878 and Britt & White a 30,000-ft mill in 1880. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a 160-yard wharf across the beach, widening to 20 yards, 30 ft above high water, with three derricks each suspending a chute, 12 ft of water alongside; heavy moorings across the cove; 130 vessels loaded in one year, and it was rated one of the best winter anchorages on this coast. White shifted his main operation to Greenwood c.1890; Whitesboro's later years are unverified.
sources: Palmer 1880 (Salmon Creek mills; Salmon Creek RR 1877 narrow gauge) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Whitesboro | MCMRHS, Whitesboro page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: The user's separate 'Salmon Creek' = this port. Coordinate source: GNIS 255234 Whitesboro Cove (39.2174008,-123.7727921)

name: Navarro Landing (Navarro Harbor)
summary: Wharf/river-improvement franchise at the Navarro mouth granted to A.W. Macpherson by Act of 18 April 1859; the Navarro mill was built 1861 by Tichenor & Hendy. Charles Fletcher, first settler, ran a shipyard at the river mouth (schooners Nevarra 50 tons, Sina 140 tons, Ocean Pearl 300 tons, per Palmer) and with the Kennedys built an inn in the 1860s for schooner crews waiting the three days it took to load. The first mill burned July 1890; a larger mill a mile upriver went bankrupt in 1893 and burned 1902; at its height the flats settlement held 500-600 people. The Navarro Lumber Co. was acquired by Albion Lumber Co. in May 1920 (the inland 'Navarro'/Wendling mill ran to Sept 1927).
sources: Palmer 1880 (1859 Macpherson Act in full; Fletcher shipyard list; Navarro mill 1861) | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Navarro River and Landing | MCMRHS, Navarro/Wendling page (1890 fire, 1893 bankruptcy, 1902 fire) | Wikipedia, 'Fort Bragg and Southeastern Railroad' (Navarro Lumber Co. to Albion Lumber May 1920; Navarro sawmill ceased Sept 1927) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Distinguish Navarro-by-the-Sea (this port) from inland Wendling, renamed Navarro 1914. Coordinate source: GNIS 229433 Navarro River (prim/mouth 39.1921239,-123.7611258)

name: Cuffey's Cove Landing
summary: Settled by Frank Farnier ('Portuguese Frank') and Nathaniel Smith; James Kenney's chute/landing franchise dates to 28 March 1868. By 1880 the village had ~50 buildings, six saloons and four chutes shipping 'immense quantities' of bark, wood, posts, pickets, ties and lumber; J.S. Kimball alone shipping 250-300,000 railroad ties a year with up to 300 men. The 1889 Coast Pilot maps three chutes in the inner cove (10, 13 and 24 ft of water) plus a 'half-wharf' steamer chute reaching 24-ft water; over 100 coasting vessels loaded annually, fed by the steam railway from the Greenwood Creek mill. L.E. White's superior new landing at Greenwood made Cuffey's obsolete in the 1890s; population had peaked ~300 in 1883.
sources: Palmer 1880, Cuffey's Cove | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Cuffeys Cove | MCMRHS, Cuffeys Cove page | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Name origin stories (bear vs. 'cuffey' for a Black settler) both period-reported; unresolved. Coordinate source: GNIS 254801 Cuffeys Cove (39.1410141,-123.7311267)

name: Chisholm Landing
summary: Single trough chute ('Chisholm chute' on the 1870 USC&GS survey) running from the cliff across the water to a rocky island, between Greenwood Landing and Cuffey's Cove. Already inactive when Davidson described it in 1889.
sources: 1870 USC&GS T-sheet; Davidson 1889:277, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal: Davidson 1889:277 'Formerly there was a chute located at the islet which is halfway between this cove [Cuffeys Cove] and Greenwood Creek Landing'; midpoint of GNIS 254801 Cuffeys Cove and GNIS 224596 Greenwood Cove

name: Greenwood Creek Landing (Greenwood, Elk)
summary: Two-stage port. By 1889 (built 1886-89 per the MPDF) a long wharf/chute complex ran from the 140-ft point over the rocky islets north of Greenwood Creek, reaching 10 ft of water, fed by the narrow-gauge Mendocino Railroad Co. (org. 1875, 3.5 mi up Greenwood Creek, T-rail, two rod locomotives) which served both this landing and Cuffey's Cove; mills included A.W. Hall's (1870-73), Dixon's (1875-77) and Helmke's first-class 50,000-ft mill (1875/76, lost to creditors, becoming the Redwood Lumber Co.). Stage two: L.E. White built a large steam sawmill and 3-ft-gauge railroad about 1890 (80,000 ft/day), with a cliff-hung rail incline to a wharf where lumber was slung by wire to moored steam schooners; sold to Goodyear Redwood Co. 1916; Goodyear bankrupt 1932 and the uninsured mill burned 1936, ending the industry. Elk once had ten hotels; the L.E. White office survives as the town museum.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Greenwood Creek Landing | Palmer 1880 (Hall, Dixon, Helmke mills; Mendocino RR Co. 1875) | Wikipedia, 'Elk, Mendocino County, California' (White, Goodyear 1916, 1932 bankruptcy, 1936 fire) | MCMRHS, Elk/Greenwood page (incline, wire slings, wharf footings) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: White's mill start '1883' appears in some accounts; Wikipedia (citing local sources) supports c.1890 production of 80k ft/day. End of sea shipping c.1930 is inferred from Goodyear collapse; mark inferred. Coordinate source: GNIS 224596 Greenwood Cove (39.1324031,-123.7225157)

name: Bridgeport Landing (Hoag's Landing, Field's Landing (Mendocino))
summary: Open landing facing the NW swell, 6⅔ mi N of Point Arena light. C. Hoag built the chute in 1870; washed away in the storms of 1877 and rebuilt 1878; owned in 1880 by Mrs. Eliza Fields, with a store and blacksmith shop at the hamlet (post office 'Miller'). Large annual shipments of tanbark, cordwood, fence posts and railroad ties (Palmer). The 1889 Coast Pilot describes the chute running from high land 100 yards inside the cliff, by trestlework to two small rocks ~100 yards offshore, its apron turned sharply south. James Dixon's mill (machinery moved from Fort Ross, 1873) and successors sawed nearby.
sources: Palmer 1880, Bridgeport | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Bridgeport Landing; Uncle Abe's Landing | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Uncle Abe's Landing, a chute 1.5 mi SE of Greenwood, was torn down and abandoned before 1889 (Coast Pilot); folded here as the next minor landing north. Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal: Davidson 1889:275 'Six and two thirds miles north one degree east (N. 1 E.) from Point Arena Light'; base = GNIS 253765 Point Arena cape (38.9557424,-123.7414086, lighthouse site)

name: New Haven Landing
summary: Tiny, rock-filled cove whose south point is the north point of Mal Paso gulch (a 280-ft-deep 'bad crossing' for teams), 5.5 mi N of Point Arena light. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a chute projected 75 yards SSE from the high north bank just beyond the breakers; a vessel lay to six mooring lines broadside, head out, in a passage only ~70 yards wide; 'a dangerous-looking place'; safe for one 80-ton vessel at a time, with a large mooring buoy outside. No independent chute at Mal Paso itself is documented in sources located.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Mal Paso and New Haven Landing | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: The user's 'Mal Paso' and 'New Haven' resolve to this one cove complex. Coordinates approximate (Mallo Pass Creek vicinity). Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal: Davidson 1889:274 - the landing's south point 'lies five and a half miles north seven degrees east (N. 7 E.) from the Light-house at Point Arena' and is 'the north point of the little cove into which empty the waters of Mal Passo Gulch'; base = GNIS 253765 Point Arena cape

name: Arena Cove Landing (Point Arena)
summary: The best semi-sheltered cove between Bodega and Mendocino; used from 1859 to land supplies, with S.B. Campbell lightering from 1862 until Mart T. Smith's February 1866 state wharf franchise (owners then Woodward & Chalfant 1870, A. McClure & Co. 1875, C.R. Arthur 1880). The 1889 Coast Pilot shows a ~100-yard wharf into 15 ft of water on the north side plus a 'very long' trough chute descending the valley slope to 10 ft of water, later joined by a clifftop wire chute (Kelley House photo shows wharf, trough chute and wire chute together); ~50 schooners a year plus a regular coasting steamer. 1879 shipments included 70,000 posts, 13.5 million shingles, 223 cords of tanbark, leather, produce and 2,300 tons of merchandise; the town itself never had a big sawmill.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Arena Cove | Palmer 1880, Arena Township (wharf franchise 1866; 1879 shipment table) | MCMRHS, Point Arena page; chutes gallery | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Palmer's 1880 shipment statistics are from wharf-owner Arthur; period but interested source. 1913 wharf/1920s rebuilds not verified here. Coordinate source: GNIS 218356 Arena Cove (38.9137983,-123.7133513); GNIS 230845 Point Arena Creek mouth (38.9137982,-123.7105734)

name: Saunders' Landing (Hearn's Landing)
summary: Chuted bluff landing half a mile NW of Iversen Point, behind Saunders Reef. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a long chute carried from the 90-ft cliff over a chasm to a 49-ft rocky islet and projected to five fathoms, where schooners loaded lumber hauled from Schooner Gulch, plus wood, ties and posts; three mooring buoys; about 17 schooners loaded yearly, and 'no possible chance of saving anything that goes ashore here.'
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Saunders Landing | Palmer 1880, Landings and Chutes | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Scott's Landing (franchise to Lew. Gerlock, 22 Feb 1870, per Palmer) lay in this Gualala-Point Arena stretch; possibly an earlier name hereabouts; unresolved. Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal, two convergent Davidson 1889:268 constructions: (a) 'the chute at this place is less than half a mile northwestwardly from Iverson Point' off GNIS 254831 Iversen Point; (b) 'Saunders Reef lies from 750 to 1230 yards west three-quarters south from the chute' off GNIS 232600 Saunders Reef (38.8526878,-123.660293) - both give ~38.853,-123.650 (within 150 m)

name: Iverson's Landing (Fergusons Cove, Rough and Ready)
summary: Rock-choked cove under Iversen Point, 8¼ mi SE of Point Arena, protected somewhat by Saunders Reef. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a small platform chute on the north bank with a wire ('trapeze') carried across the cove; vessels at the trapeze lay stern-to in 17 ft of water moored to the rocks, while the Rough and Ready point chute took vessels of 100 tons on six mooring-lines (Davidson 1889); ~30 vessels/yr loaded wood, tanbark, posts and ties, fleeing to Havens Anchorage when SW swell came in. The Rough and Ready chute on Iversen Point itself washed away three times and was being re-erected in 1885. Namesake Niels Iversen (b. Denmark 1830) rebuilt the schooners Annie Iverson (1869) and Sina Johnson (1875) in the area.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Iverson Landing/Rough and Ready Landing | Palmer 1880 (Iversen biography; schooner rebuilds) | NOAA GFNMS doghole overview | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: NOAA lists 'Iverson's Landing' and separately 'Rough and Ready' among regional dogholes; they are adjacent works at one cove complex. Coordinate source: GNIS 254831 Iversen Point (38.8468544,-123.646959)

name: Steen's Landing (Hardscratch, Signal Port)
summary: Open landing 1⅓ mi NW of Havens Neck, ten miles SE of Point Arena; formerly called Hardscratch. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a chute about 200 yards long built from the 80-ft cliff over rocks into deep water, loading lumber, firewood, posts and tanbark; two mooring buoys plus a third added 1884. Its supplying sawmill, 3.5 mi inland, was erected in 1883 (25,000 ft/day) and about eight vessels loaded per month.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Signal Port or Steens Landing | Richard H. Tooker, 'Loading by High-Line on the California Coast,' Sea Letter 6:1 (SF Maritime Museum, May 1968) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinates estimated from Coast Pilot bearings only. Coordinate source: GNIS 1666816 Signal Port (historical) (38.8290768,-123.6155687); Wikipedia Signal Port, California 38.82917,-123.61556 (agrees); GNIS 233113 Signal Port Creek mouth 38.8285212,-123.6161243

name: Nip and Tuck Landing (Phelp's, Bryne's)
summary: Open-coast chute landing one mile NW of Havens Neck, at Reesman Gulch (crossed by a 60-ft-high bridge). The 1889 Coast Pilot reports a chute from the 75-ft cliff and states the landing was 'practically abandoned'; only six vessels loaded in 1883. The schooner Caroline Medau wrecked here in October 1881.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Nip and Tuck Landing | NOAA GFNMS doghole overview (port list) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Known essentially only from the 1889 Coast Pilot; NOAA's overview also lists it. Coordinate source: GNIS 231899 Roseman Creek (prim/mouth 38.8257434,-123.6097352); identified via Davidson 1889:266: chute 'on the south side of a deep, narrow gulch... called Reesman Gulch', 'one mile north thirty-eight degrees west from Havens Neck' (GNIS 225025)

name: Fish Rock Landing (Haven's Anchorage, Anchor Bay)
summary: Cove sheltered by the twin Fish Rocks, named Havens Anchorage by the Coast Survey in 1853. State franchises: wharf to Mart T. Smith 13 May 1861; chute to E.J. Stevens 26 March 1866; landing and chute to William S. Ferguson 27 February 1870 (Palmer). Russel Stevens ran a mill at Fish Rock Gulch from 1864 (~15-18,000 ft/day) until the timber was cut out. The 1889 Coast Pilot: chute from the NE bluff point over 15 ft of water, vessel broadside with 5-6 mooring lines; wood, posts and ties shipped year-round; five or six vessels could shelter under the rocks in NW blows; 200-ton vessels could anchor close in.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Havens Anchorage or Fish Rock Landing | Palmer 1880, Arena Township landings (franchise dates; Stevens mill 1864) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Propeller Arispe lost here May 1854; Mary Zephyr stranded 1881. Palmer conflates Ferguson's Cove here; the 1889 CP applies 'Fergusons Cove' to Iverson Landing; names migrated, flag when mapping. Coordinate source: GNIS 225024 Havens Anchorage (38.800744,-123.5858452)

name: Collin's Landing (St. Ores)
summary: Exposed landing two-thirds of a mile NW of Bourns Landing. The 1889 Coast Pilot: a chute from the 80-ft cliff to an offshore rock, continued by a 300-yard wire cable ('trapeze chute') to an outer rock; the vessel beneath lay in 20 ft of water on five mooring lines. Used only in summer, ~25 cargoes a year; the lumber mill had been abandoned by 1889 but wood, posts and tanbark were still shipped.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Collins Landing | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Sparse: known almost solely from the 1889 Coast Pilot. Coordinate source: GNIS 232234 Saint Orres Creek (prim/mouth 38.7924107,-123.5641777)

name: Bourn's Landing (Bowens Landing, Bourne's)
summary: Chief shipping point for the Gualala mill, 1.5 mi NW of the river. Franchise for wharf and chutes granted to Morton Bourn 22 February 1870; the Gualala Mill Co. added its own chute in 1872 (washed away 1878 by a southeaster, rebuilt 1879). The 1889 Coast Pilot describes a 200-ft northern chute reaching 24-ft water (lumber only), a southern chute (wood, bark, ties, posts, stave-bolts), a small cove inside with two small landing-wharves and a wharf served by a railroad branch, plus a new 'trapeze' wire-rope chute; ~140 cargoes shipped yearly, six 250-ton vessels at moorings in summer. Still listed as a working landing in the 1911 Coast & Geodetic Survey.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Bowen's Landing | Palmer 1880, Landings and Chutes between Gualala and Point Arena | MCMRHS, 'Bourns Landing' (quotes C&GS 1911) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: 1889 Coast Pilot calls it Bowen's Landing; local usage Bourn(s). Coordinates approximate from Coast Pilot bearings. Coordinate source: Wikipedia 'Bowens Landing, California' coordinate 38.785,-123.562 (this is Wikipedia's coordinate); corroborated by GNIS 254655 Bourns Gulch (38.7838036,-123.5560707), GNIS 254656 Bourns Rock (38.7788001,-123.5572329), and Davidson 1889:264-265 station 'on the southwestern extremity of the point' 38-46-52 N

name: Gualala Landing (Walalla, Robinson's)
summary: The Cole brothers built the first (apron) chute in 1865; C.D. Robinson bought it in 1866 and rebuilt it in 1875 as a cable chute with a donkey engine to haul the car back (Palmer 1880). The Gualala Mill Co. (Rutherford & Webber, spring 1862; later Harmon, Dingley & the Heywoods) sawed at the river mouth until the mill burned in 1906; from the 1870s its lumber went by rail two miles north to Bourns Landing rather than over the exposed Gualala bluff chutes, which the 1889 Coast Pilot describes as two wire cable-chutes under the north bluff 'abandoned in 1884' (though the 1917 Coast Pilot again notes a wire chute). The mill company owned three schooners and ~12,000 acres of timber.
sources: Lyman L. Palmer, History of Mendocino County (Alley, Bowen & Co., 1880), Gualala/Arena Twp. mills & chutes | [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Walalla River | Wikipedia, 'Gualala River Railroad' (fire 14 Sep 1906; RR idle 1907-11) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Palmer's 5'8" gauge figure is explicit and repeated by MCMRHS. Wrecks: Skylark (1876), Three Sisters (1880). Milano Hotel NRHP #78000720 (burned 2001). Coordinate source: GNIS 253221 Gualala River (prim/mouth 38.7685224,-123.5338987); derived-from-verbal (landing on the bluff just N of the mouth)

name: Joe Tongue's Landing (Joe Tonga's)
summary: What the MPDF describes as 'a modified wire chute with a steam powered swinging boom', built in the 1880s by farmer Joe Tongue of Gualala on leased Rutherford ranch land (Sea Ranch area); shipped grain and fruit. Candidate site: the end of Fish Rock Road behind Rutherford's barn. The farm-cargo edge case of the chute system.
sources: Clark 2016; Clark 2009:17, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal AREA anchor: GNIS 224702 Gualala Point (38.7524119,-123.5266762), which lies ~1 mile S of the Gualala River mouth - matching the MPDF/Clark-Lindstrom statement 'one mile south of Gualala River'

name: Del Mar Landing
summary: Charles Meyer and William Benitz opened a landing for produce and grain at a little cove here in 1849 (lost with the rancho, 1855). The lumber-era port dates from 1898, when the Bender brothers, William and George, put up a mill just south and rigged a wire chute, adding saloon, store and lumber warehouse by 1903; the mill burned in 1910, and the wire chute probably went out of service within a few years (the 1917 Coast Pilot still notes a wire cable; the 1929 T-sheet shows none). Tanbark and split stakes were among products shipped; the topography gave loading vessels no protection.
sources: NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Del Mar Landing' | [P] US Coast Pilot 1917 and USC&GS 1929 T-sheet, as cited by NOAA | Susan M. Clark, The Del Mar Ranch (SSU thesis 1990) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Research design gives mill burning 'between 1903 and 1910'; NOAA public page says 1910. Steam schooner Klamath lost nearby 1921. On Sea Ranch land, coastal trail posts 58-59. Coordinate source: GNIS 222223 Del Mar Point (38.7410231,-123.5113979)

name: Bihler Landing (Black Point)
summary: On the former German Rancho (Ernest Rufus grant, 1846), William Bihler ranched from the 1850s and turned to lumbering in the 1860s-70s; Bihler and D.L.B. Ross had a landing and slide chute working by 1875, with a second chute following in 1876 (only the outer, reaching 23-ft water, was used; six mooring lines, three buoys). Ranch produce went out with railroad ties, staves, posts, firewood and tanbark; a summer-only landing averaging five small schooners a month (1889 Coast Pilot). A wire chute replaced the slide chutes around 1900; the Benders bought in 1904 and the port operated until 1917. The adjacent Black Point community counted more than twelve buildings, among them a hotel, a store, the post office, blacksmith and wagon shops, and a livery.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Bihler Point Landing | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Bihler Landing' | Susan M. Clark, 'The Del Mar Ranch...' (SSU thesis, 1990) and TSRA history · cited in NOAA bibliography | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: 1879 T-sheet shows the two slide chutes. Wreck: schooner Ruth (1903). On Sea Ranch land today, accessible via CA Coastal Trail (marker 1-25). Coordinate source: GNIS 219397 Black Point, Sonoma Co. (38.6790792,-123.4319533)

name: Stewarts Point Landing (Fisherman's Bay)
summary: The Fisk brothers, John and Andrew, opened the first landing here in 1867; by 1877 three trough chutes served nearby mills, though by 1885 only the middle chute was operable (to 11 ft of water, seven mooring lines; vessels to 125 tons; ~25 schooners/yr with wood, posts, tanbark, shingles). H.A. Richardson acquired the point in 1881 and added a chute of his own, and the family shipped for ~40 years; a wire chute by the 1917 Coast Pilot, rail lines, steam- and horse-powered, running out to the bluff edge, and a family fleet of sailing schooners and steam schooners; until trucking took over the freight in 1925. The settlement reached ~30 buildings and survives with its doghole-era fabric largely intact (Sonoma County Historic District).
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Stewarts Point Landing/Fishermans Bay | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Stewarts Point' | [P] US Coast Pilot 1917 (wire chute), as cited in Marx & Lawrence 2016 Research Design | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: 2016 team interviewed Harold Richardson (1919-2016). Many wrecks recorded at Fisherman's Bay (research design table, 1861-1913). Coordinate source: GNIS 235471 Stewarts Point cape (38.6546349,-123.4080645)

name: Fisk Mill Landing
summary: John C. Fisk began lumbering and milling here in 1860; Frederick M. Helmke acquired the operation in 1865 and shut the mill down in 1876, but the Kruse family kept the chute in service, handling cargo sent down from other operations such as Platt's mill 1.75 miles up the coast (at Horseshoe/Timber Gulch). The 1889 Coast Pilot: chute on the south point of the west side, vessel broadside in 14 ft with six mooring lines, four buoys; vessels to 100 tons; about 40 schooners loaded yearly with lumber, wood, bark and posts; 'quite a village' half a mile inside the point. A rare wood-and-iron capstan survives on the bluff.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Fisk Mill Cove | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Fisk Mill Cove' | Marx & Lawrence 2016 Research Design, Fisk Mill data sheet (incl. Porter 1985) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Wrecks: Archie and Fontie (1902), Carolita (1876), Grace B. Richardson (1888). Fisk cemetery (SPSP-85-3) nearby; Porter 1985 survey recorded chute remains. Coordinate source: GNIS 223554 Fisk Mill Cove (38.5968574,-123.3533421)

name: Salt Point Landing (Gerstle Cove)
summary: Joshua Hendy and Samuel Duncan brought the township's first steam sawmill here in 1853 (Hendy sold to Alex Duncan 1855; Duncan Bros. to 1860, ~30 million ft cut); the Duncans also quarried marine-terrace sandstone shipped to San Francisco and Mare Island. Before the 1870s cargo was lowered to ships on cables anchored to the cliffs; William R. Miller built a chute in 1872 and Funcke & Wasserman a second (public landing, 1876); by 1889 only the rebuilt inner chute remained (out to 13 ft of water, six mooring lines, two 80-ton vessels able to lie in the cove), abandoned by 1917. A horse-drawn wooden-rail tramway connected Miller's sawmill to the chute; Pritchard's 1969 survey found its remnant and a sandstone-lined cliff cut. On the 'earliest railroad' claim: sources located document the horse tramway but none support calling it one of California's first railroads; treat that claim as unverified.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Gerstles Cove or Salt Point Landing | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Gerstle Cove' | Marx & Lawrence 2016 Research Design, Gerstle Cove data sheet (incl. Pritchard 1969) | Salt Point State Park history (saltpoint.org): Duncan mill 1853-60, quarry stone to SF/Mare Island | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Norlina wreck (1926) off Horseshoe Point/Gerstle. Salt Point SP Archaeological District NRHP #71000207. Trinomials 4-SonS51/52 (mill+quarters up Miller Creek). Coordinate source: GNIS 224133 Gerstle Cove (38.563802,-123.3272309); GNIS 232328 Salt Point cape (38.5663021,-123.3327865) The 1853 Hendy-Duncan mill predates the doghole landing; the MPDF's canonical span is 1870-1917 (Funcke & Gerstle era).

name: Walsh Landing (Ocean Cove)
summary: Small bluff landing at Ocean Cove between Stillwater Cove and Salt Point; named for W.J. Walsh, who purchased the property 14 October 1889. The Ocean Cove local history states: 'Timber was harvested in the surrounding area, then loaded from the bluffs onto "Dog Hole" schooners, and sent to San Francisco'. A 1910 shipping-agents' table of ports of call pairs 'Salt Point Landing/Walsh's Landing.' Not among the doghole ports surveyed in the 2016 NOAA/CSP Sonoma project.
sources: 'History of Ocean Cove,' Ocean Cove Campground & Store (Walsh purchase 10/14/1889; bluff loading) | MCMRHS 'Shipping' page, 1910 ports-of-call table ('Salt Point Landing/Walsh's Landing') | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Thinnest-sourced Sonoma entry: rests on a local business-history page and the 1910 port list reproduced by the Mendocino Coast Model RR & Historical Society. Needs county-history/CDNC verification. Coordinate source: GNIS 229921 Ocean Cove (38.5551908,-123.3044528)

name: Stockhoff Cove Landing
summary: Landing or anchorage (possibly a wire chute) at Stockhoff Cove, now Stillwater Cove Regional Park. The Stockhoff homestead (late 1860s) lived by lumbering, ranching, and farming; potatoes and produce loaded here or at neighboring chutes.
sources: Rudy 2009:55; Rudy 2015:40, via the MPDF | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Coordinate source: GNIS 235498 Stockhoff Creek (prim 38.5468574,-123.2975084)

name: Stillwater Cove Landing
summary: Very small but sheltered cove usable year-round. Christian Friedrich Ruoff settled by fall 1851; after his 1854 death his widow Francesca took over the property and had a lumber chute working before the end of the 1860s ('owned by Mrs. Ruoff in 1880'). The single chute on the NW side ran from the cliff past the outer rocks into 11 ft of water; vessels lay broadside with six mooring lines (1889 Coast Pilot); 249 wood loads shipped 1868-74. No town ever formed; no photos or drawings of the chute have been found, but rebates, ring bolts, pins and wire rope survive.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Stillwater Cove | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Stillwater Cove' | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: An 1880 township history is NOAA's source for the Ruoff story (likely Munro-Fraser's History of Sonoma County, 1880; not directly consulted). Coordinate source: GNIS 1654970 Stillwater Cove (38.5458333,-123.2986111)

name: Timber Cove Landing
summary: Settlement from c.1856 with hotel, store and post office supporting a trough chute 'built sometime that decade,' 'the first such apparatus in the area' (NOAA). In 1861 George Weber and D.L.B. Ross started a sawmill on a ridge 1.5 mi inland; it ran only three years; William R. Miller's sawmill ran from 1867 and had largely stripped the nearby hills by the 1870s. 481 schooner cargoes were transhipped 1868-74; the 1889 Coast Pilot shows the single trough chute (out to 16 ft of water, 5 mooring lines, 2 buoys) loading cordwood, posts, ties, tanbark and produce. Ernest Saltzig installed a wire chute in 1921 (transplanted from Fort Ross); lumber shipping ended by 1925.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Timber Cove | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Timber Cove' | Marx & Lawrence 2016 Research Design, Timber Cove data sheet | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Windermere (iron bark, 1883) lost at Windermere Point just south; Acme (1889) at Kolmer Gulch. Cargo counts 1868-74 from NOAA ('historians documented'). Coordinate source: GNIS 236354 Timber Cove (38.5296352,-123.2711192) Active-from c.1856 per NOAA settlement history; the MPDF's canonical span opens 1860 (chute built by Benitz in the 1860s).

name: Fort Ross Landing
summary: Russian-era prehistory in one line: the Russians maintained a small wharf and shipyard here, where shipwright Vasily Grudinin built vessels here at what California State Parks calls the first shipbuilding yard in California; brigs Rumiantsev (1818), Buldakov (1820), Volga (1822), Kiakhta (1824). American era: James W. Dixon built a 180-ft trough chute with 100-ft swing apron on the north bank in 1867 (used to c.1900); William Benitz had built a stone wharf pre-1870s, expanded by George W. Call in the 1870s with warehouse and derrick (destroyed 1901 when the schooner J. Eppinger wrecked into it); a wire chute operated c.1901-1920/21, rebuilt 1910, then dismantled and its machinery moved to Timber Cove. Vessels loaded lumber, cordwood, tanbark, stone, hides, produce and passengers; a railway was cut into the cliff's northern rim from blufftop to wharf.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Fort Ross Anchorage | Marx & Lawrence 2016 Research Design, Fort Ross data sheet | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Fort Ross Cove' | Fort Ross Conservancy, 'Shipbuilding' (first ships built in California, 1818-1824) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Pomona (1908, NRHP #07000306) lies in the cove. Site trinomial CA-SON-1454/H. Ship years per fortross.org history pages (some sources give build spans 1816-18 etc.). Coordinate source: GNIS 223704 Fort Ross Cove (38.5121351,-123.2472299)

name: Russian Gulch Landing (Sonoma)
summary: Landing at the only sand-beach gulch north of the Russian River; vessels entered a 100-yard rock passage to load at a short, very steep chute built from the southeast point (1889 Coast Pilot; 11 ft at the chute end, 3 mooring buoys (Davidson 1889)). It received Rule's Landing's business in 1884 and was supplied by steam railroad from the Russian River mills; after 1900 the Western Redwood Lumber Company operated a wire chute and storage yard here (c.1904 photo). Archaeology (2016) found railroad ties, roadbeds and buried wire cable.
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Russian Gulch Landing | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Russian Gulch' | Marx & Lawrence 2016 Research Design, Russian Gulch data sheet | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: End of operations not pinned; Jenner Headlands IRMP (Sonoma Land Trust 2012) is the survey's cited local source. Wrecks nearby: D.C. Haskins 1885, Maggie Ross 1892, Joseph S. Spinney 1892, Whitelaw 1893. Coordinate source: GNIS 1723332 Russian Gulch Creek (prim/mouth 38.4668583,-123.1566714); GNIS 232048 Russian Gulch valley (38.4667517,-123.1569255)

name: Rule's Landing (Rules Head)
summary: Wire-chute-only landing under Rule's Head, 1.5 mi NW of the Russian River mouth, on the Rule family ranch (John and Elizabeth Rule, land bought 1870). The 1889 Coast Pilot: 'located in 1877, but has since been abandoned'; a wire cable ran 150 yards from the bluff to a rock, vessels mooring beneath; the owners dismantled the cable in 1884 and shifted the trade to Russian Gulch Landing. Douglass (1995) recorded railroad ties, a possible turntable, and frayed wire cable; the cove was the Russians' 'harbor sheltered for baidarkas.'
sources: [P] Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot, Rules Landing entry (wire cable, abandoned 1884) | Robert G. Douglass, Rule's Landing: A Lumber Shipping Focus on the Sonoma Coast (CDPR report, 1995) | NOAA GFNMS 'Doghole Port: Rule's Landing' | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: No historical photos of the chute located; no shipwrecks reported. Coordinates are my estimate of Rule's Head from the Coast Pilot description. Coordinate source: Derived-from-verbal: Davidson 1889:255 'It lies one and [a half] miles northwest from the mouth of Russian River, under a high head... which we have named Rules Head'; along-coast interpolation between GNIS 267200 Russian River mouth (38.4504698,-123.1294482) and GNIS 1723332 Russian Gulch Creek mouth

name: Duncan's Landing
summary: Doghole cove on Duncan's Point used to tranship lumber from the Duncan brothers' mill on the lower Russian River (the river itself being unnavigable to lumber vessels). The 1876 USC&GS T-sheet shows two trough chutes projecting into the cove with four moorings; by 1889 the railroad to Duncans Mills had eliminated water shipment. 2016 NOAA/CSP survey recorded eye bolts, chain, pins and traces of the headland railway; divers found no anchors.
sources: Marx & Lawrence, Sonoma Coast Doghole Port Project Research Design (NOAA ONMS, 2016), Duncan's Landing data sheet | Deborah Marx, 'Doghole Port: Duncan's Landing' (NOAA GFNMS) | [P] USC&GS T-sheet 1876 (two chutes, moorings) | Marx & Jaffke, Northern California Doghole Ports Maritime Cultural Landscape, NRHP MPDF draft (CA DPR, 2021)
notes: Research design says the Duncans 'established lumber mill in early 1877' at Duncans Mills; start date of the landing itself is not pinned in sources located. Wrecks: Emma Adelia (1872), Sovereign (1873). Coordinate source: GNIS 222718 Duncans Point (38.3929711,-123.0947251); Wikipedia 'Duncans Landing' (redirects to Duncans Point) 38.393,-123.0947 - same point (Wikipedia's coordinate) The Duncans' mill dates from 1860; the MPDF's canonical LANDING span opens with the 1876 T-sheet chutes.

name: Shelter Cove
date_display: c.1860s lightering; pier 1885-1930s (maintenance abandoned in the 1930s)
summary: The only semi-sheltered roadstead on the Lost Coast (Davidson 1889 describes it as the standard summer refuge). A 960-ft pier of 1885 served the southern Humboldt backcountry - tanbark, wool, hides, butter out; supplies in - by mule train and later wagon road. Its timber-products traffic was captured by Bear Harbor and Needle Rock in the 1890s, and the pier decayed until maintenance was abandoned in the 1930s; salmon fishing then rum-running sustained the place.
sources: Martha Roscoe, 'Shelter Cove,' Humboldt County Historical Society history nugget, 20 Apr 2023 | [P] Davidson, Pacific Coast Pilot (1889), pp. 300-301 (Point Delgada and Shelter Cove) - read directly | Bear Harbor NR nomination (Shelter Cove as prior outlet, its 1890s decline) | Resort Improvement District No. 1, 'About' (pier built to ship lumber, wool, hides, butter; commercial fishing from 1900s)
notes: Pier length/date from HCHS (no footnotes given). Lumber as an export is NOT documented in sources seen - Shelter Cove belongs on the map as a tanbark/ranch-produce doghole, not a lumber port proper. Coordinate source: Davidson 1889 Coast Pilot (on-disk fulltext): C&GS secondary astronomical station 40°01'13.7"N, 124°04'04.3"W on the cliff overlooking the harbor; GNIS 232947 Shelter Cove (bay) 40.02431,-124.06364 corroborates Audit: lumber export is not documented for the pier; wool, produce, and tanbark are the attested cargoes.

name: Mattole Wharf (Sea Lion Rock)

Storm-wrecked by February 1914; the trade died with the tanbark. Before 1908 the valley's bark went out by mule and wagon via Shelter Cove.

name: Eureka (Humboldt Bay)
date_display: 1850-1940s+ (first sawmill and first lumber cargo 1850; first redwood cargo 1855; timber port for over a century)
summary: California's redwood metropolis: nine mills on the bay by 1854, the first redwood cargo 1855, and by 1889 'the great lumber center of this region' with enormous shipping, direct foreign trade, and eight feeder railroads (Davidson). Its notorious shifting bar bred the earliest tug-assisted bar-crossing system on the coast (c.1852) and, from 1889-91, federal jetties. John Dolbeer's donkey engine (Eureka, Aug 1881) mechanized West Coast logging from here. The NWP's completion (23 Oct 1914) turned the lumber flow from sea to rail, though steam schooners persisted into the 1920s-30s.

name: Samoa
date_display: 1892/1894-1940s+ (Vance mill's first lumber 1894; Hammond era 1900-1956; Georgia-Pacific 1956, Louisiana-Pacific after 1972-73)

Logging lines reached Big Lagoon until fire destroyed the trestles in 1945.

name: Trinidad
date_display: 1850-c.1920s (gold-rush supply port 1850-50s; lumber wharf by 1869; mill-company port through the 1880s-90s; Hammond owned the waterfront until 1944; whaling pier in the early 20th c.)

The pier passed through Hammond hands until 1944 and hosted early-20th-century whaling.

name: Crescent City
date_display: 1853-1939 as a lumber port (town 1853; first lumber wharf/cargo 1869-70; Hobbs Wall shutdown 22 Feb 1939); harbor breakwater era 1920s+; post-1945 truck-logging revival shipped by other means
summary: Del Norte's only real port: a rock-strewn open roadstead that Davidson called the most dangerous regularly used on the coast, yet from the 1869 community mill venture and the 1871 arrival of Hobbs, Pomeroy (later Hobbs, Wall & Co.) it shipped spruce and redwood lumber and millions of boxes to San Francisco for seven decades. Hobbs Wall's mills, 12-mile Crescent City & Smith River RR (1890-94), wharf-spur locomotives (1903), and company steamers Del Norte, Mandalay, and Westport made it a company county until the sudden shutdown of February 1939.

name: Santa Cruz wharves
date_display: 1849-1931 (first chute/wharf 1849; SP removed tracks from the Municipal Wharf 1931)
summary: Santa Cruz's wharves shipped redwood, lime, and powder from 1849, climaxing with the 1875-76 Railroad Wharf built to put San Lorenzo Valley flume-and-rail lumber straight onto steamers. The South Pacific Coast narrow gauge (May 1880) then made rail to San Francisco cheaper than sea; coastal lumber shipping withered within a decade, and the county's biggest later mills (Loma Prieta, San Vicente) were rail-only operations. Sea-borne lumber here effectively ends a generation before it does on the North Coast.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Sheltered bay anchorage and village port, listed by NOAA among the regional doghole ports though it functioned mainly as a produce/potato and general-cargo port rather than a chute port. name: Usal
summary: In 1880 Palmer found only two or three buildings and a telegraph line; the industrial town came in 1889, when a mill, wharf and company town were built at the Usal Creek mouth with a railroad running about three miles up the creek; the Usal Redwood Co. built the mill, town, and 1,600-ft wharf in 1889; Robert Dollar took the operation over and started the mill up in 1893 per his own memoirs (some accounts say 1894), running it about six years (his steamer Newsboy served the port); flag this discrepancy. The mill was destroyed by fire in 1902 (with schoolhouse, warehouse and the county bridge), the railroad was dismantled (its Shay No. 1 sold to Glen Blair in 1903), and the surviving hotel burned in 1969. Palmer's 'Northport,' 16 miles north of Cottoneva with a steam-powered cable-and-cage instead of a chute (Funk & Co., resident partner Walter Fisk), lay in this vicinity; its precise relation to Usal is unresolved.

name: Reed's Sawmill (Rancho Corte Madera del Presidio) · the Mexican-period prelude
summary: The first sawmill in Marin County: John Thomas Reed (Juan Read), grantee of Rancho Corte Madera del Presidio (Figueroa, 2 Oct 1834), built a water-powered sash-saw mill in the ravine of Cascade Creek. Its construction date is genuinely disputed: the landmark tradition (CHL No. 207) says about 1833-34, while Munro-Fraser's detailed 1880 account says Reed 'erected his saw-mill in 1843, and had but just got it in operation when he died'; cutting lumber for his own adobe. The rancho's name ('cut wood for the Presidio') records the older pre-grant woodcutting trade that supplied timbers to the Presidio and Yerba Buena, not the mill's output. No Mexican-period landing or embarcadero for the mill is attested; the documented rafting of Richardson Bay timber is American-period (1849 on). The structure standing in Old Mill Park today is a 1991 reconstruction.

name: Battle at San Diego Mission
summary: First armed clash in Alta California. The Spanish camp at Cosoy was attacked. One Spaniard was killed, the muleteer Jose Maria Vegerano, aged twenty; Padre Vizcaino, the blacksmith, a soldier and a Baja California Indian were wounded, the blacksmith fighting without a cuera. Three natives were killed.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (1542–1800) (San Francisco: History Company, 1886), 137–39 · the attack of 15 August 1769 on the camp/mission at Cosoy. | San Diego, Libro de Misión, MS., 65 (mission register; Bancroft's manuscript authority for the identity of the man killed). | Francisco Palóu, Relación histórica de la vida... de Junípero Serra (Mexico, 1787), 84 · reports earlier assaults, 12–13 Aug. 1769. | NO Archives of California record attests this engagement. [null result, recorded deliberately]
notes: Bancroft I, 138 and n. 28 identifies the man killed from Serra's San Diego mission book as 'a Spanish arriero 20 years old named Jose Maria Vegerano'; the blacksmith was among the wounded, not the dead. Earlier versions of this entry named a blacksmith 'Jose Manuel Robles', a person the sources do not support.

name: Destruction of San Diego Mission
summary: 800–1,000 attackers from 9+ rancherías; dual-axis plan (mission + presidio). Defenders: Cpl. Rocha + 3 soldiers, 2 friars, 3 artisans = 11 men. Padre Jayme martyred (18 arrow wounds). Blacksmith Arroyo killed. Carpenter Urselino died of wounds. Cpl. Rocha fired muskets all night from adobe enclosure.
result: INDIGENOUS TACTICAL VICTORY; first successful mission destruction
sources: Tte. José Francisco de Ortega to Tte.-Col. Juan Bautista de Anza, San Diego, 30 Nov. 1775, 'Expediente de investigación' on the burning of Mission San Diego and the death of Fr. Luis Jayme (certified copy by Capt. Fernando de Rivera y Moncada) · Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.1–7 / Savage pp.2–9, scan n2–n8, Doc 1. | Comandante Fernando de Rivera y Moncada and Sgt. Mariano Carrillo, expediente on an Indian conspiracy which uncovered the confessions to the Nov. 1775 revolt, San Diego, 10 Aug.–4 Sept. 1776 · Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 1), tomo i. 221–232 / Savage pp.526–539, scan n223–n234, Doc 100. | Capt. Fernando de Rivera y Moncada, interrogation of the imprisoned leaders of the San Diego revolt, San Diego, 31 May–18 June 1776 · Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.327–343 / Savage pp.24–25, scan n23–n24, Doc 28. | Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, interrogation of 'el indio Carlos', capitán of the mission ranchería and principal ringleader of the 5 Nov. 1775 revolt, declarations of 11, 13 and 15 Apr. 1776 · Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. pp.294–327 / Savage p.24, scan n23, Doc 27. | Fr. Vicente Fuster, Registro de Defunciones / San Diego, Libro de Misión, MS., 74–75 (eyewitness burial entries for Fr. Luis Jayme, the mason Arroyo and the carpenter Urselino). | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:249–54 ('Destruction of San Diego').
notes: Date/casualty checks against the manuscript: ca15-d1 gives the attack as the night of 5 Nov. 1775 (the map's 5 November is right; the catalog headline reads '4–5 Nov'). DISCREPANCY ON THE TRADES: the map says 'Blacksmith Arroyo killed. Carpenter Urselino died of wounds.' Ortega's informe as catalogued calls Manuel Arroyo a MASON (albañil) killed and Felipe Romero a mason wounded, while Bancroft I:250 calls Arroyo and Romero both BLACKSMITHS sleeping in the smithy. Both agree Urselino was the carpenter and died of his wounds (buried 10 Nov). I am not reconciling this; flagging it. Also: the manuscript names the wounded escort as cabo Rocha[?], Alejo Antonio Gonzáles, Juan Álvarez and Joaquín Armenta, which supports the map's 'Cpl. Rocha'. The map's '13+ rancherías' figure belongs properly to feature reg-63, which is the same leaf.

name: Carrillo's Punishment at Alocuachomi
summary: Punitive raid near San Juan Capistrano. 3 natives killed.
sources: Cabo [Guillermo] Carrillo to Sgt. Francisco de Aguiar, report of the punitive expedition to the ranchería de Alocuachomi, 20 June 1777 · State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), Savage pp.49–51 (stamp 276), scan n275, Doc 327. | Auto of Sgt. Francisco de Aguiar ordering the attack, Misión y escolta de San Juan Capistrano, 19 June 1777 · State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), Savage pp.47–49 (stamp 274), scan n273, Doc 326. | Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, sumaria taken by Sgt. Francisco de Aguiar on the disorders in the San Juan Capistrano and San Gabriel escorts, 11 July 1777 (sumaria opened 26 May) · State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), scan n257–n264, Doc 318. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:314 · 'in June 1777 the Alocuachomi rancheria threatened the neophytes of San Juan Capistrano, and Corporal Guillermo Carrillo was sent with five men to chastise the offenders, which he did by killing three and wounding several.'
notes: The manuscript refines the map on two points. (1) COMMANDER: the officer who led the raid was Cabo GUILLERMO Carrillo, not Sgt. Mariano Carrillo; the catalog marks the authorship of ca55-d327 as inferred, but Bancroft I:314 independently names 'Corporal Guillermo Carrillo... sent with five men', and ca55-d326 records Sgt. Aguiar ordering 'Cabo Guillermo Carrillo + 5 soldiers to attack the rancheria'; three-way agreement. Consider retitling the feature 'Guillermo Carrillo's punishment at Alocuachomi'. (2) CASUALTIES: the map's '3 natives killed' is defensible but soft; the report says 'tumbamos unos tres, dos quedaron en el sitio y el otro cayó en el agua dentro del tule' (about three brought down; two dead on the spot, the third fell into the water in the tules), plus two more who fled badly wounded and two taken prisoner, one of whom got 25 lashes. Bancroft rounds this to 'killing three and wounding several'. (3) The ranchería is spelled Alocuachomi in the raid report (ca55-d327) but Alamachomi in the order of the previous day (ca55-d326); same place, Savage's reading varies. Exact date of the raid: 20 June 1777.

name: Ambush at San Juan (Briones killed)
summary: Midnight ambush near San Diego. Corporal Briones killed.
sources: Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, diligencias on the death of Cabo Garci [Brito] Murillo, with inventory of his goods, relaying Sgt. Carrillo's report of the assault on the despatch party, San Diego, 17 Aug. 1777 · State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), orig. tomo vii, pp.~166–199 / Savage pp.199–200, scan n198–n199, Doc 231. | Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, instructions to Sgt. Mariano Carrillo for a punitive campaign against the gentiles who killed Cabo Briones; Carrillo's operations report rendered 9 Oct. 1777 · State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), orig. tomo vii, pp.200–216 / Savage p.201, scan n200, Doc 233. | Gov. Felipe de Neve to the Comandante General, 15 Apr. 1778 · Provincial Records (C-A 22), orig. pp.184–185 / Savage p.97, scan n97, Doc 124. | Gov. Felipe de Neve to the Comandante General, 16 Oct. 1778 · Provincial Records (C-A 22), orig. pp.192–193 / Savage p.98, scan n98, Doc 127. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:315 · 'on August 13th four soldiers bearing despatches from General Croix to Neve were surprised at midnight, at a place called San Juan just above San Diego... who killed the corporal in command, Antonio Briones.'
notes: THE MAP'S PLACE IS RIGHT BUT AMBIGUOUS AND THE CATALOG IS PROBABLY WRONG ABOUT IT. Bancroft I:315 puts the ambush 'at a place called San Juan just above San Diego', and ca22-d127 names it precisely: the rancherías of the ARROYO DE SAN JUAN BAUTISTA. The catalog summary of ca55-d233 glosses it as 'the gentiles of San Juan [Capistrano]'; that bracketed expansion looks like an editorial error, since San Juan Capistrano is ~60 miles north of San Diego and the party was returning FROM San Diego. Recommend the map say 'Arroyo de San Juan Bautista, above San Diego' and not San Juan Capistrano. SECOND FLAG; A DATE CONTRADICTION INSIDE THE ARCHIVE: ca55-d231 is dated 17 Aug. 1777 yet its Savage abstract says the assault happened 'on ~13 Oct'; that is internally impossible (a 17 August document cannot report a 13 October event). ca22-d124 (Neve, 15 Apr. 1778) and Bancroft both give 13 AUGUST 1777, which the 17 August dateline supports. I read this as a Savage or cataloguing slip for '13 Ago'. Do not silently correct in the catalog without a leaf check. THIRD: the corporal's full name is José Antonio Briones (Bancroft gives 'Antonio Briones'); the two wounded soldiers were Felipe Santiago Tapia and Joaquín Díaz, and the caballada was driven off.
