name: Attack at La Cieneguilla (Rivera's march)
summary: From the hoja de servicios of Sargento Mariano de la Luz Verdugo: in 1769 he was one of the party that, by order of Capt. Fernando de Rivera y Moncada, "sostuvieron el ataque que hicieron los gentiles en el parage de la Cieneguilla en que se mataron 8"; the gentiles attacked and the party withstood it, with eight of the attackers killed. Verdugo's earlier 1781 service sheet describes the same action.
sources: Hoja de servicios of Sargento Mariano de la Luz Verdugo, aged 42, Monterey, 31 Dec. 1786 · Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. p.335 / Savage pp.195–96, scan n200–n201, Doc 272. | Hoja de servicios of Sargento Mariano de la Luz Verdugo, 31 Dec. 1781 (signed Diego Gonzáles) · Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 15), orig. p.57 / Savage p.66, scan n67, Doc 82.
notes: ⚠ LOCATION UNRESOLVED; the pin is a placeholder, not evidence. Corrected 2026-09-01 from the manuscript leaves themselves (C-A 15 scan n200 = Savage 195, and the parallel 1781 sheet at scan n68): the copy reads sostuvieron (not "estuvieron"), la Cieneguilla (not "La Ciénega"), and 8 killed (not 3); the numeral is an unambiguous figure-8 at full resolution. The verb reverses the sense: the gentiles attacked and Rivera's party withstood it. On place: this is a 1769 action on Rivera y Moncada's march, and Portolá's diary (Bancroft I:135 n.16) records camping "en la cieneguilla, cuio nombre puso el padre jesuita Lino" on 27 May 1769 while following Rivera's route north from Velicatá; a paraje named by a Jesuit lies in BAJA CALIFORNIA, since the Jesuits never worked in Alta California. Nothing found places this fight in Alta California, so the existing coordinate is retained only as a placeholder and is marked conjectural. The pin should probably move to the Velicatá–San Diego road or the feature be reconsidered; that is Aodhan's call, so no coordinate has been invented. The permalink id (reg-65-battle-at-la-cienega) is deliberately unchanged.

name: Toypurina's Revolt at San Gabriel
summary: MAJOR CONSPIRACY. Toypurina; female war leader of the Tongva (Gabrieleño); organized multi-village uprising against Mission San Gabriel with neophyte alcalde Nicolás José. Plan to kill padres and soldiers. Betrayed by informant before attack could succeed. Toypurina and co-conspirators arrested. She was exiled to Mission San Carlos Borromeo. One of the most important indigenous military actors in California history.
result: Conspiracy foiled; Toypurina arrested and exiled
sources: Gov. Pedro Fages to the Comandante General, San Gabriel, 30 Dec. 1785 (4 docs), with the continuation of 5 Jan. 1786 · Provincial Records (C-A 22), tomo ii, ff.131–133 (orig. pp.521–526, the San Gabriel entries at orig. pp.528–531) / Savage pp.348–351, scan n349–n351, Doc 2042. | Gov. Pedro Fages to the Comandante General, Santa Bárbara / Monterey, 1786, on Sgt. Ignacio Olivera having punished two San Gabriel rebels without authority · Provincial Records (C-A 22), tomo ii, orig. pp.540–544 / Savage pp.352–355, scan n352–n355, Doc 2043. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, I:460 and n.21 · 'In October 1785 the neophytes and gentiles were tempted by a woman, so at least said the men, into a plan to attack the mission and kill the friars... Two years later came General Ugarte's order condemning one native, Nicolás, to six years of work at the presidio followed by exile to a distant mission. The woman was sent into perpetual exile.' | Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535–1846, 247–49. | Comandante General Jacobo Ugarte y Loyola to Gov. notes: MAJOR RESULT: this feature had no manuscript link at all, and there IS one. I fetched C-A 22 leaf n350 (Savage stamp 349, tomo folio 132) and read Savage's abstract of Fages's letter to the Comandante General from San Gabriel, 30 Dec. 1785: 'Que halló aquí presos á 7 Indios cristos. y 4 gentiles INCLUSA LA AUTORA DEL MOTÍN, y dos capitancillos gentiles ademas, á cuyos cabecillas se forma la corresp.te sumaria, sentenciando á los restantes á la pena de 15 á 20 azotes.' 'La autora del motín'; the female author of the rising; is Toypurina, named here only by her role. Immediately below, the entry of 5 Jan. 1786: 'Pasa las diligs. practicadas contra los cuatro Indios cabecillas del motín (de S. Gabl.) y que quedan castigados los 17 cómplices.' So the C-A record gives eleven prisoners held at San Gabriel (7 Christians, 4 gentiles), four ringleaders tried, 17 accomplices punished. NOTE THE ARITHMETIC TENSION with Bancroft I:460, who says the corporal 'captured some twenty of the conspirators'; 11 held at San Gabriel is not 20; the counts may cover different moments. Flagging, not reconciling. TWO FURTHER CHECKS I RAN AND REPORT NEGATIVE: (a) ca22-d2034 (Fages, 'Reflections on the Gabrieleño Indians' plan to kill padres & soldiers') looked like a candidate but is dated 10 Feb. 1784; I pulled leaf n315 and the surrounding entries are all January–February 1784, so it PREDATES Toypurina by twenty months and I have not linked it. It may record a separate, earlier Gabrieleño conspiracy worth its own investigation. (b) I searched C-A 4 and C-A 23 for Ugarte's Dec. 1787 sentence (Nicolás José to six years' presidio labour and exile, Toypurina to perpetual exile) and found nothing; Bancroft cites it to Arch. Sta. Bárbara, MS., vi. 110-17, which is not a C-A document. The exile to Mission San Carlos Borromeo asserted in the map summary is not attested in anything I read here.

name: Indian Killed at Monterey Presidio
summary: Indian Choychi grabbed musket at 2 AM, wounded guard Quesadas with bayonet. Soldiers entered; Marín struck him on head; died 1½ hours later "echando sangre con espuma por la boca."

notes: Three corrections/flags. (1) The record is Sal's report of 28 Feb. 1797; it does not state the 2 a.m. hour the feature gives, so '2 AM' is unconfirmed from the catalog. (2) The feature treats 'guard Quesadas' and 'Marín' as two men; Savage names the wounded soldier 'Marín Quesadas' and the man who struck the blow 'soldier Marín'; ambiguous, possibly one person. Flagged, not reconciled. (3) For the 'result' field: surgeon Pablo Soler testified Choychi already had two fractured ribs when brought in from San Luis (injured at capture) and died more from the chest contusion than the head blow, which undercuts a flat 'killed resisting'. Bancroft vol. I has no mention of Choychi or Quesadas (grepped); episode appears unpublished, so no book source.

sources: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 9), tomo xvi, orig. pp. 906-907 / scan n240, Doc 416. Marcos Briones to Sal, San Luis Obispo, 8 Jan. 1797, 'Muerte a un Indio cristiano': Toribio killed by an old Gentile and his two sons on suspicion of having bewitched a child. | Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 9), tomo xvi, orig. pp. 794-795, 821-822 / scan n215-n217, Doc 364. Marcos Briones to Sal, San Luis Obispo, 26 Jan. 1797 · the arrest.
notes: Discrepancy flagged, not reconciled: the killer's motive differs between the two documents. Briones's first report (ca9-d416, 8 Jan.) gives the witchcraft/poisoning accusation over the man's dead daughter; the accused's own statement after arrest (ca9-d364, 26 Jan.) gives a different, more mundane reason, that a Christian in Toribio's party had approached his house. The map summary carries only the first version. ca9-d364 also adds that Toribio's body was burned. Bancroft, Hist. Cal. I, does not narrate this killing.

name: Expedition against Tulares Gathering
summary: Pursued fugitives, couldn't find them. Indian woman reported gentiles gathering "heading toward the Tulares." Plans to return "to pacify the gathering of Gentiles."
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 9), tomo xvi, orig. pp. 904-905 / scan n239-n240, Doc 415. Marcos Briones to Sal, San Luis Obispo, 14 Jan. 1797, 'Pesquisa de malhechores': the search for the malefactors, and word that the Gentiles of those parts had gathered near the headwaters as if heading for the Tulares.
notes: Leaf number corrected from n240 to n239 (the record opens on n239 and runs to n240; n240 alone lands on Doc 416, the Toribio killing = feature reg-51). Features reg-51 and reg-52 are consecutive documents in one manhunt: Toribio killed, Briones out 8 Jan. (d416), pursuit fails 14 Jan. (d415), gentiles taken 18 Jan., reported 26 Jan. (d364). Worth cross-linking on the map. The 'result: Failed pursuit' is right for 14 Jan. only; the January manhunt did in the end take the killers.

name: Amador Expedition to el Colorado
summary: Argüello orders Amador: "A lo gentiles no se los violente para hacerlos de sus rancherías." Gentiles fled "porque decían que querían bautizarlos"; feared forced baptism.
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 10), tomo xvii, orig. pp. 218-220 / Savage p. 124 (stamp) / 123 (hand), scan n123, Doc 119. Argüello to Sgt. Pedro Amador, San Francisco, 12 Apr. 1798, with Amador's endorsement dated San José, 24 Apr. 1798. | Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 10), tomo xvii, orig. p. 221 / Savage p. 125 (stamp) / 124 (hand), scan n124, Doc 120. Argüello to Borica, San Francisco, 26 Apr. 1798 · cover note.
notes: Two substantive corrections. (1) CITATION FORM: 'n218' is not a leaf; the document is at scan n123. The old citation lands a reader on an unrelated 1799 petition. (2) THE EVENT: the record does not describe an Amador expedition. It is Argüello's written order forbidding force in recruiting gentiles, with Amador's marginal endorsement reporting that 'el Mtro' (the missionary) went to el Colorado and the gentiles fled at sight of him for fear of baptism. Amador is the reporting officer, not the man who went; 'type: raid' likely needs revising. What 'el Colorado' denotes here is unresolved; in the San Francisco/San José jurisdiction it is most likely a local place name rather than the Colorado River (ca24-d943 concerns the Río Colorado but in a Baja/Santa Catalina context). Left unresolved rather than guessed. Context, not linked: the April 1798 Mission San José war scare (ca10-d81, d89, d90).

name: False Alarm: Attack on SLO, SM, Concepción
summary: Rumored multi-mission attack proved false. Viceroy Azanza "queda impuesto de la falsedad de la noticia."
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 10), tomo xvii, orig. p. 487 / Savage p. 221 (folio 219), scan leaf n221, Doc 273. Azanza to Borica, México, 6 March 1799, 'Sobre tranquilidad de los indios'. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. i, 1542-1800 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 548-49.
notes: CITATION CORRECTION: the existing text 'C-A 10, n240, p. 487' mixes two different documents. Original page 487 is right, but scan leaf n240 is NOT this document; I pulled the record that actually sits on leaf n240 (ca10-d310, Azanza to Borica, 3 Aug 1799, 'Sobre arrivo de embarcn. americana', orig. p.562, about the Anglo-American frigate Elisa and John Kendrick's supercargo) and it has nothing to do with the mission alarm. The correct leaf for p.487 is n221. DATING: the feature is dated '1799' with year confidence; the document is exactly dated 6 March 1799, and it is a viceregal ACKNOWLEDGEMENT from México, so the rumour itself circulated in California in 1798. Bancroft places the false alarm in his 1798 paragraph (Hist. Cal. i. 548-9): 'There was a false alarm of impending attack on San Miguel, San Luis, and Purisima by the Tulare and channel Indians.' I could NOT resolve Bancroft's underlying footnote (Prov. Rec., MS., iv. 285; v. 210; vi. 106-7, 100; ix. 9; Prov. St. Pap., MS., xvii. 97, 100, 106-7) to a document about THIS alarm: the Prov. St. Pap. xvii page-runs he cites map onto the April–June 1798 San José Bay-Area scare (ca10-d81 leaf n96, ca10-d89 leaf n100, ca10-d112 leaf n120), which is the other half of the same Bancroft footnote, not the SLO/San Miguel/Purísima rumour. So ca10-d273 is the only C-A record that demonstrably concerns this feature.

name: Tulares: Borica Orders Avoidance
summary: "No conviene de ningún modo mandar Neofitos ni tropa á los Tulares... por ser muchísimos los Gentiles y exponerse á una pelea fuerte." Sargento Macario Castro sent with Indian guides instead.
sources: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 24), tomo vi, orig. p. 753 / scan n560, Doc 1028. Borica to the padres of San Antonio, 'Indios fugitivos': it is on no account advisable to send neophytes or troops after the fugitive gentiles, who are too numerous and would risk a heavy loss to the spiritual conquest. | Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 24), tomo vi, orig. p. 753 / Savage p. 558 (folio 235), scan leaf n560, Doc 1029. Borica to the Padres of San Carlos, Monterey, 6 April 1799, 'Indios huidos' · order to Sgt. Macario Castro to go after nine runaway neophytes with trustworthy Indians chosen by the friars. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: ⚠ CATALOGUE ERROR FOUND AND PROVEN FROM THE LEAF IMAGE. I downloaded the BookReader JPEG of C-A 24 leaf n560 (item 168036074_80_6_2, scale 2) and read Savage's hand directly. The manuscript reads: heading 'Indios "Tulares"'; body: 'Dice qe no conviene de ningun modo mandar Neofitos ni tropa á los Tulares en solicitud del Indio huido Agustin, por ser muchissimos los Gentiles y esponerse á una pelea fuerte qe atrasaria demasiadamte la conquista espiritual. p. 753.' The published catalog record ca10... ca24-d1028 is wrong in FIVE places: (1) heading given as 'Indios fugitivos'; the leaf says 'Indios "Tulares"'; (2) 'á los Frailes'; the leaf says 'á los TULARES'; (3) 'los Indios huidos Aguini [gentiles]'; the leaf says 'del Indio huido AGUSTIN' (one named runaway, not a group); (4) 'una pérdida fuerte'; the leaf says 'una PELEA fuerte'; (5) 'desgraciadamte'; the leaf says 'demasiadamte'. The MAP FEATURE'S quotation is therefore correct and the catalog record needs amending. This should be fed back to the C-A database as a leaf-verified field correction. Savage page on this leaf is stamped 558 with hand folio 235.

name: Peralta's Failed Expedition from Santa Clara
summary: Cabo Luis Peralta (future grantee of Rancho San Antonio; Oakland/Berkeley/Alameda) "did not have satisfactory results for lack of good guides." Can't navigate into indigenous territory.
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), tomo xviii, orig. pp. 824-25 / Savage p. 334 [stamp] / 331 [hand], scan leaf n335, Doc 382. Cabo Luis Peralta to an unnamed captain, Santa Clara, 27 September 1804: 'Avisa q.e la espedicion q.e hizo contra indios gentiles no tuvo resultados satisfactorios p.r falta de buenos guias.' | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), tomo xviii, orig. pp. 851-52 [catalog field reads 'p.352'] / Savage p. 355, scan leaf n356, Doc 396. Argüello (San Francisco) to Sargento Luis Peralta, 1804: instructions for a second pursuit of the gentiles, on the indispensable condition that he take good guides. | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 11), tomo xviii, orig. pp. 355-56 [catalog field; summary gives pp. 864-66] / Savage pp. 358-59, scan leaves n359-n360, Doc 402. Argüello to Gov. Arrillaga, San Francisco, 26 October 1804: result of Peralta's SECOND expedition. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: ⚠ DATE DISCREPANCY, NOT SILENTLY RECONCILED. The map dates this feature 'February 1804'. The document it cites (C-A 11, Savage 334 / orig. pp. 824-25) is headed by Savage '1804 - Set.e 27 - Sta Clara - Cabo Luis Peralta á un Capitan (no dice cual)', i.e. 27 SEPTEMBER 1804. The map's February date is not supported by the cited manuscript. Either the map date is wrong or it rests on a source I have not seen; I did not find any February 1804 Peralta expedition record in C-A 11. Also note Savage calls Peralta 'Cabo' here and 'Sargento' six weeks later. SECOND CATALOGUE INCONSISTENCY: ca11-d396's own summary and ca11-d382's cross-reference both give the follow-up order as pp. 851-2, but d396's orig_page field reads 'p.352' and its date field reads '1804 Oct 27' while d382's note calls it '27 Set 1804'. The orig_page field of ca11-d396 looks mis-keyed and its date needs a leaf check; I have not opened that leaf image.

name: Report at Pizcache Village
summary: No combat. Oral memory of prior battle: "Other soldiers from the other side of the mountains appeared about twenty years ago." ~200 souls, chief Sujoyucomu.
sources: Fr. Pedro Muñoz, Diario de la Expedición hecha por Don Gabriel Moraga, Alférez de la Compañía de San Francisco, á los Nuevos Descubrimientos del Tular, 1806, MS. (Bancroft Library, cited by Bancroft as a titled manuscript, not part of the Archives of California series). | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), notes 27-28 (Muñoz diary, Pizcache). | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 290-92 / Savage pp. 115-18, scan leaves n117-n120, Doc 106. Arrillaga to Tte. de la Guerra, San Gabriel, 4 September 1806: orders forming the Moraga interior expedition, 25 men plus chaplain and interpreters. | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 295-96 / Savage pp. 118-19, scan leaves n120-n121, Doc 108. Arrillaga, San Diego, 9 October 1806: the Moraga column assembled at San Juan Bautista with Fr. Pedro Muñoz and the San Francisco detachment. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 111-15 / Savage B-111-115, scan leaves n262-n265, Doc 983. Arrillaga to Luis Argüello, 20 May 1806: 'Instrucciones para el reconocimiento del interior' · the standing instruction for the 1806 interior reconnaissances, including the order to keep a diary and to use faithful Indians as guides. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1885), 52-53 and n.16 (Muñoz diary abstracted; Pizcache and chief Sujoyucomu at 13 October 1806).
notes: NULL RESULT, RECORDED HONESTLY: the Muñoz diary is not in the C-A corpus. I searched all 34,567 records for 'Pizcache', 'Sujoyucomu', 'Nupchenche', 'Taulamne' and 'Latelate'; ZERO hits on every one. I also ran content searches on the diary title and on 'Moraga expedición Tulares 1806'. Bancroft cites the diary as a standalone titled MS ('Munoz, Diario de la Expedicion hecha por Don Gabriel Moraga, Alferez de la Compania de San Francisco, á los Nuevos Descubrimientos del Tular, 1806, MS.'), which in his citation system means a separate item in his collection, not a folio of the Archives of California. What C-A DOES hold is the administrative paper trail of the expedition, which is emitted below as real clickable evidence. DATING: Bancroft's abstract of the diary puts the Pizcache interview on 13 October 1806, which fits the feature's 'October 1806'. The chief's testimony as Bancroft renders it: 'a band of soldiers like these came from across the sierra (from New Mexico) 20 years ago and killed many of the Indians.'

name: Armed Confrontation at Río Guadalupe
summary: Tuolumne River area. 40 armed Indians with feather flag. Standoff; no casualties.
sources: Fr. Pedro Muñoz, Diario de la Expedición hecha por Don Gabriel Moraga... á los Nuevos Descubrimientos del Tular, 1806, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript; NOT in the Archives of California series), entry for 5 October 1806. | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), note 20. | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 295-96 / Savage pp. 118-19, scan leaves n120-n121, Doc 108. Arrillaga, San Diego, 9 October 1806: the Moraga column assembled with Fr. Pedro Muñoz. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 291-92 / scan n119-n120, Doc 106. Arrillaga to Tte. de la Guerra, 4 September 1806: the order forming the expedition, a party under Alferez Gabriel Moraga of 25 men with chaplain and interpreters, San Francisco to ready a sergeant, a corporal and eight soldiers. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 52 n.16 (Muñoz diary, entries of 2 and 5 October 1806).
notes: UNRESOLVED for a C-A manuscript of the encounter itself, same reason as reg-16: the Muñoz diary is a standalone Bancroft MS, absent from all 34,567 C-A records (searched by five distinctive diary place-names, zero hits). The pre-computed candidate list for this feature was pure noise; its top hits were the O'Cain/Peacock affair at Todos Santos and a Santa Bárbara artillery inventory, nothing to do with the Tuolumne. GEOGRAPHY NOTE: Muñoz's 'Río Guadalupe' is the STANISLAUS, not the Tuolumne. Bancroft's abstract (ii. 52 n.16) identifies the river named 'Nª Sª de Guadalupe' on 2 October as the Stanislaus, and the Rio Dolores of 1 October as the Tuolumne. The map's placement of this feature in the 'Tuolumne River area' therefore conflicts with Bancroft's identification of the stream; flagged, not reconciled. The hostile demonstration is Bancroft's 'Oct. 5th, Hostile demonstrations of the Indians, whose fears could not be removed,' with the party camped back at the Rio Guadalupe. The record link here was briefly pointed at C-A 12 Doc 105, a retirement cedula; Doc 106 is the order forming Moraga's expedition and is what this citation describes.

name: Encounter at Taulamne
summary: Tuolumne caves. ~200 souls on steep cliffs, inaccessible. Indians live in caves. Refused to descend. Said "soldiers killed and captured people." Armed passive resistance.
sources: Fr. Pedro Muñoz, Diario de la Expedición hecha por Don Gabriel Moraga... á los Nuevos Descubrimientos del Tular, 1806, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript; NOT in the Archives of California series), entry for 3 October 1806. | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), note 23. | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 295-96 / Savage pp. 118-19, scan leaves n120-n121, Doc 108. Arrillaga, San Diego, 9 October 1806: the Moraga-Muñoz column assembled. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 52 n.16 (Muñoz diary, entry of 3 October 1806).
notes: UNRESOLVED for a C-A manuscript of the encounter. Searched the whole corpus for 'Taulamne'; zero hits. Same finding as reg-16/17. DATE: Bancroft's abstract of the diary puts this at 3 October 1806, '6 l. E. up the river to a rancheria of Taulamne or Tahualamne (Tuolumne?) situated on inaccessible rocks'; the river being the Guadalupe/Stanislaus, which is consistent with the map's Knights Ferry placement. Note the ethnonym problem Bancroft himself raises: he suspects the Merced of 29 September may actually be Bear Creek 'in order to locate Tahualamne on what is now Tuolumne River', i.e. the identification of this rancheria's stream is contested in the literature. Not reconciled here.

name: Skirmish at Apaglamenes/Tationes
summary: Near Grayson, Stanislaus County. 30 armed heathen on opposite bank, "painted, bedecked with feathers." 12 shots fired. One Indian hit. "Soldier Morales came into the skirmish with half his chin shaved."
sources: Fr. José Viader, Diario ó Noticia del Viage que acabo de hacer por mandato del Sr Gobernador y Padre Presidente, con el objeto de buscar parages ó Sitios para fundar Misiones, Agosto 1810, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript, with a second copy from the Archivo de la Misión de Santa Bárbara; NOT in the Archives of California series), entry for 22 August 1810. | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), note 7 (Viader, August 1810). | [No Archives of California manuscript found for this engagement.] | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 56 and n.36 (Viader's August 1810 diary abstracted).
notes: ⚠ CITATION CORRECTION. The existing source reads 'Viader diary (Cook note 7). C-A 12.' The Viader diaries are NOT in C-A 12. I searched the whole corpus for 'Viader' (10 hits, all unrelated: mission rosters, a neophyte-wage receipt, a baptism case, Solá correspondence) and ran targeted searches for the August 1810 mission-site reconnaissance in C-A 12, 25 and 26; no record of it exists. Bancroft cites the source as 'Viader, Diario ó Noticia del Viage que acabo de hacer por mandato del Sr Gobernador y Padre Presidente, con el objeto de buscar parages ó Sitios para fundar Misiones, Agosto 1810, MS.'; a titled standalone manuscript; and adds explicitly that 'Viader's original diary in my possession and that copied from the archives of Santa Bárbara do not exactly agree in some details', i.e. the two known copies are a Bancroft Library MS and a copy from the Santa Bárbara mission archive. Neither is Archives of California. DATING/GEOGRAPHY: Bancroft's abstract places Tationes and Apaglamenes on 22 August 1810, on the far bank of the San Joaquin, which fits the feature's 'August 1810' and the Grayson, Stanislaus County placement. Bancroft also notes 'Most of the names were those of the chiefs', a caution worth carrying on the map.

name: Dawn Assault at Pescadero/Cholvones
summary: Delta; Old River area. "Before dawn we assaulted a village." 15 San José Christians recovered, 18 heathen men captured, 51 women (released; "went away very happy"). 2 prisoners escaped.
sources: Fr. José Viader, Diario de una Entrada al Río de San Joaquín, Octubre 1810, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript, with a second copy from the Archivo de la Misión de Santa Bárbara; NOT in the Archives of California series), entries of 19-22 October 1810. | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), note 12 (Viader, October 1810). | [No Archives of California manuscript found for this engagement.] | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 56-57 n.37 and 92.
notes: ⚠ CITATION CORRECTION, same as reg-19: 'Viader diary (Cook note 12). C-A 12'; the diary is Bancroft's 'Viader, Diario de una Entrada al Rio de San Joaquin, Octubre 1810, MS.', a standalone titled manuscript, not a C-A folio. Searched and not found (see reg-19 evidence). NUMBERS DISCREPANCY, FLAGGED NOT RECONCILED: the map says '15 San José Christians recovered, 18 heathen men captured, 51 women (released)'. Bancroft, summarising the same expedition at ii. 92, says 'sixteen Christian Indians were recovered and eighteen gentiles captured by a sudden attack on a rancheria, to say nothing of fifty women taken and set free; all without bloodshed.' 15 vs 16 Christians and 51 vs 50 women. The map's figures presumably come from Cook's text of the diary and Bancroft's from his own copy; Bancroft himself warns the two known copies of Viader disagree in details. Worth a footnote on the map rather than a silent choice. Bancroft's abstract also confirms 'Oct. 22d, Corporal Pico sent home with captives'; the link to reg-24's Pico.

name: Battle of Suisun
summary: MAJOR ENGAGEMENT. Alf. Moraga, 17 cavalry vs. ~120 Sespesuña/Suisun warriors. Crossed Carquines Strait by boat. Hard fight; 18 captured (released, expected to die). Survivors in 3 huts: 2 stormed, all killed; 3rd set on fire; "bravely preferred to perish in the flames." 4 Spanish wounded (23.5% rate); highest in any Spanish victory. Royal Order from Spain praised "glorious action." Moraga promoted; Herrera + Soto made sergeants.
result: Spanish tactical victory; highest casualty rate of any Spanish victory
sources: Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 25), tomo ix, orig. pp. 367-71 [= Bancroft's ix. 122-3, hand folio] / Savage pp. 371-372, scan leaves n374-n375, Doc 686. Arrillaga to the Viceroy, 28 June 1810, 'Sobre encuentro y campaña con gentiles'. | Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1016-1019 / Savage p. 313 [Bancroft cites xix. 314], scan leaf n319, Doc 395. Viceroy Venegas to the Governor, México, 12 November 1811: transmits the royal order rewarding the action of 22 May 1810. | Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 723-24 / Savage pp. 223-24 [= Bancroft's xi. 222-3], scan leaves n223-n224, Doc 831. Governor to the commandant [Estudillo], La Soledad, 26 June 1812: transmits the viceroy's note of 12 November 1811 on Moraga's 'gloriosa acción' of 22 May 1810. | Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. p. 593 / Savage B-593, scan leaf n447, Doc 1218. Arrillaga to the Comandante de San Francisco, Monterey, 16 June 1812: the real decreto granting Moraga the grade of Teniente de Caballería (⚠ this entry dates the action 20 May, not 22 May). | Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 363-66 / Savage B-363-366, scan leaf n432, Doc 1203. Arrillaga to the Comandante de San Francisco, Monterey, 5 May / 5 June 1810: among the register items, 'salida del Alférez Gabriel Moraga con 17 hombres a aprehender la ranchería de [Suymaya]'. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 91-92 and n.24. | Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales tocantes á la Alta California, MS. (Bancroft Library dictation; Bancroft short-titles it 'Vallejo, Hist. Cal., MS.'), i. 151-55. NOT part of the Archives of California series. | Juan Bautista Alvarado, Historia de California, MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), i. 69-70. NOT part of the Archives of California series.
notes: THE PAGE-NUMBER PUZZLE, SOLVED. Bancroft's 'Prov. Rec., MS., ix. 122-3' does not match the C-A record's fields at first sight (ca25-d686 is catalogued at tomo IX pp. 367-71, Savage p. 371-372, scan n374). It resolves through Savage's DUAL foliation: a neighbouring record in the same run, ca25-d649, carries savage_page '365/116', giving an offset of 249 between the stamped number and the hand folio. 371-249 = 122 and 372-249 = 123. So Savage 371-372 IS hand folio 122-123, and Bancroft was citing the hand folio. The map's citation is right and the record is right; I record the arithmetic so nobody 'corrects' it later. DATE DISCREPANCY INSIDE C-A: ca26-d1218 dates the 'gloriosa acción' to 20 May 1810 while ca26-d831, ca12-d395, Bancroft and the royal order all say 22 May. The catalog record already flags this ('⚠ fecha 20 May, no 22'). Not reconciled. NAME DISCREPANCY: the promoted corporals are 'Herrera y Soto' in ca26-d831, ca12-d395 and Bancroft, but 'José Correa y Francisco Soto' in ca26-d1218. Also 'Ventura' vs 'Buenaventura' Zúñiga. SOURCE CAUTION Bancroft raises and the map should carry: Vallejo's account describes a fight in the same region by José Sánchez in 1817 against the Suisunes under chief Malaca, and Bancroft judges 'It is possible that the author has confounded two different battles'; Alvarado, Hist. Cal., MS., i. 69-70 dates the affair 1817, puts Gabriel Moraga in command, and says Solano was captured on that occasion. Using Vallejo for 1810 detail is therefore risky. Malaca's words come from Vallejo's memoir of the 1870s reporting what Alférez Sánchez told him, not from a contemporary record, and Vallejo wrote the phrase in English. Earlier versions of this map rendered it into Spanish and presented that rendering as the source wording.

name: Tense Encounter with Tauquimenes
summary: Sacramento River branch, delta. Standoff; no combat.
sources: Fr. Ramón Abella, Diario de un registro de los ríos grandes, 1811, MS. (Bancroft Library titled manuscript; a second copy was in Duflot de Mofras's hands. NOT in the Archives of California series), entries of 23-27 October 1811. | [No Archives of California manuscript found for this encounter.] | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 321-23 and n.3.
notes: BANCROFT'S FOOTNOTE CHASED, RESULT NEGATIVE. The episode is Bancroft, Hist. Cal. ii. 321-23, and his source is 'Abella, Diario de un registro de los rios grandes, 1811, MS.'; a standalone titled manuscript, of which Duflot de Mofras also says 'Le journal manuscrit de cette exploration intéressante est entre nos mains.' Not a C-A citation. SPELLING: Bancroft renders the ethnonym 'Tarquimenes', the map 'Tauquimenes'; grep of vol2 for 'tauquimen/taquimen' returns nothing, for 'Tarquimenes' the Abella note. Worth normalising on the map. EXPEDITION DETAIL from Bancroft: Fr. Ramón Abella with Fr. Buenaventura Fortuni, Sergeant [José] Sánchez apparently commanding, 68 persons in several boats, 15 October to 30 October 1811; they named Points San Pablo and San Pedro, made the first recorded navigation of the Sacramento, and named the numerous Indians on it 'Tarquimenes'. This is a 15-day trip, so the map's 'October 1811' is right. Bancroft notes the Suisunes 'showed more timidity than hostility', consistent with the map's 'standoff, no combat', and that 'Two leagues distant was where Moraga's famous battle took place'; a direct tie to reg-21.

name: Soto's Battle
summary: LARGEST PITCHED BATTLE IN COLONIAL CA. Sgt. Soto + 12 soldiers from SF (by boat) + 100 Mission San José auxiliaries vs. ~1,000 warriors from 4 united rancherías (Unsumnes). Warriors pre-positioned on marshy island, women/children removed. "Fell upon the soldiers at landing." 3-hour battle. Soto "was at one time doubtful of the result, so reliant were the foes on their numbers, so careless of life." 1 neophyte killed (Alcalde Julio); many indigenous dead. Not a single fugitive captured.
result: Spanish tactical / INDIGENOUS STRATEGIC VICTORY; largest single-engagement indigenous army in CA
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (BANC MSS C-A 12), tomo xix, orig. pp. 1153-69 / Savage pp. 344-348, scan leaves n351-n355, Doc 425. Luis Argüello to Gov. Arrillaga, San Francisco, 31 October 1813, 'Expedición militar · Combate con los indios' (embodying Sgt. Francisco Soto's own narrative). | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 324 and n.4. | San José, Libro de Misión, MS., 25 (mission register, Mission San José). NOT in the Archives of California series. | Sgt. Francisco Soto, Expedición Militar del Sargento, 1813, MS. · Soto's own narrative, surviving embodied in Argüello's report (see the C-A entry above), not as a separately catalogued C-A document. | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), 265-77.
notes: BEST RESULT IN THE BATCH. Bancroft's footnote says of Soto's narrative that 'The narrative is embodied in a report by Argüello'; and that report survives in C-A as ca12-d425, a five-leaf abstract. The map's Savage page range should be corrected from 334-348 to 344-348 (the record spans Savage 344-348, orig. pp. 1153-69, scan leaves n351-n355). DATE: the record dates the report 31 October 1813 and the battle at dawn on the 27th, matching the map's 27 October 1813. The San José mission book puts the departure against the Unsumnes on 25 October and names the killed alcalde Julio, which the C-A record independently confirms ('one auxiliary, Julio, killed'). The C-A abstract adds a detail not in Bancroft and worth putting on the map: the Indians had taunted that 'soldiers are worth nothing on foot, only on horseback', then learned otherwise; and Soto praises the auxiliaries' obedience and valour.

name: Pico's Fight at San Joaquin Crossing
summary: San Joaquin River between Dos Palos and Los Banos. Day 9: armed heathen crossing river, Cpl. Juarez engaged; killed 2. Day 10: Indians came to attack camp at dawn. Line of battle formed. Interpreter asked what they wanted; "to fight." After firing, troops dismounted and pursued through brush. 3 killed, 1 captured. Dead included a Christian from Santa Cruz who was "the one most determined" to kill the soldiers.
sources: [Sgt. José Dolores] Pico, diary of the 1815 expedition to the San Joaquin, MS. · printed in Cook. Provenance NOT established as Archives of California; see notes. | [No Archives of California manuscript found for this engagement.] | Sherburne F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820,' University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (1960), 271-74 (Pico diary, November 1815). | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. ii, 1801-1824 (1885), 326 and n.7 (the 1815 'gran expedición': Solá's letters 14 Sept - 9 Nov; Moraga's northern party of 50 against the Pitemas; Sgt. Pico bringing in 11 Indians, Solá to Ruiz, 5 Oct 1815).
notes: ⚠ CITATION PROBLEM AND AN OPEN HISTORIOGRAPHICAL CONFLICT. (1) C-A 13 cannot hold this: q.py vol 13 shows it is Prov. St. Pap. tomo XX, whose records run 1816-1821; the 1815 material is not there. C-A 12 (tomo XIX) I searched directly and found nothing. (2) Bancroft, Hist. Cal. ii. 326, says flatly of the 1815 gran expedición: 'It is only from allusions in the archives that this affair is known, for no diary is extant.' Cook nevertheless prints a Pico diary at pp. 271-74. Either the diary surfaced after Bancroft wrote, or Cook used a copy Bancroft did not connect to this campaign. I cannot resolve that from here and will not guess. (3) Bancroft's own manuscript pointers for the 1815 campaign are 'Prov. St. Pap., Ben. Mil., MS., xlvi. 32-4' (the northern party of 50 under Gabriel Moraga against the Pitemas, out from San Francisco about 25 Sept) and 'Sola to Ruiz, Oct. 5, 1815. Id., xlvi. 5-6' (Sgt. Pico delivering 11 Indians accused of the killing of Christians and the wounding of vaqueros). Prov. St. Pap. Benicia Military is C-A 17, but Savage's abstracts in that stretch carry NO original page numbers (the orig_page field is empty throughout), so the page-interval resolver cannot reach them, and my content searches of C-A 17 for a 1815 Pico entry found nothing. This is a genuine gap, not a search failure I can close. (4) DATE: the map's 'November 9-10, 1815' is consistent with Bancroft's note that Solá's letters on this expedition run 'Sept. 14th to Nov. 9th' and that the expedition returned 1 December 1815 (Tapis to Guerra, 2 Dec).

name: Ortega's Raid on Tache
summary: Tache village, Kings River, not far west of Lemoore (Cook note [2]). Ortega attacked at dawn but village deserted; fugitive Indians had warned them "the soldiers were coming to kill them at the point of the lance." Found 3 Soledad horses. Followed into tule swamp but could not reach inhabitants.
sources: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 267–69 (Ortega's diary, in translation); Cook note [2] places Tachi territory west of Tulare Lake, villages near Lemoore. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 · Solá's 'grand expedition' of autumn 1815 in pursuit of runaways; 'Diego Olivera was one of the party from Santa Barbara, under Juan Ortega … which met another from Monterey over in the Tulares'; the expedition had returned by 1 Dec. 1815 (Tapis to Guerra, 2 Dec. 1815). | Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815 · the operational order for this raid: Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93.
notes: LEAF-VERIFIED FIELD CORRECTION: I downloaded C-A 26 scan n27 (BookReader JPEG) and read Savage's entry verbatim. It reads: 'A Sargto Juan de Ortega. / Nove 1o.; 2o con partida de Presidio de Sta Barba y 15 hombres mas hará una expedicion del 6 al 11, pr los parajes inmediatos en persecucion de gentiles: qe el Sargto Jose Dolores Pico se le unirá y entonces hará correrias pr Misiones de Sn Miguel, Sn Antº Soledad y otras, con ambas partidas. pp. 98-100.' The catalog summary for ca26-d93 says 'Con 18 hombres del Presidio de Sta Bárbara'; the leaf says the SB presidio party PLUS 15 more men ('y 15 hombres mas'). That is a catalog error worth correcting. NULL RESULT (record it): the Ortega diary Cook translated is NOT in the Archives of California so far as I can find. I grepped the whole 34,567-record catalog for Tach/Tache/Tachi (word-boundary, case-sensitive) and for diario/expedicion/tular restricted to 1815; zero diary hits. Bancroft II:326 states outright of this expedition that 'no diary is extant,' which is consistent: Cook's text must come from a repository outside C-A, and I could not establish which one. Do not fabricate a C-A link for the diary itself.

name: Pico's Raid on Cheneche
summary: Cheneche village near mouth of Mariposa Creek, north of Los Banos, on the San Joaquin River. Pre-dawn assault at 4 AM. 66 captured (Christians and heathen). Released 4 men and 12 crippled old women. "Majority of the people escaped because this village is in a bad location." Found 7 live horses and 5 recently dead.
result: Mostly escaped; bad terrain for pursuit
sources: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 270–71 (Pico's diary, in translation); Cook note [9] places the Cheneches near the mouth of Mariposa Creek. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 · Solá's grand expedition of 1815; the Monterey party met the Santa Bárbara party in the Tulares; in the south 'Sergt. Pico brought in 11 Indians charged with killing Christians and wounding vaqueros' (Solá to Ruiz, 5 Oct. 1815, Prov. St. Pap., Ben. Mil., MS., xlvi. 5-6). | Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815, ordering Sgt. José Dolores Pico to join him: Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93.
notes: Same expedition as reg-25, opposite wing. Pico commanded the Monterey party; Ortega the Santa Bárbara party; Bancroft says the two met in the Tulares. The 8 November date for Cheneche falls inside the '6 al 11' window of the order. NULL RESULT: no Pico 1815 diary exists anywhere in the C-A catalog (word-boundary greps for Cheneche, Malim, Tape/Tapee, Nupchenche across all 34,567 records returned nothing; Bancroft II:326 says no diary of this expedition is extant). Cook's source repository is not established.

name: Tapee Horse Slaughter
summary: Village of Tapee (Tape), south of the great bend of the San Joaquin River, ~20 miles west of Fresno (Cook note [9]). Pico surrounded village on both sides of river. Found 238 RECENTLY KILLED ANIMALS, "a great deal of meat quartered and dried," and 16 live animals shot with arrows or badly treated. "From Tapee to Cheneches... more than 500 dead animals." LARGEST INDIGENOUS ECONOMIC WARFARE INCIDENT.
result: INDIGENOUS ECONOMIC WARFARE; 238+ horses killed, 500+ in region
sources: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 275–76 (Pico's diary, in translation); Cook note [9] places Tape ~20 mi. west of Fresno, south of the great bend of the San Joaquin. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 · the 1815 grand expedition, its two parties, and its return on 1 December 1815. | Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815, ordering the joint correrías by the missions of San Miguel, San Antonio and Soledad 'con ambas partidas': Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: The 23 November date falls AFTER the 6–11 November window of the order, in its second phase: 'el Sargto Jose Dolores Pico se le unirá y entonces hará correrias pr Misiones de Sn Miguel, Sn Antº Soledad y otras, con ambas partidas' (verbatim from scan n27). Tapee, ~20 mi west of Fresno, lies in exactly the interior hinterland reached from San Miguel/Soledad, and Bancroft II:326 n.8 records the whole expedition returning 1 December 1815; so a 23 November action is chronologically inside it. NULL RESULT: no C-A record mentions Tape/Tapee, and no C-A record anywhere reports the 238 slaughtered horses. That figure survives only in Cook's translation of the Pico diary. Given its importance to the feature ('largest indigenous economic warfare incident'), the absence of any archival corroboration in C-A should be stated on the map rather than papered over.

name: Search for Malim Village
summary: Junction of Mariposa Creek and the San Joaquin River, near Los Banos. Guide (from Malim village) told them he knew the way, then when they arrived said he didn't know where it was; "but he did know that this was his country and we were hunting for his village." Guide given 10 lashes. Village found but inhabitants had escaped. 2 Christians from Santa Cruz captured.
sources: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 277–78 (Pico's diary, in translation); Cook note [9] places Malim between the Cheneches and the Nupchenches along the San Joaquin River. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 326 and 326 n.8 · the 1815 grand expedition and its return on 1 December 1815. | Gob. Pablo Vicente de Solá to Sgt. Juan de Ortega, Monterey, 1 Nov. 1815, ordering the joint correrías by the missions of San Miguel, San Antonio and Soledad 'con ambas partidas': Provincial Records (C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. pp. 98–100 / Savage p. 28, scan n27, Doc 93. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: 27–28 November falls in the second phase of the order (the joint correrías 'con ambas partidas'), inside the expedition's chronology (home 1 Dec. 1815 per Bancroft II:326 n.8). NULL RESULT: the catalog has no record mentioning Malim; the only C-A occurrences of anything like the name are 'Malmi' near Santa Cruz (ca13-d110/d111, June 1816); a completely different place and event, and it should NOT be linked here. The Pico diary itself is not in C-A.

name: Martinez Incident at Bubal
summary: Village of Bubal (Wowol), western shore of Tulare Lake (Cook note [6]). Fr. Luis Antonio Martinez burned village of Pusas. Lively controversy with other friars over his behavior.
sources: Sherburne F. Cook, "Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800–1820," University of California Anthropological Records 16:6 (Berkeley, 1960), 279–86 (Padre Luis Antonio Martínez's tular entrada, in translation); Cook note [6] identifies Bubal as Wowol on the shore of Tulare Lake. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 327–28 and 327 n.11 · 'Padre Luis Martinez visited these rancherias early in 1816'; the party left San Luis Obispo and visited Lucluc (28 lgs.), Tuohuala (9 l.), Gelecto (18 l.), Lihuanhilame (19 l.), Quihuame (7 l.); Telame mentioned but not visited; 'Tuohuala was called also Hubal (Bubal?).' Bancroft then narrates the ensuing quarrel among the friars over the soldiers' conduct. | Martínez, "Entrada á las Rancherías del Tular, 1816," MS · the diary itself, cited by Bancroft under his own manuscript title (Hist. Cal. II:327 n.11). | Cabot to the prefect, and Sarría to the governor, 1 June 1816: Archivo del Arzobispado [de San Francisco], MS, iii. pt. i. 46–49, 51–53, 119–20 · the inter-Franciscan controversy over the soldiers' conduct on this entrada (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:328 n.12). | Gov. Pablo Vicente de Solá to P. Fr. [Luis] Antonio Martínez, Monterey, 17 June 1816, 'Instruido de cuanto le acaeció en la Expedicion' · Prov. Rec. (BANC MSS C-A 26), tomo xi, orig. p. 334 / scan n352 (Savage 352), Doc 1127. The governor's acknowledgement of Fr. Martínez's report on the Tulares expedition; the Jun 8 entry on the same leaf names him in full as 'P. Fr. Luis Antº Martinez'.
notes: NULL RESULT, recorded honestly: there is NO Archives of California record of this entrada. What I tried: (1) word-boundary greps over all 34,567 records for Bubal, Pusas, Tach*, and the other ranchería names; nothing; (2) a full listing of every C-A record dated April–July 1816 (about 90 records, read); nothing on a tular entrada; (3) year-scoped content searches on tular/expedición/ranchería/gentil for 1816; the only hits are the Moraga/Malmi affair near Santa Cruz and routine cimarrón orders. The nearest thing is ca26-d1127 (Solá borrador, 11 June 1816, 'instruido de lo ocurrido en la expedición'), which is too vague to attach; it could equally be the Malmi raid; so I am not linking it. DATE FLAG: the feature dates this May 1816; Bancroft says Padre Luis Martínez 'visited these rancherias early in 1816.' A May date is compatible with the friars' controversy correspondence of 1 June 1816 but Bancroft does not state a month. Do not silently harmonise. NAME FLAG: Bancroft's itinerary gives 'Tuohuala … called also Hubal (Bubal?)'; the identification of Bubal with Wowol on Tulare Lake is Cook's, not the manuscript's.

name: Battle at Malime/Tasnil
summary: Near Santa Cruz. Inter-indigenous: Christians vs. gentiles. 4 killed.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 328 n.14 ('June, 1816, Moraga made a fruitless expedition against apostate Christians at Malmi rancheria near Santa Cruz. Prov. St. Pap., MS., xx. 103') and II:390 (Santa Cruz annals: the rancherías of Pitemas and of Malmi named for 1815–16). | Luis Argüello to the Gov. of Alta California, San Francisco, 21 June 1816 · Alf. Gabriel Moraga setting out in force against the apostate Indians at the ranchería/pueblo of 'Malmi' in the Santa Cruz mission jurisdiction: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. 386–88 / Savage p. 104, scan n103, Doc 110. | Luis Argüello to Gob. Solá, San Francisco, 30 June 1816 · the surprise on the apostate Christians of Malmi failed, they were no longer there: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. pp. 389–91 / Savage pp. 104–105, scan n103–n104, Doc 111.
notes: SERIOUS DISCREPANCY; do not reconcile silently. The feature says December 1816, inter-indigenous (Christians vs. gentiles), 4 killed. The only documented Malmi engagement is Gabriel Moraga's expedition of June 1816, which was a Spanish military operation, not inter-indigenous, and which FAILED because the apostates had already left; no one was killed. I listed every C-A record dated Nov 1816 – Feb 1817 (about 80 records, read) and there is no December 1816 action near Santa Cruz at all. 'Tasnil' appears nowhere: not in the 34,567-record catalog, not in Bancroft's History of California vol. II. Bancroft II:390 says only that in 1815–16 'there had been expeditions after runaway neophytes of which not much is known, but the rancherias of Pitemas and of Malmi are named.' Recommendation: either re-date this feature to June 1816 and re-describe it as a failed Spanish surprise, or mark the December 1816 / 4-killed / inter-indigenous details as unsourced. The two C-A records below are offered as the correct records for the Malmi episode, NOT as confirmation of the feature as currently written.

name: Armed Encounter on Sacramento
summary: Sacramento River, ~50 miles from SF. Standoff; Spanish retreated.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 331 and 331 n.37, citing Argüello (Luis), Hoja de Servicios, 1828, MS · a seventeen-day voyage up the Sacramento 'constantly threatened by the numerous Indians, and once landing with four men to fight them.' | Hoja de servicio of Capt. Luis Antonio Argüello, certified by Ignacio Martínez, San Francisco, 31 Dec. 1828 · records his expedition up the river debouching at San Francisco (10 men, 17 days, attacked): State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 56), tomo xi, orig. to p. 90 / Savage pp. 120–22, scan n119–n121, Doc 138.
notes: CITATION PROBLEM. I checked every occurrence of '1817' in Bancroft's Indian-affairs / explorations chapter of vol. II (the whole span from the chapter head through the notes on Indian affairs of the decade) and there is no May 1817 armed encounter on the Sacramento in Bancroft II. The bare citation 'Bancroft II.' cannot be verified as written. The closest Bancroft passage is II:331 with its note 37, resting on Luis Argüello's Hoja de Servicios: 'in this same month of May he went to explore the river that flows from the north into San Francisco Bay, that is the Sacramento, sailing on it for seventeen days, constantly threatened by the numerous Indians, and once landing with four men to fight them,' which Bancroft assigns to May 1818 but then argues 'was probably made one or two years earlier.' DATE CONFLICT, unreconciled: the hoja as catalogued in C-A reads 1808; Bancroft read May 1818; Bancroft's own guess is 1816–17; the map says May 1817. Four different dates for what may be one voyage. RESEARCH LEAD, not a claim: the May 1817 Sacramento voyage of Luis Argüello with Padres Narciso Durán and Ramón Abella is documented by Durán's own diary, which is not in C-A; if that is the map compiler's real source, the citation should be changed from 'Bancroft II.' to Durán's diary. I did not verify this and am not asserting it.

name: Skirmish with Fugitives on Sacramento
summary: Sacramento delta island. Minor skirmish; 1 wounded.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885) · citation as given on the feature; the specific engagement could not be located in this volume.
notes: UNRESOLVED, recorded as a finding. What I tried: (1) grepped every '1817' occurrence in Bancroft II's explorations-and-Indian-affairs chapter; no May 1817 Sacramento skirmish exists there, so the feature's 'Bancroft II.' citation cannot be substantiated; (2) listed every C-A record dated April–July 1817 (about 40 records, read in full); nothing on a river expedition; (3) year-scoped content searches on Sacramento / San Joaquín / lancha / expedición for 1817; nothing. The one C-A item close in kind, ca26-d161 (Solá, 10 June 1817, 'El Sargto. distinguido Juan Ortega no pudo coger a los indios fugitivos'), gives no location and I am deliberately NOT linking it. I also considered ca56-d138 (Luis Argüello's hoja, the 17-day Sacramento voyage under attack, linked on reg-31) but the feature's two distinguishing details; a delta island and one man wounded; appear nowhere in that record, and attaching it here would be exactly the kind of plausible-looking wrong link that is worse than a gap. RESEARCH LEAD, not a claim: the Argüello–Durán voyage of May 1817 is documented by Fray Narciso Durán's diary, which is outside the C-A series; if that is the compiler's real source the citation needs changing. Unverified.

name: Campaign against Muquelenis
summary: Mokelumne, eastern delta. Spanish reported success.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 335 and 335 nn. 31–32 · 'Victory of Sanchez over the Moquelumnes'; 27 pagans killed, 20 wounded, 16 captured, 49 horses taken; Padre Durán names the offending gentiles Muquelemes. | Solá's borradores, pt. 4 (artillery and campaigns), San Juan Bautista / Rancho del Rey / Monterey, Jul.–Dec. 1819 · the successful campaign against the Ranchería de los Muquelemnes reported to the Viceroy, Padre Narciso Durán named: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 54), tomo i, Savage pp. 239–46, scan n238–n245, Doc 154. | Gob. Solá to Tte. Gabriel Moraga, San Carlos, 24 Sept. 1819 · the instruction forming the multi-pronged 1819 campaign, including 'a SF party of 20–25 under Sgt. Sánchez via San José, and a launch with a cannon by water': Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 421–22 / Savage pp. 228–29, scan n227–n228, Doc 284. | Gob. Solá to de la Guerra, 7 Oct. 1819, 'Campaña contra indios' · approving that each presidio mount its own expedition within its own demarcation: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. pp. 425–30 / Savage pp. 232–33, scan n231–n232, Doc 288. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Gob. Solá to de la Guerra (in México), Monterey, 6 Jan. 1820 · the 1819 expeditions had poor results, but Sgt. Sánchez's was 'muy brillante'; recommends him for the grade of alférez: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 17), orig. p. 455 / Savage p. 241, scan n240, Doc 300. | Padre Narciso Durán to Solá, 2 June and 28 Oct. 1819: Archivo del Arzobispado [de San Francisco], MS, iii. pt. ii. 82–84, 104–105 · the letters in which the offending gentiles are named 'Muquelemes' (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:335 n.32). | Amador, "Memorias," MS, 15–16 · the eyewitness account of José María Amador, one of the five soldiers wounded in the fight (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. II:335 and n.32).
notes: Strongest C-A result in this batch. Bancroft II:335 supplies the detail the feature compresses to 'Spanish reported success': Sgt. José Sánchez marched from San Francisco by way of San José in early October 1819 with 25 men, fought in the region of modern Stockton, killed 27, wounded 20, captured 16 and took 49 horses, losing one neophyte ally with five soldiers wounded (one of them José María Amador); the force was back before the end of October and Sánchez was recommended for promotion. Padre Durán's naming of the offenders as 'Muquelemes' is, Bancroft notes, perhaps the first writing of the name. ONE DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: Savage's abstract of ca17-d300 describes Sánchez's expedition as being in the Santa Cruz direction, whereas Bancroft places the fight in the lower San Joaquin near Stockton. The leaf has not been re-read to settle whether that is Savage's error, Solá's, or a second expedition. Also noted: the catalog summary of ca54-d154 itself carries an internal cross-reference '= mil-history register #33', so that one record is not fully independent of the register being annotated; I have therefore rested the verification on the Bancroft correspondence and on ca17-d284, which are independent.

name: Garcia's Battle at Jayaya/Tape
summary: Beyond Santa Rita, near SJB. Spanish nearly defeated; chaotic retreat.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 338–39, note 38 · the fight at the rancherías of Jayaya and Tape beyond Santa Rita, from Garcia, Hechos, MS., 10–15. | García (Inocente), "Hechos Históricos de California," MS, 10–15 · the participant's own dictated narrative, the sole source for this engagement.
notes: UNRESOLVED for C-A, and the reason matters. Bancroft prints this episode inside his closing note on Californio personal narratives, where he says explicitly that such items are 'statements more or less inaccurate but founded on facts not clearly recorded in the archives, which it would be hazardous to embody in chronological history.' In other words, Bancroft himself found no archival record of it. My own search agrees: word-boundary greps across all 34,567 C-A records for Jayay* and Tape/Tapee return nothing, and a search for Inocente García in the period returns only his later career (Rancho Natividad 1827, administrator of Mission San Miguel 1839–40). Bancroft's version supplies detail the feature omits and should be carried on the map: six men including Inocente García, under Sgt. José Dolores Pico, accompanied Padre Felipe Arroyo de la Cuesta, with thirty Indian auxiliaries out of San Juan Bautista, past Santa Rita to the rancherías of Jayaya and Tape to collect girls promised as converts; the chief was absent, a fight followed, most of the party ran, García and a few continued against the sergeant's orders and rescued all but two who were killed, along with all the horses; Pico put García in the stocks and the governor pardoned him at Arroyo's intercession. DATE FLAG: Bancroft gives no year for this item; the feature's 'ca. 1815–20' is an editorial estimate, not a source statement.

name: Boronda's Campaign at Tachi
summary: Tachi village, west of Tulare Lake near Lemoore (Cook note [2]: "not far west of Lemoore"). Same village Ortega raided in Nov 1815. "Arrows raining; underground defenses." Indigenous fortification.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 338–39, note 38 · '1812, etc., the Indians of Tachi had pits from which they discharged their arrows, into which the soldiers' horses often fell. Boronda, Notas, 15'; and '1813, Boronda gives some details of an expedition to Tachi in the Tulares region under Sergt. Espinoza. Notas, MS., 13–15.' | Boronda (José Canuto), "Notas Históricas sobre California," MS, 13–15 (the Tachi expedition under Sgt. Espinoza) and 15 (the arrow pits); cf. p. 2 (the river Reyes and Tache Lake, in connection with the 1815 grand expedition, which Boronda accompanied as a soldier).
notes: UNRESOLVED for C-A, plus a possible duplication problem worth the compiler's attention. (1) DATE CONFLICT: the feature dates this ca. 1815–20; Bancroft dates Boronda's Tachi expedition to 1813, under Sgt. Espinoza, and dates the arrow-pits detail to '1812, etc.' Neither is 1815–20. (2) POSSIBLE DUPLICATE OF reg-25: Bancroft also notes that 'Boronda, Notas, MS., 2, mentions the river Reyes and Tache Lake in connection with what seems to be this expedition'; meaning Solá's grand expedition of November 1815, which Boronda accompanied as a soldier. That is precisely the expedition in which Ortega raided Tache on 10 November 1815 (reg-25). So part of the Boronda Tachi material may be a second, dictation-based telling of reg-25 rather than a separate engagement, and the map may be double-counting. I am flagging this, not asserting it. (3) C-A search: word-boundary greps of all 34,567 records for Tach/Tache/Tachi return nothing; a search for an Espinosa expedition returns only ca12-d297 (Sgt. Miguel Espinosa, 13 Oct. 1809, San Antonio, a 20-day reconnaissance of a ranchería) which is four years early and unnamed as to place; I am deliberately NOT linking it. I also considered attaching ca26-d93 (the November 1815 order, linked on reg-25) but Bancroft's dating of the Boronda Tachi expedition to 1813 under Espinoza argues against it, so no link is offered.

The Albatross itself was NOT captured - only the Lydia was taken as prize, so the feature's result line should say one of the two ships escaped.

summary: 4 English frigates (22–24 guns each) raided Gulf of California shipping. Gov. Arrillaga: "sin ningunos elementos de defensa." 50-man militia raised; battery formed at Puerto Escondido.

name: Bouchard's Attack on Monterey
summary: MAJOR NAVAL RAID. Argentine privateer Bouchard: Argentina (38 guns + 2 howitzers) + Santa Rosa (26 guns), ~285 crew. Spanish: 40 defenders (25 cavalry, 4 veteran artillery, 11 militia). Nov 21: 2-hour artillery duel; J.J. Vallejo's beach battery did most damage; 5+ insurgents killed. Nov 22: 400 men landed with 4 field pieces; Estrada's 25 men overwhelmed. Solá retreated to Salinas, saving archives + 6,000 cartridges. Presidio burned Nov 26-27. Damage: ~$10,000. Only foreign capture of a California capital.
result: Only time a California presidio fell to an enemy; Monterey burned

notes: FORCE FIGURES DISAGREE and the feature flags none of it. Sola's own report (C-A 25 Doc 923): two frigates of 38 and 28 guns, MORE THAN 500 men. Pre-raid warning (C-A 26 Doc 1162): 34 and 18-20 guns, 250 men. C-A 55 Doc 339: 34 and 18, 230 crew. Prisoner Taylor (C-A 13 Doc 33): 235 crew. The feature's 38+2 howitzers / 26 guns / ~285 crew matches none of these. DATES: feature says Nov 20-26; Sola says the ships appeared on the 21st and 23rd; C-A 17 Doc 292 fixes the occupation at 22-25 Nov; C-A 13 Doc 293 (27 Nov) says the castillo and presidio were fired 'yesterday' (26 Nov); the Viceroy was told 24 Nov (C-A 13 Doc 66). Vallejo's beach battery is likewise absent from C-A; Bancroft attributes it entirely to the Californio dictations.

name: Bouchard's Raid on Refugio Ranch
summary: Dec 2: Bouchard landed, plundered and burned Ortega's ranch, killed cattle. Sgt. Carlos Carrillo with 30 men reached Sta Inés at 11:30 PM. Padres sent 40 armed neophytes + 35 more from SLO. Spanish ambush party captured 3 insurgents (Lt. William Taylor of Boston, Martin Romero, Mateo José Pascual).
result: Ranch destroyed; 3 insurgents captured by ambush
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), II:235-38. | Padre Ullibarri to Fr. Mariano Payeras, Santa Ines, 3 and 4 Jan. 1819, Archivo del Arzobispado (Arch. Arzob.), MS., iii, pt. ii, 24-26. | Correspondence of Payeras, Uria, Rodriguez and Martinez on the neophyte levies, Arch. Arzob., MS., iii, pt. ii, 35-37, 41; Arch. Sta Barbara, MS., vi, 277-80. | Sgt. Carlos Antonio Carrillo to Capt. Jose de la Guerra, Santa Ines, 2 Dec. 1818, 11.30 p.m., in Guerra, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS., iv, 197. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. i.1023-1029 / Savage pp. 225-227, scan n224-n226, Doc 285: Jose de la Guerra to Gov. Sola, 6 Dec. 1818 (Bancroft's 'Prov. St. Pap., MS., xx. 223'). | Provincial State Papers (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. i.119-120 / Savage pp. 35-37 (fol. 119-120), scan n34-n36, Doc 33: deposition of Lt. William Taylor of Boston, taken at Santa Ynes, Dec. 1818. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 13), tomo xx / Savage p. 38 (fol. 121-122), scan n36-n38, Doc 34: deposition of Martin Romero, Santa Ynes, Dec. 1818. | Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 17), tomo xl-lii, orig. p. 383 / Savage pp. 208-210, scan n207-n209, Doc 260: Gov. Sola to Capt. de la Guerra, Dec. 1818 (borrador), 'Desaprueba sus relaciones con los enemigos.'
notes: Bancroft II:236-37 nn.25-29 name every manuscript behind this episode; only some are in C-A. Date discrepancy to flag: Savage dated the Taylor deposition 'Abril 5' and the Romero deposition 'Oct 5' though both must be Dec 1818 / Jan 1819 (the catalog flags both). Bancroft's page arithmetic runs ~2 pp. behind Savage's foliation in C-A 13 (his 'xx. 223' = Savage p.225); the match here rests on content, not arithmetic. Bancroft himself resolves the Pascual puzzle: the negro Mateo Jose Pascual taken at Refugio was exchanged and then surrendered again at San Juan Capistrano, which is why he appears in both dossiers.

name: Bouchard at San Juan Capistrano
summary: Dec 14-15: Alf. Santiago Argüello with 30 men from San Diego posted on hill. Bouchard landed, requested supplies, refused. Minor damage; straw houses burned, wine/brandy spilled. 4 insurgent deserters surrendered (John Rose, Scotch drummer; Pedro Zaldíbar; Nicolás Chavarría; Mateo José Pascual).
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), II:240-42. | Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 17), tomo xl-lii, orig. p. 385 / Savage p. 214, scan n213, Doc 264: Gov. Sola to Tte. Jose Maria Ruiz, Monterey, 18 Dec. 1818. | Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 17), tomo xl-lii, orig. p. 386 / Savage pp. 215-216, scan n214-n215, Doc 266: Gov. Sola to Alf. Santiago Arguello, 18/19 Dec. 1818. | Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 17), tomo xlix (C-A 17 covers tomos xl-lii), 66-72 / Savage pp. 255-261, scan n254-n260, Doc 318: 'Declaraciones de insurgentes de la expedicion de Bouchard,' taken by Alf. Santiago Arguello at Mission San Juan Capistrano, 29 Dec. 1818. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. i.189-190 / Savage p. 63, scan n62, Doc 64: Conde del Venadito to the Governor, Mexico, 28 Oct. 1819 (Bancroft's 'Prov. St. Pap., MS., xx. 62'). | Provincial State Papers (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. i.331-334 / Savage pp. 88-91, scan n87-n90, Doc 95: Jose de la Guerra y Noriega to Gov. Sola, Santa Barbara, 6 Apr. 1819. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 13), tomo xx, orig. i.355-357 / Savage pp. 91-93, scan n90-n92, Doc 96: Alf. Santiago Arguello to Gov. Sola, San Diego, 7 Apr. 1819.
notes: Bancroft II:241 n.38 is the key: 'Names of the prisoners with their testimony. Prov. St. Pap., MS., xx. 62; Id., Ben. Mil., xlix. 66-72. Oct. 28, 1819, viceroy orders proceedings ... Prov. St. Pap., MS., xx. 62. Sola's communications to commandants Guerra and Ruiz on Dec. 18, 19 ... Prov. St. Pap., Ben. Mil., MS., xlix. 25-7.' All four resolve into C-A 13 and C-A 17. Name discrepancy to flag: the map (following Bancroft) gives 'Nicolas Chavarria of Bogota,' the C-A 17 depositions give 'Nicolas Blanco ... of Santa Fe,' and the viceroy's 1819 order gives 'Nicolas Echeverria (Santa Fe).' Three forms of one man; the manuscripts do not support 'Bogota.' The viceregal order also dates the desertion 'Oct/Nov 1818,' against the 15-16 Dec date the contemporary correspondence establishes.

name: Santa Clara Uprising Threat
summary: Fray Diego de Noboa warns: rancherías augmented, "rompimiento muy semejante al de Sonora" (uprising like Sonora). Exiled gentiles from Monterey/Santa Cruz fled with Christians. "Situación muy crítica."
sources: Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii-xiii, orig. pp. 129-133 / Savage pp. 50-54, scan n49-n53, Doc 86: Jose Perez Fernandez to Gov. Arrillaga, 15 Mar. 1794, 'Critica situacion, debiles escoltas,' enclosing Fr. Diego de Noboa's letter of 14 Mar. 1794 (at Savage p. 53 / scan n52). | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii-xiii, orig. pp. 127-128 / Savage p. 50, scan n49, Doc 85: Jose Perez Fernandez to Gov. Arrillaga, 1 Mar. 1794.
notes: The catalog entry for ca7-d86 carries its own cross-reference to this very map feature ('= prior mil-hist #43, at Sav p.53'), so the existing pointer and the record agree. One element of the map text is not evidenced in the catalog summary: 'Exiled gentiles from Monterey/Santa Cruz fled with Christians.' That detail, if correct, sits inside Noboa's enclosed letter on Savage p. 53 (scan n52) and I could not confirm it from the record without reading the leaf image; treat it as unverified. Bancroft's History of California does not narrate this warning at all (vol. 1 mentions Noboa only in the Santa Clara mission-statistics chapter), so the C-A document is the sole known source and there is no printed footnote to mine.

name: Stockade at Mission San José
summary: Estacada ordered: 70 varas long, 60 varas wide. Soldiers must carry arms at all times; weekly arms and cartridge inspection. Pedro Amador instructions.
sources: Provincial State Papers (C-A 9), tomo xvi / orig. pp. 54-55, scan n33, Doc 33: Sgt. Pedro Amador, 'Prevenciones al Cabo sobre los trabajos y el servicio,' Mission San Jose, 28 June 1797. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 9), tomo xvi / Savage pp. 51-53, scan n32-n33, Doc 32: diary of Sgt. Pedro Amador, expedition to found Mission San Jose, 9-28 June 1797. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 9), tomo xvi / Savage p. 48, scan n30, Doc 26: Comte. Jose Dario Arguello to Gov. Borica, San Francisco, 30 Sept. 1797, 'Sobre un proyecto de ataque.'. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: One wording correction for the map text: the document says the stockade plaza was marked out 70 varas long and 60 varas at its NARROWEST point ('60 at the narrowest'), not 60 varas wide; the enclosure was therefore irregular, not a rectangle. Bancroft's History of California carries no footnote to this order, so the C-A record stands alone. Amador's instructions were issued the day he closed his founding diary (28 June 1797), which is why the two records sit on adjacent leaves.

name: Indian Prisoners at San Diego
summary: "Indios presidiarios" maintained at $693/year at San Diego presidio. Indigenous prisoners as fiscal/military burden.
sources: Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 16), tomo xx-xxxix, orig. pp. 297-98 / Savage p. 181, scan n180, Doc 284: Habilitado Manuel Rodriguez, San Diego, account of 31 Dec. 1802, 'Gasto por presos.' | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii-xiii, orig. pp. xiii.50-51, scan n239, Doc 345: Comte. Antonio Grajera to Gov. Borica, San Diego, Sept. 1795 (rations of the Indian prisoners). | Provincial Records (C-A 23), tomo iii-iv, orig. pp. 61-62 / Savage p. 325, scan n330, Doc 864: Gov. Borica to the comandantes of San Diego and Santa Barbara, Monterey, 1796 (undated). Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Provincial Records (C-A 24), tomo v-vii, orig. p. 659 / Savage p. 508, scan n509, Doc 909: Gov. Borica to Fr. Martin de Landaeta, Monterey, 3 Apr. 1797.
notes: Two corrections to the map text. (1) DATE: the $693 figure is a single year-end account dated 31 Dec. 1802, not a 1794-1808 range; the range should be dropped or re-labelled as the span of the supporting records. (2) WORDING: the catalog summary reads 'presidio convicts (presidiarios), numbering 26 and up to 48' - it does NOT say they were Indians. The map's phrase 'indios presidiarios' is therefore unverified from this record; the ethnicity of the San Diego convicts is an inference (a reasonable one, given the separate Indian-prisoner records below, but an inference). I have not read the leaf image to see whether Savage's Spanish uses 'indios'; that would settle it. The three supporting records are genuine Indian-prisoner records at San Diego but none carries the $693 figure.

name: Neophyte Hermenegildo Condemned to Death
summary: Neophyte sentenced to capital punishment at San Diego. Extreme measure.
sources: Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 16), tomo xx-xxxix, orig. pp. 625-52 / Savage pp. 401-402, scan n400-n401, Doc 644: sentence by fiscal Ignacio Martinez, San Diego, 22 Mar. 1807. | Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 16), tomo xx-xxxix, orig. pp. 197-232 / Savage p. 313, scan n312, Doc 533: criminal case before fiscal Ignacio Martinez, San Diego, 20 Dec. 1807. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: Discrepancy to flag, not to reconcile. C-A 16 Doc 533 (Savage p. 313, 20 Dec. 1807, same fiscal Ignacio Martinez, same presidio) tries the neophytes Anastacio Cholopian, HERMENEGILDO and Atilano for the homicide of the Indian Juan and sentences the latter two to eight years in the San Blas arsenals. If that is the same Hermenegildo, the March death sentence was not carried out but revised on review - which would change the map's stated result from 'capital punishment' to 'death sentence, apparently commuted.' The catalog does not identify the two men with each other and the March record names no victim, so I have NOT merged them. Bancroft's History of California does not mention the case (his only Hermenegildos are Sal and an escolta soldier), so there is no printed footnote to arbitrate. Resolving this needs a read of Savage leaves n312 and n400-401.

name: Arms Inventory ALL CA Presidios
summary: Complete "Relación del Armamento" at San Gabriel. ALL 5 presidios: 263 swords (72 short), 376 mohanas (22 short), 289 escopetas (51 short), 434 pistol pairs. SF: 32 swords (13 short), 55 mohanas, 39 escopetas (12 short).

The map's per-presidio San Francisco line (32 swords/13 short, 55 mohanas, 39 escopetas/12 short) is NOT recoverable from the Savage abstract, which records only column heads and totals; it must come from the table on the leaf.
