II:274-277 / n297, the Dec-1780 arms state, noting only 39 of 195 escopetas were new and the swords too brittle to repair).

name: Chumash Revolt · Santa Inés
summary: LARGEST INDIGENOUS UPRISING IN CALIFORNIA. Trigger: flogging of Purísima neophyte by Cpl. Cota. Feb 21 afternoon: neophytes attacked soldiers, set fire to "a large part of mission buildings." Sgt. Anastasio Carrillo arrived next day with reinforcements. Hostile Indians fled to Purísima.
result: Chumash driven off; revolt spreads to La Purísima and Santa Barbara
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II: 1801-1824 (San Francisco: History Company, 1886), 527-36. | Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535-1846 (Santa Clara/Berkeley, 2001), 323-65 (Rafael González narrative). | Antonio Ripoll, 'Levantamiento de Indios en Santa Bárbara, 1824,' MS (Bancroft Library) · Ripoll's report of 5 May 1824 to Fr. Sarría. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. pp. 148-150 / scan n219-n221 (Savage 216-218), Doc 285: Gov. Luis Argüello to the Ministro de Guerra y Marina, Monterey, 21 April 1824 · official report of the revolt. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. p. 72 / scan n100 (Savage 101/100), Doc 134: Argüello to Comte. Ramírez, Monterey, 10 March 1824. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. pp. 75-76 / scan n105 (Savage 106/105), Doc 140: Argüello to Sgt. Ignacio Vallejo, Monterey, 24 March 1824 · the 2 a.m. dispatch. | Departmental State Papers (BANC MSS C-A 27), tomo I, orig. pp. 112-115, 130-131 / scan n31 (Savage 32), Doc 41: Capt. José Romero to Gov. Argüello, San Gabriel, 17 April 1824.
notes: The C-A series holds no eyewitness parte of the 21 Feb Santa Inés fight; Bancroft says as much ('Details of what happened here are not known'). All his Santa Inés detail is from Ripoll, Osio, Ord and the Archivo del Arzobispado; non-C-A. The four records above are the government correspondence the event generated, the strongest manuscript link available. DATE FLAG: C-A abstracts give the rising as 21-22 Feb; Osio (Bancroft II:530 n.43) says it began at Santa Inés on Saturday. Bancroft followed the official documents; the map follows Bancroft. Not reconciled. ALSO: ca18-d46 (C-A 18, LIV.50 / n101) records the Santa Inés indios Benito and Bernabé sentenced for 'la sublevación y asesinatos' but is dated 29 Jan 1824, BEFORE the revolt; a Savage date error or mis-keyed sequence. Not emitted until the leaf is checked.

name: Chumash Revolt · La Purísima Seized
summary: Same afternoon as Sta Inés. Cpl. Tapia + 4-5 soldiers defended families through night; surrendered when powder ran out. 4 white travelers killed (Sepúlveda, Sotelo + 2). 7 Indians killed. ~400 neophytes then fortified mission: palisades, loopholes in adobe, mounted old cannon + 2 swivel-guns, drilled for month. Padre Rodríguez stayed; "no disposition to molest him."
result: INDIGENOUS VICTORY; Chumash held fortified mission for 29 days
sources: Bancroft, History of California, II:528-33. | La Purísima Concepción, Libro de Misión, MS., 11 (mission burial register; Santa Barbara Mission Archive-Library). | Beebe and Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair, 323-65. | Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 18), tomo LVII, orig. 624-44 / scan n188-n189, Doc 161: trial and sentences, Misión de la Purísima, 23 March 1824 (tribunal: José de la Guerra, José Estrada, Subtte. Francisco de Haro). | Departmental State Papers (BANC MSS C-A 27), tomo II, orig. pp. 571-576 / scan n147-n150 (Savage 157-160), Doc 167: Lt. José Estrada, parte y detalle of the retaking of La Purísima, 16 March 1824 (copy certified by José Mª Estudillo, Monterey, 6 Oct 1826). Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. p. 217 / scan n291 (Savage 288/287), Doc 414: Argüello to the Comandante of San Francisco, Monterey, 26 March 1824.
notes: The 29-day occupation, Tapia's night defence and Padre Rodríguez's decision to stay are known only from Bancroft's non-C-A sources (Osio, Ord, Sarría in the Archivo del Arzobispado, Valdés). No C-A record narrates the night of 21-22 February at La Purísima; the C-A evidence is retrospective (the trial, the retaking parte, the governor's letterbook). Stated as inference, not fact. Companion C-A records not emitted, to avoid duplicating the recapture feature: ca46-d334 (25 Mar 1824, the same Estrada parte copied to a second correspondent) and ca56-d41 (C-A 56, XIV·334-335 / n19, the 26-name captive roster of those 'tomados en el alzamiento de las misiones [Purísima], Sta Barbª y Sta Inés', leaf-verified 2026-07-06).

name: Chumash Revolt · Santa Barbara
summary: Feb 22: Neophytes under Andrés armed themselves. Fought Capt. Guerra's troops "several hours" from behind corridor pillars with guns and arrows. Indians: 2 killed, 3 wounded (28 total dead later). Spanish: 4 wounded. Indians took property (respected church), fled to hills then Tulares. Ripoll "sat at a window at the presidio overlooking the mission, weeping."
result: Chumash strategic withdrawal to Tulares; retained autonomy for 4 months
sources: Antonio Ripoll, 'Levantamiento de Indios en Santa Bárbara, 1824,' MS (Bancroft Library), Ripoll's report of 5 May 1824 to Fr. Sarría. | María de las Angustias de la Guerra Ord, 'Ocurrencias en California,' MS (Bancroft Library dictation, 1878), 7-11. | Bancroft, History of California, II:530-31. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. pp. 148-150 / scan n219-n221 (Savage 216-218), Doc 285: Argüello to the Ministro de Guerra y Marina, Monterey, 21 April 1824. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. pp. 73-74 / scan n102-n103 (Savage 103/102), Doc 138: Argüello to Comte. Ramírez, Monterey, 31 March 1824. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. p. 16 / scan n25 (Savage 26/25), Doc 43: Argüello to the Ministro de Estado, Monterey, 24 July 1824. | State Papers, Sacramento (BANC MSS C-A 56), tomo XIV, orig. 334-335 / scan n19 (Savage 20), Doc 41: 'Lista de Indios presos por revolucionarios y Ladrones,' n.d. [1824].
notes: WARNING FOR ANY LATER EDITOR: ca46-d196 (C-A 46, Savage 149/148, scan n150, 15 Apr 1824) ranks first on content search here and looks perfect; Guerra's confidential parte on 'una acc.n reñida 5 1/2 horas, contra los Indios sublevados de la Mis.n de S.ta Bárb.a'. It is NOT the 22 Feb fight at the mission. Bancroft II:533-34 places that 5-hour action on 9 April at Buenavista Lake, when Lt. Narciso Fabregat took 80 men into the Tulares after the Santa Bárbara fugitives; the document concerns Fabregat's unexplained retreat. Deliberately not linked. ALSO: the map's '28 total dead later' is not in C-A at all; Bancroft II:531 n.44 takes it from Santa Barbara, Libro de Misión, MS., 45-6 (twelve buried by end of February plus a later certificate of sixteen more buried by their companions), a mission register, other-archive.

name: Recapture of La Purísima
summary: Lt. Estrada: 109 men (16 artillery, 23 cavalry, 35 infantry, 35 Indian auxiliaries) + 4-pounder. 8 AM attack. 400 neophytes returned fire from cannon, swivels, muskets + arrows. Neophyte guns ineffective; "ignorance of gunners." Canon may have burst, killing defenders. Cavalry cut off escape. P. Rodríguez interceded. Over at 10:30 AM. Indians: 16 killed, many wounded. Spanish: 3 wounded (1 mortal). 7 sentenced to death + shot. 4 ringleaders: 10 yrs exile.
result: Mexican victory; 2.5 hour battle; 7 Chumash leaders executed
sources: Departmental State Papers (BANC MSS C-A 27), tomo II, orig. pp. 571-576 / scan n147-n150 (Savage 157-160), Doc 167: Lt. José Estrada, parte y detalle of the assault and retaking of Mission La Purísima, 16 March 1824 (copy certified by José Mª Estudillo, Monterey, 6 October 1826). | Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 18), tomo LVII, orig. 624-44 / scan n188-n189, Doc 161: depositions, fallo and sentences, Misión de la Purísima, 23 March 1824. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 46), tomo I, orig. pp. 148-150 / scan n219-n221 (Savage 216-218), Doc 285: Argüello to the Ministro de Guerra y Marina, Monterey, 21 April 1824, forwarding Estrada's parte. | Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military) (BANC MSS C-A 20), tomo LXXXVIII, orig. p. 817 / scan n471 (Savage 472/69), Doc 497: Ministro de Guerra Terán to Comte. Luis A. Argüello, México, 31 July 1824 · rewards for the action. | Bancroft, History of California, II:532-34. | Rafael González, 'Experiencias de un soldado de California,' MS (Bancroft Library dictation, 1878).
notes: FORCE-SIZE DISCREPANCY, not reconciled. The map's 109 men (16 artillery, 23 cavalry, 35 infantry, 35 auxiliaries) is Bancroft's figure at II:531 n.45, citing 'Dept. St. Pap., Ben. Mil., MS., lviii. 7; lxxxvii. 64' (= C-A 18 and C-A 20), and it describes the force SENT SOUTH, not the force at the mission. Estrada's own parte (ca27-d167) says 80 men reached La Purísima, and ca46-d196 independently calls it 'una divis.n (aunq.e pequeña) de 80 homb.s'. I searched C-A 18 and C-A 20 for the two estado documents behind Bancroft's breakdown and could not identify them: UNRESOLVED, and I have not guessed one. Also: ca27-d167 is a certified copy made 6 Oct 1826, not the 1824 original; and the map dates the parte 16 March while Argüello's letterbook (ca46-d334, ca46-d414) says 17 March, probably action-report vs covering letter, unverified.

name: Estanislao's First Revolt · Sánchez Defeated
summary: ESTANISLAO; "a neophyte of more than ordinary ability, educated at Mission San José, of which establishment he was at one time alcalde." Ran away 1827-28 with CIPRIANO. By Nov 1828 PP. Durán and Viader warned Martínez of general rising. Earlier ~20-man expedition accomplished nothing. Estanislao continued "insulting challenges to the soldiers." May 5-8: Alf. Sánchez with ~40 men + damaged swivel-gun. Divided into 6 parties of 6 under Cpls. Piña, Berreyesa, Soto. 2 of Piña's men "so rash as to enter the wood"; killed. "Ammunition exhausted, men tired out, weather excessively hot." Estanislao left unconquered. Cpl. Soto and pvts. Peña and Pacheco praised for gallantry.
result: INDIGENOUS VICTORY; Sánchez's force repulsed with heavy losses (~50% casualty rate)
sources: José Sánchez, 'Campaña contra Estanislao y sus Indios sublevados, 1829,' MS (Bancroft Library), dated San José, 10 May 1829. | Fr. Narciso Durán and Fr. José Viader to Comte. Ignacio Martínez, 9 November 1828; Martínez to Echeandía, 20 November 1828 · Archivo del Arzobispado, Santa Bárbara, MS., v. pt. i. 68-70. | Beebe and Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair, 366-412. | Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco, 1885), 110-12. | State Papers, Missions and Colonization (BANC MSS C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp. 37-44 / scan n15-n20 (Savage 16-21), Doc 10: Alférez José Sánchez to Comte. Ignacio Martínez, San José, 16 May 1829 · report of the first expedition against Estanislao. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 48), tomo VII, orig. pp. 546-547 / scan n149, Doc 353: Gov. José Mª Echeandía to the Comandante of San Francisco, 8 May 1829 · order for the expedition. | Departmental Records (BANC MSS C-A 48), tomo VII, orig. pp. 606-608 / scan n172, Doc 423: Echeandía to the Comandante of San Francisco, 3 June 1829.
notes: DISCREPANCIES, flagged not reconciled. (1) ca53-d10 names 'cabo Antonio Soto, soldiers Manuel Piña & Tomás Pacheco'; Bancroft III:111 n.53 has 'Corp. Soto and privates Manuel Peña and Lorenzo Pacheco'. The map follows Bancroft. Two of three given names differ; a leaf check at n15-n20 would settle it. (2) Casualties: C-A gives 2 dead + 8 wounded + 3 auxiliaries wounded (1 mortally); Bancroft gives 2 dead, 8 wounded, ELEVEN auxiliaries wounded. The map's '~50% casualty rate' follows neither and looks like the map author's own arithmetic. (3) Bancroft flagged his order-date as suspect ('May 6th, probably an error in date'); the C-A copy reads 8 May 1829, still after Sánchez's 5 May departure. (4) METHOD: ca48-d353 was found by CONTENT search; 'Dept. Rec., MS., vii. 149' through the page resolver returns ca48-d38, a friar-loyalty roster; right arithmetic, wrong document.

name: Estanislao's Revolt · Vallejo's Expedition
summary: VALLEJO'S 3RD COMMAND; prior campaigns: Sierra Nevada from S. Miguel (1 killed, 15 wounded), Tulares (35 men, "slain 48 Indians, no casualties"). 107 men + 3-pounder. Set impenetrable wood on fire. Sánchez with 25 men fought 2+ hrs in burning wood. Vallejo with 37 men found "pits and ditches arranged with considerable skill"; "Indians could never have been dislodged except by the agency employed." Pursued to Arroyo Seco: "some negotiations" then Indians declared "they would die rather than surrender." Cut road through chaparral with axes; 8 wounded; ammunition ran out. Night: Indians escaped one by one. Morning: only dead bodies + 3 women. ATROCITY: Piña records 6+ captives killed. Osio: "order of no quarter given by Vallejo, infuriated auxiliaries wrought terrible carnage, pits for defences utilized as graves." Fiscal concluded: only 1 man + 1 woman killed; woman "unjustifiably by soldier Joaquín Alvarado." Martínez: "no decisive results obtained." Pardoned Oct 7, 1829.
result: Pyrrhic Mexican victory; Estanislao escaped; atrocity investigation
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 110-14. | St. Pap., Missions and Colonization (C-A 53), tomo ii. 24-36 / Savage 12-16, scan n11-n15, Doc 9. Mariano G. Vallejo (San José) to the comandante of the port of San Francisco, 4 June 1829 - official battle report of the campaign against Estanislao. | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (C-A 19), tomo lxx. 518-541 / Savage 45, scan n45, Doc 47. Lt. Ignacio Martínez, fiscal, San Francisco, 31 Oct. 1829 - inquiry into the Indians killed on the punitive expedition. | Departmental Records (C-A 48), tomo vii. 797-98, scan n229, Doc 614. Echeandía to the comandante of San Francisco, 7 Oct. 1829 - 'Perdón á Indios sublevados'. | St. Pap., Missions and Colonization (C-A 53), tomo ii. 37-44 / Savage 16-21, scan n15-n20, Doc 10. Alf. José Sánchez (San José) to comandante Ignacio Martínez, 16 May 1829 - report of the FIRST, failed expedition against Estanislao. | Departmental Records (C-A 48), tomo vii. 546-47, scan n149, Doc 353. Echeandía to the comandante of San Francisco, 8 May 1829 - orders the expedition under alférez José Sánchez, with a 3-pounder. | Departmental Records (C-A 48), tomo vii. 606-08, scan n172, Doc 423. Echeandía, 3 June 1829 - 'Expedición contra Indios': deplores the casualties of Sánchez's expedition and demands the pormenores, the diario and the parte oficial. | Vallejo, Campaña contra Estanislao y sus Indios sublevados, 1829, MS. (Bancroft Library). | Piña, Diario de la Expedición al Valle de San José, 1829, MS. (Bancroft Library) - the diary of artillery corporal Joaquín Piña, 19 May to 13 June 1829. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), i. 174, 175; xx. 280. | Antonio María Osio, Historia de California, MS., 126-38 (Bancroft dictation; published as The History of Alta California, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 1996). | William Heath Davis, Glimpses of the Past in California, 282-89.
notes: Two discrepancies to flag, not reconciled. (1) CASUALTIES: the map text (from Bancroft) says the fiscal found 'only 1 man + 1 woman killed'; Vallejo's own report (ca53-d9) states 'several rebels + 3 women killed, 3 women captured' and 11 men + 2 auxiliaries wounded. Savage's abstract of Vallejo and the fiscal's finding do not agree, and Bancroft prints both without resolving them. (2) DATES: the map header reads 'May 29 - Jun 4, 1829'; ca53-d9 says the force set out 26 May with 107 men, a cannon and 2,500 cartridges, and the report is dated at San José 4 June. Bancroft's 29 May is the San Joaquin crossing, not the departure. Also note ca19-d47's catalogue summary hedges the commander's forename ('Gonzalo?'); the hedge is resolved by the record's own content, which names soldier Alvarado exactly as Bancroft's footnote does.

name: Vallejo vs. Guapos (Sotoyomes)
summary: VALLEJO'S SONOMA FRONTIER. Cainameros (allies near Sta Rosa) attacked by Sotoyomes/"Guapos"; 22 killed, 50 wounded. Chiefs appealed to Vallejo. Apr 1: 50 soldiers + 100 Indians + Cainamero force. Salvador Vallejo commanded one division. Apr 4: Battle in Geyser region hills. Guapos "routed and driven back to their rancherías, where most of them were killed." Apr 7: back at Sonoma, zero casualties. Jun 7: TREATY with 7 tribes (Yoloytoy, Guilitoy, Ansactoy, Liguaytoy, Aclutoy, Churuptoy, Guapos). Approved by Gov. Chico. 1837: Chief Zampay of Yoloytoy revolted; captured by Solano + Salvador Vallejo; eventually became "peaceful citizen and industrious farmer."
result: Decisive Mexican victory; zero casualties; 7-tribe treaty followed
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 70-72. | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (Military) (C-A 20), tomo lxxxi. 530 / Savage 237, scan n236, Doc 279. Gov. Mariano Chico (San Gabriel) to Mariano G. Vallejo, 27 June 1836 - approves the treaties Vallejo made on the northern frontier with several Indian tribes. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 104 - Vallejo's orders for assembling troops, 28 March 1836. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 105 - report of the campaign, 8 April 1836 (Salvador Vallejo commanded one division). | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 193 - Comandante General Gutiérrez thanks Lt. Vallejo and his men for their gallantry, 21 April 1836. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iii. 119, 217 - the treaty of 7 June 1836 with the chiefs of seven tribes. | No C-A manuscript located for the battle of 1-7 April 1836 in the Geyser region.
notes: The existing citation 'Dept. St. Pap. Ben. Mil. LXXXI.25-7' does resolve into C-A 20, but the only record in that neighbourhood whose content concerns the treaty is ca20-d279, Chico's approval of 27 June 1836. I found NO record carrying the text of the seven-tribe treaty of 7 June 1836 itself; I checked ca20-d275 through ca20-d288 individually and they are musters, pay budgets, mail arrangements and recruiting notes. The treaty text is therefore either unabstracted by Savage or survives only in Vallejo, Doc., iii. 119, 217. Second flag: I could find NO C-A record of the 1-7 April 1836 battle in the Geyser hills. Bancroft himself cites only Vallejo Documentos for it, which is consistent with the Sonoma frontier's operational correspondence living in C-B rather than C-A.

name: Battle of Soscol · Horse Thieves
summary: 50 Indian horse-thieves crossed Sacramento, appeared at Soscol with band of tame horses, aiming to stampede Sonoma horses. 34 killed in battle with Vallejo's men; rest surrendered. Chief CUMUCHÍ shot at Sonoma for his crimes.
result: Decisive Mexican victory; 34 killed, 0 Mexican casualties
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 72-73. | Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo iv. 498-501 / Savage 223, scan n220, Doc 253. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma) to Juan Bautista Alvarado, 7 August 1838 - reports the August 1838 encounter with predatory Indians, prisoners taken, and asks to found a new establishment to contain the depredations. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), v. 124 - Vallejo's circular to the authorities, 3 August 1838, with Cumuchí's confession about the droves of stolen horses on the Sacramento in charge of the Moquelumnes.
notes: DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: Bancroft (from Vallejo, Doc., v. 124) gives 34 killed and names the executed chief Cumuchí; the C-A record, Vallejo's own letter of 7 August 1838, says only 'tuvo un encuentro con algunos Indios depredadores y mataron algunos' and that he holds some prisoners. Savage's abstract carries no number and no chief's name. I regex-grepped the entire catalogue for Cumuchi / Cumuchí / Soscol / Suscol and got zero hits, so the name Cumuchí and the figure 34 rest solely on the C-B circular. Note also that the map dates the engagement to August 1838 and places it at Soscol; Vallejo's C-A letter is dated Sonoma, 7 August 1838 and does not name the place.

name: Capture of Zampay (Yoloytoy)
summary: Chief ZAMPAY of the Yoloytoy broke the 1836 treaty, "committing many outrages and trying to arouse the Sotoyomes again." Head chief MOTI offered to aid his capture. Combined forces of SOLANO and SALVADOR VALLEJO effected capture. Zampay held captive at Sonoma but eventually "became a peaceful citizen and industrious farmer."
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 72. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), iv. 250, 256 - M. G. Vallejo to his brothers Salvador and Jesús, 25-26 June 1837. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xxxii. 104 - Alvarado thanks Salvador Vallejo for his gallant achievement, 26 July 1837. | Salvador Vallejo, Notas Históricas sobre California, MS., 7-65 (Bancroft Library dictation). | Mariano G. Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales (Historia de California), MS., iii. 230-38, 298-99, 299-304 (Bancroft Library dictation). | No C-A manuscript located for the capture of Zampay, June 1837.
notes: This is a recorded null for the C-A series. Every manuscript Bancroft cites for the Zampay episode is in the Vallejo Documentos (C-B) or is a Bancroft dictation. The map's existing citation is already correct as to collection; my only correction is that it is not a C-A citation and should not be expected to yield an archivesofcalifornia.com link.

name: Sacking of Pacheco/Sánchez Ranchos
summary: Indians sacked ranchos of Pacheco and Sánchez near San Juan Bautista: killed 1 white man, "outraging several women, burning the buildings, and destroying all they could lay their hands on." Sánchez rancho also attacked March 1837 (2 Indians killed). Riflemen at Monterey demanded $2 each before pursuing.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 75-76. | Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo iv. 468-469 / Savage 213-214, scan n210-n211, Doc 238. Antonio María Osio (Monterey) to his cousin [José Castro], 24 July 1838 - 'Relativo á depredaciones de Indios'. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), v. 116-17, 129. | Hartnell, Narrativa, MS., 5 (Bancroft Library dictation); Mariano G. Vallejo, Historia de California, MS., iii. 378-80.
notes: Partial coverage, flagged. Osio's letter (ca29-d238) attests the Pacheco rancho attack - one gente de razón killed and several wounded - and adds two murders at Hartnell's rancho that Bancroft does not mention in his text. It does NOT mention the Sánchez rancho, the sexual assaults, or the burning of the buildings; those details come from Vallejo, Doc., v. 116-17, 129 and from Hartnell's Narrativa. So this record confirms the engagement but not every element of the map's summary. Note also that Bancroft's footnote cites Hartnell, Narrativa, MS., 5 - and Osio's letter is the contemporaneous report of the killings at Hartnell's own rancho, an independent corroboration Bancroft did not use.

name: Death of Yozcolo at Santa Clara
summary: Party of YOZCOLOS attacked neophytes guarding wheat-fields at Santa Clara, killing 1. Leader DIOSCULO/YOZCOLO was killed and "his head set up on a pole at the mission." This is the same Yoscolo linked to Estanislao by Davis; confirmed ex-neophyte resistance leader.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 76. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), viii. 4, 41; and viii. 46 (21 August 1839, a 75-man party returned to San José from the pursuit of eleven runaways, two killed). | No C-A manuscript located for the death of Yozcolo at Santa Clara, July 1839. Bancroft's 'St. Pap., Miss., MS., ix. 60-1' does not resolve to a Santa Clara record in C-A 51.
notes: Recorded null with a positive finding about the citation. The map's existing citation 'St. Pap., Miss., MS., ix. 60-1' does NOT resolve to a Santa Clara document in the C-A series. I tested both possible readings of Bancroft's tomo pagination against C-A 51 and both fail, and I verified one of them against the leaf image rather than the catalogue. A user clicking this feature should be told the manuscript is not currently locatable in C-A, not sent to a wrong leaf.

name: Prado Mesa Ambush on Río de Estanislao
summary: Alf. PRADO MESA on expedition against thieves on "Río de Estanislao" (Stanislaus River). Surprised by the foe. 3 citizen volunteers killed, Mesa wounded, 6 of his men wounded, many weapons lost. Desiderio Briones left behind; found 7 days later by Francisco Palomares. "This disaster caused much excitement and alarm. The Indians became bolder than ever."
result: INDIGENOUS VICTORY; Mexican force routed with heavy losses
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 76. | Dept. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43), tomo iv. 19 (Savage stamp 245), orig. pp. 72-73, scan n245, Doc 546. Manuel Jimeno (Monterey) to the Prefect of the 1st District, 15 December 1839 - on the 'suceso desgraciado' of alférez Prado's party against Indian horse-thieves; alférez Rafael Pinto marches with 15 soldiers to Mission San José. | Departmental Records (C-A 49), tomo x. 75 / Savage x·17, scan n172, Doc 451. Gov. Alvarado (Monterey) to the administrator of San José, 13 December 1839 - alférez Rafael Pinto sallies with 15 soldiers against the Tulare Indians. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 29), tomo iv. 725-26 / Savage 287, scan n282, Doc 360. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma) to Gov. Alvarado, 26 December 1839 - 'Sobre depredaciones de indios en San José. Falta de fuerza pública.'. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xxv. 249; viii. 368, 373, 375, 382, 394-95. | San José Archives, MS., i. 43-46 (the Pueblo Papers of San José).
notes: This feature resolves unusually cleanly: two of Bancroft's footnote citations land on exactly the right record by their own page numbers, and a third lands one page off in the direction I verified independently for C-A 29. Note the map's date, 'December 1839', is right: the disaster is reported to Monterey by 13 December and the governor's relief order goes out the same day. None of the three C-A records gives the casualty figures; the three killed, Mesa wounded, six wounded and Desiderio Briones found seven days later all come from Vallejo, Doc., and from the San José Archives.

name: Sonoma Native Infantry Revolt
summary: Vallejo's own Indian infantry company; "about 25 selected Indians given Spanish names on the rosters, armed with muskets"; attempted revolt. "Many of the number were killed in a fight, and nine were subsequently shot." A trained indigenous military unit turned against its commanders.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 74. | Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 30), tomo v. 17-18 / Savage 6, scan n5, Doc 7. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma), 12 April 1840 - 'Sobre sublevación de tropa': the frontier infantry company rose on the night of the 9th, meaning to destroy the cavalry and kill Chief Solano; alférez Lázaro Piña with many rancherías and gentiles under their chiefs attacked them, killed many and shot those taken. | Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 30), tomo v. 19-21 / Savage 6, scan n5, Doc 8. Mariano G. Vallejo (Sonoma) to the Jefe de las Californias, 13 April 1840 - forwards the document on what happened on the frontier, explaining that it kept him from going to San Francisco for the sailing of the ship carrying the foreign prisoners. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), viii. 192; xiv. 18; xxxiii. 56-57; and Vallejo, Historia de California, MS., iv. 166-68.
notes: DATE CORRECTION and a discrepancy. (1) The map dates this 'April 1840' with month confidence; Vallejo's own letter fixes the rising to the night of 9 April 1840, so the date can be tightened to 9-12 April 1840. (2) DISCREPANCY: Savage's abstract says the rebels were attacked by alférez Lázaro Piña together with many rancherías and gentiles under their own chiefs, who 'matan á muchos y fusilan á los cogidos' - killed many and shot those taken. It gives no number. Bancroft's 'nine were subsequently shot' comes from Vallejo, Doc., viii. 192 / xiv. 18 / xxxiii. 56-57, not from this record. (3) A detail the map omits and the manuscript supplies: the mutineers' stated aim was to destroy the cavalry and kill Chief Solano, and the force that put them down was itself largely indigenous.

name: CLEAR LAKE MASSACRE · Salvador Vallejo
summary: LARGEST SINGLE-DAY DEATH TOLL IN CALIFORNIA. Capt. SALVADOR VALLEJO: 70 Californians + 200 auxiliary Indians. 12 soldiers + 30 auxiliaries reached island of "Moth" by rafts. Night attack 8-11 PM. 170 INDIANS KILLED. Official report placed island "near Cape Mendocino"; actually Clear Lake. Bojorges: real objective was slave-raiding ("to obtain Indian laborers and servants"). Dr. Sandels: attack was "in the absence of all the fighting men." Negro deserter "shot in the back." Governor ordered investigation; result unknown. Tribes: Mottiyomi, Chiliyomi, Holiyomi, Tuliyomi, Supuyomi, + 4 more.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 162-63. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 342 - Salvador Vallejo, from Mendocino, to M. G. Vallejo, 13 March 1843, describing the previous evening's fight. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 354 - Col. M. G. Vallejo's report to the governor, 1 April 1843, naming the tribes (Mottiyomi, Chiliyomi, Holiyomi, Tuliyomi, Supuyomi, Paguenjelayomi, Sicomyomi, Hayomi, Clustinomayomi). | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 361 - on the killing of the negro deserter. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS. (BANC MSS C-B), xi. 366 - the governor to Vallejo, 26 April 1843, ordering a strict investigation because 'the public mind is troubled about the killing of so many Indians'. | Juan Bojorges, Recuerdos sobre Historia de California, MS., 24-37 (Bancroft Library dictation). | G. M. Waseurtz af Sandels, A Sojourn in California by the King's Orphan (Sandels's narrative), for the eyewitness account of the party's return to Sonoma. | No C-A manuscript located for the Clear Lake massacre of 12-13 March 1843.
notes: Recorded null for the C-A series, and I want to be explicit about why: this is one of the best-documented atrocities on the map and none of its documentation is in the Archives of California. Every manuscript Bancroft used is in Vallejo Documentos (BANC MSS C-B), because the Sonoma frontier command's operational correspondence went into Vallejo's private files rather than the departmental archive. The map's existing citation is accurate as to the documents; it simply names a collection that will never yield an archivesofcalifornia.com link. Note also the geography flag Bancroft himself raises and the map repeats: Salvador Vallejo's official report placed the island near Cape Mendocino, and Bancroft concludes on Bojorges's evidence that the scene was Clear Lake.

name: Chaguanosos Steal 1,200 Horses from SLO
summary: CHAGUANOSOS (Shawnees from New Mexico, under Canadian chiefs, in league with trappers). Stole 1,200 horses from San Luis Obispo. "Well armed, ready for any kind of profitable adventure." Pursuers from LA saw "the foe retiring deliberately and independently" but "thought it imprudent to risk a conflict, especially when they saw that among the Chaguanosos there were more Americans than Indians."
result: Raiders escaped unchallenged; Mexicans too afraid to attack
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. IV: 1840-1845 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 77. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 316-318, scan n506, Doc 1248. Circular from the Santa Bárbara administration to San Fernando and Los Angeles, 26 April 1840, relaying San Luis Obispo's report of the 24th that a party of Chaguanosos drove off several caballadas. | Dept. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43), tomo iv. 21 (Savage stamp 247), orig. pp. 87-88, scan n247, Doc 554. Manuel Jimeno to the Encargado del Juzgado de 1a Instancia of the 1st District, Monterey, 9 May 1840 - the Chaguanosos have stolen 1,000 horses at San Luis Obispo. | Dept. St. Pap., San José (C-A 45), orig. pp. 314-15 / Savage stamp 250, hand 71, scan n251, Doc 83. Manuel Jimeno to the juez of San José, Monterey, 9 May 1840 - heading 'Chaguanosos': the Chaguanoso rustlers entered the San Luis Obispo establishment, took more than 1,000 animals and threatened the servants. | Departmental Records (C-A 49), tomo xi. 69 / Savage xi·14, scan n219, Doc 562. Casarín to the juez of San Luis Obispo, Monterey, May 1840 - pursue the 'extranjeros chaguanosos' who stole more than 1,000 head. | Departmental Records (C-A 49), tomo xi. 63-65 / Savage xi·12, scan n217, Doc 557. Casarín to the juez de paz of San José, Monterey, 27 April 1840 - orders him to coordinate with Castro to pursue the Chaguanosos. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 426-429, scan n525-n526, Doc 1292. Tiburcio Tapia to the jueces de paz 1o and 2o, 23 May 1840 - a 10-man advance guard sent to observe the enemy; the raiders had gone with the caballada and darkness prevented tracking; the pursuit party inventoried at 13 men, 4 muskets, 7 pairs of pistols, 19 lances, 22 sabres, 445 cartridges. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 430-432, scan n526, Doc 1293. Ignacio Palomares (San Bernardino) to the juez de paz, 19 May 1840 - combat report: of a 23-man party, in an attack on the Chaguanosos there were deaths; he broke off as tired horses let his men fall to the raiders. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 461-469, scan n533-n534, Doc 1308. Juan Bautista Leandri to the Prefect, May 1840 - three documents including the campaign report of 30 May: the 36-man party under José Antonio Carrillo returned the night of the 28th; on the 25th it overtook the thieves at the paraje 'agua de Ramón' about 100 leagues out; 'El número de ladrones que componía la retaguardia era la de 20 hombres Ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos.' | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados tomo iv, doc pp. 492-498, scan n539-n540, Doc 1321. Felipe Lugo to the Prefect, 9 June 1840 - transcribes Carrillo's campaign parte: the 36-man party set out at 3 a.m. on 23 May, tracked raiders who had a four-day start with about 3,000 head; the rearguard, surprised just before sunset at 'agua de Ramón', 'se componía de 20 hombres todos rifleros' and fled headlong, abandoning gear and about 500 cattle dead of hunger and thirst; not pursued further for the bad state of the horses and want of provisions. | Dept. St. Pap., Benicia, Prefecturas y Juzgados, MS., vi. 69-70; Duflot de Mofras, Exploration du Territoire de l'Oregon, i. 379.
notes: This is the richest feature in the batch: nine C-A records, two of them matching Bancroft's footnote page citations exactly. NUMBERS DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: the map and Bancroft say 1,200 horses; the two governor's circulars of 9 May 1840 (ca43-d554, ca45-d83) say 1,000 and 'mas de 1000 bestias'; Casarín's order (ca49-d562) says 1,000+; and Carrillo's own campaign parte (ca34-d1321, ca34-d1308) says the raiders were driving about 3,000 head and lost more than half of them, abandoning about 1,500 dead animals. The manuscripts do not support a single figure. DATE: the map says April 1840; the San Luis Obispo report is dated 24 April, relayed 26 April, and the governor's circulars follow on 9 May, with the Los Angeles pursuit running 19-30 May. CORRECTION to the map's claim that the pursuers never engaged: ca34-d1293 records Palomares's party of 23 actually attacking the Chaguanosos with deaths on the field before he broke off, and ca34-d1307 records him recovering the caballadas beyond the Matanceras with one man wounded and one unaccounted for. Bancroft's 'thought it imprudent to risk a conflict' describes Carrillo's later party, not Palomares's.

name: Indian Attacks near San Diego
summary: Late-period indigenous military action near San Diego. Juana Machado's firsthand account describes continued frontier violence in the Mexican period.
sources: Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535-1846 (Santa Clara and Berkeley: Santa Clara University / Heyday Books, 2001), 413-19 - the Juana Machado account. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), orig. pp. 420-424 / Savage 86-89, scan n87-n90, Doc 188. Agustín V. Zamorano to the ayuntamiento, San Diego, 29 May 1837 - the Jacum battle and the call for a general expedition. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 34), Prefecturas y Juzgados, doc pp. 437-38, scan n281-n282, Doc 676. José Antonio Estudillo (San Diego) to the Juez 1er Constitucional, 26 June 1837 - San Diego forms a 23-man guard to repel the continual threatened invasion by the sierra Indians, who 'han devastado, incendiado los ranchos' of the district. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), orig. pp. 433-434 / Savage 92, scan n93, Doc 193. Gov. Alvarado to the alcalde, Santa Bárbara, 3 August 1837 - aid Capt. Pablo de la Portilla with every resource 'para la persecución de los indios que han cometido depredaciones en Sn Diego'. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), tomo xii. 212-214 / Savage xii·17, scan n198, Doc 463. Manuel Jimeno to Tapia, Monterey, 22 November 1837 - 'Sublevación de gentiles en la frontera Sur (S. Diego)': approves the measures for defending the port of San Diego; the Comandante de la Frontera reported the invasion without stating its causes, which Padre Caballero and the comandante are to report. | Dept. St. Pap., Angeles (C-A 37), tomo xii. 234-236 / Savage xii·22, scan n203, Doc 473. Manuel Jimeno to the Prefect of the 2nd District, Monterey, 7 November 1837 - 'Sobre medidas contra indios sublevados en San Diego'. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement.
notes: Two things the map should know. (1) This feature is a generic container ('Late-period indigenous military action near San Diego, 1837') resting on a single printed testimonio. The C-A series documents that year on the San Diego frontier in detail, and I have supplied five records that between them give a chronology: the Jacum battle of May 1837, the 23-man guard formed at San Diego in June, Alvarado's August order to reinforce Portilla's pursuit, and the November rising of the sierra gentiles. (2) ca37-d188 is not a background paper, it is the record of a distinct engagement in which the Californio force was beaten - 'QUEDÓ EL CAMPO PR LOS ENEMIGOS'. If the map carries or should carry a separate 'Battle of Jacum, 1837' feature, that record belongs to it, and linking it here is second best. I have flagged it rather than quietly folding it in. Note also that the Juana Machado testimonio is a Bancroft Library dictation ('Los tiempos pasados de la Alta California') that Beebe and Senkewicz translate and print; the map cites the printed book, which is correct as it stands.

name: Indian Attacks near Guadalupe
summary: Late frontier violence near Guadalupe (Santa Barbara County). José Luciano Espinosa and María Gracia accounts describe indigenous raids in the final years before American conquest.
sources: Rose Marie Beebe and Robert M. Senkewicz, eds., Lands of Promise and Despair: Chronicles of Early California, 1535-1846 (Santa Clara and Berkeley: Santa Clara University / Heyday Books, 2001), 420-27 - the José Luciano Espinosa and María Gracia accounts. | No C-A manuscript located for an Indian attack near Guadalupe, Santa Barbara County, in 1840.
notes: A GEOGRAPHY FLAG that the map's owner needs to resolve before any link is attached. The feature is plotted at 34.97 / -120.57, which is Guadalupe in Santa Barbara County (Rancho Guadalupe, near Santa Maria), and the summary glosses it that way. I could not find a single C-A record of an Indian attack at that Guadalupe in any year, let alone 1840: I grepped the whole catalogue for Arellanes, Nipomo, Rancho Guadalupe and Olivera, and listed every 1840 record mentioning Santa Bárbara, San Luis Obispo or La Purísima, and the 1840 material for that stretch of coast is entirely the Graham affair, the Carrillo conspiracy depositions, and presidial musters. The ONLY 'Indian attack near Guadalupe' documented in the corpus is at Mission Guadalupe del Norte on the BAJA CALIFORNIA frontier, in the San Diego demarcation - about 500 miles south of where the pin sits. Two candidate records are named in my evidence below, deliberately NOT emitted as links. Someone should check Beebe and Senkewicz pp. 420-427 to see which Guadalupe José Luciano Espinosa and María Gracia are actually talking about; if it is the Baja mission, both the pin and the summary's 'Santa Barbara County' gloss are wrong. Second, smaller flag: the map dates the feature 1840 with year confidence, while the Baja Guadalupe siege records are dated 1839.

name: Castillo de San Joaquín fires on the Saturnina (friendly fire)
summary: Earliest known shore-battery firing at San Francisco. Hermenegildo Sal's guard sighted a sail at 8 a.m. and fired a warning shot; getting no reply, manned the Cantil Blanco battery (8 cannon; the future Castillo de San Joaquín / Fort Point) intending to sink her, and fired 8 cannon-shots from 11 a.m. until 5 p.m. Pilot Juan Carrasco then identified her as the Spanish navy schooner Saturnina, carrying Bodega y Quadra's Nootka dispatches, driven in for water.
result: Friendly-fire blunder; predates the 1803 Lelia Byrd as a battery-fires-on-ship episode
sources: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), tomo i. 304-5 / scan n68-69, Doc 130 - Hermenegildo Sal (San Francisco) to Gob. Arrillaga, 10 Sept. 1792, 'Haber hecho fuego contra un buque espanol por equivocacion.'
notes: Bancroft NULL RESULT (recorded per the null-results rule): grepped vol1 for Saturnina, Carrasco, 'by mistake', 'fired upon' and read I:490-532. Bancroft nowhere narrates this friendly-fire episode, so there is no book source and no footnote to mine. The one Saturnina passage (I:532) is Borica's 1794 gulf voyage. Vessel identity corroborated but NOT linked: ca6-d141 has the goleta Saturnina 'procedente de Nuca' as the Limites-expedition schooner, ca6-d199 gives her alias 'La Orcasitas'.

name: English ships at Bodega Bay (Indian intelligence)
summary: An Indian "de las Islas" reports two ships at Puerto de la Bodega, ashore 4 days taking water and wood, hunting deer, and trading otter skins for cattle; the sailors believed English. Sal to Arrillaga. Foreign use of unguarded Bodega as the back door to SF Bay during the Nootka-crisis / Vancouver season. Related to #41 (1793 English ship at Bodega with cannons on land).
result: Coastal-defense intelligence; consecutive-year foreign presence at the bay Spain meant to occupy
sources: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), tomo i. 296 / scan n66-67, Doc 124 - Hermenegildo Sal (San Francisco) to Gob. Arrillaga, 8 Oct. 1792, 'Buques ingleses en Bodega.' | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (San Francisco, 1884), 516 n.29.
notes: Bancroft's footnote cites 'St. Pap., Sac., MS., vi. 67-8' and ca55-d124's Savage page is 67-68, so for C-A 55 tomo vi Bancroft's page = the record's savage_page column (his next cite, 'Id., vi. 98', likewise lands on ca55-d160 savage 98, the Jan 1793 second sighting the map assigns to feature #41). Useful resolver rule, but note it does NOT hold for tomo vii (see reg-92). I found no Arrillaga reply or Prov. Rec. counterpart for the Oct 1792 report.

name: The "Sochem" engagement
summary: After gentiles killed a Christian Indian of Mission San Miguel, an alférez + 5 soldiers seized 3 of the killers; on the return ~300 armed Indians attacked the patrol. The soldiers killed 1, wounded 2 and withdrew, but the alférez's horse was killed and the 3 captives escaped. Grajera then fortified against a feared assault on the mission.
sources: Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xiii. 507-509 / scan n441-442, Doc 567 - Antonio Grajera (San Diego) to Gob. Borica, 13 May 1795: clash at the rancheria 'Sochem' behind Mission San Miguel. | Provincial Records (C-A 24), tomo v. 322 / scan n139-140, Doc 223 - Gob. Borica (Monterey) to Antonio Grajera (San Diego), 7 June 1795. | Provincial Records (C-A 24), tomo v. 175-6 / scan n375, Doc 570 - Gob. Borica to the Viceroy, 1795, 'Sobre Indios de Jacom, S.n Diego.' | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xiii. 188-189 / scan n299-300, Doc 403 - Viceroy Branciforte (Mexico) to Gob. Borica, 18 Sept. 1795. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (San Francisco, 1884), 652-53 (and I:547).
notes: Location now CONFIRMED, not inferred: ca24-d570 places the pursuit at 'la Rancheria de Jacom [Jacum/Jacumba]' with the return toward 'la mis.n de S.n Miguel' 5-6 leagues off, and Bancroft I:653 calls San Miguel a Dominican establishment 'in La Frontera' - i.e. San Miguel de la Frontera, Baja California, not San Miguel Arcangel. DISCREPANCIES flagged, not reconciled: (1) the rancheria is 'Sochem' in ca7-d567 but 'Jacom' in ca24-d570; (2) attacker strength ~300 in ca7-d567 vs ~200 in ca24-d223, ca24-d570 and Bancroft; (3) Bancroft dates it 'May or June 1795' and 'June', the C-A records 17-18 Apr 1795. Bancroft's footnote page arithmetic (Prov. Rec. v. 227-8, Prov. St. Pap. xiii. 215-16) does not resolve to these records; the links rest on content, not page match.

name: San Luis Obispo Indian conspiracy
summary: A thwarted mission uprising: instigators Miguel and Marito used beads as recruitment currency; La Purísima gentiles were jailed and set to forced labor; the commandant downplayed it. Part of the 1794 unrest arc with the Santa Clara / SF crisis (#43); recurs in Arrillaga's "Estado de las Californias" (ringleaders sent to SF-fort forced labor).
sources: Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 263 / scan n104, Doc 166 - Goycoechea to Arrillaga, 20 Sept. 1794, 'Sedicion de Indios' at San Luis. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 268-269 / scan n106-107, Doc 171 - Goycoechea to Arrillaga, 12 Sept. 1794: declarations of the imprisoned La Purisima gentiles. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 273 / scan n108, Doc 174 - Goycoechea to Arrillaga, 4 Sept. 1794: Alf. Pablo Cota returns from La Purisima with the accomplices. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 491-498 / scan n192-202, Doc 287 - Arrillaga to Borica, 1794, 'Estado de las Californias' / Papel de Puntos, pts. 22-25. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 271-272 / scan n108, Doc 173 - Goycoechea to Arrillaga, 4 Sept. 1794: the indio 'Chuarquin' held in grillos. DOES NOT BELONG TO THIS FEATURE. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (San Francisco, 1884), 547 and 689.
notes: NAME DISCREPANCY flagged: the instigators are 'Miguel & Marito' in ca7-d174 but 'Miguel & Morillo' in ca7-d287. Bancroft (I:547 n.42 and I:689 n.51) cites Prov. St. Pap. xii. 33, 49-53, 100-4, 124-32, 192-4 for this episode; I ran those through the resolver and they land on unrelated records (Santa Cruz sailors, Loreto musters), i.e. Bancroft's tomo-xii page numbers do not agree with the catalog's page column for C-A 7. The links here rest wholly on content, not page arithmetic. Bancroft also disagrees on scale: he says 'five ringleaders' condemned, ca7-d174 reports 9 Indians + 17 gentiles brought in.

name: The Charquín uprising at Mission San Francisco
summary: The Christian Indian Charquín rebelled at Mission San Francisco, took up arms against the mission Christians, and held ~20 mission women and children captive in the sierra; reported by Sgt. Miguel Pacheco. An early-1790s armed mission revolt led by a baptized Indian; a precursor to the Bay Area resistance cluster (#7 / #9).
sources: State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 55), tomo vii. 57-64 / scan n159-163, Doc 207, item No 3 - Hermenegildo Sal, habilitado (San Francisco), to Gob. int. Arrillaga, 27 Feb. 1793. | Provincial Records (C-A 22), tomo ii. 585-589 / scan n362-364, Doc 2046 - Gob. Arrillaga (Monterey) to the Comandante of San Francisco, 1793: 'aprehension de Charquin.' | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 491-498 / scan n192-202, Doc 287 - Arrillaga to Borica, 1794, 'Estado de las Californias,' pts. 22-25. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 7), tomo xii. 271-272 / scan n108, Doc 173 - Goycoechea to Arrillaga, 4 Sept. 1794: the indio 'Chuarquin' held in grillos at Santa Barbara, to be sent to San Diego. | Provincial State Papers (C-A 8), tomo xiv. 228-229 / scan n69-70, Doc 117 - diary of Alf. Pablo Cota, Santa Barbara, 28 Apr.-3 May 1795: attempted arrest of Mateo Charquin at 'Calabaguala.' | Provincial State Papers (C-A 8), tomo xiv. 237 / scan n72, Doc 122 - Goycoechea to Gob. Borica, 15 May 1795: escape of the prisoner Charquin. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. I (San Francisco, 1884), 709 n.27.
notes: DATE: refine 'ca. 1792-93' to February 1793 - the source letter is 27 Feb 1793 and Bancroft says 'In February 1793 a new convert named Charquin ran away.' CATALOG DEFECT worth reporting upstream: two other records (ca22-d2046, ca55-d264) carry internal cross-references reading 'cf. C-A 55 Doc 212' for Charquin; that pointer is wrong in the catalog itself and is the likely origin of the map's bad link. PAGE DISCREPANCY: Bancroft cites St. Pap., Sac., MS., vii. 24-5, which does not match the catalog's p.vii.57-64 / savage 160-64; the identification rests on content (Charquin, 20 women and children captive, Feb 1793), not arithmetic.

name: Capture & execution of the outlaw Pomponio
summary: From Ignacio Martínez's hoja de servicios: with only a cabo + 2 soldiers he ran down and captured the cimarrón Christian José/Pomponio at the cañada de Novato after a firefight (one comrade wounded). Guilty of "innumerables robos, homicidios" (one victim a soldier), Pomponio was shot at Monterey by government order. The death sentence survives in C-A 17 Doc 389, a Consejo de Guerra condemning him for killing soldado Manuel Varela.
result: Spanish counter-banditry; Pomponio executed at Monterey
sources: Provincial State Papers, Benicia Military (C-A 17), tomo lii. 7 / scan n349, Doc 389 - Consejo de Guerra, Monterey, 6 Feb. [1824; catalog reads 1821], death sentence of 'el indio Pomponio' for the killing of soldado Manuel Varela. | Departmental State Papers, Benicia Military (C-A 18), tomo lxvi. 962-963 / scan n418-419, Doc 365 - hoja de servicios of Capt. Ignacio Martinez, San Francisco, 31 Dec. 1828. | State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 56), tomo xi. 823-825 / scan n179-181, Doc 182 - hoja de servicios of Capt. Ignacio Martinez, certified by Echeandia, San Diego, 11 Aug. 1829. | State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 56), tomo xi. 623-628 / scan n98-101, Doc 108 - Ignacio Martinez (San Francisco) to Luis Arguello, 31 July 1823: the Ponponio pursuit. | State Papers, Sacramento (C-A 56), tomo xi. 537-538 / scan n81, Doc 487 - Ignacio Martinez to Luis Antonio Arguello, 1 Apr. 1823: Ponponio raids near the Rancho de San Pedro. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Departmental Records (C-A 46), tomo i. 213-214 / scan n287, Doc 406 - Gov. Luis Antonio Arguello (Monterey) to the Comandante of San Francisco, 20 Jan. 1824: 'Sentenciado a Muerte.' | Departmental State Papers, San Jose (C-A 44), tomo i. 513-517 / scan n112, Doc 85 - Gob. Sola to the Comandante of San Jose, 1820-21: Pomponio taken in a theft. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1885), 537 and n.59; also II:510. | Archivo del Arzobispado (Santa Barbara), MS., iv. pt. i. 29 - report of 21 Mar. 1820: 20 runaways from Mission San Francisco, 'Pomponio and his company committing ravages.'
notes: DATE CONFLICT, flagged not reconciled. The catalog dates ca17-d389 to 6 Feb 1821; Bancroft II:537 puts the same court-martial (same signers) at 6 Feb 1824 with execution 6 Sept 1824; ca46-d406 (20 Jan 1824) reports the consejo de oficiales de guerra held at Monterey on 14 Jan 1824 and Arguello's approval of the death sentence. Decisive against 1821: Luis Antonio Arguello, who signs, only became governor in Nov 1822. I judge the catalog's 1821 year very likely a mis-dating, but I have not seen the leaf, so I am not overwriting it. Second discrepancy: ca18-d365 places the capture at the canada de Novato (as Bancroft does), ca56-d182 at the 'Canada de Nuestra Senora'.

name: The Solís Revolt
summary: A convict-sergeant pronunciamiento: presidiario Sgt. Joaquín Solís and subcomisario José Mª Herrera seized Monterey against Gov. Echeandía; marched south; the SF garrison fired a salute and raised the flag to welcome them; defeated at Santa Bárbara (Pacheco's counter-revolution). Leaders deported to San Blas on the Volunteer. Prosecution built a "revolución por España" charge and named a foreign-merchant circle (Hartnell/Spence/Anderson/Stearns) on both sides.
result: Mexican-period military coup; suppressed; leaders deported
sources: Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 19), tomo LXIX–LXXVII, orig. pp. 578–598 / Savage pp. 16–20, scan n16–n20, Doc 20: sumaria on the Solis conspiracy, Subtte. Ramirez, 24 Mar 1830. | Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military) (C-A 19), tomo LXIX–LXXVII, Savage p. 151, scan n154, Doc 145: umbrella header of the Solis trial dossier, Echeandia, Monterey, 12 Nov 1829. | Dep. summary: After Gov. Victoria's overthrow, Vicente Sánchez and the convict José Antonio Ávila armed a band of presidiarios (weapons from Santa Bárbara) against Zamorano's northern faction. Ávila's party split from Sánchez past San Buenaventura and surrendered at Mission Santa Inés; dismissed under the 25 Apr 1832 amnesty. The endpoint of the Solís→anti-Victoria arc.

name: Pursuit & killing of the fugitive Valerio

Rodrigo del Pliego, Monterey, 6 Aug 1830. | Dep. name: Felipe Briones killed at Cerro de Bolbones
summary: Felipe Briones killed trying to recover horses from Indians near the Cerro de Bolbones (Mt Diablo area).
sources: Dept. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43), tomos i-viii, Doc 728, orig. pp.456-57 / scan n337: Ignacio Peralta, Rancho San Antonio, 12 Jan 1840, to the Prefecto - 'Robo de Caballada por los indios a Felipe Briones, quien los siguio con 4 hombres a los indios que lo mataron.' | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. iv (1840-1845) (San Francisco: History Co., 1886), 76 n70. | Vallejo, Documentos para la Historia de California, MS., ix. 20 (BANC MSS C-B, Bancroft Library).

Searched q.py for 'Briones' across all volumes: the only other Briones hits are 18th-century soldiers (Marcos, Vicente, cabo Briones) and Desiderio Briones, wounded on the Estanislao in Dec 1839 - a different man and a different fight.

name: Cochrane squadron raid on Mission Todos Santos
summary: Ships of "la Escuadra del Lord Cochrane" entered Cabo de Cortés and attacked Mission Todos Santos at night; the inhabitants defended themselves, killing the lieutenant + 4 men, mortally wounding 3, and capturing the rest; a 13-man landing party. Gov. Solá ordered church silver withdrawn from the coast.
sources: St. Pap., Sacramento (C-A 54), tomo i, Doc 149 (Savage pp.212-13 / scan n211-n212): Gov. Pablo Vicente de Sola, Monterey, 30 Mar [1823 per Savage], circular to the friars and commandants of Monterey and San Francisco - ships of 'la Escuadra del Lord Cochrane' entered Cabo San Lucas (Cabo de Cortes) and attacked Mission Todos Santos on 18 Feb; the inhabitants killed the lieutenant and four men, mortally wounded three, and captured the rest of a thirteen-man raiding party. Sola orders church silver and valuables withdrawn from the coast. | St. Pap., Sacramento (C-A 55), tomos vi-ix, Doc 84, orig. p.i.153-154 / Savage p.46, scan n45: Sola, 5 May 1822, to Jose Romero - Lord Cochrane's privateers at Cabo San Lucas, Feb 1822, including the brig El Alcion; missions San Jose and Todos Santos sacked. | St. Pap., Sacramento (C-A 56), tomos x-xix, Doc 397, orig. pp.xviii.20-21 / Savage pp.347-350, scan n346-n349: Gov. of the Californias, Monterey, 4 May 1822, to the Padre Prefecto, relaying Lt. Jose Manuel Ruiz's report of Cochrane's insurgent squadron ravaging Baja California, Feb-Mar 1822. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Dept. St. Pap. (C-A 27), tomos i-ii, Doc 2, orig. pp.3-6 / Savage p.3, scan n2: Sola, Monterey, 29 Mar 1822, to the commandants of Santa Barbara and San Diego - defence against Lord Cochrane's squadron, quoting Gov. Capt. Jose Dario Arguello of Baja California via the mission cordillera; the attack on Mission San Jose del Cabo, 1 Feb, with about twelve prisoners taken by the defenders.
notes: The Savage copy dates Solá's circular 30 Mar 1823 and the raid itself 18 Feb; the Cochrane operations off the Californias belong to 1822, and three independent volumes (C-A 27, 55, 56) place the squadron at Cabo San Lucas in February 1822. Event year shown as circa 1822. ⚠ An earlier version of this record cited 'C-A 54 Doc 2051', a document number that no longer exists after the volume was re-itemised; the correct record is C-A 54 Doc 149. DATE DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled. Savage heads the C-A 54 circular '1823 Mar 30' with the raid on '18 Feb', while three other C-A records put the same raid in Feb 1822: ca27-d2 (29 Mar 1822), ca55-d84 (5 May 1822), ca56-d397 (4 May 1822). 1822 also fits Bancroft ii. 474 (the San Francisco Javier 'captured by one of Cochrane's fleet at Cape San Lucas'). Likeliest a slip of a year in Savage's heading, but I did not check the heading against the leaf, so both readings stand. Note too that the records disagree on the mission: d2 has San Jose del Cabo on 1 Feb with ~12 prisoners, d84 has both San Jose and Todos Santos sacked, d149 has Todos Santos on 18 Feb with 13 raiders - probably successive landings by one squadron.

St. Pap. (C-A 11), tomo xviii, Doc 472, orig. pp.388-89 (Savage's cross-ref pp.1008-9) / Savage pp.391-92, scan n392-n393: Ruiz, San Vicente, 9 May 1804, to Arrillaga - forwards to the Habilitado the inventories of the effects of the deceased Juan Camacho and Jose Peiquera. | Prov. (C-A 11), tomo xviii, Doc 481, orig. pp.392-93 (Savage's cross-ref pp.1028-30) / Savage pp.395-96, scan n396-n397: Ruiz, San Vicente, 6 Oct 1804, to Arrillaga - the fight at Santa Catalina, in which the gentiles engaged are identified as the same men who killed the soldiers.

name: Spanish Yuma Punitive Campaign
summary: Neve and Capt. José Antonio Romeu (108 men) march down the Colorado; Romeu with 40 men and 12 Indian allies (Jalchedunes/Cocomaricopas) routs the Yuma cavalry ('crecida mortandad'), 4 soldiers wounded; Fages escorts the rescued captives. name: Tule balsa shipwreck at the Farallones
summary: Mission San Francisco Indians navigated by sea in tule balsas to evangelize gentiles on the opposite shore; currents carried one balsa onto the Farallones, where 2 of the 4 Indians drowned. Not a military engagement; an indigenous open-water navigation datum at the Bay mouth.
sources: Pérez Fernández to Gov. Borica, 30 Nov 1794. Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 7), tomo xii–xiii, 72–73 / Savage 29–30, scan n28–n29, Doc 54.
notes: The catalog record places the drowning on 'the 4th of the month' in a letter of 30 Nov 1794, i.e. 4 Nov 1794; the map's bare '1794' can be tightened to Nov 1794, but I have not read the leaf image to confirm the day, so I state it as what the catalog summary says. The record also shows the balsa voyages were not free-standing: they sit inside Pérez Fernández's refusal of extra escort soldiers for a missionary 'conquista de gentiles' across the bay toward Marin, which is the administrative context the map's 'evangelize gentiles on the opposite shore' comes from.

name: Horse-theft raid & punitive expedition (140-head caballada)
summary: 'Indios malhechores' drove off a caballada of 140 head from the national rancho; Gov. Argüello sent Alf. Santiago Argüello with 34 troops to punish the raiders and the rancherías that harbor them ('por cortar de raiz los daños'). In a related San Diego–frontier action, 14 of 15 neophyte auxiliaries who fought were killed, and ~40 raiders later burned a San Diego rancho.

(2) DATE/EPISODE SEPARATION: the '14 of 15 neophyte auxiliaries killed' and the ~40 raiders who burned a San Diego rancho are reported in a letter of 17 Dec 1824 to the Governor of Baja California (ca46-d212 head, ca46-d213 tail), five months after the July caballada raid and on the Baja/San Diego frontier. The map's date range 'Jun–Jul 1824' is confirmed: Argüello's order is 30 Jun, the raid the night of the 1st (July), the report 31 Jul 1824.

name: Surrender of the Spanish squadron at Monterey
summary: The Spanish ship-of-the-line Asia and brig Constante; Spain's last Pacific force after the loss of Peru; put into Monterey and capitulated to the Mexican Nation, their crews swearing 'el solemne juramento de sujetarse á las leyes de los Estados Unidos Mejicanos.' Argüello tapped the Asia's powder to arm the near-empty San Francisco and Monterey batteries; pilot Juan Malarín carried the acta de Capitulación to Mexico City.

The interregnum then splintered; the Diputación installed Pío Pico, Los Angeles proclaimed Echeandía, Zamorano rose in the north; 'casi inevitable el derramamiento de sangre.'

name: The anti-Micheltorena revolt · Cahuenga/Providencia
summary: The last Californio overthrow of a Mexican-appointed governor. The Asamblea Departamental 'desconoce la autoridad… de M. Micheltorena,' charging his 'relaciones secretas con el extranjero Sutter' (Sutter marched for Micheltorena; M.G. Vallejo corresponded against him). name: Ambush of the San Diego pursuit party (Dominican frontier)
summary: A San Diego troop detachment pursuing Dominican-mission cimarrones (runaway neophytes) was ambushed on the Baja frontier; the action left 15 Indians dead, including a leader from Mission San Miguel; a frontier engagement in the same season as the Chumash Revolt further north.

The Baja/Dominican frontier falls outside his Alta California annals, so no book source is offered here. The two C-A records agree on all details (15 killed, the San Miguel cabecilla, the rancho house burned); ca46-d335 supplies the leader's name (Fidelis), the rancho name (San Isidoro) and the two wounded invalidos (Ignacio and Jose Lopez) that the San Diego report leaves blank.

name: Gentile attack on mission neophytes · '21 neophytes killed'
summary: A report of 21 neophytes killed by gentiles on the interior frontier of the San Diego district; evidence for the raiding-economy pressure on mission populations in the 1820s, and for inter-indigenous violence between mission and independent communities.
sources: José Ignacio Bernal(?) (San José) to the Comandante, 3 Nov 1826 · reports 21 Christian Indians killed by gentiles. Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 27), Departmental State Papers, tomo I–II, orig. pp.498–500 / Savage p.~136 / scan n130, Doc 145. | Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III (1825–1840), San Francisco: The History Company, 1886, pp.109–110 and p.110 n.51.
notes: Location not given in the abstract; conjectural pin in the SD interior. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE FEATURE TEXT. (1) The feature places this 'on the interior frontier of the San Diego district'. The manuscript is written from SAN JOSÉ; the victims were Mission San José neophytes killed by gentiles in the Cosumnes/San Joaquin country. It is a northern, not a southern, episode, and it is the outrage that provoked alférez José Sánchez's Nov 1826 Cosumnes campaign (Bancroft III:110). (2) Casualty figure: the manuscript says 21; Bancroft's narrative text says 'twenty or thirty of whom were killed, or at least never returned' while his own footnote quotes the 21 from this document. Page-system note: Bancroft cites 'Dept. St. Pap., MS., i. 135', which matches the record's SAVAGE page (~136), not its original tomo page (p.498–500).

name: Martínez's 'campaña en los Ríos'
summary: Ignacio Martínez's 1827 campaign into the Delta rivers against the runaway and rebel Indians of Missions San José and Santa Clara; 2 soldiers killed. The precursor operation to the 1829 Estanislao campaigns, in the same theater.
sources: Ignacio Martínez (San Francisco) to Gov. José María Echeandía, 31 May 1827 · reports the campaign 'en los Ríos'. St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp.21–23 / Savage p.12 / scan n11, Doc 8.
notes: NULL RESULT, recorded deliberately. I could find no second manuscript for this campaign. (a) Bancroft: grepped vol3 for 'en los Rios', 'los Rios', 'Martinez' (60+ hits read in context) and for every 'St. Pap., Miss. and Colon., MS., ii.' citation; he cites that tomo at pp.6, 91, 96, 200–308 etc. but never pp.21–23, and his 'Los Rios' references are all 1829 Estanislao, not 1827. Bancroft appears simply not to narrate this campaign. (b) DB: searched C-A 47 (Dept. Records 1827) and C-A 18 (DSP Benicia Mil., 1827) for an Echeandía reply or a service-record entry; nothing on subject. So ca53-d8 is, on present evidence, the sole record of the engagement; which is itself worth stating on the map.

name: The great 1840 horse-raid campaign ('agua de Ramón')
summary: A multi-week mounted campaign, not a single skirmish. Chaguanosos drove off three mare-herds from Mission San Gabriel (14 May); the LA vecino-militia mobilized (13→36 men, 4 muskets, 19 lances); Ignacio Palomares's ~23-man party was routed; relief columns held the Puerta del Cajón and recovered the herds at the 'agua de Ramón' surprise. Leandri's report: the rearguard was '20 hombres Ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos; pero tenían á más otra gente,' driving 1,000+ head, ~1,500 driven to death in flight.
result: Raiders routed one militia party; herds recovered at agua de Ramón

(3) Bancroft IV:76–77 is thin and partly contradicts the manuscripts: he pins the great 1840 theft to SAN LUIS OBISPO in April (1,200 horses) and says the pursuers 'thought it imprudent to risk a conflict'; the C-A 34 E29 dossier documents the San Gabriel theft of 14 May and a real engagement at the agua de Ramón.
