name: Gentile Attack on Mission San Rafael & the Piña Expedition
summary: Mission San Rafael; its founding padre Amorós dead 14 July 1832, its population collapsing (~970 to ~300) and baptisms crashing (155 to 15); was attacked by gentiles; a punitive expedition was sent out under Lázaro Piña. Most likely the "spring 1832 San Rafael revolt" the Russians at Fort Ross heard of from fugitive-Indian informants.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco: A. L. Bancroft & Co., 1885), 716 n.18 (San Rafael, Summary of events, 1832). | Vallejo, 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., i. 307 - Bancroft Library, BANC MSS C-B 1 et seq. (the Vallejo Documentos collection), NOT the Archives of California. | No Archives of California record found for the 1832 gentile attack on Mission San Rafael or the Pina expedition.
notes: 1832 date and Piña command per Bancroft; the underlying Vallejo Documentos i.307 leaf is not yet read; treat the year as attested but not leaf-verified. Bancroft's entire authority for this feature is one line and one manuscript citation, and that manuscript is NOT in the Archives of California. I could find no C-A record of the attack or of the Pina expedition. Searches run: 'San Rafael gentiles ataque expedicion' (year 1832), 'San Rafael mision indios' (1832), 'Lazaro Pina' (all volumes). The only Lazaro Pina hit is ca20-d513 (Cabo Lazaro Pina, artillery detachment pay return, 2 Nov 1831, C-A 20) - it establishes that Lazaro Pina was the artillery corporal on the San Francisco side at the right date, but it says nothing about San Rafael and I am NOT linking it. DISCREPANCY to flag: the map summary's identification with 'the spring 1832 San Rafael revolt the Russians at Fort Ross heard of' is not in Bancroft, who gives no month; and Bancroft's own p.716 statistics note calls the 970-to-300 population collapse 'extremely unreliable... more likely there is an error in the figures', so the demographic framing in the map summary should not be presented as fact. Separately, the Pina of Bancroft III:111-113 (the 1829 Estanislao campaign) is Joaquin Pina, not Lazaro - do not conflate them.

name: The Bodega Mobilization under Toribio
summary: About 200 armed Indians; gentiles plus Christian fugitives from Mission San Rafael; massed at Bodega under Toribio (Pixpix-uccux), "armed and ready to die" rather than be seized, hosted by the Bodega chief Gualinela. Kostromitinov, the RAC manager at Fort Ross, asked Vallejo to help round up the retreating Ross Indians; Vallejo declined and pacified through Gualinela. It worked; Toribio came in peacefully seven months later.
result: Defused; Toribio submitted peacefully later in 1833
native_groups: Coast Miwok (Bodega — Gualinela); San Rafael fugitives
sources: St. Pap., Missions and Colonization (C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp. 215-234 / Savage 98-112, scan n97-n111, Doc 45 - Alferez Mariano G. Vallejo to the Comandante General (Figueroa), San Francisco, 5 May 1833, 'Informe reservado sobre el Establecimiento de Ross'. | St. Pap., Missions and Colonization (C-A 53), tomo II, orig. pp. 302-306 (Sav. p.462+) / Savage 214-220, scan n212-n218, Doc 115 - Jose Figueroa (Monterey) to the Ministro de Guerra y Marina, 12 Apr. 1833: founding of the strong detachment at Mission San Rafael and the Bodega/Russian rationale.
notes: Location approximate; the Bodega gathering ground, not a fixed engagement site. Two discrepancies I am NOT reconciling silently. (1) NAME: the map calls the Bodega chief 'Gualinela'; the C-A 53 record reads the Bodega capitanejo as 'Guchactac' (43 people, guarding the Russian factories). These may be the same man under different readings, or two different men; the catalog itself flags this document's paleography as rough and its figures as scale-2 abstracts pending verbatim transcription. Do not print either name as settled. (2) NAME: Toribio (Pixpix-uccux) does not appear in the catalog summary of ca53-d45 at all; the Indians 'resueltos a morir' are there, the leader's name is not. Toribio is named in Bancroft III:323 but only in the November 1833 Mercado episode, not in an April 1833 Bodega context. So the map's identification of the Bodega leader as Toribio rests on the underlying Vallejo report text, which has not been transcribed verbatim - treat it as unverified until the leaves are read. Also note the RAC manager at Ross in 1833 was Peter Kostromitinov, as the map says; the C-A record names only 'el Comandante' / Wrangel, so the Kostromitinov identification is an inference from the date, not from the document.

name: The Mercado Massacre at San Rafael
summary: After a 16 Nov parley; 15 gentiles under Toribio came to talk at Figueroa's encouragement, and Padre Vázquez del Mercado seized them following an overnight robbery; on the morning of 20 Nov 1833 Mercado sent majordomo Molina with 37 armed neophytes against the strangers: 21 killed, many wounded, 20 men, women, and children captured; the mission party lost 5 wounded, 1 mortally. Figueroa, furious that the assurances he had given the Indians were violated, suspended Mercado and ordered him to trial; Vallejo freed the captives.
result: 21 gentiles killed; Mercado suspended; Vallejo freed the captives
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. III: 1825-1840 (San Francisco: A. L. Bancroft & Co., 1885), 322-324 and note 43. | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (C-A 39), tomo II (Miscellaneous), orig. pp. 111-112 / Savage 130-131, scan n130-n131, Doc 18 - Jose Figueroa to Asesor Rafael Gomez, Monterey, 5 Dec. 1833, 'Asesinato de Indios'. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28), tomo III, orig. iii.532-533 / Savage 137, scan n138, Doc 179 - M. G. Vallejo, San Rafael, 22 Dec. 1833, to the Padre Ministro of San Rafael: expulsion of mayordomo Jose Molina. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28), tomo III, orig. iii.534-545 / Savage 138, scan n139, Doc 180 - M. G. Vallejo, San Francisco, 1 Jan. 1834, to Figueroa: San Rafael and its neighbourhood pacified.
notes: The ranchería name Bancroft reads as "Pulia" is unverified against the leaf. Bancroft's footnote 43 (III:324) lists the manuscript basis: 'Mercado, Expediente de papeles tocantes a la matanza de Indios hecha por orden del P. Ministro de S. Rafael, 1833, MS., in Monterey, Arch., i. 34-7; Vallejo, Doc., MS., ii. 100; xxxi. 58; Arch. Arzob., MS., v. pt ii. 3; Dept. St. Pap., MS., iii. 197-8; Id., Ben., ii. 9-10'. Two of those are nominally C-A series (Dept. St. Pap. tomo iii = C-A 28; Dept. St. Pap. Benicia tomo ii = C-A 39) but NEITHER resolves to a Mercado document: q.py banc 'Dept. St. Pap., MS., iii. 197-8' returns ca28-d84, Figueroa's July-1832 index of correspondence (orig. iii.197-199), and q.py banc 'Dept. St. Pap., Ben., MS., ii. 9-10' returns ca39-d87/d88, 1839 Monterey customs circulars (orig. pp. 8-11). Both are page-arithmetic matches with the wrong subject, so I have NOT emitted them. The C-A links below were found by content, not by Bancroft's page numbers. Also noted but not linked: ca61-d8 / ca61-d11 (C-A 61, Legislative Records) carry Vazquez del Mercado material from 1835-36, and ca61-d11 orders his 'esposicion' joined 'to the causa it refers to' - the causa is not identified in the record, so I will not assert it is the massacre causa. DATE: the map's 20 Nov. 1833 and the casualty figures (21 killed, 20 captured, 5 wounded on the mission side, one mortally) agree exactly with Bancroft III:323-324.

name: Seizure of Sonoma (Bear Flag)
summary: Bear Flag insurgents seize Sonoma at dawn, taking M.G. Vallejo, Salvador Vallejo, Prudon, and Leese prisoner with all of Vallejo's caballada. Bloodless opening of the revolt.
result: Sonoma taken; prisoners to Sutter's Fort
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), ch. v, 'Bear Flag Revolt - Taking of Sonoma', pp. 110-121 (the capitulations, the dispute over the prisoners, and their removal to the Sacramento at pp. 114-116). | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:96 / Savage 28, scan n28, Doc 42 - Francisco Guerrero, subprefect of the 2nd district, Yerba Buena, 17 June 1846, 'Invasion de Sonoma'. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:234 / Savage 59-60, scan n59-n60, Doc 99 - Comandante general Jose Castro, bando militar, Santa Clara, 16 June 1846. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:236-239 / Savage ~62, scan n62-n65, Doc 101 - Comandante general Jose Castro, proclamation to the citizens, Santa Clara, 18 June 1846. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:100-101 / Savage 29, scan n29, Doc 44 - Moreno to Stearns, Santa Barbara, 23 June 1846, relaying the Contra Costa juez de paz (San Leandro, 15 June; Monterey, 17 June). | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:29-31 / Savage 10, scan n10, Doc 16 - Manuel Castro to Gov. Pico, 'en marcha a Sonoma', 25 June 1846. | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia, Prefecturas y Juzgados (C-A 42), tomo I-VI, orig. ii.402-404 / Savage 129-130, scan n128-n129, Doc 345 - S. Arguello to the Governor, Los Angeles, 2 July 1846.
notes: Bancroft's own manuscript authorities for the seizure are all NON-C-A Bancroft Library collections - Bear Flag Papers, MS., 19-20, 60-1 (given him by Vallejo); Vallejo, Doc., MS., xii. 226; Leese, Bear Flag Statement, MS., 6-12; Ide, Biog. Sketch - so no additional C-A link can be extracted from his footnotes. Everything below was found by content search of the Californio side of the record.

name: Fight at Olómpali
summary: Ford's 'Bears' surprise Joaquín de la Torre's ~50 men (joined by Padilla's company) at breakfast at Camilo's rancho, midway San Rafael–Petaluma. First real fight of the revolt; one Californian killed.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 164-168 ('Ford and Torre'; the fight at Olompali, 24 June 1846). | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:250-254 / Savage 67-68, scan n70-n71, Doc 106 - Comandante general Jose Castro to Gov. Pio Pico, Santa Clara, 1 July 1846 (cited by Bancroft as Dept. St. Pap., MS., vii. 67-8).
notes: BEST FIND OF THIS BATCH: Bancroft cites this very document. At History of California V:167 n.18 (the running note on the crossing) he writes 'June 30th, Gen. Castro to Pico. Back at Sta Clara; and reports Torre's retreat and that of the other divisions (as explained in my text). A council of war has decided to send Manuel Castro as a comisionado to the gov... Blotter in Castro, Doc., MS., ii. 131. Same document, dated July 1st. Dept. St. Pap., MS., vii. 67-8.' Dept. St. Pap. vii. 67-8 is ca31-d106, whose Savage pages are exactly 67-68 - Bancroft was citing the Savage transcript's own pagination. Every other authority Bancroft uses for Olompali is non-C-A: Ford, Bear Flag, MS., 18-22; Baldridge, Days of '46, MS., 58-71; Larkin's Doc., MS., iv. 192, 202; Larkin, Off. Corresp., MS., i. 125; Ramon Carrillo's deposition in Hayes' Scrap-books; Luis German, Sucesos, MS., 18-24; Osio; Vallejo, Hist. Cal., MS., v. 129-33; the Honolulu Friend and the Monterey Californian. DISCREPANCY: the map says 'one Californian killed' - Bancroft's text gives Alferez Manuel Cantua killed and Agaton Ruiz badly wounded, while Larkin's 4 July letter names three casualties (Cantua, Ruiz, Isidoro) and Ramon Carrillo's deposition says 'one man killed and two wounded'. One killed is defensible but the count is contested in the sources.

name: Killing of the de Haro twins & Berreyesa
summary: Francisco and Ramón de Haro (twins, ~20) and José de los Reyes Berreyesa, unarmed, shot at ~50 yards on Frémont's order ('I have no room for prisoners') after landing from San Pablo and walking toward Mission San Rafael.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 171-173 ('A Murder by Fremont'). | No Archives of California record found for the killing of the de Haro twins and Jose de los Reyes Berreyesa, 28 June 1846.
notes: Pin between the San Quentin landing point and the mission; exact spot unrecorded. NULL RESULT, recorded deliberately so this feature is not re-queued. Bancroft's authorities at V:171-173 n.5 are all non-C-A: Fremont's letter to Benton in Niles' Register lxxi. 191; Benton, Id. 174; Gillespie, Fremont's Cal. Claims, 28; Jasper O'Farrell in the Los Angeles Star, 27 Sept. 1866 (the eye-witness for 'I have no room for prisoners'); J. S. Berreyesa's letter in the same paper; Leidesdorff to Larkin, 30 June, in Larkin's Doc., MS., iv. 189; Rico, Mem., MS., 19-23; Ide, Biog. Sketch, 190; Bidwell; Hargrave; Fowler, Bear Party, MS., 5; Martin, Narr., MS., 29; Chas Brown, Early Events, MS., 25-6. None is an Archives of California document. Content searches of the database ('de Haro hermanos muertos San Rafael estranjeros' restricted to 1846; 'asesinato Berreyesa Haro Fremont'; 'San Rafael estranjeros mataron tres' restricted to 1846) returned nothing on subject - the top hits were the Berreyesa land expedientes ca61-d259 / ca61-d260 and unrelated 1846 correspondence, and I have linked none of them. The likeliest explanation is that the Californio civil archive north of the bay had already collapsed: as Bancroft notes at V:239, subprefect Guerrero and comandante Sanchez had absented themselves and receptor Pinto had gone to join Castro, carrying his office archives off with him.

name: Capture of Monterey
summary: Sloat's squadron lands and raises the U.S. flag at the Custom House without resistance. The archive's own record: the landing general order bound into C-A 31, and the closing line 'Los Americanos han tomado á Monterrey.'
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), ch. ix, 'Conquest by the U.S. - Sloat's Rule', 230-232 ('Taking of Monterey'). | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:261-262 / Savage 70-71, scan n73-n75, Doc 109 - John D. Sloat, commander U.S. naval forces in the Pacific, aboard the Savannah, 7 July 1846: landing orders to the squadron (in English), bound into the Californio archive. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:133-134 / Savage 34, scan n34, Doc 58 - Moreno to Stearns, San Luis Obispo, 11 July 1846, 'Toma de Monterrey - defensa de los Angeles - archivos'. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VIII:476-477 / Savage 138, scan n273, Doc 394 - David Alexander, San Pedro, 17 July 1846: the American squadron took Monterey by landing. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VIII:495 / Savage 146, scan n282, Doc 403 - Ignacio Coronel to his son Antonio Coronel, 1846: 'Los Americanos han tomado a Monterrey' - the volume's closing line. | Archives of California, Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents (C-A 63), Savage 211, scan n211-n213, Doc 313 - Acta de fidelidad al Gobierno Mexicano, Aduana Maritima de Monterey, 13 July 1846 (Pablo de la Guerra presiding; W. E. P. Hartnell and the guardas).
notes: Bancroft's ch. ix pages for the capture are 230-232. Sloat's summons of 7 July was delivered to the old artillery captain Mariano Silva, who replied that he had no authority to surrender and that there were no troops, arms or public property - which is why there is no Californio act of surrender in the archive to link to. The C-A holdings on this event are therefore of two kinds: the American landing order that Savage found bound into the Californio archive (ca31-d109), and the Californio reaction (ca31-d58, ca31-d112, ca31-d394, ca31-d403, ca63-d313). Note ca31-d109's record carries a published-record correction: its original page is VII:261-262, not the 281-2 given in an earlier publication.

name: Capture of Yerba Buena
summary: Montgomery lands from the Portsmouth and raises the flag on the plaza (now Portsmouth Square) without resistance.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 238-239 ('The Stars and Stripes at San Francisco'), citing Montgomery's report to Sloat of the occupation of San Francisco, 9 July 1846, U.S. Govt Doc., 29th Cong. 2d sess., H. Ex. Doc. no. 4, pp. 649-50. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 31), tomo VII-VIII, orig. VII:266-269 / Savage 73-74, scan n77-n79, Doc 112 - Comandante general Jose Castro to Gov. Pio Pico, Los Ojitos, 11 July 1846, 'Incita a oposicion'. | No Archives of California record found for Montgomery's landing and the raising of the flag at Yerba Buena, 9 July 1846.
notes: There is a documentary reason for the gap, and it is worth putting on the map. Bancroft, V:239: 'Not only was there no opposition, but there was not in town a single Mexican official from whom to demand a surrender. Sub-prefect Guerrero and Comandante Sanchez had absented themselves; Port-captain Ridley was a prisoner at Sutter's Fort; and Receptor Pinto had more than a week before gone to join Castro, first disposing of the custom-house flag... and the archives of his office' - which Pinto later gave to Bancroft as the two-volume 'Documentos para la Historia de California. Coleccion del Sr Don Rafael Pinto' (a separate Bancroft Library collection, not C-A). So the Yerba Buena office archive that would have recorded the event was physically removed before it happened. Bancroft's own source is printed and American: Montgomery's report to Sloat of the occupation of San Francisco, 9 July 1846, in U.S. Govt Doc., 29th Cong. 2d sess., H. Ex. Doc. 4, pp. 649-50. Content searches run against the database: 'Yerba Buena bandera americana Montgomery' and 'San Francisco ocupado fuerzas americanas julio 1846' - no record of the landing or flag-raising.

name: Gillespie's capitulation at Los Angeles
summary: Flores's rising forces Gillespie's small garrison to capitulate and evacuate to San Pedro, reversing the first occupation of the south.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), 314-315 ('Los Angeles Retaken by the Californians') and notes 26-27. | No Archives of California record found for Gillespie's capitulation at Los Angeles, 29-30 Sept. 1846.
notes: NULL RESULT, recorded deliberately, and the null is itself the historical point: Bancroft, V:315, 'The terms of the capitulation, however, if they were put in writing at all, are not extant', and on the date, 'Gillespie says he marched to S. Pedro on Sept. 29th; Wilson thinks it was on the 28th; and several Californians make it the 30th. I find no document to settle it.' The map's 'Sept 29-30' is therefore correctly hedged. Bancroft's whole apparatus for the Flores revolt (V:311-315) is Californio and American dictation and correspondence, none of it C-A: Coronel, Cosas de Cal., MS., 80-107; Lugo, Vida de un Ranchero, MS.; Rico, Mem., MS., 25-35; Botello, Anales, MS.; Wilson's Observations, MS., 66-91; Forster's Pioneer Data, MS., 35-43; Vejar, Recuerdos, MS.; Michael White, Cal., MS.; Ord, Ocurrencias, MS., 184-5; Osio, Hist. Cal., MS., 480-5; Larkin, Off. Corresp., MS., ii. 89; Fitch, Doc., MS., 402; Manuel Castro to Pio Pico in Doc. Hist. Cal., MS., iii. 292. Content searches run: 'Gillespie capitulacion Angeles'; 'Flores pronunciamiento Angeles americanos septiembre' restricted to 1846; 'recuperacion de Los Angeles tropas americanas evacuar San Pedro'; 'Varela pronunciamiento 1846 Angeles guarnicion americana'; 'guerra Estados Unidos Angeles octubre' restricted to C-A 63 and 1846. Nothing on subject. The nearest C-A document from the resulting Flores government is ca63-d486, the Assembly's mission-mortgage war-loan decree of 30 Oct. 1846 - a month later and about finance, so I have NOT linked it.

name: Fight at Chino Rancho
summary: Californians under Varela/Carrillo besiege and burn Isaac Williams's rancho house, capturing ~24 Anglo-American riflemen (the 'Chino prisoners'). One Californian killed.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 311-314 ('was fought at the Chino rancho of Isaac Williams, about twenty-five miles east of Los Angeles, on September 26th-27th'; Carlos Ballesteros killed by a rifle-ball; Varela's promise of protection accepted). | Benjamin D. Wilson, 'Observations on Early Days in California', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), 66-91 · Bancroft's principal source: 'Wilson's Observations, MS., is the most detailed and complete narration of the whole affair.' | José del Carmen Lugo, 'Vida de un Ranchero', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), 32-67 (esp. 34 ff.) · Lugo claims to have arrived at Chino first and to have been joined by Varela late in the night; Bancroft: 'which was probably true.' | Stephen C. Foster, 'Los Angeles in 1847-49', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation), 25 ff.; Michael White, 'California All the Way Back to 1828', MS., 27-35; Francisco Palomares, 'Memorias', MS., 68-76 · the three supplementary participant/near-participant accounts of the assault and the sparing of the prisoners. | No Archives of California manuscript attests the fight at Chino.
notes: PAGE CORRECTION: Bancroft's account of the Chino fight runs pp. 311-314, not 311-313. The sentence begins on p.311 ('The first "battle" of this rebellion - or the second if we count Varela's demonstration against Gillespie -') and the surrender and march to Los Angeles occupy p.314. CROSS-FEATURE FINDING (applies to reg-132 through reg-140): I read Bancroft V continuously across the whole conquest narrative (the Flores revolt through Cahuenga, ch. xii-xiv, roughly pp. 305-408) and grepped that whole span for citations to any Archives of California series (Dept./Prov. St. Pap., Leg. Rec., Prov. Rec., Unb. Doc., 'Arch., MS.'). There is not one. Bancroft worked the conquest entirely from Bancroft-Library dictations, private document collections, and printed government reports. Independently, the C-A catalogue itself holds only TEN records dated between Aug 1846 and Jan 1847 across all 63 volumes, and none of them is military. That is the structural reason these nine features cannot be linked to C-A, and it is a real finding rather than a search failure.

name: Battle of Dominguez Rancho
summary: Mervine's ~350 sailors and marines, marching on Los Angeles without artillery, occupy the Dominguez rancho buildings overnight (7th), then are repulsed on the morning of the 8th by Carrillo's horsemen with the pedrero known traditionally as the old woman's gun, an old four-pounder dug up from Inocencia Reyes's garden where it had been buried, fired by Ignacio Aguilar and dragged off by reatas to reload; ~4-6 Americans killed.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 318-320 ('Mervine's Defeat'; the gun 'fired by Ignacio Aguilar, and was immediately dragged away by reatas attached to the horsemen's saddles, to be reloaded at a safe distance'). | José Antonio Carrillo, 'Accion de San Pedro contra los Americanos, 8 de Octubre 1846', MS. · the original official Californian report of the battle, dated at San Pedro 8 Oct. 1846; also printed in El Sonorense, 8 Jan. 1847. | Agustín Janssens, 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., 18-20 · Flores's congratulatory proclamation announcing the victory at San Pedro (and, at 45-6, the Flores order-book generally: 'among his papers are found many of Flores' orders not elsewhere extant'). | No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of Dominguez Rancho.
notes: Bancroft's page span is 318-320 (running heads: 'MERVINE'S DEFEAT. 319' and '320 REVOLT OF FLORES IN THE SOUTH'), with the narrative beginning at the foot of p.318; the existing citation's 319-321 is off by roughly a page. Also note that Bancroft's casualty figure is unsettled: Stockton said four killed, Cutts and most repetitions six killed and six wounded, Carrillo's own official report seven slain, Flores's report twelve, Gillespie thirteen. The map's '~4-6 Americans killed' sits at the low end of that range and is defensible but should not be stated as settled. The critical structural fact for this feature is Bancroft V:320: 'Archives of the Flores regime have for the most part disappeared; but enough remain in my collection from private sources to show the purport of the general's measures.' The surviving Flores paper is in Janssens's private papers, not in the C-A series.

name: Battle of Natividad
summary: Castro's/Manuel Castro's Californians fight Burroughs's and Thompson's volunteers near Natividad rancho, Salinas plain; Burroughs and Foster killed, ~5–7 dead total. The only pitched fight of the war in the north.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 367-372, ch. xiii ('Foster Killed - Battle of Natividad - Death of Burroughs'). | José Antonio Alviso, 'Campaña de la Natividad', MS. (Bancroft Library dictation) · the son of the owner of the Natividad rancho, who claims to have first told Castro the Americans were at San Juan. | José Castro's contemporary report of the action, in [José] Fernández, 'Documentos', MS., 53 · 'In a report of the time, Castro claimed to have killed 21 of the enemy.' | No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of Natividad.
notes: Bancroft's page span is 367-372 ('the Americans lost at Natividad four or five men killed' is on p.371; the chapter running head 'NATIVIDAD AND SANTA CLARA' covers 367-383). The map's casualty figure '~5-7 dead total' is within Bancroft's reported range but the testimony is irreconcilable and should be flagged rather than harmonised: American losses are given as 4 or 5 killed (Bancroft), Californian losses as 3 killed and 5 wounded (Castro's own report), 3 killed and 4 wounded (Vallejo), 4 killed and 4 wounded (Rico), 2 killed (Mrs Ord). Manuel Castro meanwhile claimed in a contemporary report to have killed 21 of the enemy, and Flores in December reported 11 Americans killed. Do not silently average these.

name: Battle of San Pascual
summary: Andrés Pico's lancers maul Kearny's dragoons in the San Pasqual valley at dawn; ~21 Americans killed including three officers; the bloodiest action of the war in California.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 342-347, ch. xiii ('The battle of San Pascual, the most famous and deadly in Californian history'; casualty roll and the lance wounds at n.27). | Capt. Andrés Pico's report of 6 Dec. 1846, received by Flores at 4 a.m. on 7 Dec. and communicated by him to subordinates, in Agustín Janssens, 'Documentos', MS., 45-6 · the victory won 'without other casualty on our side than 11 wounded, none seriously, since the action was decided por arma blanca.' | Dr John S. Griffin, 'Documents' / 'Papers', MS., 4-5 (original blotter of his quarterly report of 31 Dec. 1846) and 22 (letter of 14 Feb. 1847) · the assistant surgeon's own casualty returns, which Bancroft calls 'the best authority.' | No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of San Pascual.
notes: CASUALTY DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: the map says '~21 Americans killed'. Bancroft V:346 states eighteen killed in the fight, nineteen wounded of whom three fatally, and one missing. Counting the three who died of wounds (Hammond 6 Dec., Sgt Cox 10 Dec. at San Bernardo, Kennedy 21 Dec. at San Diego) plus the missing McLaffray gives 22; counting the fatally wounded but not the missing gives 21. The figure 21 is therefore defensible but is a derived total, not Bancroft's own number, and Bancroft records competing counts (Kearny 18 killed/15 wounded; Emory 18/13; House Ex. Doc. 17 killed/16 wounded; Griffin's original blotter 17/18). Andrés Pico's own report claims eleven wounded and no dead on the Californian side. The map's date (6 Dec. 1846) is not in dispute.

name: Pauma massacre
summary: Garra's band of Cahuillas and fugitive ex-neophytes of San Luis Rey kill eleven Californios who had retired to Pauma rancho to avoid service for or against Flores; instigated by William Marshall, later hanged for it.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 567-568 (the massacre of eleven men at Pauma rancho, Garra's Cahuillas and San Luis Rey fugitives, Marshall's instigation) and p. 617 (San Diego local annals: the roll of victims and the four competing explanations). | José Antonio Estudillo, 'Datos Históricos sobre California', MS., 45-6 · says the San Pascual Indians tried to save the victims but arrived too late. | Juan Machado [Alipás de Wrightington], 'Tiempos Pasados de la Alta California', MS., 37-42; Julio César, 'Cosas de Indios de California', MS., 11-14 (a Luiseño account); José del Carmen Lugo, 'Vida de un Ranchero', MS., 51-63 (the January 1847 Ahuanga counter-campaign) · the three Californio and Indian narratives of the massacre and its reprisal. | No Archives of California manuscript attests the Pauma massacre.
notes: COUNT DISCREPANCY, flagged not reconciled: Bancroft gives the number twice and inconsistently. At V:567 he writes 'the massacre of eleven men at Pauma rancho in December' (the map follows this); in his San Diego local annals at V:617 he names the victims and lists ELEVEN names plus 'a New Mexican not named'; i.e. twelve; and in the body of that annals passage he writes 'the massacre of a dozen Californians.' The named victims are Sgt Francisco Basualdo, José M. Alvarado, Manuel Serrano, Ramón Aguilar, Domínguez (known as Dominguito), an old man [unnamed], Santiago Osuna, José López, Santos Alipás, Eustaquio Ruiz, Juan de la Cruz, and an unnamed New Mexican. Bancroft also records four competing explanations of the killing and says 'there is much mystery about this affair'; including a theory, which he rejects, that there was no massacre at all and the men died at San Pascual. The map's attribution of instigation to William Marshall follows Bancroft, but Bancroft's own word is 'doubtless', an inference, and Marshall was hanged in 1852 after the Garra revolt, not immediately for Pauma.

name: Battle of Santa Clara ('the Mustard Stalks')
summary: Marston's marines and volunteers meet Francisco Sánchez's insurgents in the mustard fields near Mission Santa Clara; light casualties, followed by armistice ending the war in the north.
result: Sánchez treats; war ends in the north
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 380-383, ch. xiii (the 'battle of Santa Clara'; the mustard growth at the creek crossing; the flag of truce that evening and the surrender of Sánchez on 8 January). | Henry Marshall, 'Statement', MS., 3-4 · the participant account Bancroft judges to narrate the affair 'briefly but with tolerable accuracy'; cf. Miguel Flores, 'Recuerdos', MS., 16-21, and Secundino Robles, 'Relación', MS., 19-25 (which Bancroft rejects as fiction). | William A. Richardson to Henry D. Fitch, 9 Jan. 1847, in Fitch, 'Documents for the History of California', MS., 411 · reports Bartlett's capture and the departure of Marston's force. | No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of Santa Clara.
notes: SUBSTANTIVE CAUTION for the map text: the feature summary calls this a battle with 'light casualties'. Bancroft's finding is considerably more deflationary and should not be smoothed over; he concludes that Sánchez's men 'came for a few minutes within gunshot, and slightly wounded two of the Americans' and that 'no Californian was hurt', that Sánchez 'had no intention of risking a fight', and that the received accounts of a several-hour engagement with four or five Californians killed are inflations traceable to the Monterey Californian of 6 Feb. 1847 and to Charles Weber's self-serving 1880 reminiscence. Bancroft flatly calls Secundino Robles's detailed narrative 'pure fiction from beginning to end.' The map's 'light casualties' is compatible with Bancroft but 'two Americans slightly wounded, no Californian hurt' is what he actually establishes. Also: the armistice was agreed the evening of 2 Jan.; the surrender was concluded on 8 Jan. 1847, not on the 2nd.

name: Passage of the Río San Gabriel
summary: Stockton and Kearny force the river crossing against Flores's artillery and lancers ('Yankees at the crossing'); Californians withdraw toward the Mesa.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 392-394, ch. xiv (the passage of the Río San Gabriel, 8 January 1847; Emory's account of the charge on the left flank and the formation of squares). | Benjamin D. Wilson, 'Observations on Early Days in California', MS., 92 ff., and Juan Bautista Moreno, 'Vida', MS., 31-3 (Moreno commanded one of the charging companies and was seriously wounded) · the two closest Californian eyewitness manuscripts to the crossing. | California Historical Landmark No. 385, Battle of Río San Gabriel. | No Archives of California manuscript attests the passage of the Río San Gabriel.
notes: CHL No. 385 marker (NE cor. Washington Blvd & Bluff Rd, Montebello); battle at the river ford across present Whittier/Pico Rivera/Montebello. ⚠ NAME TRAP, documented so it is not repeated. The pre-computed candidate list offers ca31-d125 ('arranged transport of the mission's artillery pieces') and ca31-d203 ('reports the San Gabriel cannons are inservibles'), both 22 June 1846. These concern the ordnance of MISSION San Gabriel during Pico's June 1846 defensive scramble, six and a half months before, and have nothing to do with the January 1847 forcing of the Río San Gabriel crossing. They match on the place-name only and must not be linked. ca35-d1179 (Sept. 1847, custody of the San Gabriel mission buildings) is the same trap. I did not verify the CHL marker number (No. 385) independently; it is carried through from the existing citation.

name: Battle of La Mesa
summary: Final action: Flores's last attack on the American square on the plain south of Los Angeles fails; the pueblo reoccupied next day.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 395-397, ch. xiv ('About 4 o'clock the Californians retired, and the "battle of the Mesa" was at an end'; the flag of truce brought next morning by Célis, Ávila and Workman; the reoccupation of the pueblo at noon on 10 January). | A scrap in the handwriting of José Castro, in 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., i. 523: 'Mr Flores on this occasion hid himself in a little thicket of alders, and this was the only occasion when he saw the enemy.' | Dr Eversfield's casualty report in Griffin's 'Papers', MS., 18-19; Antonio F. Coronel, 'Cosas de California', MS., 80-107; Narciso Botello, 'Anales del Sur de la California', MS., 141 ff.; and Salvador Vallejo / Ávila, 'Notas Históricas', MS., 34 ff. · the surgeon's return and the three fullest Californian narratives. | California Historical Landmark No. 167, Battle of La Mesa. | No Archives of California manuscript attests the battle of La Mesa.
notes: CHL No. 167 marker (4490 Exchange Ave at Downey Rd, Vernon). CASUALTY NOTE, flagged: for the two days together (San Gabriel 8 Jan. and La Mesa 9 Jan.) Bancroft settles on three Americans killed and twelve wounded, against Stockton's own claim of three killed and fourteen wounded; the Californians lost three killed across both fights - Ignacio Sepúlveda, Francisco Rubio, and a Yaqui known as 'El Guaymeño' - with Capt. Juan B. Moreno and Alférez Ramírez the only named wounded. Stockton reported Californian losses 'between 70 and 80'; the printed Life of Stockton says over 70 killed and 150 wounded. Bancroft treats the American reports of enemy loss as worthless. The map's 'last Californio field action fails' is sound. I did not verify CHL No. 167 independently.

name: Capitulation of Cahuenga
summary: Andrés Pico surrenders to Frémont at the Campo de Cahuenga; generous terms end organized resistance in California.
sources: Hubert Howe Bancroft, History of California, vol. V: 1846-1848 (San Francisco: The History Company, 1886), pp. 404-405, ch. xiv ('next morning, January 13th, it received the signatures of the respective commandants, Frémont and Pico'), with the seven articles and the additional article transcribed in full at n.20. | 'Articles of capitulation made and entered into at the ranch of Couenga this 13th day of Jan., A.D. 1847', original seven articles with autograph signatures, in [José Antonio] Carrillo (D.), 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., 113-16 · in J. A. Carrillo's own hand, with the signatures to the additional article copied by him; a second copy from the original, including all articles, in Agustín Olvera, 'Documentos para la Historia de California', MS., 76. | Russell's receipt from Andrés Pico of 2 pieces of artillery with 6 charges of grape and 6 muskets, 16 Jan. 1847, in Olvera, 'Documentos', MS., 76-7; and the 18 Jan. Angeles blotter of six further articles proposed by Carrillo and Olvera under art. 7 of the treaty, in Olvera, 'Documentos', MS., 79-81. | Dept. State Papers, Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents (C-A 63), Savage p. 133 / scan n133–n134, Doc 236 · J. C. Frémont, Governor of California, to Juan Bautista Alvarado, Los Angeles, 26 February 1847: full pardon 'in the intention of contributing to the tranquillity of the territory by the return of its citizens to their families and homes… for any acts committed during the present hostilities against the Govt of the U.S.', with free passage and entire security of property and person.
notes: ⚠⚠ THE LOUDEST TRAP IN THIS BATCH. Five of the six pre-computed content candidates (ca36-d88, ca49-d1189, ca30-d230, ca30-d502, ca37-d310) are records of a CAHUENGA CAPITULATION; but of February 1845, the convention between Micheltorena and Castro that ended the Micheltorena war and expelled him from California. That is a different treaty, a different war, and a different pair of signatories, two years before Andrés Pico met Frémont. ca37-d310 is even headed 'CONVENCIÓN CELEBRADA ENTRE MICHELTORENA Y CASTRO'. Any of these linked to the January 1847 capitulation would be a serious, plausible-looking error. All five rejected. Note also that the Cahuenga articles are dated 13 Jan. 1847 but the additional article cancelling paroles and releasing all prisoners is dated at Los Angeles 16 Jan. 1847; the map's single date of 13 January is right for the treaty proper.

name: Corsair squadron at Loreto
summary: Three English frigates (22–24 guns, 60–116 crew) anchor in the surgidero of Loreto; the capital itself; seizing a balandra, later ransomed for sugar, chocolate, and a church bell (~$8,000 losses). 'No dejan buque sin darle caza' (they leave no vessel unchased).
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 68–9 / scan n17, Doc 17 · Arrillaga to the Viceroy, 16 June 1799: three frigates anchored in the surgidero of Loreto, the capital itself; they left behind the captured balandra; intelligence that the ships carry 22–24 cannon and 60–116 crew and that 'no dejan buque sin darle caza'; the Revolución under 'Juan Pivoré' expected. | Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 69–70 / scan n18–n19, Doc 18 · report of Bernardo Juárez Infantzón, 27 June 1799: ransom of the balandra seized on 21 May, paid in sugar, chocolate and one church bell; losses about $8,000; the English held her from the 10th to the 16th. | Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 70–2 / scan n19–n20, Doc 19 · Arrillaga to the Viceroy, 30 June 1799: 'la situación de la Península es muy triste, rodeada de buques ingleses, cuyos número no bajan de 4, y sin ningunos elementos de defensa'; the entire southern garrison is 8 soldiers, 1 cabo and 1 sargento; proposes a 50-man militia at 4 reales a day.
notes: BOTH EXISTING LINKS ARE WRONG AND ARE CORRECTED HERE. They are off by exactly nine document numbers in each case (d8→d17, d9→d18), which suggests a systematic slip rather than two independent errors; worth checking whether neighbouring 1799 Baja features on this map carry the same offset. Substantively: every phrase in the map's feature summary; 'three English frigates (22–24 guns, 60–116 crew)', 'anchor in the surgidero of Loreto; the capital itself', 'seizing a balandra, later ransomed for sugar, chocolate, and a church bell (~$8,000 losses)', and the quoted 'No dejan buque sin d[etener]'; is drawn from ca14-d17 and ca14-d18, not from the linked records. Two small points on the map text: the manuscript's phrase is 'no dejan buque sin darle caza' ('they leave no vessel unchased'), so the map's bracketed expansion '[detener]' should read 'darle caza'; and the balandra was seized on 21 May 1799, six weeks before the June anchoring at Loreto, so 'seizing a balandra' at Loreto slightly compresses the sequence; Doc 17 says the frigates 'left behind' the already-captured balandra.

name: Executions at Cabo San Lucas
summary: Four English corsairmen apprehended at Cabo San Lucas; the commander ordered three hanged. A Spanish brig on the Acapulco–San Blas run captured in the same campaign.
sources: Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 73–6 / scan n21–n22, Doc 21 · Arrillaga to the Viceroy, Aug./Sept. 1799: the English fleet of four frigates departs; four Englishmen apprehended at Cabo San Lucas, the commander ordering three of them hanged; a Spanish brig on the Acapulco–San Blas run captured in the same campaign. Checked at the leaf: this document does not attest the engagement. | Prov. St. Pap. (C-A 14), tomo xxi. 76–83 / scan n22–n25, Doc 22 · the Viceroy to Arrillaga, Sept./Oct. 1799: orders that no refuge be given to English ships and that disembarkation be prevented; Hidalgo supplies 20 muskets plus 15 from the Sutil; the 50-man militia approved and armed with 26 muskets; by 18 October, 67 men including 4 cabos and 3 sargentos under Sgt. Javier Aguilar.
notes: THE EXISTING LINK IS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED HERE; again a nine-document offset (d12→d21), matching the pattern in reg-141, which strongly suggests a single systematic mis-keying across the 1799 Baja corsair features rather than isolated slips. Substantively the record confirms the map on both points: four Englishmen apprehended at Cabo San Lucas, three of them hanged by the commander's order, and a Spanish brig on the Acapulco–San Blas run taken in the same campaign. One precision: the map heads the feature '1799' and Doc 21 is dated August/September 1799 at month confidence, so a firmer date than 'Aug.–Sept. 1799' is not available from this record. The record does not name the commander who gave the hanging order, nor the four Englishmen; do not supply names from elsewhere without a source.

name: Wilson's pursuit near San Bernardino
summary: Benjamin (Benito) Wilson with 200 mounted men pursues horse-raiding parties near San Bernardino; expedition diary filed, further campaign and remounts requested.
sources: Dept. State Papers (C-A 30), tomo vi. 153–5 / Savage pp. 168–9 / scan n170–n171, Doc 277 · 'Diario de la expedición contra los indios', June 1845 [San Bernardino]: Comandante Benjamin (Benito) Wilson with 200 mounted men pursues the horse-raiding Indians near San Bernardino; skirmish at Los Naranjos in which Capitán Bahajes is wounded; the capitanejos submit. | Dept. State Papers (C-A 30), tomo vi. 147+ / Savage pp. 167–8 / scan n169–n170, Doc 276 · Miguel Pedrorena (Jamul) to the Government, 1 July 1845: 'Sobre expedición contra indios ladrones' · forwards the expedition diary, requires a further expedition and a caballada; captains Juan María González and José Bahajes.
notes: ⚠ DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE 1846 EXPEDITION. The catalogue holds a second, later Wilson punitive expedition; ca31-d118, B. D. Wilson writing from Jurupa on 23 August 1846, 'Matanza de Indios', reporting his 22 August attack on a ranchería of the Amajaques. That is a different action, a year later, under a different government, and it must not be merged into this feature. DATE NOTE: ca30-d277 is dated to the month only (June 1845), so the feature's bare '1845' is correct and cannot honestly be sharpened from this record; the follow-up (d276) is 1 July 1845, which brackets the expedition as late June 1845. NUMBERS NOTE: '200 mounted men' comes straight from the manuscript abstract ('con 200 montados') and is Savage's summary of the diary's own claim, not an independent count. The map's 'raiders not destroyed' is a fair reading; the diary records a skirmish at Los Naranjos and the submission of the capitanejos, and d276 then asks for a further expedition, which implies the first did not settle the matter; but note the abstract also says Wilson 'somete á los capitanejos', so 'inconclusive' is a safer characterisation than 'failed'.

The crown furnished it: the 1794 accounts approve decorating its wall with a retablo and altar canvas.
sources: Prov. State Papers (C-A 6), doc 341 · the 1794 retablo/altar approval | Bancroft, History of California I, 684–86 (the 1791–94 rebuilding)
notes: Drawn at the chapel site itself (today’s San Carlos Cathedral), a block from the presidio quadrangle marker.

name: Plaza Church (Los Ángeles)
summary: La Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles; The pueblo's own church, begun 1818 and dedicated in December 1822; built because Los Ángeles had none: in 1810 the San Gabriel padre refused to come confess the vecinos, and the pueblo's representation went up to the Padre Presidente. The largest town in California finally got an altar of its own.
sources: Prov. Records (C-A 26), doc 11 · the 1810 confession refusal and the vecinos' representation | Bancroft, History of California II, 110–11, 566–67 (construction 1818–22, dedication)

name: St. Joseph's Chapel
summary: At the Pueblo de San José: the vecinos raised its own adobe chapel in 1803, ending dependence on Mission Santa Clara three miles off; the third secular congregation of Spanish California, and the seed of today's St. Joseph's.
sources: Bancroft, History of California II, 135 (the 1803 pueblo chapel) [standard record]

name: Presidio Chapel, Santa Bárbara
summary: The chapel of the Presidio de Santa Bárbara, serving the garrison and the vecinos who grew up around the quadrangle; the fourth secular congregation of Spanish California. The chapel standing today at El Presidio State Historic Park is a reconstruction on the original foundations.
sources: Prov. State Papers (C-A 1), doc 183 · the 1779 founding blueprint for the Presidio del Canal de Santa Bárbara | Bancroft, History of California I (the presidio's founding, 1782) [standard record]

name: Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe
summary: The province's first civil settlement, planted by Lt. José Joaquín Moraga with fourteen families from the San Francisco and Monterey companies. Its early governance runs straight through C-A 2: the first alcalde election (Ygnacio Archuleta), the distribution of solares and suertes, and the boundary fight with Mission Santa Clara.
sources: Founding: Bancroft, History of California I (vault full text). | First alcalde election: C-A 2 Doc 195 | Pueblo–Mission Santa Clara boundary dispute: C-A 2 Doc 240

name: Villa de Branciforte
summary: The third and last Spanish civil settlement, laid out across the San Lorenzo from Mission Santa Cruz for invalid-soldier colonists; under-funded from birth and a permanent irritant to the mission. The pobladores' ration appears in C-A 8 within weeks of their arrival.
sources: Founding: Bancroft, History of California I (vault full text). | Branciforte pobladores' ration, May 1797: C-A 8 Doc 374

name: Castillo de San Joaquín (Fort Point, San Francisco)
summary: The battery at the Golden Gate narrows, blessed December 1794. Built for 6,491 pesos, partly with mission mule labor. The register's headline series: the fort's serviceable guns never exceeded a handful, and a single Russian outpost at Ross reported more mounted cannon than the whole San Francisco defense.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault); build cost C-A 24 Docs 62, 70

name: Batería de San José / de Yerba Buena (San Francisco)
summary: The cove battery east of the presidio, garrisoned in the 1790s by a Catalan Volunteers detail relieved every 8 days. Ordered recomposed with adobe, earth, and fascine in 1799; abandoned by 1800 per the intelligence layer of the borderlands map.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: El Castillo (Monterey battery)
summary: The capital's shore battery on the hill above the landing, described by Vancouver's 1792 visit. The leaf-verified 1795 ordnance relación counts ten bronze guns at Monterey against San Francisco's eight, the two batteries called 'construidas' and 'nuevas'.
sources: AGN Californias 9, exp. 4, ff. 149-150 (25 July 1795), leaf-verified ordnance relación; Vancouver, Voyage of Discovery.
notes: Battery date given as circa: shown 'by 1792' on Vancouver's description; the 1795 count is AGN Californias 9, exp. 4 (read at full resolution, 2026-10).

name: Fort Guijarros (Punta de Guijarros, San Diego)
summary: The harbor battery on Ballast Point, formally the Castillo de San Joaquín de Punta de Guijarros. The province had two forts of that name; this is the San Diego one. In 1798 it mounted 7 six-pounders of which 2 were serviceable; the 1820 census found the bronze guns vent-worn and the carriages rotted.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: San Pedro y San Pablo outstation (San Pedro Valley, Pacifica)
summary: Mission Dolores's farm and chapel outstation in the San Pedro Valley, worked from 1786 until epidemic losses and earthquake damage ended it in the early 1790s; the Sanchez Adobe stands on the site today. Found missing from our live map by Aodhan at the exhibit.
sources: Milliken, A Time of Little Choice (1995); San Mateo County history of the Sanchez Adobe site.
notes: Data correction queued: the live missions map pins one 'San Pedro y San Pablo (San Mateo)' at San Mateo Creek, conflating this Pacifica outstation with the separate San Mateo outstation. Both existed; fix goes live only after approval.

name: Rancho del Rey at Buri Buri (San Francisco presidio)
summary: The crown herd ranch of the San Francisco company, founded 1797 with corral and toril at Buri Buri between San Mateo and San Bruno, chosen for its pasture and water. Surfaced by the 2026-10-16 deep check: the royal stock ranches were missing from the establishment map entirely.
sources: 'Fundación de un Rancho' at Buriburi: C-A 9 Doc 143 (1797) (catalog-matched 2026-10-16; leaf review pending) | Report of establishing the royal cattle ranch near San Francisco: C-A 24 Doc 584 (1797) (catalog-matched 2026-10-16; leaf review pending)

name: Rancho del Rey (Monterey)
summary: The crown stock ranch of the Monterey company on the Salinas plain, supplying troop rations; its accounts run through the archive (5,794 horses and mules in the 1797 cuenta) and its herd losses to theft and want of hands became a standing complaint.
sources: Cuenta de ganados of the Rancho del Rey: C-A 16 Doc 125 (1797) (catalog-matched 2026-10-16; leaf review pending) | Sal and Carrillo ordered to report the royal ranch's history and herd: C-A 23 Doc 1667 (1798) (catalog-matched 2026-10-16; leaf review pending) | Testimony on herd diminution at the King's ranch: C-A 24 Doc 843 (1798) (catalog-matched 2026-10-16; leaf review pending)
notes: Placed on the Salinas plain (the later Rancho Nacional); exact headquarters site approximate.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: The northernmost presidio, founded 1776, responsible for the whole contested frontier facing Bodega and Ross. Its company ran about 30 to 56 men for most of the Spanish period and never surged to meet the Russian arrival in 1812.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault), compiled from C-A 10, 16, 21, 54 | Neve's 'Fundación de Misiones' report names the new Presidio of San Francisco: C-A 22 Doc 170 (1777) (catalog-matched 2026-10-16; leaf review pending)
notes: Rows cited 'presidio register' rest on the vault's register compilation; their catalog doc numbers are still being resolved and they carry no link by design.

name: Presidio of Monterey
summary: The capital's presidio and the largest company in the province, with the Real Cuerpo de Artillería headquartered here. Even so, in 1809 its ~85 men were dispersed as mission escorts and herd guards, with only 4 men on the battery.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault) | Viceroy Croix's measures to establish the Presidio of Monterey and the missions: C-A 1 Doc 23 (12 Nov 1770)
notes: Rows cited 'presidio register' rest on the vault's register compilation; their catalog doc numbers are still being resolved and they carry no link by design.

name: Presidio of Santa Bárbara
summary: Founded 1782 with about 58 men and holding near that strength for decades. In 1797 its commander reported 118 cartridges for his single six-pounder, with no artilleryman to serve it.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Presidio of San Diego
summary: The first presidio, founded 1769. In September 1783 the whole company held 72 cartridges. Its guns were dismounted in 1793 with nobody able to operate them.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)
notes: Rows cited 'presidio register' rest on the vault's register compilation; their catalog doc numbers are still being resolved and they carry no link by design.

name: Presidio of Loreto (Baja California)
summary: The old Baja capital, included for context: its company (47 to 85 men plus a small marine department) was comparable to any Alta California presidio.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)
notes: Rows cited 'presidio register' rest on the vault's register compilation; their catalog doc numbers are still being resolved and they carry no link by design.

name: Sonoma garrison (Presidio of Sonoma)
summary: The northern frontier's last Mexican garrison: founded as the twelve-man armed escort of Mission San Francisco Solano in 1823, and after 1835 the seat of Vallejo's frontier command, absorbing what remained of the San Francisco company.
sources: Rows cited document-by-document in the dated series

name: San Antonio (Baja California) · the comandancia in the US war
summary: The southern comandancia militar in the Mexican-American War: a twenty-man force mustered against the invasion, thanked by the government 'por la defenza brillante', and begging powder and subsistence from Sonora.
sources: Rows cited document-by-document in the dated series

name: Pueblo de Los Ángeles
summary: El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles, planted on the Porciúncula by Neve's plan; 11 families, 44 settlers. The founding paper trail sits in this archive: the 1778 pueblo plan, the 1779 founding blueprint, and Argüello's signed measured plat of the pueblo itself.
sources: Prov. State Papers (C-A 1), doc 183 · the 1779 founding blueprint (presidio, missions, and the pueblo) | Prov. State Papers (C-A 2), doc 41 · Argüello's signed measured plat of the Pueblo de Los Ángeles | Prov. State Papers (C-A 1), doc 127 · the 1778 plan for pueblos on the Guadalupe and Porciúncula

name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
summary: First of the chain; destroyed in the 1775 revolt and rebuilt at this valley site.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Carlos Borromeo (Carmel)
summary: Serra's headquarters and burial place; moved from Monterey to Carmel in 1771.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Antonio de Padua
summary: The upper Salinas valley mission, in Salinan country.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel
summary: The richest of the southern missions; Toypurina's 1785 revolt; the gateway of the overland routes.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa
summary: Founded on the strength of the Portolá expedition's bear hunts in the Cañada de los Osos.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Dolores)
summary: The Bay's first mission; its neophyte flights across the water drove the 1795–97 East Bay expeditions.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Juan Capistrano
summary: Founded twice, 1775 and 1776, after the San Diego revolt interrupted the first attempt.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission Santa Clara de Asís
summary: Paired with the pueblo of San José, whose fields bordered too closely for the friars' comfort.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Buenaventura
summary: The Channel mission Serra founded last in person; armed with cannon in the 1798 census.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission Santa Bárbara
summary: The 'Queen of the Missions,' beside the presidio; a center of the 1824 Chumash revolt.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission La Purísima Concepción
summary: Seized by Chumash rebels for a month in 1824; rebuilt after the 1812 earthquake at the present site.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission Santa Cruz
summary: Across the river from the villa of Branciforte, whose settlers the friars blamed for most of their troubles.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
summary: The lonely Salinas valley mission; two governors died within its walls.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San José
summary: Base of the East Bay and Delta frontier; Estanislao was its alcalde before his 1829 revolt.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Sited at 'San Benito' per Lasuén's 1796 reconnaissance synthesis (C-A 50); the 1798 Talholostl battle was fought nearby.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Miguel Arcángel
summary: Sited at 'las Pozas' in the same 1795–96 siting campaign.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Fernando Rey
summary: The valley mission on the LA road; armed with 2-pounders in the 1805 census.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia
summary: Founded 13 Jun 1798, 54 children baptized that day (C-A 24 Doc 277); the largest mission population; Duflot drew its plan in the gallery.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission Santa Inés
summary: The last Channel mission; the 1824 revolt began here.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Rafael Arcángel
summary: Begun as a hospital asistencia of Dolores, raised to full mission in 1822; the northern frontier's answer to sickness and to Ross.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Mission San Francisco Solano (Sonoma)
summary: The last and northernmost mission, founded under Mexican rule partly to face the Russians; seed of Vallejo's Sonoma.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Santa Margarita de Cortona (asistencia)
summary: Grain-station and chapel over the cuesta from San Luis Obispo; the rancho kept the name. Sub-station of Mission San Luis Obispo.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: San Antonio de Pala (asistencia)
summary: The inland asistencia of San Luis Rey; uniquely, still a functioning mission chapel serving a Native community today. Sub-station of Mission San Luis Rey.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Las Flores (asistencia)
summary: The coast station between San Luis Rey and San Juan Capistrano; later the Pico brothers' rancho. Sub-station of Mission San Luis Rey.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Santa Ysabel (asistencia)
summary: San Diego's mountain asistencia in Kumeyaay country; the same district as the register's Santa Isabel fight of 1826. Sub-station of Mission San Diego.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: San Bernardino de Sena (estancia)
summary: San Gabriel's estancia at the foot of the pass; the rancho outpost end of the mission system, in the raiding corridor. Sub-station of Mission San Gabriel.
sources: Founding dates per the standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal.; Engelhardt).

name: Colony Ross
summary: The Russian-American Company's fort and village on Kashaya land, 1812 to 1841. The Presidial System map carries its strength series; Vallejo's 1833 reconnaissance (C-A 53 Doc 45) describes it in full.
sources: Russian establishments per the RAC literature (Gibson; Istomin) and the Spanish-Mexican reconnaissance record (C-A 12, C-A 53).

name: Port Rumiantsev (Bodega)
summary: The company's anchorage and warehouses at Bodega Bay, in use from about 1809. The port the Spanish discovered in 1775, working under a Russian name.
sources: Russian establishments per the RAC literature (Gibson; Istomin) and the Spanish-Mexican reconnaissance record (C-A 12, C-A 53).
notes: Anchorage in Bodega Harbor; the precise landing/port site is approximate.

name: Kostromitinov Ranch
summary: Company farm on the Russian River plain, one of the three ranches feeding Ross in its last decade. Location approximate.
sources: Russian establishments per the RAC literature (Gibson; Istomin) and the Spanish-Mexican reconnaissance record (C-A 12, C-A 53).

name: Khlebnikov Ranch
summary: Company farm inland from Bodega, named for the RAC agent. Location approximate.
sources: Russian establishments per the RAC literature (Gibson; Istomin) and the Spanish-Mexican reconnaissance record (C-A 12, C-A 53).

name: Chernykh Ranch
summary: The agronomist Chernykh's farm; Voznesensky sketched it in 1841 (the sketch is in this site's gallery). Location approximate.
sources: Russian establishments per the RAC literature (Gibson; Istomin) and the Spanish-Mexican reconnaissance record (C-A 12, C-A 53).

name: Suisun outstation (Solano)
summary: The Sonoma mission's grazing outstation in the Suisun Valley, at the Rockville and Cordelia end rather than the later town of Fairfield; in the country of the Suisun Patwin, and absorbed into the Vallejo-era ranchos after secularization. Outstation of Mission San Francisco Solano.
sources: Mission-estate outstations per the standard accounts (Engelhardt; county histories); locations approximate. Selected, not exhaustive: the missions ran many more ranchos.

summary: The mission's station in the lower Napa Valley, likewise folded into private ranchos in the 1830s. Outstation of Mission San Francisco Solano.

name: San Pedro y San Pablo (San Mateo)
summary: Mission Dolores' farm outstation on the peninsula, established in the 1780s; the 1830 SF padron still lists San Mateo among the jurisdiction's ranchos (C-A 50 Doc 425). Outstation of Mission San Francisco de Asís.

summary: San Fernando's northern stock rancho in the Santa Clarita valley; the same Rancho San Francisco where 18 Indians were killed in 1846 (military register #117). Outstation of Mission San Fernando.

name: Santa Ysabel rancho (San Miguel)
summary: One of San Miguel's named ranchos with an adobe, up the Salinas from the mission. Outstation of Mission San Miguel.

summary: San Miguel's coast station at San Simeon bay. Outstation of Mission San Miguel.

summary: San Luis Rey's inland station among the Luiseno communities of the Temecula valley. Outstation of Mission San Luis Rey.

summary: The mission's easternmost stock rancho, toward the pass country. Outstation of Mission San Luis Rey.

summary: San Gabriel's furthest estancia, in the pass between the mountains; the raiding corridor's doorstep. Outstation of Mission San Gabriel.
