name: Sutter's Fort (New Helvetia)
summary: Sutter's Mexican land-grant colony at the Sacramento-American confluence, founded 1839. Buyer of Ross's movable property in 1841, magnet for the overland emigrants, and the hinge between the mission-rancho world and the American conquest. The anti-Micheltorena revolt charged the governor with his 'relaciones secretas' with Sutter (C-A 61).
sources: Standard accounts (Bancroft, Hist. Cal., IV); cf. Leg. Rec. (C-A 61) Doc 19

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: 1797. Moraga 1806 departure; Viader 1810 Aug return.

name: Mission San Fernando
summary: 1797. Moraga 1806 arrival.

name: Mission San José
summary: 1797. Viader/Moraga 1810 departure point.

name: Mission Santa Clara
summary: 1777. Viader 1810 Oct return.

name: Mission San Miguel
summary: 1797. Moraga 1807 stop.

name: Monterey Presidio
summary: Moraga 1807 departure.

name: Mission San Rafael
summary: 1817. First establishment north of SF Bay. Site selected by Moraga. Founded 83 days after Hagemeister-Pomo treaty.

name: Fort Ross
summary: 1812. Russian-American Company. Kuskov. 95 Russians + ~80 Aleut hunters. Moraga visited 1812, 1813, 1814.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: 1776. Founded by José Joaquín Moraga (Gabriel's father). Gabriel served here as Alférez 1806–1818.

name: Monterey
summary: Departure. 25 cavalry under Alférez Gabriel Moraga. Sgt. Miguel Espinosa. 8 horses each.

name: Mission San Miguel
summary: 'We went from Monterey to San Miguel Mission.'
sources: Felipe Santiago García's reminiscence, taken down by Alexander S. Taylor, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California' (1958), ch. III, 254-256.

name: Buena Vista Lake
summary: 'From there to the Laguna we called Buena Vista in one day and a half.' Went after runaway neophytes — 'did not get any.'
sources: Cook note 46: 'This expedition of 1807 is otherwise unrecorded.' | Felipe Santiago García's reminiscence, taken down by Alexander S. Taylor, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California' (1958), ch. III, 254-256.

name: Mountains — Salinas de Cortéz
summary: 'We went away into the Snowy Mountains, 'or near where the snow was'.' Indians stole half the horses and killed two men. 'Portezuelo' with great quantities of nitre.
sources: Cook note 47: possibly entrance to Gorge of Kern R., E of Bakersfield | Felipe Santiago García's reminiscence, taken down by Alexander S. Taylor, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California' (1958), ch. III, 254-256.

name: San Joaquin River (crossings)
summary: 'We crossed the San Joaquin River several times and everywhere there was Indians.'
sources: Felipe Santiago García's reminiscence, taken down by Alexander S. Taylor, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California' (1958), ch. III, 254-256.

name: Mission San José
summary: 'The Captain made up his mind to go back by the way of San Jose Mission where we arrived in good order.'
sources: Felipe Santiago García's reminiscence, taken down by Alexander S. Taylor, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California' (1958), ch. III, 254-256.

name: Mission San José
summary: Aug 15, 1810. Departed 5:30pm with Lt. Moraga, Cadet Estrada, 1 corporal, 3 soldiers, 4 neophytes.

name: Valley of San José — Pool
summary: Aug 15. 6 leagues N. 'Good water. So near and so well known to everyone.'
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Walnut Creek
summary: Aug 16 (lunch). 6 leagues N. 'Good water but runs in very small amount.' Killed 2 bears and a deer.
sources: Cook note 1: route via Sunol, Dublin, Walnut Creek | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: End of Walnut Creek — Estuaries
summary: Aug 16. 6 more leagues N. 'Beginning of some estuaries on the NE side of a fine plain.' Big walnut trees.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: San Joaquin R. / Tulpunes — Antioch
summary: Aug 18. 7 leagues E. 'Quarter-league wide, apparently very deep, reached by tides.' Large oak forest. Tulpunes not seen.
sources: Cook note 2: at or near Antioch. Julpunes oak forest to Brentwood. | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Oak Forest — Oakley
summary: Aug 18. 2 more leagues E. Good country, no water except the river.
sources: Cook note 2: halt near Oakley

name: Pescadero / Cholvones — Bethany
summary: Aug 19. 10 leagues SE. Lake in oak grove. Interpreter met heathen Guanats. The Guanats told him, in Viader's words, 'They say that the Christian fugitives from San José are on the opposite shore.'
sources: Cook note 3: Bethany. Lakes vanished. | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Tomchom Village
summary: Aug 20. 3 leagues SSE. 'No wild Indian showed himself.'
sources: Cook note 4: north of Tracy | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Cuyens Village
summary: Aug 20. 2½ leagues further. Chief Cuyens. 15 Indians brought fish. 4 stayed the night.
sources: Cook note 4: left bank, 3 mi above highway bridge

name: Maijem Village
summary: Aug 21. 2½–3 leagues. Dry stream bed. Indians came 'with great trepidation' then disappeared.
sources: Cook note 5: ~2 mi NNE of Vernalis | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Opposite Bozenats Village
summary: Aug 21. 2 leagues. Indians on far bank 'refused to come near, yelled with much vigor.'
sources: Cook note 6: right bank, E of Vernalis | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: SKIRMISH — Tationes / Apaglamenes
summary: Aug 22. 2 leagues + 1 league. 30 armed heathen on opposite bank. Then Tationes village. Apaglamenes and Tationes attacked — 'painted, bedecked with feathers.' 12 shots fired. One Indian hit.
sources: Cook note 7: ~2 mi SE of Grayson | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Lakes near Willow Grove
summary: Aug 22 afternoon. 3 leagues. 'Neither firewood nor good land.'
sources: Cook note 8: probably E of Patterson | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Creek — Orestimba
summary: Aug 23. 3½ leagues. 'Great heat forced us to jump in for a swim.'
sources: Cook note 9: Orestimba Cr., E of Crows Landing | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Pond — NE of Gustine
summary: Aug 23. 4 leagues. 'No wood or brush to cook supper or even make chocolate.'
sources: Cook note 10: 3–4 mi NE of Gustine. Southernmost point. | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: San Luis Gonzaga
summary: Aug 24. Turned back W! 10 leagues. Explored — 'no more water than a few pools.' Not suitable for mission.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Ausaymas Creek
summary: Aug 26. SW over mountains. 'Caught forty fish including six trout.' Already the plain of San Juan Bautista.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Aug 27. 5 leagues SW. 'With a good breakfast we brought the expedition to an end.' Signed Fr. José Viader, Aug 28, 1810.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Mission San José
summary: Oct 19, 1810. Left ~2pm with Lt. Moraga, 23 soldiers, ~50 armed Christian Indians.

name: Valley of San José
summary: Oct 19. 6 leagues NE. Willow grove with good water.

name: Pescadero / Cholvones — Bethany
summary: Oct 20. 9 leagues ENE. 'Arrived very late so as not to be seen or heard. Placed our people in position to attack a dance.'
sources: Cook note 11: Mission San José to Bethany = ~32 mi | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Bolbones Villages — Old River
summary: Oct 21. 'Before dawn we assaulted a village.' Captured 15 San Jose Christians, 18 heathen men, 51 women. Women released — 'went away very happy.' Two prisoners escaped.
sources: Cook note 12: two villages on Old River / Union I. | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Jusmites
summary: Oct 22. 2½ leagues SE along river. 'Oak groves, willow thickets, ponds.'
sources: Cook note 14 | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Tugites
summary: Oct 22. 2½ more leagues. 'All the country seen thus far has wood, with water in the river and lakes, but the land is low, flooded, and without stone.'
sources: Cook note 14 | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Cuyens Village
summary: Oct 23. Met friendly Cuyens Indians. 'Bearing as a gift three very big, red, salmon.'
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Mayem Village
summary: Oct 23. 4 leagues total. 'Approached us with much fear and a tendency to prevaricate.' Deny harboring Christians. Lt. threatens flogging.
sources: Cook note 14: Mayem 9 leagues from Pescadero | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Ford Opposite Taualames
summary: Oct 23 afternoon. 2 leagues. 'Ford across the river — very bad, wide and deep.' Crossed without incident. Sent boy to village.
sources: Cook note 14–15 | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Toward Tuolumne — Blocked
summary: Oct 24. Scouted N toward Tuolumne (Dolores), 2–3 leagues away. 'On account of so many sloughs, swamps, and ponds we turned back.'
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Past Apelamenes & Tatives
summary: Oct 24 afternoon. 6 leagues SSE. 'Passed in front of the Apelamenes and Tatives Indians, who had fought us on the former occasion.'
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Merced River
summary: Oct 24. Reached Merced R. 'Almost swimming the horses.' Much wood — oak, cypress, cottonwood.
sources: Cook note 15 | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Crossed San Joaquin
summary: Oct 25. SW. 'Crossed several other swampy sloughs. Southward no more trees, only tules.'
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: 'Battle / Shaving Place'
summary: Oct 25. 2½ leagues downstream. 'At this point now, as previously, the soldiers shave themselves.' Viader identifies the shaving place as the scene of the August skirmish, so this stop is plotted where that engagement is fixed.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Orestimba Creek — Apalamenes
summary: Oct 25. 1 league. 'Allies of the Tatives when they fought us.' Creek dry. 'Least bad spot — only firewood, river water, and good fish.'
sources: Cook note 9/16 | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Opposite Taualames (return)
summary: Oct 25. 2 leagues. 'Refused to come out, saying they were afraid. They guessed right for they would have been taken captive.'
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Del Puerto Creek — Corpus Christi
summary: Oct 25. 3 leagues W. 'Spent the night without water for the horses. Had to dig a well in the sand.'
sources: Cook note 16: Del Puerto Cr. | Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: El Toro
summary: Oct 26. 6 leagues W. Mountains, bad trails. Lunch stop.

name: San Guillermo
summary: Oct 26. 6 more leagues W. 'Extremely bad trail.' Pools of good water.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Old Village of Patenos
summary: Oct 27. 6 leagues W. Lunch stop.
sources: Cook note 16: through hills NE of Mt. Hamilton

name: Mission Santa Clara
summary: Oct 27. 5 leagues NW. 'In good condition, thanks be to God.' Signed Fr. José Viader, Oct 28, 1810.
sources: Fr. José Viader, diary of the expedition of 15-28 August / 19-27 October 1810, in S. F. Cook, 'Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820' (1960), ch. V.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: May 1810. Governor Arrillaga orders Moraga to pursue the Suisun, who have killed 16 Christians over 3 years. Moraga departs with 17 men.
sources: Arrillaga report, Prov. Rec. ix. 122–3 (C-A 25).

name: Overland March — East Bay Hills
summary: Route overland from the Presidio, skirting the south shore of the Bay toward the Strait. Exact route unknown but likely through modern Oakland/Richmond hills.
sources: No diary survives for this expedition.

name: Carquinez Strait Crossing
summary: Troops had no boats. Found a single small vessel. 'With great sacrifice, the Ensign embarked his troops and horses, making several crossings.' Multiple trips across the narrows.
sources: Arrillaga report. Vallejo calls it the 'Karkin-aku pass.'

name: Skirmish on Suisun Creek
summary: Initial engagement. After crossing the strait, troops fought Suisun warriors along the banks of a creek. Vallejo (via Sánchez): the Suisun chief drew the Spanish inland toward the main body of warriors. Sgt. Francisco Soto left as rear guard with horses.
sources: Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos, i. 151-5. Vallejo attributes to Sánchez (1817) but likely describes 1810.

name: Battle at the Malaca rancheria
summary: Main engagement, May 22, 1810. Captured 18 gentiles (released — too wounded to transport). Survivors retreated into 3 tule huts. 2 corporals (Herrera, Soto) and 2 soldiers (Briones, Zúñiga) wounded. After 2 huts stormed, 3rd set on fire. Defenders burned alive rather than surrender. ~120 Suisun fighters. Chief Malaca's speech: 'It is better to die free than to live as slaves, despised by our Puy.'
sources: Bancroft II, p. 91 fn. 24. Arrillaga: Prov. Rec. ix. 122–3. Royal Order: Prov. St. Pap. xix. 314. Vallejo: MS. i. 151-5. | Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo, Recuerdos Históricos y Personales tocante a la Alta California, Tomo 1, ch. 10, trans. Beebe and Senkewicz, 151, recounting Alférez José Sánchez's narration. Vallejo's footnote records that the phrase stands in English in the original manuscript.
notes: Malaca's words come from Vallejo's memoir of the 1870s reporting what Alférez Sánchez told him, not from a contemporary record, and Vallejo wrote the phrase in English. Earlier versions of this map rendered it into Spanish and presented that rendering as the source wording. Bancroft flags the provenance problem directly: Vallejo places this fight with Jose Sanchez in 1817 rather than Moraga in 1810, Alvarado dates it 1817 but puts Moraga in command, and Bancroft concludes 'It is possible that the author has confounded two different battles' (History of California II, n. 29). Malaca's words reach us only through that account. Malaca is named as a village in the contemporary Spanish record; the reading of Malaca as a chief comes from Vallejo's later recollection, which is also the only source for the speech quoted here.

name: Return Crossing — Carquinez Strait
summary: Vallejo: 'At dawn they tried to ford a creek and came back over the Carquines Strait.' Return to south shore after the battle.
sources: Vallejo, Recuerdos, i. 151-5.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Moraga returns to the Presidio. Arrillaga reports to the Viceroy on 28 June 1810. The viceroy transmitted the royal order of 19 August 1811 on 12 November 1811: Moraga promoted to brevet Lieutenant of Cavalry.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: October 3, 1810. Governor orders Moraga to investigate Russian fur-hunting at Bodega Bay. 10-day reconnaissance.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, n. 281: 'Gabriel Moragas Diary of his Expedition to the Port of Bodega, Oct. 3, 1810, Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79. Diary survives in the Archives of California.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay from the Presidio to the Marin shore. Method uncertain — possibly native balsas or a borrowed vessel.
sources: SF Presidio had limited boat access. See boat-problem article.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Passed through future site of Mission San Rafael. Bancroft: 'The site was probably selected on the advice of Moraga, who had several times passed it on his way to and from Bodega.'
sources: Bancroft, II, p. 330.

name: Novato / Olompali Area
summary: Route north through Marin. Approximate — following the natural corridor through the Novato gap toward Petaluma Creek and the coast.
sources: Exact route not specified in diary abstract.

name: Petaluma Creek / Estuary
summary: Likely crossed or followed Petaluma Creek toward the coast. Natural route from interior Marin to Bodega Bay.
sources: Route reconstruction based on geography.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Arrived at Bodega Bay. Found an American ship and Alaskan Indians (Aleut hunters working for the Russian-American Company). 10-day reconnaissance of the area. Wrote a diary of the expedition.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: finds an American ship and Alaskan Indians. Diary: Prov. St. Pap., XII, 276–79.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns after ten days. The diary reports not a Russian but an American vessel and crew otter-hunting at Bodega, with Alaskan (Unalaska) hunters among them. The Russian establishment at Bodega and Ross comes later.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: Late August 1812 (departed 25 August, returned 1 September). Argüello sends Moraga with 4 men to investigate construction of a small Russian fort on the Sonoma coast. Fort Ross had been dedicated Sept. 10, 1812 — but Kuskov had been building since spring.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay to the Marin shore.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Through future Mission San Rafael site. Moraga's repeated passage through here informed his later recommendation of the site.

name: Petaluma Creek Area
summary: North through Marin toward the coast. Approximate route.

name: Bodega Bay
summary: Passed through or near Bodega Bay en route to Fort Ross.

name: Fort Ross
summary: Moraga identifies the Russian settlement: a brigantine-anchored base with a 150-yard-square stockade and cannon. Notes the Russians' friendly manner. Fort Ross had been dedicated by Kuskov with 95 Russians and ~80 Aleut hunters.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: 150-yard-square stockade and cannon; notes the Russians friendly manner.'

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to SF. Report filed with Argüello.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: January 1813. Moraga drives 20 cattle and 3 horses to Fort Ross — practical diplomacy. Returns again in 1814 with Cadet Gervasio Argüello.
sources: Langelier & Rosen, Ch. 3.

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed bay to Marin shore with livestock.

name: San Rafael Area
summary: Through future mission site, driving cattle north.

name: Bodega Bay Area
summary: Through Bodega country toward Fort Ross.

name: Fort Ross
summary: Jan. 1813: Delivered 20 cattle, 3 horses as goodwill gesture. 1814 return: accompanied by Cadet Gervasio Argüello. Wrote a report describing 40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon, glass windows in the commandant's house. Also carried official demands for Russian withdrawal.
sources: Langelier & Rosen: 40 gente de razón and many Kodiak Indians, cannon guarding the place, and glass windows in the commandants house.'

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to SF Presidio.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: c. 1817. Moraga reconnoiters the site north of the Bay for a new establishment. He had passed through this area multiple times on trips to Bodega and Fort Ross since 1810.
sources: Bancroft II, p. 330: 'The site was probably selected on the advice of Moraga.'

name: Bay Crossing — to Marin
summary: Crossed the bay to the Marin shore. SF Presidio had no proper boat from Feb. 1816 to Nov. 1818 — crossing method uncertain. Possibly native tule balsas.
sources: See boat-problem article. Vallejo mentions 'a small boat belonging to the San Francisco presidio.'

name: Mission San Rafael Site
summary: Moraga selects this site — 5 leagues north of the Presidio, on the other side of the Bay. Warmer climate, near homeland of many SF neophytes. Mission founded Dec. 14, 1817 under Fr. Luis Gil y Taboada, escorted by Cpl. José Herrera (wounded at Suisun 1810, promoted to Sgt.). Vallejo says the Suisun victory led directly to the decision to found the mission.
sources: Solá letter: Prov. Rec. ix. 583–604 (C-A 25). Founded 83 days after Hagemeister-Pomo treaty.

name: Return to Presidio
summary: Returns to the Presidio with his recommendation. Governor Solá approves the plan in consultation with Prefect Sarría.

name: The 19 Chumash rancherías of the channel, counted 1796
summary: The colonial state's one attempt to count the people it had not yet reduced. A nominal census of about nineteen coastal Chumash rancherías, each entered with its own name, its captain's name in his own language, its distance from the last, and its number of gentile souls: 1,983 people over 31 leagues of coast. It closes with a proposal to instruct them in their own rancherías rather than force them into the missions, with grain as the inducement.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 200 · *Rancherías de Gentiles*, 12 March 1796.
notes: ⚠ Placed on the channel as a group. The nineteen rancherías are named individually in the manuscript; itemising and locating them requires a leaf-by-leaf read, which has not been done. This feature stands for the census, not for a single place.

name: The rancherías behind Carmel, in Serra's padrón of 1781
summary: Serra counted his neophytes not as a mission population but by the rancherías they came from: San Carlos 23 married men and 1 widower, San José 14, Santa Teresa 21, San Miguel 15, San Francisco 18; 96 adult males in all. Behind the mission's single number stand five named communities. Since the mission's founding 659 Indians had been baptised and 243 had died.
sources: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Mil.) (C-A 15) Doc 163 · padrón of the neophyte Indians of Mission San Carlos, by Serra, 22 December 1781.
notes: ⚠ The ranchería names here are the mission's Spanish names for them, recorded at Carmel. Their locations are not given in the document.

name: Coast Miwok place-names in the limits of Mission San Rafael, 1828
summary: A boundary description that is also a gazetteer. Setting the limits of Mission San Rafael, the document runs west some eight leagues to the estero coming from the port of Bodega 'llamado de Tamales' (Tomales), and north nine leagues over the sierra to the plains of Livantonomi[?], where a house and sown fields were to draw the gentilidad in 'con suavidad y blandura'. It carries a dense layer of Coast Miwok names: the ranchería of Olompalí, the Laguna Ocolom, the cañadas de las Gallinas.
sources: Archives of California, Misc. (C-A 62) Doc 57 · *Límites de Misión San Rafael Arcángel*, 1828.
notes: ⚠ Placed between San Rafael and Tomales Bay to span the described limits; the boundary itself is not mapped here.

name: The ranchería de Amajaba (Mojave), 1819
summary: The furthest place the Californian military reached toward. In 1819 the ranchería de Amajaba was reported to have threatened Missions San Gabriel and San Fernando, and Moraga was ordered to march with fifty men; thirty-five cavalry from both presidios, fifteen Mazatlán troops under Fabregat, four artillerymen and a cannon with grape and ball; to make the *capitanejos* surrender the fugitive Christian Indians, then leave garrisons of fifteen at each mission.
sources: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Mil.) (C-A 17) Doc 296 · order for the Amajaba campaign, Monterey, 1819.
notes: ⚠ Placed at the Mojave villages on the Colorado. The document names the people, not a mapped location.

name: The ranchería called Sespesuya, across the estero, 1810
summary: Arrillaga ordered Alférez Gabriel Moraga of the San Francisco company against the gentiles of the ranchería 'llamada Sespesuya' north of the presidio, who in three years of nominal peace had killed sixteen Christians. The ranchería lay across the estero de San Francisco and the troops had no launches; 'las tropas no tienen lanchas'; so they crossed by relays in one small boat found on the shore. Moraga took eighteen gentile prisoners, released because they were too badly wounded.
sources: Prov. Rec. (C-A 25) Doc 500 · 'Sobre encuentro y campaña con gentiles', 1810.
notes: ⚠ CONJECTURAL. The document says only 'north of the presidio' and 'across the estero de San Francisco'. The pin marks the north bay generally and should not be read as a located site.

name: The rancherías of Tinoqui and Napalayagua, 1790
summary: Interior Chumash politics visible through a colonial patrol. A Santa Bárbara sergeant sent after a deserter to the ranchería de Tinoqui was joined by nine Indians of Napalayagua, 'enemies of Tinoqui'. The camp was attacked from the rear by more than sixty; soldiers Gabriel Espinosa and Ignacio Carlón were killed. The record preserves an alliance and an enmity between two named communities that the territorial map cannot show.
sources: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Mil.) (C-A 15) Doc 296 · the 1790 interior-Chumash ambush of a Santa Bárbara patrol.
notes: ⚠ CONJECTURAL. Placed in the interior behind Santa Bárbara; neither ranchería's site is given in the document.

name: The ranchería of Huilantuliyami, 1823
summary: A corporal took a small party to the ranchería 'nombrada Huilantuliyami' after runaway Christian Indians, and was reprimanded for it: no such sortie 'debe verificarse sin ántes consultarlo', given the risk to so small a party against 'una Rancheria tan belicosa como es la de Huilantuliyami'. At least ten men should have been sent. The archive names the place because the army was afraid of it.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (C-A 46) Doc 88 · headed 'Indios', Monterey, 1823.
notes: ⚠ CONJECTURAL. Placed in the San Joaquín/Tulares interior, the usual destination of Monterey-district fugitive pursuits. The document gives no location.

name: Toma de posesión of the Mar del Sur (and Golfo de San Miguel, named 25 Sept)
date_display: 1513-09-29 (St Michael's day; first sight and naming of the gulf 1513-09-25; further autos de posesión around the gulf in October 1513)
summary: Per Oviedo (who read and later held Valderrábano's original testimonio): at vespers, as the tide rose, Balboa took in hand a banner/pendón real painted with the Virgin and Child above the royal arms of Castile and León, and with naked sword and shield waded knee-deep into the salt water, pacing about and proclaiming: «Vivan los muy altos é muy poderosos Reyes don Fernando é doña Johana... en cuyo nombre é por la corona real de Castilla tomo é aprehendo la possesion real é corporal é actualmente destas mares é tierras é costas é puertos é islas australes, con todos sus anexos é reynos é provinçias que les pertenesçen...», offering to defend it against any prince 'chripstiano ó infiel'; 'é assi hiço sus autos de possesion... y como no ovo ni paresçió contradiçion alguna, lo pidió por testimonio.' On 25 Sept, on the summit, the party knelt, sang the Te Deum, erected a tall wooden cross, named the gulf San Miguel, and Valderrábano recorded the 67 names. In October Balboa repeated the autos around the gulf ('añadiendo possesion á possesion é auto á auto'), designated the islet of San Simón as coto y padrón, the marker standing opposite the Pearl Island (Isla Rica), which he named but never landed on, again with named witnesses (Bartolomé Hurtado, Francisco Pizarro, Martín de los Reyes piloto, Esteban Barrantes, Martín Ruiz, Fernando Hidalgo, Andrés de Vera presbítero) before Valderrábano
sources: Original notarial testimonio by Andrés de Valderrábano, No surviving exemplar known in any archive. Oviedo states he personally saw and read the signed testimonio ('el qual testimonio yo vi é leí, y el mismo escribano me lo enseñó') and that Valderrábano's and Balboa's papers came into his own hands after their execution at Acla (Jan 1519). Not in AGI; neither Medina nor Altolaguirre could print an original. [lost] | Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, Historia general y natural de las Indias, ed. José Amador de los Ríos, t. III (Madrid: Real Academia de la Historia, 1853), lib. XXIX, caps. III-IV, pp. 10-17 (roll of the 67 at pp. 11-12; possession formula at p. 13; October autos and witness list pp. 16-17) | Antonio de Herrera, Historia general de los hechos de los castellanos, Década I, libro X (Madrid, 1601) | Pedro Mártir de Anglería, De Orbe Novo, Década III (first printed 1516). Early description based on letters and returning participants; no act text. | José Toribio Medina, El descubrimiento del Océano Pacífico: Vasco Núñez de Balboa, Hernando de Magallanes y sus compañeros, t. I (Santiago de Chile: Imprenta Universitaria, 1913), pp. 88-98 (Critical reprint of 'el acta' (the Valderrábano roll, from Oviedo) with footnotes correcting the names, plus full narrative of both ceremonies) | José Toribio Medina, El descubrimiento del Océano Pacífico, t. II: Documentos relativos a Núñez de Balboa (Santiago de Chile, 1913), pp. 355-364 (probanza of Alonso Martín de Don Benito, Lima, 26 Oct 1535) | Ángel de Altolaguirre y Duvale, Vasco Núñez de Balboa (Madrid, 1914), estudio pp. LXXXIX-XCII and Apéndice núm. 18 (appendix pagination pp. 47-49)
notes: Two-stage ceremony: 25 Sept (summit: Te Deum, cross, naming of Golfo de San Miguel, roll of 67) and 29 Sept (wading possession of the sea). Coordinates are for the Gulf of San Miguel generally; the exact shore (territory of cacique Chiapes, near the Río Sabana mouth) is traditional, not documented to the meter.

name: Auto de posesión of the puerto y bahía de Santa Cruz.
date_display: 1535-05-03 (Day of the Holy Cross; followed on 1535-05-10 by the auto of public reading of the 1529 royal provision naming Cortés governor, same escribano)
summary: Per the acta (full text read): about midday 3 May 1535 Cortés landed 'con gente é caballos' on the beach, declared before the escribano that in the King's name and by virtue of his 1529 capitulación he took 'la tenencia é posesión de la dicha tierra, nuevamente descobierta... é de todas las demás que desde ella se comunican'; named the port 'el puerto é baya de Santa Cruz'; walked over the land from one part to another, threw sand about, struck certain trees with his sword, ordered the company to hold him as His Majesty's Governor, 'é hizo otros abtos de posesión', all 'pacíficamente, sin contradicion', and demanded testimonio, which Martín de Castro gave under his sign
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 21 (old signature 1-1-2/21, 'Part 9a' per Wagner 1929) - the acta was filed as an exhibit in the Proceso del Marqués del Valle over northern discovery rights, presented in the Consejo de Indias by Íñigo López on 13 March 1540, and presented again by Íñigo López de Mondragón on 3 March 1550; a 2020s PARES-derived snippet places the related autos at PATRONATO,21,N.2,R.4 (ramo-level signature INFERRED, not directly confirmed; the PARES catalogue could not be reached to confirm it) | Archivo General de Indias, Seville (the 'figura de la tierra' filed with the acta), AGI, MP-MEXICO,6 - 'Mapa de la Nueva Tierra de Santa Cruz... descubierta por Hernán Cortés en 1535', identified by Torres Lanzas as found with the acta of possession [digitized] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville (possible second exemplar), AGI, Patronato, 16 - cited by M.ª Montserrat León Guerrero (2013) as 'Auto de posesión y descubrimiento de California por la corona de Castilla y León. Santa Cruz, 3 de mayo de 1535. AGI, Patronato 16'; unverified against PARES. | Colección de documentos inéditos... de América y Oceanía [CDI, Pacheco-Cárdenas-Torres de Mendoza, 1st series], t. XV (Madrid, 1871), pp. 306-308 (within the Proceso del Marqués del Valle, printed from p. 300 et seq.). The act is also commonly said to be printed in tomo IV (Madrid, 1865); that attribution is unverified. | CDI, 1st series, t. XII (Madrid, 1869), pp. 490-496. | H. R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast of America in the Sixteenth Century (San Francisco: California Historical Society, 1929), p. 6 (narrative) and p. 296, Plate II note (AGI signature 1-1-2/21 Part 9a and the accompanying map) | H. H. Bancroft, History of the North Mexican States, vol. I (San Francisco, 1884), pp. 51-52 and n. 39. | W. Michael Mathes, The Conquistador in California: 1535. The Voyage of Fernando Cortés to Baja California in Chronicles and Documents, Baja California Travels Series 31 (Los Angeles: Dawson's Book Shop, 1973), section 'The act of possession and discovery' (123 pp. total; exact pages not verified). FULL ENGLISH TRANSLATION of the act of possession, with the other expedition documents.
notes: Sovereign possession preceding the (failed) colony. The chronological index of the CDI (t. XXXIII, 1880) confirms no separate 3 May 1535 acta entry under 1535 - it was printed only inside the Proceso in t. XV.

name: Acta de posesión at El Puerto de los Puertos, Bahía de la Posesión.
date_display: 1539-09-18 (date as given in the acta; Preciado also describes the ceremony, adding that a cross was set up on the hill)
summary: Per the acta (Wagner/Wright translation): Ulloa 'actually and in reality took possession for the Marqués in the name of the Emperor... placing his hand upon his sword and saying that if any person disputed it, he was ready to defend such possession, cutting trees with his sword, moving stones from one place to another and taking water out of the sea and throwing it upon the land, all which was done in token of said possession'; Palencia drew the instrument with his notarial mark; per Preciado a cross was erected on the hill.
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.11 (VERIFIED via UNM Scholes finding aid to AGI Patronato: 'Acompaña una relación del viaje y actos de posesión de varios puertos...', 74 pp., dated Isla de los Cedros 5 April 1540; Wagner's old signature 1-1-2/20, No. 5, R. 11) - a legalized copy made in Mexico City 29 May 1540; the seven actas are appended to Ulloa's relación. | H. R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast (1929), ch. I, translation of Ulloa's relación by Irene A. Wright at pp. 15-50; the seven actas at pp. 46-49; notes pp. 297-318. FULL ENGLISH TRANSLATION of all the actas de posesión and the relación. | Julio Le Riverend (ed.), Cartas de relación de la conquista de América (México: Editorial Nueva España, [c. 1945]), t. I, pp. 642-695 (Spanish text of Ulloa's 'Memoria y relación del viaje...' (per León Guerrero 2013, who notes it was 'publicada varias veces')) | Francisco Preciado, 'Discorso sopra la Relatione di Francisco Ulloa', in G. B. Ramusio, Terzo volume delle Navigationi et Viaggi (Venice, 1556), ff. 341r-353v; English in Richard Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, vol. III (London, 1600)
notes: First of seven notarial instruments by Pedro de Palencia appended to the relación. A second instrument dated 10 Sept 1539 at the Río/Cabo de San Pedro y San Pablo (26.5°, Sinaloa coast) is NOT a possession but a notarized declaration that Ulloa was commencing his exploration there.

name: Acta de posesión at the Ancón de San Andrés y Mar Bermejo.
summary: Formal possession for the Marqués del Valle in the Emperor's name 'actually and in reality; placing his hand upon his sword, saying that if any person disputed it he was ready to defend it, cutting trees with his sword, pulling up grass, moving stones from one place to another... and taking water from the sea and throwing it upon the land'. Ulloa's narrative adds he landed on a sand-bar to take the possession. First European possession at the mouth of the Colorado; from this voyage the gulf was called Mar Bermejo
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.11 (as above - all seven actas travel with the relación) | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), pp. 46-47 (acta translation); Spanish text quoted in part in espanaenlahistoria.org and in M. León Guerrero, 'Reconocimiento de la isla de California', Revista de Estudios Colombinos 9 (2013), pp. 37-52.

name: Acta de posesión at the Bahía de San Marcos.
date_display: 1539-10-06 (so the acta; Wagner notes San Marcos' feast is 7 Oct; Ulloa's narrative implies possession on Thursday 4 Oct)
summary: Same notarial formula: hand on sword, offer to defend, cutting trees, pulling up stones and grass, throwing sea-water on the land, 'all in token of the said possession'
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.11. | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), p. 47 (acta translation); notes 62-63 p. 308. Full acta in English translation.

name: Acta de posesión at the Río Carrizal.
summary: Same formula: possession taken 'actually and in reality' for the Marqués in the Emperor's name; sword, trees, stones, sea-water.
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.11. | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), p. 48 (acta translation); note 73 p. 308. Full acta in English translation.

name: Acta de posesión at the Bahía de Santa Catalina, Punta de la Trinidad.
date_display: 1539-12-01 (so the acta; Ulloa's narrative puts the possession on Thursday 4 Dec)
summary: Possession 'actually and in reality' for the Marqués in the Emperor's name; hand on sword, cutting trees, moving stones 'all in token of the said possession' (this acta omits the sea-water clause)
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.11. | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), p. 48 (acta translation); note 24 (Punta Tosco identification). Full acta in English translation.

name: Acta de posesión on the Isla de los Cedros.
date_display: 1540-01-20 (so the acta; Wagner note 138 argues the ceremony actually occurred 21 Jan)
summary: Same notarial formula: hand on sword, offer to defend, cutting trees, moving stones, throwing sea-water on the land. Preciado's narrative does not describe the taking of possession but the chapter heading in Ramusio states it
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.11 (the legalized copy is itself dated from Isla de los Cedros 5 April 1540 / Mexico City 29 May 1540) | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), pp. 48-49 (acta translation); note 138 p. 311. Full acta in English translation.
notes: Last of the seven Palencia instruments. Ulloa sailed north past Cabo del Engaño with the Trinidad after 5 April 1540; his furthest possessions end here.

name: Possession at the Puerto de la Posesión.
summary: Per the relación: 'The following Tuesday Captain Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo went ashore and took possession in the name of His Majesty and the most illustrious Don Antonio de Mendoza, naming it Puerto de la Posesion.' Wagner (1929, 419, Appendix III n. 7) notes that 'There was a regular established form to be used in taking possession', citing the Ulloa actas as the model; Mendoza's standing instructions required possession-taking
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.13 (VERIFIED: UNM Scholes finding aid and recent scholarship) - the anonymous third-person summary relación headed 'Jhoan Paez' (Wagner: Juan Páez de Castro's file copy), 17 ff.; the original full diary and any notarial actas are lost. Copies: Juan Bautista Muñoz copy, Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid; Navarrete copy, vol. 19 of his MSS, Depósito Hidrográfico (now Museo Naval), Madrid. | Buckingham Smith, Colección de varios documentos para la historia de la Florida y tierras adyacentes (London, 1857), pp. 173-189. First printing of the FULL SPANISH TEXT (from the Navarrete copy) | Colección de documentos inéditos... de América y Oceanía [CDI, 1st series], t. XIV (Madrid, 1870), pp. 165-191: 'Relación del descubrimiento que hizo Juan Rodríguez, navegando por la contracosta del Mar del Sur al Norte, hecha por Juan Páez' (start page verified from the collection's chronological index, t. XXXIII; closing page per standard bibliographies). FULL SPANISH TEXT printed from the AGI original (carelessly, per Wagner) | Alexander S. Taylor, The First Voyage to the Coast of California... by Cabrillo and Ferrelo (San Francisco, 1853). First (defective) English translation. | [Richard Stuart Evans, trans.], 'Translation from the Spanish of the Account by the Pilot Ferrel of the Voyage of Cabrillo along the West Coast of North America in 1542', with notes by H. W. Henshaw, in Report upon U.S. Geographical Surveys West of the One Hundredth Meridian, vol. VII (Washington: GPO, 1879), Appendix to Part I, pp. 293-314. FULL ENGLISH TRANSLATION. | H. E. Bolton, Spanish Exploration in the Southwest, 1542-1706 (New York: Scribner's, 1916), pp. 13-39. FULL ENGLISH TRANSLATION (revised from Evans) | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), ch. IV, translation pp. 79-93; bibliographical note p. 319; notes pp. 329-335; Appendix No. VIII, facsimile of the relación, pp. 450-463; Herrera's derivative account translated at pp. 426-430. FULL ENGLISH TRANSLATION with facsimile of the manuscript.
notes: Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), 13: 'The first recorded acta of possession by Cabrillo was made north of Punta Antonio, the modern name for what was probably Cabo del Engaño.' The site is deliberately beyond Ulloa's farthest point; the bay is today Bahía de San Quintín.

name: Possession at the Cabo/Puerto de Santa María.
date_display: 1542-09-08/11 (anchored and named the cape Friday 8 Sept, the Virgin's nativity; 'Here they took possession and remained until the following Monday')
summary: Relación: at the watering place, where c. 40 Indians with bows appeared, 'Here they took possession and remained until the following Monday' - no further detail given in the summary.
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.13 (same summary relación) | Same editions as the Puerto de la Posesión entry: Smith 1857, 173-189; CDI XIV, 165-191; Evans/Henshaw 1879, 293-314; Bolton 1916, 13-39; Wagner 1929, 79-93 (this passage at pp. 83-84, note 64 p. 333). Full text/translation of the relación including this one-line possession notice.
notes: In the MS the name is abbreviated 's.m.'; Navarrete/Smith wrongly expanded a later occurrence as San Martín (Wagner note 62)

name: Possession at the Puerto de San Mateo.
date_display: 1542-09-17/22 (arrived Sunday 17 Sept; 'They took possession and were there until the following Saturday', the 23rd; San Mateo's day = 21 Sept)
summary: Relación: good closed port named 'San Mateo', herds like 'the sheep of Peru' (antelope) seen; 'They took possession and were there until the following Saturday'
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.13. | Same editions; Wagner 1929 passage at p. 84, note 66 p. 333. Full text/translation including the possession notice.

name: Possession at the Pueblo de las Canoas (Xucu)
date_display: 1542-10-10/13 (anchored Tuesday 10 Oct; 'Here they took possession and remained until Friday, the 13th')
summary: Relación: town of large houses 'like those of New Spain', fine canoes of 12-13 Indians each; 'Here they took possession and remained until Friday, the 13th'
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.13. | Same editions; Wagner 1929 passage at p. 86, note 77 p. 334. Full text/translation including the possession notice.
notes: First documented act of possession on the coast of the present state of California.

name: Isla de Posesión (possession inferred from the naming)
date_display: 1542-10-18/25 (islands reached and named 'Islas de San Lucas' from 18 Oct; on departing Wednesday 25 Oct 'they named it [the windward island with the good port] Posesion')
summary: No ceremony is described; the relación records only the name 'Posesion'. Wagner: 'the name Posesion first given San Miguel Island indicates that possession was also taken there.' Cabrillo wintered there, broke a limb, and died on the island 3 Jan 1543 ('isla de Posesion... capitán de los dichos navíos'); Ferrer renamed the islands the 'Isla de Juan Rodriguez' (singular, for San Miguel)
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Patronato, 20, N.5, R.13. | Same editions; Wagner 1929 pp. 86-87 (naming), p. 89 ff. (wintering and death), analysis p. 74, note 90 p. 335. Full text/translation; the act itself is attested only by the toponym.
notes: Also note the NEGATIVE at San Miguel (San Diego Bay), 28 Sept - 3 Oct 1542: the surviving relación records NO act of possession there, despite the later tradition; and at the Bahía de los Pinos (Monterey Bay, mid-Nov 1542) possession was intended but the surf prevented a landing (Wagner p. 74; index 'Possession intended, 178')

name: Drake: post, plate and sixpence at "Nova Albion"
date_display: Cession ceremony 26 June 1579; the post with engraved plate + sixpence set up at departure, c. 21–23 July
summary: Monument post with engraved plate and sixpence; Miwok "crowning" read as voluntary cession (World Encompassed)
sources: Vaux (ed.), The World Encompassed (Hakluyt Soc. XVI, 1854), 225-26; Hakluyt 1589; the possession passage. | Bolton, "Francis Drake's Plate of Brass," CHSQ 16 (1937); the plate. PROVEN HOAX 1977; cite only historiographically. | The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake, ed. W. S. W. Vaux (Hakluyt Society, 1st ser. XVI, London, 1854), pp. 115 (anchoring 17 June, departure 23 July), 126-29 (26 June cession ceremony), 132-33 (plate and sixpence monument); Appendix No. I (Hakluyt 1589 text) pp. 225-26. | The Plate of Brass Reexamined: A Report (Berkeley: Bancroft Library, 1977); the metallurgical proof of the hoax.
notes: English consent-theater on the same shore as Cermeño 1595. The brass plate Bolton published in 1937 was shown by metallurgical analysis in 1977 to be a modern forgery; it is cited here only as historiography. The permalink for this entry keeps its original slug; the act's date of record is 26 June 1579.

name: Possession of the Puerto de San Lucas and its land.
date_display: 1587-10-18 (Sunday, day of San Lucas; the inland entrada and the fatal skirmish followed 19-20 Oct)
summary: Per Unamuno's relación: on a hill near the shore strewn with pearl-oyster shells, 'as it seemed to be a suitable place to take possession in His Majesty's name of the port and the country, seeing that I and the rest of the party had landed and traversed the country round about... quietly and pacifically, as in territory belonging to his domain, I did so in the name of King Philip, our master, in due legal form, through Diego Vasquez Mexia... in his capacity of Justicia, setting up a cross as a sign of the Christian faith and of the possession taken in His Majesty's name of the port and the country, cutting branches from the trees which grew thereabouts, and performing the other customary ceremonies.'
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, Audiencia de México, 21 (INFERRED: Wagner cites old signature 58-3-10 = the Viceroy Villamanrique's letter of 10 Dec 1587 enclosing 'a certified copy' of Unamuno's account; the old-to-modern conversion 58-3-X -> México X+11 is confirmed by the Cermeño case, 58-3-12 = México 23 and 58-3-16 = México 27) | Henry R. Wagner (trans. Irene A. Wright), 'The Voyage of Pedro de Unamuno to California in 1587,' California Historical Society Quarterly 2:2 (July 1923), pp. 140-160 (English translation of Unamuno's journal including the full possession passage of 18 Oct 1587) | Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast of America in the Sixteenth Century, CHS Special Publication 4 (San Francisco, 1929), ch. 'The Voyage of Pedro de Unamuno,' pp. 139-153 (possession passage at pp. 144-145); facsimile of the Unamuno account, appendix X, pp. 481-504. English translation (revised Wright text) + facsimile of the Spanish manuscript. Translation at pp. 141-151, the possession at 144-145, notes to the chapter at 364-67; Appendix X reproduces a facsimile of the Unamuno account, pp. 481-504. | AGI, Patronato, Leg. 25 (R.32 per Servín 1963 n.27); the 1587 certified copy (Antonio de Castro, "cotejado"; Wagner’s old signature 1-1-3/25); a second 1587 copy at old 58-3-10; Muñoz transcript RAH Madrid vol. 38. PARES unconfirmed (rate-limited)
notes: The joint account of the voyage by Unamuno and the pilot Alonso Gómez, which the viceroy also forwarded, 'has never been found' (Wagner)

name: Possession of the land and port named La Baya de San Francisco.
date_display: 1595-11-07 (ship anchored midday 6 Nov; captain landed with 22 men the morning of the 7th and took possession the same day)
summary: Per the Declaración/derrotero: 'Y el dicho día que saltó el dicho capitán con la dicha jente en tierra pidió a todos le fuesen testigos como en nombre del Rey nuestro señor tomaua posesión de la tierra e puerto, al qual le pusso por nombre la baya de San Francisco que la bautizó el Reverendo Padre fray Francisco de la Conçepçión de la horden de Sant Francisco de los Descalços que uiene en la dicha nao' (AGI, México, 23, N.50\3, ff. 6-7, quoted in Piedade 2006); the company then marched with the banner to the Indian village. No separate acta instrument is known - the possession is recorded within the voyage records
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, AGI, México, 23, N.50 - 'Relación de lo sucedido en el viaje...' (enclosed with the Conde de Monterrey's letter of 19 April 1596; Wagner's old signature 58-3-12); AGI, México, 23, N.50\3 - 'Derrotero y relación del descubrimiento que hizo Sebastián...', the possession at ff. 6-7; AGI, México, 23, N.50\4 - testimonies on the loss of the San Agustín and the Información on the character of the land at the bay (the 'two autos' Wagner translated) | Archivo General de Indias, Seville (second copy of the relación), AGI, México, 27, N.18 (Wagner's old signature 58-3-16; a slightly later, somewhat faulty copy) | Museo Naval / Depósito Hidrográfico, Madrid (Navarrete copies of the Velasco and Monterrey letters), Colección Navarrete (used by Carrasco 1882); related copies also in the Sutro Collection, San Francisco (used by Griffin 1891) | H. R. Wagner, 'The Voyage to California of Sebastian Rodriguez Cermeño in 1595', California Historical Society Quarterly 3:1 (April 1924), pp. 3-24. | Wagner, Spanish Voyages (1929), ch. IX, pp. 154-167 (translation incl. the Declaración, possession passage at p. 158); Appendix No. XI, FACSIMILE of the Declaración of Cermeño, pp. 505-532; bibliographical note p. 368. Translation plus photographic facsimile of the Declaración. | Francisco Carrasco y Guisasola, Documentos referentes al reconocimiento de las costas de las Californias... (Madrid: Dirección de Hidrografía, 1882), docs. 4-7. | George Butler Griffin, 'Documents from the Sutro Collection', Publications of the Historical Society of Southern California, vol. 2, pt. 1 (Los Angeles, 1891) | Carla Delgado de Piedade, 'Sebastião Rodrigues Soromenho: um piloto português nos navios da rota de Manila', Anuario de Estudios Americanos 63:1 (2006), pp. 157-186 (possession quoted at pp. 180, from AGI México 23, N.50\3, ff. 6-7) | C. E. Chapman, article on the Cermeño voyage, Southwestern Historical Quarterly (January 1920); substance in his History of California: The Spanish Period (1921), ch. X. First extended notice; description only.
notes: One of the two surviving roteiros omits the ceremony (Piedade). Drake had claimed the same bay for England 17 June/July 1579 ('Nova Albion') - excluded here as non-Spanish. | Pin offset ~4–6 km for display (site overlaps its neighbors); documented site = 38.03, -122.94.

name: Puerto de San Sebastián / Villa de San Felipe / Reino de Nueva Andalucía.
date_display: 1596-09-04 (circa; ceremony 'otro día' after the 3 Sept landfall per Vizcaíno's relación; expedition stayed at the bay 3-10 Sept 1596)
summary: Per Vizcaíno's own relación (quoted verbatim in Mathes): a tent town with streets and plaza was laid out; the next day, before ~200 Indians, 'con la solemnidad que se requería hincado el estandarte Real en tierra tomé possessión de ella en el nombre de Su Magestad y púsele por nombre a la Villa San Phillipe, al Puerto San Sebastián y el Reyno Nueba Andaluzía.' At the possession the friars said mass at an altar ashore, carrying the image of Nuestra Señora in procession from the beach; an Indian principal with ~800 followers knelt before the image. Large crosses were left standing when the expedition departed
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Patronato, Legajo 20 (Parte 2), Ramo 17; 'Relación del descubrimiento de las Californias por el capitán Sebastián Vizcaíno' (12 pp., dated 16 April 1598) and 'Copia de la Relación de Sebastián Vizcaíno de 1598, con notaciones al margen' (17 pp.); same ramo holds the asiento y capitulación of 1597 [unknown. PARES search endpoint returned 429 during check (control search failed, so a null is worthless); Patronato series is widely digitized on PARES (INFERRED)] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Wagner's old pressmarks), Old signature 141-1-1: 'Vizcaino's original account of this expedition' (Wagner 1929, ch. X n.14), with his account dated 8 Dec 1596 and the abridged account of 16 Apr 1598; related viceregal letters in old 58-3-12 and 58-3-13 (modern equivalents not established here) | Francisco Carrasco y Guisasola, Documentos referentes al reconocimiento de las costas de las Californias desde el Cabo de San Lucas al de Mendocino (Madrid: Dirección de Hidrografía, 1882), document no. 14 ('Vizcaíno's account of his voyage, the undated one' per Wagner); exact pages not established. Full Spanish text of Vizcaíno's relación of the 1596 voyage, which contains the possession passage; no digitization found. | Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast of America in the Sixteenth Century (San Francisco: California Historical Society, 1929), ch. X 'The Antecedents of Sebastian Vizcaino's Voyage of 1602', pp. 168-179 (possession at pp. 171-172); source notes pp. 375-377. | W. Michael Mathes, 'Importancia de Cabo San Lucas en la historia' (La Paz: Gobierno de BCS, 1980), pp. 30-34. | W. Michael Mathes, Californiana I: Documentos para la historia de la demarcación comercial de California, 1583-1632, 2 vols. (Madrid: José Porrúa Turanzas, 1965). INFERRED to print the 1596-98 relaciones in full with AGI signatures (Mathes's quoted texts derive from this corpus); doc/page not verified. Full Spanish texts (INFERRED) | George Butler Griffin, 'Documents from the Sutro Collection', Publications of the Historical Society of Southern California II.1 (Los Angeles, 1891), 5-73; translates the related 1596-97 correspondence (Monterrey letter 29 Feb 1596; Vizcaíno letter 27 Feb 1597; First Memorial), NOT the relación with the possession passage. Translations of related correspondence only.
notes: The act claimed the whole 'Reyno Nueba Andaluzía', i.e. the Californias, not just the port. Separate written acta not located; the relación is the surviving witness. Settlement abandoned within days when the expedition moved north to La Paz.

name: Puerto y Villa de La Paz (renaming of Cortés's Santa Cruz)
date_display: 1596-09-13 (arrival and naming per Mathes; settlement occupied until abandonment, final departure 28 Oct 1596)
summary: Renaming of Cortés's Bahía de Santa Cruz as 'La Paz' because the Guaycura/Pericú received the Spaniards peacefully; a town was laid out and occupied ca. 13 Sept - 28 Oct 1596. NO separate formal act of sovereign possession at La Paz is documented in the printed extracts of Vizcaíno's relación consulted; the sovereign claim had been made days earlier at San Felipe for the whole 'kingdom'
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Same relaciones as the San Felipe act: Patronato, Legajo 20 (Parte 2), Ramo 17; Wagner old pressmark 141-1-1 [unknown. PARES endpoint unreachable at check (429)] | Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast (1929), pp. 171-172. | W. Michael Mathes, 'Importancia de Cabo San Lucas en la historia' (1980), p. 34 (Description only ('el 13 de septiembre fue recibido por un grupo de pericúes pacíficos, poniendo por ello el nombre de La Paz a la bahía y a la colonia')) | Carrasco y Guisasola, Documentos (1882), doc. no. 14. Full Spanish text of the relación covering the La Paz episode; pages not establi.
notes: Settlement renamed; the kingdom-wide act of record was San Felipe, 4 Sept.

name: La Toma: possession of the kingdoms and provinces of New Mexico
summary: Solemn high mass, sermon, blessing of the royal standard, then Oñate read the long written act: 'En el nombre de la Santísima Trinidad...', taking 'una, dos y tres veces... tomo y aprehendo la tenencia y posesión real y actual, civil y natural, en este dicho Río del Norte, sin exceptuar cosa alguna' of all the kingdoms and provinces of New Mexico for Philip II, with a cross raised and the requerimiento framework invoked; notarized by Pérez de Donís; feasting and a comedy followed ('the first Thanksgiving' tradition). A written, witnessed, notarized instrument survives
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Patronato, Legajo 22, Ramo 13; 'Testimonio de la toma de posesión de las provincias de Nuevo México por el gobernador don Juan de Oñate en nombre del Rey Felipe II', 30 April 1598, 7 pp., naming the ten friar-witnesses; same ramo holds the obediencias y vasallajes of the pueblos and the Itinerario copy (4 Oct 1599) [unknown. PARES search endpoint 429 at check; Patronato series widely digitized on PARES (INFERRED); Scholes transcripts at UNM CSWR MSS 841] | 'Treslado de la posesión que en nombre de Su Magestad tomó Don Juan de Oñate, de los Reynos y Provincias de la Nueva México...', in Pacheco & Cárdenas, Colección de documentos inéditos... de América y Oceanía (CDI, 1.ª serie), XVI (Madrid, 1871), 88-141 (act of 30 April 1598 at the head, followed by the acts of obedience and vassalage). Full Spanish act text. | Gaspar Pérez de Villagrá, Historia de la Nueva México (Alcalá de Henares, 1610), fols. 114-132; the prose act inserted at Canto XIV ('DE COMO SE TOMO Y APREHENDIO LA POSSESION DE LA NUEVA TIERRA'); reprinted Mexico: Museo Nacional, 1900 (ed. González Obregón), digitized by the Library of Congress; modern bilingual ed. M. Encinias, A. Rodríguez, J. P. Sánchez (Albuquerque: UNM Press, 1992). Full Spanish act text (prose, within the epic); 1992 edition gives English translation. | George P. Hammond and Agapito Rey, Don Juan de Oñate, Colonizer of New Mexico, 1595-1628 (Albuquerque: University of New Mexico Press, 1953), I, 329-336, the possession formula at 334-335. Full English translation of the act, which begins 'I take and seize tenancy and possession, real and actual, civil and natural, one, two, and three times.' | Itinerario ('Discurso de las jornadas que hizo el Campo de Su Magestad...'), CDI XVI, 228-276 (La Toma noticed at p. 242); trans. Hammond & Rey, Oñate, I. Contemporary description of the ceremony (diary form) | Bolton, Spanish Exploration in the Southwest (1916), pp. 199-211 (introduction, source census) and 212-222 (Oñate to the viceroy, 2 March 1599, mentioning 'at which river I took possession, in the name of his Majesty, of all these kingdoms') | Doralicia Carmona Dávila, Memoria Política de México, 'La toma de posesión. Juan de Oñate (Selección)' (Open-access Spanish text (selection) of the act, opening 'En el nombre de la Santísima Trinidad y de la Individua Unidad Eterna...')
notes: Inland comparandum on the Rio Grande, not a Pacific-coast act; mapped for comparison with the coastal ceremonies. Off-map inland comparandum, kept for comparison with the coastal acts. A second, ecclesiastical act. Oñate's delivery of possession of the provinces to the Franciscans, 8/9 Sept 1598 at San Juan de los Caballeros; survives separately ('Relación de cómo los Padres de San Francisco se encargaron...', AGI, transcript in the Lowery Collection, Library of Congress; Bolton 1916, p. 208). Oñate's later possession at the Gulf of California (25 Jan 1605) falls outside this cluster.

name: Puerto de San Diego (naming; mass of the feast of San Diego. NO act of possession)
date_display: 1602-11-10 (arrival) and 1602-11-12 (mass per the diary; Bolton notes the date confusion; junta on the 11th per the Libro Diario, feast of San Diego de Alcalá = 13 Nov)
summary: A hut was built ashore and mass was said 'in celebration of the feast of Señor San Diego', after which the general held a council on refitting; the bay (Cabrillo's San Miguel) was renamed San Diego. The official diary records NO act of possession, no standard, no notarial instrument; a mass and a naming only
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Audiencia de México, Legajo 372; certified copy ('Corregido con el libro original de Su Magd...') of the expedition diary, authenticated in Mexico City 8 Dec 1603 by escribano mayor Diego de Santiago; begins 'Reynando el rrey don Phelipe nuestro señor...' [not digitized so far as found (PARES check blocked by 429; no digitization located)] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Audiencia de México, Legajo 25, N.10. Conde de Monterrey's instructions to Vizcaíno, Mexico, 18 March 1602 (demarcation only; no mandate to take possession or settle), and Monterrey's letter to the king, 31 May 1602. | Newberry Library, Chicago, VAULT Ayer MS 1038. Fray Antonio de la Ascensión, 'Relación de la jornada que hizo el general Sevastián Vizcayno al descubrimiento de las Californias el año de 1602' (quarto, 248 pp., last 11 pp. autograph, signed; dated by ArchiveGrid 12 Oct 1620, by Wagner c. 1611) [not digitized so far as found] | Herbert E. Bolton (ed.), Spanish Exploration in the Southwest, 1542-1706 (New York: Scribner's, 1916), 'Diary of Sebastián Vizcaíno, 1602-1603', pp. 52-103; San Diego episode at pp. 80-82. | Carrasco y Guisasola, Documentos referentes al reconocimiento de las costas de las Californias (Madrid, 1882): diary pp. 68-107; Libro Diario (juntas) pp. 109-148; Derrotero of Palacios pp. 149-172. Full Spanish texts of the diary, the junta records, and the sailing directions. | Edward Baranowski, 'Documents from the 1602-1603 Sebastián Vizcaíno Expedition up the California Coast', eScholarship (University of California), open access. | Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast (1929), ch.
