Full English translation of Ascensión's long account; San Diego: mass and naming. | Juan de Torquemada, Monarquía Indiana (Seville, 1615), I, lib. V; 1723 Barcia ed. I, 693-725 (reprinted in Venegas/Burriel, Noticia de la California, Madrid 1757, III, 22-139). Near-verbatim early printed derivative of Ascensión's account; description only.
notes: the primary record shows mass only. Any modern claim of a 1602 possession at San Diego is unsupported by the diary, the Libro Diario, or Ascensión.

name: Puerto de Monterey (naming in honor of Viceroy Conde de Monterrey; mass under the great oak. NO act of possession recorded)
date_display: 1602-12-16 (anchored 7 p.m.) and 1602-12-17 (landing, hut/arbor under 'una gran encina', masses; junta on dispatching the Santo Tomás; the almiranta sailed 29 Dec 1602)
summary: Diary (AGI México 372): hut made by 'a great oak near the shore', mass said, the port found 'the best port that could be desired'; port named Monterey for the viceroy. Ascensión (Ayer MS 1038, trans. Wagner pp. 242-245): a large tent-church set up 'under the shade of a very large live-oak', Mass of the Holy Ghost sung, then the junta that sent the Santo Tomás home with the sick and the reports/charts. NO possession formula, standard, cross-raising as claim, or escritura appears in the diary, the Libro Diario, Vizcaíno's letter of 28 Dec 1602 written at Monterey, or either Ascensión account
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Audiencia de México, Legajo 372; certified copy of the expedition diary (chaps. 13-14 cover Monterey), Mexico, 8 Dec 1603, escribano Diego de Santiago [not digitized so far as found (PARES endpoint 429 at check)] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Audiencia de Guadalajara, Legajo 133. Vizcaíno to the king/Council, 'deste puerto de Monterey a 28 de diziembre de 1602' (reports discoveries; no possession) | Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid, MS 3042. Fray Antonio de la Ascensión, 'Relación breve en que se da noticia del descubrimiento...' (1620), which states the three Carmelites had been designated so the commissary might 'tomar la posesión del Reyno de las Californias' in the king's name; an empowerment, with no act recorded at any port [unknown; BNE's Biblioteca Digital Hispánica not checked successfully] | Newberry Library, Chicago, VAULT Ayer MS 1038. Ascensión's long Relación (the base of Torquemada and of Wagner's ch. XI translation) [not digitized so far as found] | Bancroft Library, Berkeley (derived set), Complete set of the 32 coastal pianos (vistas de costa) of the voyage, redrawn 1603 by Enrico Martínez (per Bolton 1916, p. 49) | Bolton, Spanish Exploration in the Southwest (1916), diary pp. 52-103. Monterey at pp. 91-93; Ascensión's Relación breve translated at pp. 104-134. | Carrasco y Guisasola, Documentos (1882): diary pp. 68-107 (Monterey chapters); Libro Diario pp. 109-148 (junta of 16 Dec at pp. 128-129); Derrotero p. 169 (description of the bay). Full Spanish texts. | Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast (1929), pp. 242-248 (Ascensión's account of Monterey, chs. IX-X of the Relación), and 'The Project to Settle Monterey', pp. 283 ff | Baranowski, 'Documents from the 1602-1603 Sebastián Vizcaíno Expedition', eScholarship. | Ascensión, 'Relación breve...', printed in Pacheco & Cárdenas, Colección de documentos inéditos... de América y Oceanía (CDI, 1.ª serie), VIII (Madrid, 1867), 539-574, from BNE MS 3042 (Full Spanish text of the 1620 Relación breve (recommends future possession-taking; records none in 1602-03)) | Torquemada, Monarquía Indiana (1615) I, lib. V (1723 ed. I, 693-725). Early printed description derived from Ascensión.
notes: The expedition's commission (Real Orden 27 Sept 1599; instructions 18 Mar 1602, AGI México 25 N.10) was demarcation only; Monterrey even had Vizcaíno served a 'notificación muy apretada' not to linger in the gulf. Formal sovereign possession at Monterey waited until Portolá/Serra, 1770. The oak ('Vizcaíno-Serra oak') tradition marks the mass site, not a possession.

name: Oñate at the Colorado mouth; "Port of the Conversion of San Pablo"
date_display: 1605-01-25 (day of the Conversion of St. Paul)
summary: Oñate's overland party reached the head of the Gulf and took possession at the river mouth he named the Port of the Conversion of San Pablo (25 Jan 1605, the feast of the Conversion). The record is Zárate Salmerón's Relaciones (1626), a compilation from expedition reports; no escribano is named, so the ceremony's detail is limited to the quoted statement
sources: Zárate Salmerón, Relaciones §§54-55, trans. Bolton, Spanish Exploration in the Southwest, 1542-1706 (1916), 277-78;. Same geography as Ulloa 1539 and Alarcón 1540. | H. E. Bolton, Spanish Exploration in the Southwest, 1542-1706 (1916), pp. 268-280 ('The Journey of Oñate to California by Land, [Zárate, 1626]'), possession at pp. 277-78; full text verified on IA.

name: Bahía de La Paz, named Nuestra Señora de La Paz; the province proclaimed Provincia de la Santísima Trinidad de las Californias.
date_display: Bay entered 30 Mar–1 Apr 1683; the possession instrument signed 5 April
summary: Atondo y Antillón's ships entered the bay at the end of March 1683 and a formal proclamation was issued on 1 April. The company went ashore on the 2nd and set up a cross of palmetto. On the 5th the whole party landed under the royal standard, with gunfire and cheers for Carlos II, and the admiral claimed the country for the king, calling the province Santísima Trinidad de las Californias and the anchorage Nuestra Señora de la Paz. Kino and Goñi performed the ecclesiastical possession the same day, and the notary Diego de Salas drew the instrument, signed on 5 April by the admiral, the priests, four officers and the notary himself.
sources: Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries I, 65; Bolton, Kino's Historical Memoir I, 39-40; Servín 1963 n.32 (Servín's quote says vivas 'for Charles III'; king in 1683 was Carlos II, follow Bolton) | Bolton, Kino's Historical Memoir of Pimeria Alta (Cleveland, 1919), I, 39-40 and n. 24 (act in Alegre, Hist. III, 43-45; Kino/Goni acts in Sobre pertenencia; dates from the acts) | Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries of California, I (1908), 64-65 (notary Diego de Salas; signatories Otondo, Kino, Gogni, Guijosa, four officers; names from Alegre III, 43) | Francisco Javier Alegre, Historia de la Compania de Jesus en Nueva-Espana, t. III (Mexico, 1842), 43-45; the printed text of Atondo's formal act (lead per Bolton n.24; not consulted)
notes: Pin offset ~4–6 km for display (site overlaps its neighbors); documented site = 24.16, -110.31. | Vivas were for CARLOS II (Bolton, Kino I:39-40). Servín 1963 prints "Charles III," a misprint; it should not be quoted The permalink for this entry keeps its original slug; the act's date of record is 5 April 1683.

name: San Bruno, gulf coast c. 26.5°N north of Loreto, Baja California Sur.
date_display: 1683-10 (landed 6 Oct, San Bruno's day; formal possession at the new settlement before month's end)
summary: After La Paz failed, Atondo landed in October 1683 at a bay far to the north of it, in twenty-six and a half degrees, which he named San Bruno for the saint of the day, and took formal possession again in the king's name 'con las acostumbradas ceremonias.' Venegas, recording the act, called it one repeated many times with more pomp than fruit. San Bruno was the last place formally claimed in the peninsula before Loreto in 1697
sources: Engelhardt I, the San Bruno founding passage; Venegas, Noticia de la California (Madrid, 1757), pte. II, 229-30 (= I, 165 of the 1944 Mexico ed., per Servín n.33); Servín 1963 nn.33-34. Servín: the last act before Loreto 1697. | Miguel Venegas, Noticia de la California, y de su conquista temporal, y espiritual, t. I (Madrid, 1757), pte. II, pp. 219-220; landing 6 Oct, naming for the feast, possession 'con las acostumbradas ceremonias' | Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries of California, I (1908), 66. | Bolton, Kino's Historical Memoir of Pimeria Alta, I, 40 (6 Oct landing at San Bruno)
notes: Pin offset ~4–6 km for display (site overlaps its neighbors); documented site = 26.23, -111.4. pagination (via Servín n.33), unverified against the open editions.

name: Loreto (Conchó), Bahía de San Dionisio: the founding of the mission and the possession of the peninsula.
date_display: 19 Oct 1697 landing and procession; 25 Oct the formal possession; the mission’s official founding date
summary: Salvatierra's company came ashore at the bay of San Dionisio on Saturday 19 October 1697, put up a tent chapel and set a large cross, and carried the image of Our Lady of Loreto from the ship in procession. Possession of the country was taken for the king in the customary form. Palóu's Noticias assigns the formal possession of the peninsula and the first Mass to 25 October, and that is the date the mission afterwards kept as its founding.
sources: Engelhardt I, 77 and 430 (quoting Palóu, Noticias I) | Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries of California, I (1908), 76-77 and 430.

name: San Fernando de Velicatá, interior-frontier Baja California.
summary: On Pentecost Sunday, 14 May 1769, at the frontier station of San Fernando de Velicata, Portola took solemn possession of the country in the name of the Spanish king while Serra blessed the chapel and the cross and founded the mission the same morning, naming Fray Miguel de la Campa its missionary. It is the one act on the overland route where a sovereign possession and a mission founding were performed together
sources: Palóu, Vida cap. xv, 69-70 and Noticias I cap. viii, quoted in Engelhardt I, 357-58. A sovereign-possession act proper, not just a founding. | Palou, Francisco Palou's Life and Apostolic Labors of the Venerable Father Junipero Serra, intro. G. W. James (Pasadena, 1913), cap. XV, pp. 68-70. | Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries of California, I (1908), 356-358 (Serra diary extract + Palou quote, n. 4) | Palóu, Life of Junípero Serra, trans. C. Scott Williams, with introduction and notes by G. W. James (Pasadena, 1913), 68–70; Serra’s diary extract in Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries I, 356–58.

name: Posesión del Puerto de Monterrey y fundación del presidio y misión de San Carlos de Monterrey (the 'Instrumento auténtico' of possession)
date_display: 1770-06-03 (Pentecost Sunday); officers' certifications dated 9 and 11 June 1770
summary: Enramada built and cross made ready beside the oak where Vizcaíno's Carmelites said mass in 1602; bells hung and rung; Veni Creator Spiritus; water blessed, cross planted, blessed and venerated; beach and fields sprinkled against 'infernal enemies'; sung mass by Serra before the image of Our Lady given by Abp. Lorenzana; sermon; Salve; Te Deum. Then Portolá took formal civil possession in the name of Carlos III: royal standard raised and saluted, grass pulled, stones thrown, 'performing all the acts of possession', everything recorded in the written instrument ('se solemnizó la Posesión el día 3 de Junio con Instrumento auténtico que extendió el Comandante en Gefe D. Gaspar de Portolá, y certificaron los demás Oficiales de ambas Expediciones, asegurando todos ser aquel el mismo Puerto de Monterrey'; with the identical landmarks of Vizcaíno's relations and Cabrera Bueno's derrotero). Cannon of the San Antonio and musketry throughout; officers and friars then dined on the beach. Mission San Carlos founded the same day by Serra
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville. Audiencia de Guadalajara, legajo 417 (Chapman's old signature 104-3-3), AGI, Guadalajara, 417 ('Expediente relativo a la expedición a los puertos de San Diego y Monterrey, en California...'); certified copy of the possession instrument/oath, 3 pp., enclosed with Portolá to Croix, San Blas, 1 Aug 1770. Chapman, Catalogue (1919), no. 1489 (p. 230): '1770. June 9. Monterey. Gaspar de Portolá, Juan Pérez, Miguel del Pino and Pedro Fages (June 11). [Formal oath to the effect that Portolá has taken possession of the port of Monterey described by Vizcaino and Cabrera Bueno]. C. 3pp. 104-3-3. Enc.w.1529' | Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City. Ramo Californias, AGN, Californias, vol. 76 as numbered in 1913 ('Correspondencia, 1759 a 1773'): 'Autos of possession at Monterrey, by Portolá, Pérez, Pino, and Fages. June 3, June 11, 1770', filed as enclosures to the viceroy–Portolá correspondence (Portolá letters of San Diego 4 Jul 1769; Monterey 15 Jun 1770; San Blas 1 Aug 1770). Bolton, Guide to Materials...Principal Archives of Mexico (1913), p. 171. | Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City. Ramo Californias (modern numbering), AGN, Californias, vol. 66, exp. 52, ff. 114-115v: Fages and Costansó to Viceroy Croix, 'Puerto de San Carlos Monterey', 13 June 1770, reporting the arrival at Monterey (eyewitness report accompanying the possession dispatches); also exp. 53 (Fages, 13 Jun 1770, ff. 116-116v), exps. 54-55 (Fages, 1 Jul 1770, ff. 117-127v) [not digitized] | Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City. Ramo Historia, AGN, Historia, tomo 396: original of Costansó's field diary of the expedition (per Teggart, APCH II no. 4 introduction); Sutro Library, San Francisco, holds contemporary copies of the Costansó and Vila diaries [not digitized] | Estracto de noticias del Puerto de Monterrey, de la Mission, y Presidio que se han establecido en él con la denominación de San Carlos... (México: Imprenta del Superior Gobierno, 16 Aug 1770), 8 pp.; the official printed account (two 1770 editions exist) | 'The Official Account of the Portolá Expedition of 1769-1770', Publications of the Academy of Pacific Coast History, vol. 1, no. 2 (Berkeley, 1909); facsimile, Spanish text and English translation of the Estracto; possession passage at pp. 22-23 (Spanish p. 22, translation p. 23) | Palóu, Relación histórica de la vida y apostólicas tareas del venerable padre fray Junípero Serra (México, 1787), ch. XXII; English: Francisco Palóu's Life and Apostolic Labors of the Venerable Father Junípero Serra, trans. C. Scott Williams, intro. G. W. James (Pasadena, 1913), pp. 98-99 (Serra's eyewitness letter to Palóu, Monterey, feast of San Antonio = 13 June 1770, describing the whole ceremony incl. 'the officers performed the ceremony of taking formal possession of the land in the name of the King') and pp. 104-105 (translation of the Extracto); also trans. M. Geiger (Washington, 1955) (Full translation of Serra's 13 June 1770 eyewitness letter; ceremony description, not the act text) | Palóu, Noticias de la Nueva California, trans. H. E. Bolton, Historical Memoirs of New California (Berkeley: UC Press, 1926), vol. II, pp. 289-295 (ch. XXIII 'Formal possession is taken in the name of His Majesty of the port of Monterey' and ch. XXIV); Bolton's note 163 at II, 384-385 lists the unpublished MSS: 'Formal Act of Possession of Monterey, June 3, 1770, signed by Portolá; certificates to the same effect by Miguel del Pino and Juan Pérez, June 3, and by Pedro Fages, June 11, 1770', Crespí to Andrés 11 Jun 1770, Serra to Andrés 12 Jun 1770, Fages/Costansó letters, and Portolá to Croix 'encloses act of possession'. Spanish text in Documentos para la Historia de México, 4a ser. (1857) and the 1874 San Francisco ed | Serra to Fr. Juan Andrés (guardian of San Fernando), Monterey, 12 June 1770; trans. Antonine Tibesar, Writings of Junípero Serra (Washington: Academy of American Franciscan History, 1955), vol. I; ceremony passage at 1:169 (page as cited in K. Cherry, 'Serra and Sacred Song at the Founding of California's First Missions', Cal Poly); Serra to Gálvez, 2 July 1770 ('account of the formal act of possession at Monterey', AGI copy = Chapman no. 1509, p. 232) also in Tibesar I (Translation of Serra's fullest eyewitness letters; description of the ceremony, not the act text) | Costansó, Diario Histórico de los Viages de Mar, y Tierra hechos al Norte de la California (México, 24 Oct 1770); trans. in 'The Narrative of the Portolá Expedition of 1769-1770 by Miguel Costansó', ed. A. van Hemert-Engert and F. J. Teggart, APCH Publications vol. 1, no. 4 (Berkeley, 1910), Monterey occupation at pp. 150-159 | Engelhardt, The Missions and Missionaries of California, vol. II (San Francisco, 1912), act of possession at pp. 76-77; open full text.
notes: THE INSTRUMENT SURVIVES in at least two archival copies: the signed autos sent to the viceroy (AGN Californias, old vol. 76) and a certified copy sent via Croix to Spain (AGI Guadalajara 417, old 104-3-3). Chapman heads the AGI copy '9 June' with Fages certifying 11 June; Bolton's two independent listings date the act 3 June with certificates 3 and 11 June; i.e., instrument of 3 June, certifications 9/11 June. Bolton (1926) listed the instrument among unpublished manuscripts, but its text is printed in Engelhardt, Missions and Missionaries II, and is quoted in this entry. Old-to-new signature equivalence 104-3-3 = Guadalajara 417 rests on exact content match (same expediente, same Portolá/Fages/Serra/Costansó letters); one step short of a printed concordance, so treat as very-high-confidence INFERRED. The PARES catalogue could not be reached, so Guadalajara 417's digitization status is UNKNOWN, not negative. AGN's modern Repositorio (Californias fondo digitised per-expediente) does not surface the autos at item level in either modern vol. 66 or modern vol. 76 (both walked expediente-by-expediente, 2026-10-26); the ramo was renumbered after 1913 and the autos were not relocated; no images.

name: Puerto de la Santisima Trinidad.
summary: Per Sierra's eyewitness diary: cross adored on the beach, Te Deum Laudamus chanted, procession of officers and most of both crews to the hilltop, cross set up, 'the Commandant took formal possession of the territory, in accordance with the instructions of his Excellency the Viceroy Don Antonio Maria Bucareli'; Campa's Mass and sermon; gun volleys answered by the ships' cannon; port named for the feast of the Santisima Trinidad. Mourelle (Barrington trans., 483-84) adds: crews marched in two bodies, square formed as a chapel on the mountain top, 'possession taken, with all the requisites enjoined by our instructions.' Ceremony followed the Bucareli/Perez formulario of 24 Dec 1773 (AGN Historia 68). Menzies (Vancouver expedition) found the cross still standing 2 May 1793, inscribed 'Carolus III Dei G. Hyspaniarum Rex' (Wagner's note in CHSQ 9:3). An LC Geography & Map Division Spanish atlas sheet, 'Plano del Puerto nombrado de la Sma Trinidad... 1775', marks 'A. Monte de la Cruz y posesion'
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Estado, Legajo 38, Docs. 6 and 7 (Hezeta's two escrituras de posesion, Trinidad + Rada de Bucareli; which number is which act not established) = modern PARES ESTADO,38A,N.6 / N.7 (INFERRED from the verified match Servin Doc. 8 = PARES ESTADO,38A,N.8) (digitization unconfirmed; the sibling units N.5 and N.8 are digitized) | Archivo General de la Nacion, Mexico City, Historia, vol. 324 (diaries of Hezeta, Bodega, Mourelle; Campa also in Historia vol. 3) per Wagner, Cartography I, 177 [not digitized (AGN Repositorio has no Historia fondo online - registered null)] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, ESTADO,38A,N.5 - Mourelle's 1775 diary copy, 32 hojas, PARES id 64436 (eyewitness account) [digitized (64 images on PARES)] | Fray Benito de la Sierra, 'Fray Benito de la Sierra's Account of the Hezeta Expedition to the Northwest Coast in 1775', ed. H. R. Wagner, trans. A. J. Baker, California Historical Society Quarterly 9, no. 3 (Sept 1930): 201-242, Trinidad ceremony at 219-220; translation of eyewitness diary; full ceremony description (not the act text) | [F. A. Mourelle], 'Journal of a Voyage in 1775...', in Daines Barrington, Miscellanies (London: J. Nichols, 1781), journal pp. 469-556 (narrative 471-525; tables 526-556), Trinidad possession at 483-484; contemporary English translation of Mourelle's journal; eyewitness description o. | Miguel de la Campa, A Journal of Explorations Northward Along the Coast from Monterey in the Year 1775, ed. John Galvin (San Francisco: John Howell-Books, 1964) | Bruno de Hezeta, For Honor and Country: The Diary of Bruno de Hezeta, trans./ed. Herbert K. Beals (Portland: Oregon Historical Society Press, 1985), 166 pp | H. H. Bancroft, History of California, I (San Francisco, 1884), 242-243 (description only ('landed and took formal possession... raising the cross, and a mass by Father Campa')) | Francisco Palou, 'Heceta, Expedicion maritima hasta el grado cincuenta y ocho...', in Noticias de la Nueva California (SF 1874 ed.), ii, 219-257; Eng. in H. E. Bolton, Historical Memoirs of New California (Berkeley, 1926)
notes: The escritura text itself appears never to have been printed; the formulario (Servin 243-46) is the act's template verbatim. Servin n.7 verbatim: 'Escrituras de posesion tomada por Bruno de Hezeta, MSS, A.G.I., Seville, Estado, Legajo 38, Docs. 6 and 7...'. Bancroft's authorities list also records a Bancroft Library MS 'Perez (Juan), Formulario, Escripturas de Posesion, 1773' - a Berkeley copy of the formulario.

name: Rada de Bucareli (anchorage; point named Punta de los Martires)
date_display: 14 July 1775 (the eyewitness diaries. Sierra, Mourelle; are unanimous; a 12 July date in some modern summaries is unsupported)
summary: Sierra (eyewitness, in the launch): 'the Commandant, I, the pilot and the surgeon and twenty armed men went in the launch to take possession of the land, which was done without opposition but with the greatest possible haste and without mass being said, because the weather and the position of the Frigate did not admit of any delay' (CHSQ 9:3, 227). Cross erected (Bancroft NWC I, 160-61). Same morning, a few miles south, the Sonora's seven-man watering party (led by Pedro Santa Ana per Mourelle) was killed by Quinault warriors at the river mouth (Wagner, 1933 field identification: Moclips River); Bodega named the point Punta de los Martires. The planned simultaneous possession from the Sonora was thereby aborted
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Estado, Legajo 38, Docs. 6 and 7 (Hezeta's two escrituras; this act one of the two) = PARES ESTADO,38A,N.6/N.7 (INFERRED) [unknown (PARES 429 on)] | Archivo General de la Nacion, Mexico City, Historia, vol. 324 (Hezeta diario and other 1775 diaries, per Wagner I, 177) [not digitized] | Sierra diary, CHSQ 9:3 (1930): 227-228 (eyewitness translation; ceremony and naming 'Rada de Bucareli', observed 47 deg 25 min) | Bancroft, History of the Northwest Coast, I (1884), 160-161. | Mourelle in Barrington, Miscellanies (1781), 495-497 (Sonora-side account: order to 'jointly take possession of this part of the coast', the landing party, the massacre) | Beals, For Honor and Country (1985); full translation of Hezeta's diary covering the 14 July act; pages unverified. | Wagner, Cartography of the Northwest Coast, I (1937), 176. | Sierra account, CHSQ 9:3 (1930), pp. 201-242 (as above). Translation of eyewitness description. | Barrington, Miscellanies (1781), Mourelle journal pp. 469-556 (narrative 471-525; tables 526-556). Translation describing the expedition (Mourelle was on the Sonora)
notes: Revillagigedo's 1793 informe gives the official latitude 'the Roadstead of Bucareli in 47 deg 24 min' with 'the respective formal possessions being taken' (quoted in Wagner's intro, CHSQ 9:3, 205). Bancroft (NWC I, 160) could not find 'Rada de Bucareli' in the original narratives and knew it from Navarrete and the 1793 informe; Sierra's diary (published 1930, after Bancroft) does carry the name.

name: Puerto de los Remedios (Puerto de Nuestra Senora de los Remedios)
date_display: 1775-08-18 (Mourelle's journal: entered 9 a.m., landed about noon 'the same day'; Wagner, Cartography I, 176 dates it 19 August - unresolved one-day conflict; Spanish latitude 57 deg 18 min Mourelle / 57 deg 20 min Bodega and the 1793 informe)
summary: Mourelle (Barrington trans., 504): 'having posted ourselves in the safest place we could fix upon, we planted the cross with all proper devotion, cutting another on a rock, and displaying the Spanish colours, agreeable to our instructions on that head. When we had thus taken possession of the country...'. No Mass possible (no priest). The local Tlingit afterwards removed the planted cross and set it up in front of their house, making open-armed signs
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Estado, Legajo 38, Doc. 9 (escritura de posesion by Bodega y Quadra, per Servin n.7) = PARES ESTADO,38A,N.9 (inferred; digitization unconfirmed) | Archivo del Museo Naval, Madrid, AMN Ms.0622, item N.1 (contemporary copy of Bodega's 1775 'Navegacion...' journal - eyewitness account; same volume holds Arteaga's and Mourelle's 1779 diaries) [digitized (Biblioteca Virtual de Defensa record BMDB20160046304, 554 images, free download)] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, ESTADO,38A,N.5 (Mourelle 1775 diary copy, PARES id 64436) [digitized (64 images)] | Mourelle in Barrington, Miscellanies (1781), 503-504; eyewitness translation of the landing and possession. | Bodega's own narrative (as furnished to the Santiago), in Sierra/Wagner, CHSQ 9:3 (1930): 240 and nn. 34-35. | Herbert K. Beals (ed./trans.), 'Journal of Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra, 1775', in Four Travel Journals: The Americas, Antarctica and Africa 1775-1874, Hakluyt Society, Third Series 18 (London, 2007) | Wagner, Cartography of the Northwest Coast, I (1937), 176-177; description + the Sea Lion Bay site identification against Salisbury Sound. | 'Navegacion hecha por Don Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra... a los descubrimientos de los mares y costa septentrional de California', in Coleccion de diarios y relaciones para la historia de los viajes y descubrimientos (Madrid: Instituto Historico de Marina, 1943-). Spanish text of Bodega's 1775 journal (tomo/pages unverified) | Barrington, Miscellanies (1781), Mourelle journal, Remedios passage ('We named this port de los Remedios... planted the cross with all proper devotion'), pp. 469-556 (narrative 471-525; tables 526-556). English translation DESCRIBING the act.
notes: San Jacinto (Mt. Edgecumbe) named 16 Aug; Cabo del Engano 57 deg 02 min and Puerto Guadalupe 57 deg 11 min named 17-18 Aug (no act at Guadalupe). The one-day date conflict (18 vs 19 Aug) should be settled from the escritura itself (PARES N.9) or Beals 2007.

name: Puerto de Bucareli / Entrada de Bucareli.
date_display: 1775-08-24 (entered 2 p.m. doubling the cape at 55 deg 17 min; PARES catalogue of the escritura: 'que tomo el 24 de agosto de 1775')
summary: Mourelle landed 'with the same precautions as at Los Remedios', took possession in the king's name and raised a cross (Wagner I, 177: 'He sent Mourelle ashore, who took possession and raised a cross, naming it Entrada de Bucareli'); no Indians seen, though a hut and paths proved habitation; wood and water taken on a second landing
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, ESTADO,38A,N.8 (= Servin's 'Estado, Leg. 38, Doc. 8'): 'Testimonio autorizado del acta de posesion del puerto de Bucareli, que tomo el 24 de agosto de 1775, Francisco Antonio Maurelle, piloto de la goleta La Sonora, en nombre del rey...', certified Mexico 9 Dec 1775, 7 folios; PARES description id 64439 [digitized (16 images on PARES)] | Archivo del Museo Naval, Madrid, AMN Ms.0622, item N.1, ca. images 50-61 ('Salida de la Entrada y Puerto de Bucareli' at image 061) - Bodega's journal [digitized (BVD record BMDB20160046304)] | Mourelle in Barrington, Miscellanies (1781), 508-509; eyewitness translation by the man who performed the act. | Bodega narrative in Sierra/Wagner, CHSQ 9:3 (1930): 240-241 and n. 36 (description: 'so exceedingly placid, sheltered and pleasant that on the 24th of August they took possession of it') | Voyage of the Sonora in the Second Bucareli Expedition..., Barrington's translation reprinted with notes (San Francisco: Thomas C. Russell, 1920); reprint of the Mourelle journal translation. | Wagner, Cartography of the Northwest Coast, I (1937), 177; description and location. | Beals (ed.), Four Travel Journals (Hakluyt Society 2007), Bodega 1775 journal; full translation; pages unverified. | Barrington, Miscellanies (1781), Mourelle journal, Bucareli passage ('He also directed me to take possession for his Majesty of this part of the coast, and name it Bucarelly'), pp. 469-556 (narrative 471-525; tables 526-556). English translation DESCRIBING the act.
notes: CAUTION: the PARES catalogue title says Maurelle acted 'por indisposicion de Bruno de Hezeta, comandante de la expedicion'; the Sonora had separated from Hezeta on 31 July - the indisposed officer on the spot was Bodega (Mourelle's own journal). The cataloguer compressed/erred; cite the document, not the catalogue phrase. The 1793 Revillagigedo informe lists 'the archipelago and port of the same name [Bucareli] in 55 deg 18 min' among the formal possessions.

name: Puerto de la Bodega (= Tomales Bay per Edwards/Cook), California.
summary: Bodega and Mourelle anchored one night; the longboat was smashed at the entrance and no act of possession is recorded in any eyewitness text. In April 1793 the viceregal office nonetheless grounded Spain's claim in this visit. Bodega 'anchored in the port of his name in 38° 18' close to San Francisco and took possession of it.' Mapped as a claim, not an act
sources: Wagner's intro, CHSQ 9:3 (1930), 205. Contradicted by the eyewitness 1775 record (scurvy crew, canoe smashed, no recorded landing ceremony) and by Cook, Flood Tide 83 ('four formal acts of possession far to the north' = Trinidad, Grenville, Remedios, Bucareli). Enter as a retrospective viceregal CLAIM, not a verified act; but a census built for this project cannot omit the row. | H. R. Wagner (intro) in 'Fray Benito de la Sierra's Account of the Hezeta Expedition to the Northwest Coast in 1775', California Historical Society Quarterly 9:3 (1930), p. 205 (Revillagigedo report of 12 Apr 1793, quoted verbatim) and the Sierra account + Wagner n.40 (3 Oct 1775 arrival, no ceremony).

name: Formal possession of the Presidio de San Francisco (patron San Francisco de Asís)
date_display: 1776-09-17 (feast of the Impression of the Stigmata of St. Francis)
summary: Holy Cross blessed, venerated and raised; solemn sung mass by Palóu; 'the gentlemen performed the ceremony of taking formal possession' in the name of the sovereign (Palóu); procession into the chapel singing the Te Deum; peals of bells, salvos of cannon from the San Carlos and the shore, and musketry (which frightened the Yelamu away for days); banquet given by Moraga. Site = the square laid out 92 varas on a side per Cañizares's plan
sources: Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City, Palóu, Noticias de la Nueva California, the 'Figueroa manuscript'. Bolton's translation made 'from the manuscript in the Archives of Mexico' (title page, Hist. Mem. 1926); exact modern AGN classification not verified. | Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City ('Archivo General y Público'), Moraga's official account/report of the founding of San Francisco, 1776; 'the unpublished official manuscript in the Archivo General y Público, Mexico' (Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions III, preface); ramo/volume not stated. | 'Palóu's Account of the Founding of San Francisco, 1776' (from the Noticias), in H. E. Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions, vol. III: The San Francisco Colony (Berkeley, 1930), pp. 383-405; possession ceremony at pp. 393-395. | 'Moraga's Account of the Founding of San Francisco, 1776', in Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions III, pp. 407-420 (Full translation of the commanding officer's own unpublished report; the second eyewitness account) | Palóu, Vida (1787), SF founding account; trans. C. Scott Williams (1913), pp. 203-205: 'Formal possession of the presidio was taken on the 17th of September... The officers then performed the solemn act of taking possession in the name of Our Sovereign, with a cannonade from vessel and shore'. Translation of Palóu's first-person description. | Palóu, Noticias, trans. Bolton, Historical Memoirs of New California, vol. IV (1926) (SF founding chapters; page numbers not verified; vol. IV not in the open IA set consulted); H. E. Bolton, An Outpost of Empire (= Anza's California Expeditions I, 1930), pp. 469-471; Z. S. Eldredge, The Beginnings of San Francisco (San Francisco, 1912), I, pp. 150-151; Bancroft, History of California I, pp. 288-289. Translations/descriptions of the ceremony; none prints any instrument (none is known) | Palóu, Historical Memoirs of New California, trans. Bolton (1926), vol. IV, pp. 125-127 (ceremony; arrival and layout at pp. 121-125) - pages per the NPS Presidio of San Francisco Historic Resource Study footnotes 39, 44, 45. Eyewitness DESCRIPTION in English translation (vol. IV not on IA) | Palóu, Noticias de la Nueva California (San Francisco: CHS, 1874), 4 vols. (Spanish text). Spanish original of the same account.

name: Formal possession/founding of Mission San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores), 'la Laguna de los Dolores'
date_display: 1776-10-09 per Palóu's Vida and Bancroft (the mission's official founding date); 1776-10-08 per Palóu's own Noticias account (ceremony planned for 4 Oct, postponed until Moraga returned on the 7th)
summary: Church/site blessed (3 Oct); on the founding day the site was blessed, the Holy Cross set up, procession with the image of St. Francis carried on a frame, first High Mass sung by Palóu with sermon on St. Francis; repeated salvos of muskets and the bark's swivel-guns brought ashore, and rockets; feast (two beeves). Palóu's Vida calls the presidio rite the model: this was 'the formal possession of the Mission', delayed from 17 Sept. Religious/mission possession in the king's name and that of the College of San Fernando; distinct from a sovereignty claim over territory (that was Monterey 1770)
sources: Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City, Palóu, Noticias (Figueroa MS) and Moraga's founding report (see presidio entry); no separate act/instrument of the mission founding located. | 'Palóu's Account of the Founding of San Francisco, 1776', Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions III, pp. 400-401 (ceremony 'on the 8th of the same month'). Full translation of Palóu's account of the mission founding ceremony. | Palóu, Vida, trans. Williams (1913), pp. 207-208 ('This they did on the 9th of October. After having blessed the site, set up the Holy Cross, and made a procession...'). Translation; gives 9 Oct. | Bolton, An Outpost of Empire (Anza I, 1930), pp. 471-472 (follows the Noticias: ceremony 8 Oct); Bancroft, History of California I, pp. 292-293 (gives 9 Oct 'solemne función'; notes no orders from Rivera ever came)

name: Cook at Point Possession, Cook Inlet.
summary: Flag displayed, possession taken, bottle with coins buried (per Cook's journal)
sources: Cook and King, A Voyage to the Pacific Ocean (London, 1784), vol. II, bk. IV, pp. 396–97 (1 June 1778: flag displayed, possession in the king’s name, bottle with 1772 coins buried; naming of Point Possession)

name: Puerto de Santiago (island named Santa Maria Magdalena)
date_display: Possession 21 July 1779 per Riobó (eyewitness); 23 July per Wagner, Cartography I, 194; unresolved
summary: Officers and chaplains went ashore in procession, raised a large cross, cannon and musket salutes, Te Deum sung, litany and prayers (Tovell, 94-95). Riobo (eyewitness): 'we arrived at a large harbor... We called it St. James the Apostle because at that time we were celebrating the novena of the Saint... Here we took possession of this harbor in the name of the King. It is situated in 60 degrees 13 minutes north latitude' (CHR 4:2, 227-28). Plan of the port made by pilot Jose Camacho
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Estado, Legajo 38, Doc. 12 (escritura de la posesion tomada por Ignacio Arteaga, per Servin n.8; the same Doc. 12 also carries Quiros's Regla act) = PARES ESTADO,38A,N.12 (inferred; digitization unconfirmed) | Archivo General de la Nacion, Mexico City, Historia (Historical Section), vols. 63-64 (original 1779 diaries of Arteaga, Bodega, Quiros, Camacho, Pantoja, Canizares, Aguirre, per Wagner I, 195); Mourelle's 1779 diary = W. A. Clark Jr. Library, Los Angeles [not digitized (no AGN Historia fondo online)] | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, certified diary copies: Est. Aud. Mex. 18, Docs. 13-19 (Wagner I, 195-96); also ESTADO,38A,N.13 (Arteaga diary copy, 210 fols., PARES id 64444, digitized 428 imgs) and ESTADO,38A,N.14 (Quiros diary copy, 70 fols., PARES id 64445, digitized 140 imgs) [digitized (N.13 and N.14 on PARES)] | University of Santa Clara Archives, California, Riobo commonplace-book extract (the MS Thornton translated) | [Fr. Juan Antonio Garcia Riobo], 'An Account of the Voyage Made by the Frigates Princesa and Favorita in the Year 1799 [recte 1779] from San Blas to Northern Alaska', trans. Walter Thornton SJ, Catholic Historical Review 4, no. 2 (July 1918): 222-229, Santiago possession at 227-228. translation of eyewitness chaplain's account; description only. | Wagner, Cartography of the Northwest Coast, I (1937), 194-195; description, dating, latitude analysis of the possession spot. | Bancroft, History of Alaska 1730-1885 (San Francisco, 1886), 219; description ('The usual forms of taking possession were observed') | H. R. Wagner, 'Creation of Rights of Sovereignty through Symbolic Acts', Pacific Historical Review 7 (Dec 1938): 297-326, at 312-313; census/location of the 1779 acts (cited by Servin n.8; content not independently examined)
notes: Wagner I, 195 (as printed): 'Certified copies of the various acts of possession were sent to Spain, the originals still existing in the Archivo General de Indias, Cor. Virreyes, Volume 125' - internally inconsistent; 'Cor[respondencia de] Virreyes, Volume 125' is AGN citation style, and the sentence logic (copies TO Spain, originals elsewhere) points to AGN Correspondencia de Virreyes vol. 125 for the retained originals. Treat the AGI Estado 38 items as the certified copies sent to Spain. Flagged, unresolved.

name: Nuestra Senora de la Regla (ensenada de Nuestra Senora de la Regla; island group incl. Isla de San Aniceto)
date_display: 1779-08-02 (anchored 9 a.m. 2 Aug, 'a day memorable for our religious order' - the Franciscan Portiuncula feast; Wagner: possession the day after the 1 Aug anchorage at San Aniceto, i.e. 2 Aug)
summary: 'We took possession for the second time in the name of the king in a bay not far from there and gave it the name of Our Lady de Regla' (Riobo, CHR 4:2, 229). Formal possession with the usual forms; largest island named Isla de la Regla per Bancroft; chart legend read by Bancroft: 'haviendose tomado segda posesion en la Ysla de San Antonio [sic]', cross marked at the NW point of San Aniceto; position 59 deg 8 min N, 49 deg 11 min W of San Blas
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Estado, Legajo 38, Doc. 12 (Quiros's escritura, same numero as Arteaga's Santiago act, per Servin n.8) = PARES ESTADO,38A,N.12 (INFERRED) [unknown (PARES 429 on)] | Archivo General de la Nacion, Mexico City, Historia vols. 63-64 (1779 diaries, per Wagner I, 195) [not digitized] | Riobo trans. Thornton, Catholic Historical Review 4:2 (July 1918): 229; eyewitness translation; description only. | Carlos Maria de Bustamante, Suplemento a la Historia de los tres siglos de Mexico... del padre Andres Cavo, III (Mexico, 1836), 35 (Spanish printed account of the act of possession taken at Regla (per Wagner I, 195; not independently read)) | Wagner, Cartography of the Northwest Coast, I (1937), 194-195; description, actors (Quiros, Bodega, Mourelle), latitude analysis. | Bancroft, History of Alaska (1886), 220 and n. 49; description + the Azanza-instruccion chart legend locating the possession cross.
notes: Second and last possession of the 1779 voyage; Iliamna volcano sighted and named Miranda from this anchorage. Site precision is split between Port Chatham (mainland bay, modern accounts) and the NW point of Elizabeth Island (contemporary chart legend) - do not state either as settled.

name: Founding and formal possession of the site of the Real Presidio de Santa Bárbara.
summary: Timber cut for a large cross, a hut-chapel and altar table; Serra blessed the ground and the Holy Cross, which was raised and venerated; first mass attended by governor, officers and troops; sermon; per Palóu the ceremony concluded 'by the formal act of taking possession of the site, without the slightest opposition on the part of the natives'; Bancroft (from Neve's and Serra's letters) records mass and a chanted alabado on 21 April. A secondary account (California Military Museum, uncited detail) adds flag-raising and the grass-pulling ritual. Mission Santa Barbara was NOT founded until 4/16 Dec 1786; only the presidio in 1782
sources: Bancroft Library, Berkeley. Archives of California (Savage transcripts; the original provincial archives burned in San Francisco, 1906), Provincial Records, MS, ii. 61-62, 64: Neve to Commandant-General Teodoro de Croix, 24 April 1782, reporting the founding (Bancroft, Hist. Cal. I, 377 n.10); also Croix to Neve, 22 July 1782, approving, Prov. St. Pap., MS, iii. 232-233. | Santa Barbara Mission Archive-Library (originals); Bancroft Library copy = 'Archivo de Santa Bárbara' transcripts, Serra letter of 29 April 1782 on the founding (Bancroft's citation: Arch. Sta. Bárbara, MS, ix. 293-294); presidio baptismal register with Serra's autograph founding title; in the original register Serra wrote 'esta misión de Santa Bárbara' with 'misión' struck out and 'presidio' written above (register cited by Bancroft as Arch. Sta. Bárbara, MS, vii. 32-33) | Palóu, Vida (1787), ch. LIII-LIV; trans. C. Scott Williams (1913), pp. 249-251: Serra 'blessed the ground and the Holy Cross... said the first Mass... preached an eloquent sermon, concluding the ceremony by the formal act of taking possession of the site'; also trans. M. Geiger (1955) | Bancroft, History of California I (1884), pp. 377-378 ('The formal establishing was on April 21st, when Serra said mass and chanted an alabado'), with n.10 citing Neve to Croix 24 Apr 1782, Serra 29 Apr 1782, the presidio baptismal book, and Croix's approval of 22 Jul 1782 (Description with the archival citations (the closest thing to a calendar of the founding records)) | Serra's 1782 correspondence in A. Tibesar, ed., Writings of Junípero Serra, 4 vols. (Washington, 1955-66); the April-May 1782 letters (volume/pages not verified); 'The Founders of Santa Barbara', California State Military Museum (secondary, with the register anecdote). Translations of Serra's letters; secondary description.

name: Shelikhov possession at Kodiak.
summary: Settlement founded at Three Saints Bay. Russian possession asserted by occupation; no discrete marker or possession ceremony at Kodiak is described in the sources read. The plates-and-crests instrument begins with the 1788 voyage and the 1790 Kokh instruction
sources: Shelikhov, Voyage (1791; English translation 1981). Description only | H. H. Bancroft, History of Alaska, 1730-1885 (Works XXXIII, San Francisco, 1886), pp. 223-31 (arrival 3 Aug 1784, Three Saints Bay, subjection claims; possession-tablet evidence at p. 223 n.1 and p. 231 n.) | G. I. Shelikhov, A Voyage to America 1783-1786, trans. Marina Ramsay, ed. R. A. Pierce (Kingston: Limestone Press, 1981). REAL, on IA but access-restricted (401 on full text)
notes: Possession by settlement.

name: Lapérouse at Port des Français (bottle burial)
summary: Claimed purchase of the island from the Tlingit chief; bottle with act buried.
sources: Milet-Mureau (ed.), Voyage de La Pérouse autour du monde (Paris, 1797); English trans. London 1799. Port des Français (Lituya Bay), July 1786: purchase of the island from the Tlingit chief and bottle with act buried on Cenotaph Island. | A Voyage Round the World, in the Years 1785, 1786, 1787, and 1788, by J.F.G. de la Perouse (London, 1798), vol. II, ch. VIII, pp. 95-96 (island purchase; bottle with act of possession and bronze medal buried) | L. A. Milet-Mureau (ed.), Voyage de La Perouse autour du monde (Paris: Imprimerie de la Republique, 1797), t. II. French original (pagination not verified)

name: Izmailov/Bocharov imperial crests at Yakutat.
date_display: June 1788 (Yakutat reached 11 June; crests/plates placed before the late-June departure)
summary: Imperial crests/plates distributed and buried; possession marks.
sources: The Shelikhov appendix, with Bolkhovitinov. Description only | H. H. Bancroft, History of Alaska, 1730-1885 (Works XXXIII, 1886), pp. 266-69, citing Shelikof, Putesh., ii. 2-3, 7 and Ismailof's Journal, 14-15. | Izmailov-Bocharov voyage journal, printed as part ii of Shelikhov's Puteshestvie (1791); English in Shelikhov, A Voyage to America 1783-1786 (Limestone Press, 1981), IA-restricted.

name: Meares' claimed land purchase from Maquinna.
summary: Claimed purchase of shore land; the consent claim litigated in the Nootka crisis.
sources: Meares, Voyages Made in the Years 1788 and 1789 (London, 1790), pp. 114–15 (Maquilla "consented to grant us a spot of ground," May 1788) | John Meares, Voyages Made in the Years 1788 and 1789, from China to the North West Coast of America (London, 1790), pp. 114-15. | Authentic Copy of the Memorial to the Right Honourable William Wyndham Grenville... of Lieutenant John Mears, dated 30th April 1790 (London, 1790), with enclosures. | F. W. Howay (ed.), The Dixon-Meares Controversy (1929; repr. 1969) | Authentic Copy of the Memorial to the... House of Commons by Lieut. John Mears (London, 1790); the purchase claim as litigated in the Nootka crisis.

name: Puerto de Flores (toma de posesión, first of the 1788 voyage)
summary: Procession along the beach; large cross and altar to Our Lady of the Rosary set up; Mass; cross fastened with iron spikes to a tall pine facing the interior of the island, carved 'Carolus Tertius Hispaniarium et Indiarum Rex' and 'Year of 1788'; musketry volleys answered by 4-gun salutes from each ship (eyewitness: Haro's diary)
sources: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Madrid, Estado, Leg. 4289 (cited from Servín n.9; AHN legajos 4289-4290 are confirmed as Martínez-voyage material by the DCB bibliography, but the catalogue record could not be opened) | Bancroft Library, Berkeley (19th-c. copy), 'Cuarta exploración de descubrimientos de la costa septentrional de California hasta los 61 grados... por... José Martínez... 1788', in Viages al Norte de California, MS No. VII [not digitized] | Archivo General de la Nación, México (Martínez 1788 material), Historia, vol. 61, exp. 14 (cited in DCB bibliography for Martínez; content attribution to the 1788 voyage INFERRED) [not digitized] | Gonzalo López de Haro, 'Spaniards and Russians Meet in Alaskan Waters, 1788: The Voyage of the Princesa and the San Carlos to Prince William Sound, Kodiak, and Unalaska', trans. and ed. Katrina H. Moore (1975 typescript), pp. 5-6 (English translation of Haro's eyewitness diary account of the 1 June 1788 ceremony (not the formal escritura)) | Timo C. Allan, 'Discoverers & Possessors: Symbolic Acts of Possession and Spain's Struggle for Sovereignty on the North Pacific Coast' (MA thesis, University of Alaska Fairbanks, 2002), Appendix E, pp. 142-143. Reprints the Moore translation of Haro's eyewitness account in full. | H. H. Bancroft, History of Alaska, 1730-1885 (San Francisco, 1886), 271. Description only: 'Here they took possession and remained till the 15th of June.'
notes: First of what Allan calls 'a string of claiming ceremonies' on the 1788 voyage. Servín n.9 cites six acts for the voyage at AHN Estado 4289; that count is not independently confirmed here.

name: Toma de posesión at Unalaska (anchorage off the northern point)
date_display: 1788-07-21 (Bancroft; the Princesa entered the Russian harbor on 28 July)
summary: 'Martinez on July 21st took possession in the name of Spain' (Bancroft, from the expedition MS); details of ritual not given.
sources: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Madrid, Estado, Leg. 4289 (INFERRED from the Servín n.9 lead; unverified) | Bancroft Library, Berkeley (copy), Cuarta exploración..., Viages al Norte de California, MS No. VII, at p. 312 ff. [not digitized] | H. H. Bancroft, History of Alaska (1886), 272. Description only.

name: Toma de posesión of the Puerto de Santa Cruz, Bahía de San Lorenzo de Nuca, and the whole coast.
date_display: 1789-06-24 (Wednesday, feast of St John; act states lat 49°33'N, long 20°18' W of San Blas)
summary: Full formulary: adoration of the cross, Te Deum, proclamation in the name of Carlos III invoking the 1774 discovery and Alexander VI's bull of 4 May 1493; sword gestures (cutting trees/branches, moving stones) 'without opposition'; procession with cross, Litany, cross planted with cairn of stones; port named Santa Cruz; High Mass (first in the land) and sermon; second cross cut and carved I.N.R.I. / Carolus tertius, Rex Hispaniorum; notarized instrument signed by all
sources: Archivo General de Indias, Seville, old pressmark '90-3-18' - 'Instrument of possession, San Lorenzo de Nootka, June 24, 1789' (Manning 1905, n.121; modern signature equivalent not established here - Manning's 90-3-18 items are the viceregal correspondence series, cf. name: Vancouver at Possession Sound.
summary: On 4 June 1792, George III's birthday, the crews were served a double allowance of grog to drink the king's health and Vancouver went ashore about one o'clock with Broughton and his officers, 'pursuing the usual formalities' and under a royal salute from the vessels. He took possession of the coast from New Albion in latitude 39 degrees 20 minutes north to the entrance of the supposed strait of Juan de Fuca, naming the interior sea the Gulf of Georgia and the continent binding it New Georgia. The branch of Admiralty Inlet where it was done he named Possession Sound. The ceremony came two years after the Nootka Convention was supposed to have closed the age of such acts
sources: Vancouver, A Voyage of Discovery (London, 1798 1st ed.), vol. name: Hagemeister treaty with Kashaya chiefs.
summary: Signed instrument of cession/amity; title by indigenous consent.
sources: Protocol of the meeting at Colony Ross between the Indian tribal chiefs and Captain-Lieutenant Hagemeister, 22 September 1817. Archives of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire, published by the Fort Ross Conservancy Digital Library in the 2012 bicentennial collection of sixteen documents
notes: Russia grounded its title in recorded indigenous consent, where Spain grounded its own in the papal bull of 1493. The protocol was signed by the Russian witnesses; the chiefs assented orally, so it is better described as recorded consent than as a mutually signed treaty.

name: Valenila asks Golovnin for the Russian flag.

notes: Spain's own 1773 sailing instructions had told its navigators to gather intelligence about rival ships from Native memory. In 1818 that same channel reported to Russia instead. Name spelling varies by witness: Valenila in Golovnin, Vallí-éla in the later literature.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: The northernmost presidio, founded 1776, responsible for the whole contested frontier facing Bodega and Ross. Its company ran about 30 to 56 men for most of the Spanish period and never surged to meet the Russian arrival in 1812. In 1794 its own inspection called it 'abierto y sin defensa ninguna': tule-roofed houses renewed yearly, chapel and warehouses threatening ruin; the March 1831 review counts 44 men all told. At independence the company counted itself whole: June 1822, fuerza efectiva with the militias, 127 men, eight of them artillerymen.
result: Roughly 30 to 70 men guarding the Golden Gate across five decades
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault), compiled from C-A 10, 16, 21, 54 | SF presidio condition report, Jun 1794 · 'abierto y sin defensa' (C-A 14), doc 100 | San Francisco company, Mar 1831 · 44 hombres (C-A 19), doc 76 | Estado de fuerza efectiva (veterana y milicias), San Francisco, 26 Jun 1822 · total 127 (C-A 18), doc 1

name: Castillo de San Joaquín (Fort Point, San Francisco)
summary: The battery at the Golden Gate narrows, blessed December 1794. Built for 6,491 pesos, partly with mission mule labor. The register's headline series: the fort's serviceable guns never exceeded a handful, and a single Russian outpost at Ross reported more mounted cannon than the whole San Francisco defense.
result: Never more than about six serviceable guns at any count, and usually fewer
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault); build cost C-A 24 Docs 62, 70
notes: The 1793 '6 vs 2' is resolved: the leaf of C-A 14 (n101, read 2026-09-14) says 2, agreeing with C-A 15; the 6 is a catalogue-summary defect, errata pending. The 1823 copies agree on the 3 heavy guns and disagree only on the powder figure; the earlier '2 (or 3)' note was wrong and the Doc 98 citation was a mis-reference (that record is a cadet discharge).

name: Batería de Yerba Buena (San Francisco)
summary: The cove battery east of the presidio, garrisoned in the 1790s by a Catalan Volunteers detail relieved every 8 days. Ordered recomposed with adobe, earth, and fascine in 1799; abandoned by 1800 per the intelligence layer of the borderlands map.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault)

name: Presidio of Monterey
summary: The capital's presidio and the largest company in the province, with the Real Cuerpo de Artillería headquartered here. Even so, in 1809 its ~85 men were dispersed as mission escorts and herd guards, with only 4 men on the battery. Its Mexican-era arithmetic survives month by month: March 1829, a lieutenant, an alférez, sergeants, ten corporals and sixty soldiers drawing $1,668, Mariano Vallejo keeping the books as habilitado; by November 1833 the same company musters 35 men.
result: The largest single garrison, comparable to Ross's combined personnel, 100+ miles from the contested ground
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault) | Monterey company pay & strength, Mar 1829 · Vallejo habilitado (C-A 19), doc 9 | Monterey company, Nov 1833 · 35 hombres (C-A 19), doc 207 | Monterey muster roll & arms report, Apr 1797 (C-A 54), doc 3
notes: Rows cited 'presidio register' rest on the vault's register compilation; their catalog doc numbers are still being resolved and they carry no link by design.

name: Presidio of Santa Bárbara
summary: Founded 1782 with about 58 men and holding near that strength for decades. In 1797 its commander reported 118 cartridges for his single six-pounder, with no artilleryman to serve it. Its 1788 munitions account runs the escopeta cartridges down from 3,784 to 2,634 across the year, gunflints 1,900 to 1,685: consumption bookkeeping, round by round. The Mexican-era returns continue the series: Goycoechea's November 1797 estado de la fuerza, and Ibarra's Christmas 1834 garrison return.

name: Presidio of San Diego
summary: The first presidio, founded 1769. In September 1783 the whole company held 72 cartridges. Its guns were dismounted in 1793 with nobody able to operate them. The 1827 company roster counts 69 present, captain's chair vacant, its Habilitado General away in Guadalajara.

name: Fort Guijarros (Punta de Guijarros, San Diego)
summary: The harbor battery on Ballast Point, formally the Castillo de San Joaquín de Punta de Guijarros. The province had two forts of that name; this is the San Diego one. In 1798 it mounted 7 six-pounders of which 2 were serviceable; the 1820 census found the bronze guns vent-worn and the carriages rotted.

name: Presidio of Loreto (Baja California)
summary: The old Baja capital, included for context: its company (47 to 85 men plus a small marine department) was comparable to any Alta California presidio. Its treasury side survives at full length: the Real Tribunal audited the 1781–82 presidio accounts, and the habilitado's nine-year cuenta general (1781–89) runs the company's money at 144,527 pesos of cargo.
sources: Presidio garrison & artillery register (vault) | Reparos of the Loreto presidio accounts, 1781–82 (C-A 3), doc 236 | Estrada's nine-year cuenta general of the Loreto caudales, 1781–89 · 144,527 pesos (C-A 5), doc 204
notes: Rows cited 'presidio register' rest on the vault's register compilation; their catalog doc numbers are still being resolved and they carry no link by design.

name: Colony Ross (Russian benchmark)
summary: The measuring stick. A single Russian-American Company outpost, founded September 1812 (the ~95 Russians + ~80 Alaska Native hunters figure is the later literature's; Moraga's reconnaissance reported ~80 men). A 1813 Spanish intelligence report credited it with about 13 mounted cannon; Moraga's 1814 eyewitness reconnaissance counted 8 cannon in two corner towers with embrasures for far more. Either figure matches or exceeds the serviceable artillery of the entire San Francisco defense in the same decade.
result: One Russian fort ≈ the principal Spanish fort, in guns and in men
sources: Rows cited document-by-document in the dated series (C-A 12, 20, 53, 56)
notes: Both the Ross figure (a Spanish estimate) and the SF figure (a Spanish self-inventory) are Spanish-sourced, so the comparison is internally consistent. The defensible claim is order-of-magnitude parity, not a precise gun-for-gun ratio.

name: The artillery of California · the guns and the men who served them
summary: The province's artillery as a series: the headline is the 5 September 1818 count of every gun in California; 58 pieces by calibre and metal, 3 useless, carriages failing for want of ironwork; now paired with the manning record around it: the Real Cuerpo detachment of 1795 named man by man, the militia-gunner allocations of 1817, the 62 militia gunners counted the same day as the 58 guns, and the shrinking corps musters of 1827 and 1836. The series has earlier and later rungs: in 1797 the viceroy shuffled two- and three-pounder cannon from San Miguel and Loreto to fortify the new frontier mission, and a San Diego gunner coaxed a broken 24-pounder back into service; by December 1835 the artillery company itself musters by presidio: Monterey five corporals, a drummer and eleven gunners; San Francisco one and four; Santa Bárbara one and five.
result: The whole province's ordnance in one table
sources: Prov. St. Pap., Benicia (Mil.) (C-A 17) Doc 324 · province-wide artillery inventory, Monterey, 5 September 1818. | Branciforte: fortify Santa Catalina with cannon from San Miguel + Loreto, Mar 1797 (C-A 8), doc 399 | 'Compostura de un cañón' · one of the three 24-pounders repaired, Jul 1797 (C-A 10), doc 161 | Fuerza de Artillería by presidio, 3 Dec 1835 (C-A 20), doc 241
notes: Placed at Monterey, where the return was drawn. The guns it lists were distributed across the province; see each presidio and fort.

name: Sutter's Fort (Nueva Helvecia)
summary: The counter-benchmark at the era's other end: a private fort on the Sacramento, held by a naturalized foreigner whom the government first deputized as its frontier justice, then armed itself against. Its owner bought the departing Russians' properties in 1841–42, marched an artillery-equipped private force in the 1845 civil war, and appears in the Asamblea's treason charge against the sitting governor.
result: By 1845: a private force with newer artillery than most presidios; deputized, purchased into the Russians' place, then named in a treason charge
sources: C-A 30, 49, 61 · the New Helvetia records named in the dated series; the fort's establishment context from C-A 49 Doc 582
notes: Armament of the fort itself is deliberately not totalled here: the catalogue records the Russian-property purchase and the 1845 field artillery, not a fort inventory. What can be said from the record is sourced line by line above.

name: Sonoma garrison (Presidio of Sonoma)
summary: The northern frontier's last Mexican garrison: founded as the twelve-man armed escort of Mission San Francisco Solano in 1823, and after 1835 the seat of Vallejo's frontier command, absorbing what remained of the San Francisco company.
result: 1823: twelve men and one mounted gun; 1836: the San Francisco company, 24 strong, mustered at Sonoma
sources: Rows cited document-by-document in the dated series

name: The force of the province, counted whole
summary: Province-wide force returns, reinforcement squadrons and musket allocations that counted Alta California's soldiery as a single figure; including the allocations that existed only on paper. The floor of the curve is documented twice over: in 1804 the governor, writing from Loreto, reported 'el mal estado de los Presidios y escasez de tropa'; and an 1833 muster analysis found only 35 men present in all California, the company's bulk at Santa Bárbara with Figueroa, and ten men holding the capital. The reinforcements came counted too: the Mazatlán squadron's 1819 detachment for Alta California boarded the Cosak as a full estado de fuerza: a captain, two lieutenants, two alféreces, sergeants, drummers, corporals and men, itemized before they sailed.
result: 1828: 320 muskets allotted to the Californias on paper; an allocation, not a delivery
sources: Rows cited document-by-document in the dated series | Gov. to Viceroy, 8 May 1804 · 'mal estado de los Presidios y escasez de tropa' (C-A 25), doc 1050 | Muster analysis, Sept 1833 · 35 men present in California (C-A 19), doc 221 | Estado de fuerza of the Mazatlán-squadron detachment aboard the 'Cosak' under Capt. Pablo de la Portilla, 13 Jul 1819 (C-A 13), doc 86

result: 1847–48: twenty men, eight arrobas of powder, and a commendation

name: Suscol / Soscol (Mariano G. Vallejo)
summary: About 84,000 acres that General Mariano G. Vallejo bought from Governor Micheltorena in 1843, adjoining his Rancho Petaluma on the west and running east to Rancho Suisun and south to the Carquinez Strait and San Pablo Bay, taking in Mare Island and the sites of the towns Vallejo would sell: Benicia (sold with Larkin and Semple in 1846–47 and named for his wife) and the city of Vallejo, briefly the state capital. The United States rejected the claim: in United States v. Vallejo (1862) the Supreme Court held that the governor had no authority to sell public land, voiding what would have been the largest grant of the north bay.
sources: Diseño: “Map of Suscol” (Bancroft Land Case Maps) | U.S. land-claim case no. 318 (Vallejo, claimant), Northern District of California
notes: Reconstructed: western edge on Rancho Petaluma's confirmed boundary; south and east follow the real Carquinez Strait and San Pablo Bay shoreline (OpenStreetMap), taking in the Benicia and Vallejo townsites. Never U.S.-surveyed (the claim was rejected).

name: Mare Island / Isla de la Yegua (Victor Castro)
summary: The island of Mare Island (Isla de la Yegua), about 900 acres, granted to Victor Castro — provisionally by the secretary Jimeno in 1840 and in fee by Governor Alvarado in 1841. Castro sold it to John B. Frisbie and B. R. Simmons; the U.S. Navy bought the island in 1853 for its Pacific shipyard. The grant overlapped Vallejo's Suscol claim and its title was likewise contested.
sources: U.S. land-claim case no. 311 (Mare Island; Bissell, claimant), Northern District of California
notes: Boundary is Mare Island's own shoreline (OpenStreetMap); the grant was the whole island. Vallejo's Suscol claim overlapped it; the U.S. Navy took the island in 1853 for its Pacific shipyard.

sources: Boundary: NAHC/CNRA California Land Grants (PLSS reconstruction)

name: Suscol / Soscol (Mariano G. Vallejo)
summary: About 84,000 acres that General Mariano G. Vallejo bought from Governor Micheltorena in 1843, adjoining his Rancho Petaluma on the west and running east to Rancho Suisun and south to the Carquinez Strait and San Pablo Bay, taking in Mare Island and the sites of the towns Vallejo would sell: Benicia (sold with Larkin and Semple in 1846–47 and named for his wife) and the city of Vallejo, briefly the state capital. The United States rejected the claim: in United States v. Vallejo (1862) the Supreme Court held that the governor had no authority to sell public land, voiding what would have been the largest grant of the north bay.
sources: Diseño: “Map of Suscol” (Bancroft Land Case Maps) | U.S. land-claim case no. 318 (Vallejo, claimant), Northern District of California
notes: Reconstructed: western edge on Rancho Petaluma's confirmed boundary; south and east follow the real Carquinez Strait and San Pablo Bay shoreline (OpenStreetMap), taking in the Benicia and Vallejo townsites. Never U.S.-surveyed (the claim was rejected).

name: Mare Island / Isla de la Yegua (Victor Castro)
summary: The island of Mare Island (Isla de la Yegua), about 900 acres, granted to Victor Castro — provisionally by the secretary Jimeno in 1840 and in fee by Governor Alvarado in 1841. Castro sold it to John B. Frisbie and B. R. Simmons; the U.S. Navy bought the island in 1853 for its Pacific shipyard. The grant overlapped Vallejo's Suscol claim and its title was likewise contested.
sources: U.S. land-claim case no. 311 (Mare Island; Bissell, claimant), Northern District of California
notes: Boundary is Mare Island's own shoreline (OpenStreetMap); the grant was the whole island. Vallejo's Suscol claim overlapped it; the U.S. Navy took the island in 1853 for its Pacific shipyard.

name: Echeandía opens partial emancipation
summary: Gov. Echeandía's emancipation program begins: qualified neophytes of the southern missions may leave mission discipline, with individual segregation licenses following (Gil Riela and Andrés Ibarra among the first named). The 1826 San Diego dossier ties the friars' constitutional oath to neophyte emancipation and floats a neophyte pueblo at San Fernando or San Luis Rey.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 27) Doc 127 (the 1826 oath-and-emancipation dossier). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 47) Doc 71 (segregation of Gil Riela, 30 Apr 1826).
notes: The proclamation's own text is not in the vault surveys; its execution is. Standard accounts date the proclamation July 1826.

name: Pre-secularization land census ordered
summary: The Diputación orders every mission to report its lands and boundaries before year's end; the first territorial step toward disentailment. The resulting 1828 'Informes sobre terrenos y ganados' series, with each mission's cattle brand, survives in the State Papers: Missions volumes.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Monterey (C-A 43) Doc 1 (bando, 7 Oct 1827). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Docs 402–412, 418 (the 1828 informes).

name: Echeandía's secularization decree
summary: 'Ley secularizando las Misiones, declarándolas pueblos'; 33 articles converting the missions to pueblos under the 1813 Cortes law, San Gabriel and San Carlos first, extended to all by art. 24. Read to the neophytes at the Monterey-district missions that January; suspended by Gov. Victoria within days, denounced to Mexico, and annulled by the central government in April 1832.
sources: Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 224 (the 33 articles, complete). | St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 29 (the decree). | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 3–5 (promulgation to the neophytes, Jan 1831).
notes: The C-A 49 copy sits after Nov-1831 letters in the volume; the surveys flag the year for verification against Bancroft/Hutchinson.

name: The Mexican secularization law of Aug 17, 1833
summary: The national statute: 'Sobre secularización de las misiones de Alta y Baja California,' converting each mission to a secular parish. The Californian archive's own copy survives in the Superior Government State Papers, with the 26 Nov 1833 colonization companion law that underwrote the Híjar-Padrés colony.
sources: Sup. Govt. St. Pap. (C-A 57) Doc 93, orig. pp. 415–416. | Sup. Govt. St. Pap. (C-A 57) Doc 94 (the 26 Nov 1833 colonization law).

name: Gómez Farías: all missions, four months
summary: The general secularization decree from Mexico: ALL the republic's missions to be secularized within four months. It reached California as Figueroa and the Diputación were already drafting their own, more gradual machinery.
sources: Sup. Govt. St. Pap. (C-A 57) Doc 95.

name: Figueroa's Reglamento Provisional
summary: The instrument that actually dismantled the system: missions partially converted to pueblos; each family head a solar of up to 400 varas and half the livestock; article 18 barring the Indians from alienating their grants; article 22 barring mass slaughter of herds. Enacted through the Diputación's article-by-article debate that July, with same-day instructions to the comisionados; general inventories, dissolution of the monjerío, rancherías of 25 families eligible to form pueblos.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 78, Sav. 253–257 (the printed reglamento). | C-A 53 Doc 79 (Instrucciones para los Comisionados, 12 prevenciones). | Leg. Rec. (C-A 60) Doc 2 (the Diputación debate, Jul 1834). | Leg. Rec. (C-A 59) Doc 31 (the c. 1828–30 'Plan para convertir en pueblos las Misiones', the Diputación blueprint).

name: Alvarado's administrators' reglamento
summary: A ~14-article code for the mission administrators; render accounts, no credit against mission property 'por ningún pretexto,' padrón of neophytes; the government's attempt to police the men it had put over the ex-mission estates. A further mission decree followed on 17 Apr 1839.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., San José (C-A 45) Doc 68 (the reglamento). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 639 (the 17 Apr 1839 decree, sent to Durán).
notes: The standard accounts' 'Jan 17, 1839 regulation' matches neither vault instrument exactly; both are shown.

name: Administrators suppressed, mayordomos created
summary: Alvarado's 1 March 1840 decree suppresses the mission administrators and replaces them with mayordomos under the Visitador's oversight; the government's verdict on six years of administrator rule. Emancipation power was reserved exclusively to the government that October.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Decrees & Despatches (C-A 36) Doc 63, tomo p. 155. | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 646 (16 copies to Durán, 8 Apr 1840). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 596 (emancipation reserved to the government, 23 Oct 1840).

name: Micheltorena returns 12 missions to the friars
summary: The reversal: twelve named missions returned to the padres 'como en tutoría de los Indígenas,' remitting an eighth of their products; after a February order suspending all further alienation of mission lands. The 3 April circular ordering administrators to hand over names ten of them.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 175, Sav. 669–674. | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 1043 (the handover circular, 3 Apr 1843). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 1016 (the Feb 1843 alienation freeze).

name: Pico's sale-and-lease reglamento
summary: The 23-article 'Reglamento para la enajenación y arriendo de las Misiones': sell San Rafael, Dolores, Soledad, San Miguel, and La Purísima; lease the rest for nine years. Chapter 4 declares the neophytes freed and 'no estando obligados á servir á los arrendatarios'; article 20 lets Indians petition for inalienable title to their house and garden plots. Andrés Pico and Juan Manso had been inventorying the missions since May; the commission's object expressly their arrendamiento.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Decrees & Despatches (C-A 36) Doc 107 (verbatim, 23 arts.). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 1225 (the commission's lease mandate, 1 Jul 1845). | C-A 53 Doc 191 (Pico & Manso commissioned, 11 Jul 1845).

name: Mexico orders the sales suspended
summary: The supreme government, learning what the Department 'ha dispuesto' with the missions, orders all alienation proceedings reported and suspended. The sales went ahead anyway.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 181.

name: The Assembly authorizes outright sale
summary: Pico's government, invoking the common defense 'en caso de una invasión extranjera,' authorizes auctioning the missions to pay their creditors, any surplus to each mission's Indian community. The June 1846 deeds of sale cite this decree as their authority.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Decrees & Despatches (C-A 36) Doc 110. | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 160 (the San Buenaventura escritura quoting the 13 Apr decree).

name: The Assembly annuls Pico's sales
summary: With the American conquest underway, the Departmental Assembly annuls the mission sales (art. 1) while continuing the leases (art. 3). The U.S. courts finished the job: the Supreme Court later voided the San Gabriel and San Luis Rey sales.
sources: Unbound Docs. (C-A 63) Doc 479 (verbatim abstract). | U.S. v. Workman (1863) per Caragozian, CSCHS (standard account).

name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
summary: Secularized under the 1834 program; José Joaquín Ortega administered the ex-mission from April 1835. Sold to Santiago Argüello in the last weeks of Mexican rule.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Docs 57–58 (inventory & plano). | Unbound Docs. (C-A 63) Doc 393 (the Argüello sale, 8 Jun 1846). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: An 1847 charge alleged the Argüello bill of sale was ante-dated (C-A 63 Doc 190).

name: Mission San Luis Rey
summary: The richest inventory in the record: $203,787 existencia across the mission and its ranchos (Pala, Santa Margarita, Temécula, San Jacinto). Pío Pico, first a comisionado, administered it to 1840; removed only under threat of punishment; and its Luiseño residents mounted the most sustained documented resistance to the new order.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 15 (the 1835 general inventory). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 657 (the forced handover order, 23 Jul 1840). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The Cot & Pico sale of 1846 is not in the vault surveys; the July 1846 Marrón handover is.

name: Mission San Juan Capistrano
summary: The earliest secularization; Echeandía's pilot; and in 1841 the first ex-mission formally converted to a pueblo, with a 17-article reglamento and a land repartimiento naming its neófitos libres. Sold in December 1845 for $710.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 46: handover inventory of Mission San Juan Capistrano, 1838 (warehouse goods, wine and oil, soap, forge, carpentry, loom, bakery, shoemaking, tannery). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The two vault sale records disagree on the second buyer; 'James McKinley' (C-A 51 Doc 161) vs 'Santiago Machado' (the título, C-A 63 Doc 508c). Both shown; unresolved.

name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel
summary: Handed from Fr. Estenaga to comisionado Nicolás Gutiérrez in November 1834 with 12,980 cattle on its books; by the 1840 inventory the herd had collapsed to 72. Leased under Pico's program; the lease drive began here; and in the vault record assigned to Henry Dalton in February 1846.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 16 (the 1834 handover accounts). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 54 (the 1840 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The Reid & Workman sale of June 1846 is not in the vault surveys as read; the U.S. Supreme Court later voided the San Gabriel sale (standard account).

name: Mission San Fernando Rey
summary: Entrega to comisionado Antonio del Valle in December 1834; a decade later, leased to Andrés Pico and Juan Manso, then sold to Eulogio Célis in June 1846 for $14,000 'para sostener la integridad del Territorio.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 28: Antonio del Valle, secularization inventory of Mission San Fernando, 26 July 1835 (active credits $5,736; buildings $15,511; 32,000 black-grape vines; workshop tools; church and sacristy). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 445 (the 1834 entrega). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: Lease figures differ between the two vault records ($1,120 vs $1,125); both shown.

name: Mission San Buenaventura
summary: Among the last secularized: Gov. Chico ordered Fr. Blas Ordaz to hand it to Carlos Carrillo in June 1836 amid the constitutional-oath fight. Sold to its lessee José Arnaz in June 1846; 'dueño legítimo… para siempre'; followed by an 1846–48 asset-stripping dossier.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 157 (the Chico expediente). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 160 (the deed of sale). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The 1846–48 fraud dossier on the lease is C-A 63 Doc 464.

name: Mission Santa Bárbara
summary: Comisionado Anastacio Carrillo took the richest coastal plant in the 1835 inventory; $113,960 existencia including Rancho Dos Pueblos; with $2,484 in goods distributed to the Indians. Leased in December 1845 to Nicolás Den and Daniel Hill.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 29: Raymundo Carrillo, active credits $15,390.87 and liabilities $4,628.37 of Mission Santa Barbara, 25 October 1838. | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 443 (the 1835 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission Santa Inés
summary: Secularized in the 1836 wave on Chico's order; Fr. Jimeno handed it to José María Covarrubias that August with an existencia of $56,437; down to $39,284 within six months. Leased in 1845 to Covarrubias himself with Joaquín Carrillo.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 36 (the 1836 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission La Purísima Concepción
summary: Inventoried under article 15 of Figueroa's reglamento by comisionado Domingo Carrillo, with William Dana as appraiser: existencia $62,088.50 including ranchos Todos Santos and Guadalupe. One of the five missions Pico's reglamento listed for outright sale; bought by John Temple for $10,110 in December 1845.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 25: comisionado Domingo Carrillo to administrator Joaquin Carrillo, secularization handover inventory of Mission La Purisima, 18 August 1838 (total $27,981; credits $1,774; liabilities $1,371). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 439 (the 1834 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The survey flags the inventory digits as scale-2 reads pending verification.

name: Mission San Luis Obispo
summary: A revolving door of administrators (Trujillo, Moreno, Ayala, Canet, Bonilla); 253 souls in 1834. Erected into a pueblo in July 1844; its emancipados barred from selling their lands; then sold in December 1845 to Scott, Wilson & McKinley.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 118: handover inventory of Mission San Luis Obispo, 1836, with asset valuations by category. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The $510 price is the standard account; the vault record gives the buyers, not the price.

name: Mission San Miguel Arcángel
summary: In January 1831 its neophytes refused Echeandía's secularization outright; 'quieren seguir bajo el actual sistema'; and in 1831 asked to remain 'en estado de Comunidad.' Listed for outright sale in Pico's reglamento; the vault holds no sale record.
