sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Doc 3 (the neophytes' refusal, Jan 1831). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The 1846 Ríos & Reed purchase is the standard account; not found in the vault surveys.

name: Mission San Antonio de Padua
summary: Fr. Pedro Cabot delivered the mission to comisionado Manuel Crespo in November 1834; the 1836 inventory totaled $93,122 across eleven named ranchos, with $13,602 distributed to the Indians and a 'Pueblo de San Antonio' of 557 souls. Offered in 1845, it drew no bidders and was never sold.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 24: Mariano Soberanes to Jose Ramirez, secularization handover inventory of the pueblo of San Antonio, 10 October 1835 (total $7,883). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 448 (the 1834 entrega). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
summary: Inventoried in August 1835 (~$47,297; Savage himself noted the figures don't reconcile); 177 souls by 1837. Sold in June 1846 to Feliciano Soberanes, the same encargado instructed in 1840 that 'ningún indígena será forzado á servir á un particular.'
sources: Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission San Carlos Borromeo (Carmel)
summary: One of the two missions Echeandía's 1831 decree named to go first. By 1839 juez interino Marcelino Escobar held the buildings under a room-by-room inventory, with solares assigned; two to the neófitos Josecillo and Antonio. Its surplus buildings were saleable under the 1845 reglamento; no sale appears in the vault.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Juzgados (C-A 33) Doc 8 (the 1839 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Handed over in May 1835 with a $147,413 existencia including Rancho San Felipe, and a padrón of 63 emancipated Indians holding $5,120 in land. An 1849 retrospective recorded it 'declarada pueblo' a dozen years earlier, its mission houses destroyed for materials.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 14 (the 1835 handover). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission Santa Cruz
summary: Comisionado Ignacio del Valle inventoried ~$84,354 in December 1835. Listed for outright sale in Pico's reglamento; no sale appears in the vault; and in 1849 Hartnell judged that the priest 'has no right at all to sell any real estate or the mission Sta Cruz.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 53: comisionado Ignacio del Valle to Fr. Antonio del Real, inventory of the church and library of Mission Santa Cruz, 1 December 1835 (church $7,550; ornaments and furniture $23,383; library of 152 volumes). | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 452 (the 1835 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission Santa Clara de Asís
summary: Administered by the Estradas, then Ignacio Alviso, whose 1840 handover inventory counted 3,847 cattle (down from 5,500 the year before). Its mission houses were barred from sale in 1845; in 1849 the priests leased Santa Clara and San José together to James D. Steinberger for $22,000.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 99 (the 1840 handover). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission San José
summary: Still the great stock estate of the north after secularization; José de Jesús Vallejo's 1840 receipt counted 20,000 cattle and 15,000 sheep; while draining $16,809 to the government. Hartnell's 1840 visita found 589 souls who 'quieren otro administrador.'
sources: Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The reported 1845/46 sale is disputed between the standard accounts and not in the vault; left open.

name: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Dolores)
summary: Inventoried at $67,227 in July 1835 under comisionados Ignacio del Valle and José Joaquín Estudillo; by the 1841 padrón, 78 souls remained. One of the five listed for outright sale in 1845; no sale record survives in the vault.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 27 (the 1835 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.

name: Mission San Rafael Arcángel
summary: The poorest inventory of the set ($18,474, with Rancho Nicasio at $7,256), but the most direct distribution: 343 Indians received rams, ewes, horses, and mares by name. By Hartnell's 1840 visita they refused a mayordomo altogether; 'no querían ya misión.'
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51), Doc 117: inventory of the extinguished Mission San Rafael at handover, 1836, with a credits and debits ledger. | St. Pap., Missions (C-A 50) Doc 458 (the 1834 inventory). | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: The reported $8,000 sale of 1846 is the standard account; no vault record.

name: Mission San Francisco Solano (Sonoma)
summary: Secularized under M. G. Vallejo as comisionado (standard account); the vault's mission-property record names Vallejo, Salvador Vallejo, and mayordomo Antonio Ortega, and shows the mission's stock drawn down for the frontier colony and recruitment in 1835. Its final disposition does not appear in the vault surveys.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Doc 140. | Secularization year per the standard accounts (Krell; cross-checked against CA State Parks / NPS) · year grain.
notes: Excluded (with San Rafael) from the Diputación's c. 1828–30 pueblo plan as too new.

name: The Híjar-Padrés colony lands at San Diego
summary: The brigantine Natalia; the Compañía Cosmopolitana's own ship; reaches San Diego with Director General José María Híjar, Buenaventura Araujo, and 129 colonists, the vanguard of the ~204-person colonization scheme budgeted at 45,206 pesos under the 26 Nov 1833 law. The mission estates were to be its endowment.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Doc 243 (the arrival report, 4 Sep 1834). | St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Docs 51–53, 90–93 (appointment, roster, budget).

name: Figueroa keeps the missions: the contramando
summary: Santa Anna's countermand; carried north 'por extraordinario violento'; orders Figueroa not to hand Híjar the political command; the Diputación's acuerdo goes further: neither the command 'ni los bienes de las Misiones, que son propiedad de los indios.' The colony is stranded, and the principle that the estates belong to the Indians is stated at its plainest.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA: Official Corr. (C-A 37) Doc 73 (the countermand, leaf-verified). | C-A 37 Doc 78 (the Diputación acuerdo, 22 Oct 1834).

name: Araujo and the armed rising at San Gabriel
summary: In the colony crisis's ugliest episode, ~200 armed Indians briefly seize Fr. Estenaga at San Gabriel; colony officer Buenaventura Araujo is charged with instigating the rising. Ten northern missions are nonetheless ordered to provision the stranded colonists for a year.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 249, 253, 257–260 (the Araujo proceedings).

name: Híjar and Padrés deported on the Loriot
summary: After the Los Angeles plot to depose Figueroa and halt secularization, the colony's leadership is shipped to Mexico: the Loriot's six-article instructions name Híjar, Padrés, Francisco Torres, and Apalátegui among the deportees. Figueroa's manifesto had already given the government's verdict: 'el verdadero y único objeto de su plan es el robo de los bienes de las misiones.' Padrés protested his rights from on board.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 29) Doc 25 (the Loriot instructions). | Dep. St. Pap., Benicia (C-A 39) Docs 187–…, and C-A 29 Docs 11–30 (the crisis dossier).

name: Hartnell named Visitador General
summary: William Hartnell is named Visitador of the missions at $2,000 a year; the government's inspector over its own administrators; his salary apportioned mission by mission. His two circuits of 1839–40 produced the most unsparing record of the ex-mission estates that survives.
sources: Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 397 (the appointment). | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49) Doc 434 (the salary apportionment).
notes: He resigned 6 Oct 1840 and ceased functions 7 Nov 1840 (C-A 49 Doc 660; C-A 51 Doc 150).

name: The southern visita: 'los indios son acreedores'
summary: Hartnell's report on the missions from San Diego to San Fernando: the San Dieguito Indians 'son acreedores á la tierra que reclaman'; San Juan Capistrano's community memorial against administrator Argüello arrives 'firmado por José Fermín á nombre de la comunidad'; San Fernando counts 416 souls, its Rancho San Francisco 'taken from them and given to Antonio del Valle.'
sources: Gurcke and Farris (eds.), The Diary and Copybook of William E. P. Hartnell, Visitador General of the Missions of Alta California, 1839-1840 (CMSA / Arthur H. Clark, 2004). Page references for this entry are not yet recorded. | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49), Doc 470: the Visitador Hartnell sets out, 1839.

name: San Rafael: 'no querían ya misión'
summary: On the northern circuit Hartnell finds the San Rafael Indians refusing mayordomo Gregorio Briones and refusing the institution itself; 'no querían ya misión.' His 14 May report to Jimeno Casarín is the keystone document of Indian liberty in the northern ex-missions.
sources: Gurcke and Farris (eds.), The Diary and Copybook of William E. P. Hartnell, Visitador General of the Missions of Alta California, 1839-1840 (CMSA / Arthur H. Clark, 2004). Page references for this entry are not yet recorded.

name: Vallejo arrests the Visitador
summary: At Yerba Buena, M. G. Vallejo intercepts and arrests Hartnell rather than let the inspection reach his Sonoma frontier arrangements; the plainest demonstration of where power over the ex-mission estates actually lay.
sources: Gurcke and Farris (eds.), The Diary and Copybook of William E. P. Hartnell, Visitador General of the Missions of Alta California, 1839-1840 (CMSA / Arthur H. Clark, 2004). Page references for this entry are not yet recorded.

name: San José visita: 589 souls, 50 lashes
summary: Hartnell counts 589 souls at Mission San José, records punishments running to 50 lashes; double his own 25-lash cap; and the Indians' verdict: 'quieren otro administrador.'
sources: Gurcke and Farris (eds.), The Diary and Copybook of William E. P. Hartnell, Visitador General of the Missions of Alta California, 1839-1840 (CMSA / Arthur H. Clark, 2004). Page references for this entry are not yet recorded.

name: San Diego district: Pico, Temecula, and inventory fraud
summary: The southern return visit: Pico has told the Indians the governor gave him Temecula; Las Flores brings its complaints; and comisionado Carlos Castro's inventory fraud is recorded; the Visitador's file on how the estates were actually being run.
sources: Gurcke and Farris (eds.), The Diary and Copybook of William E. P. Hartnell, Visitador General of the Missions of Alta California, 1839-1840 (CMSA / Arthur H. Clark, 2004). Page references for this entry are not yet recorded. | Dep. Rec. (C-A 49), Doc 623: on the office and salary of Hartnell as Visitador de Misiones, 1840.

name: San Miguel refuses secularization
summary: Read Echeandía's bando, the San Miguel neophytes answer that 'quieren seguir bajo el actual sistema'; while San Luis Obispo's elect four Indian comisarios de policía under it. The record of divided Indian judgments on emancipation, at the very start.
sources: Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 3–5 (the promulgation record).
notes: Later (1831) they ask to remain 'en estado de Comunidad.'

name: The southern missions demand the promised land
summary: Neophytes of San Diego, San Juan Capistrano, San Gabriel, and San Luis Rey mobilize to demand the land distribution Echeandía had promised; proclaiming the reformer governor against his replacement. Secularization's first mass Indian politics.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., LA (C-A 34) Doc 330. | Dep. St. Pap. (C-A 28) Docs 115–116.

name: San Luis Rey refuses to work
summary: Portilla's reports from San Luis Rey: the Luiseños refuse absolutely to return to mission labor; reportedly in the words 'somos libres, no queremos volver, no queremos trabajar', a sentence not yet traced to a document. The plainest statement of what emancipation meant to the emancipated.
sources: Reports of Capt. Pablo de la Portilla from San Luis Rey, December 1834 to March 1835. The exact document has not been identified in the Archives of California catalogue, and the Spanish sentence quoted in this entry has not been located in any source consulted; it should be treated as unverified until the manuscript is found.

name: 'Que no nos pelen las nalgas á azotes'
summary: The San Juan Capistrano neophytes; fewer than 60 still working, the rest fleeing; petition Alvarado against their administrator in their own unsparing words: that they not be flogged raw. Received weeks into Hartnell's visitaduría, it is the Indian-voice document of the administrator era.
sources: St. Pap., Missions (C-A 51) Doc 47 (the petition).

name: The Las Flores bargain
summary: Figueroa's oficio records the pueblo de Las Flores; the neophyte pueblo created from San Luis Rey's asistencia; accepting liberty in exchange for subsisting on its own labor. One of the few documented free-Indian pueblos of the secularization.
sources: Unbound Docs. (C-A 63) Doc 15 (transcribing the 29 May 1835 oficio).

name: Temecula and Pala stand armed against the Picos
summary: When the Picos moved on Temecula; Pico telling the Indians the governor had given it to him; the juzgado record shows the rancherías in arms: 'toda la gente está armada.' The Luiseño ranchos defended the land through the juzgado and, when needed, with weapons in hand.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Benicia Mil. (C-A 20) Doc 226 (the Temecula land conspiracy record: the land 'propiedad de todos').

name: José Cupertino petitions for absolute emancipation
summary: A sixty-year-old Santa Clara man, in service since childhood, petitions for his absolute emancipation; the individual face of the paper freedom the decade had constructed.
sources: Dep. St. Pap., Prefecturas y Juzgados (C-A 42) Doc 687.

name: 'Como á hija de la Misión': Feliciana Valdés claims land
summary: An Indian woman petitions for her share of the secularized lands 'como á hija de la Misión'; a daughter's claim on the estate. Hartnell denied it; the file preserves a woman's legal argument for what secularization had promised.
sources: St. Pap., Missions & Colonization (C-A 53) Docs 168–172.

name: Cabrillo passes this coast northbound
summary: The first European ships along this shore, standing well out; no landing on this stretch. Ferrelo repassed in 1543. Course generalized (interpretive).
sources: After the exhibit panel; Cabrillo relation (Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast).

name: The Manila ships' landfall run
summary: Returning galleons made their American landfall to the north and ran south along this coast for Acapulco, year after year from 1565 until 1815. Only the first two centuries of that run fall inside the period this map covers, and no galleon ever entered the bay: the line is the traffic that passed the Gate without finding it. Course generalized and interpretive.
sources: After the exhibit panel; Schurz, The Manila Galleon.

name: Drake careens in 'a faire and good bay'
summary: Five weeks ashore among the Coast Miwok. The quoted phrase is from the narrative Hakluyt printed, which has the ship driven back south from forty-three degrees until 'it pleased God to send us into a faire and good bay, with a good winde to enter the same', and anchoring there on 17 June; its own heading says Drake landed where he found 'a faire and goodly haven'. The World Encompassed, the 1628 account usually cited for the landfall, words it differently: the ship 'fell with a conuenient and fit harborough' in 38 degrees 30 minutes and lay there until 23 July. The landing site is a long-running argument; Drakes Bay is the prevailing identification and the one the exhibit panel follows.
sources: Hakluyt's narrative of the voyage, printed in W. S. W. Vaux (ed.), The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (London: Hakluyt Society, 1854), Appendix V no. I. | The World Encompassed (1628), as printed in W. S. W. Vaux (ed.), The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (London: Hakluyt Society, 1854). | After the Mission Dolores exhibit panel; cf. the landing-site controversy literature.
notes: Site identification debated; shown at Drakes Bay per the panel.

name: The San Agustin wrecks under Cermeno
summary: The Manila ship sent to survey the coast anchored in the bay behind Point Reyes and was driven ashore; the crew ran south in an open launch, surveying as they went. Her porcelain cargo still washes into Coast Miwok sites.
sources: Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast of America in the Sixteenth Century (San Francisco: California Historical Society, 1929), chap. IX, 'The Voyage of Cermeno'; after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel.

name: The San Carlos enters the bay
date_display: 5 August 1775 (entry); the ship moved to Angel Island later that month
summary: Ayala brought the first ship through the Gate, at night, with the launch sent in ahead of the packet. The San Carlos anchored inside on arrival and only afterwards moved to the island Ayala named for Our Lady of the Angels, where she lay for the rest of a stay of forty-four days while Jose de Canizares surveyed the bay by longboat and Juan Bautista de Aguirre took the southern arm. The land expedition Ayala was waiting for never appeared. The entry is dated 5 August 1775 from the ship's own diaries, published by Galvin in 1971; Bancroft, who had only Palou and no diary or map of the survey, put the entry on the night of 1 August and the move to Angel Island on the 2nd, taking the island's name from that day.
sources: Galvin (ed.), The First Spanish Entry into San Francisco Bay, 1775 (San Francisco: John Howell Books, 1971); after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel. | Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 188-89, for the divergent chronology.

name: The bay discovered from Sweeney Ridge
summary: The first European sight of San Francisco Bay, and not by the party sent to look for it. On 1 November 1769 Sergeant Ortega went north with a small party and three days' provisions to settle whether Monterey had been passed; while he was away, on 2 November, soldiers from the camp went up these hills after deer and came back with word of a great inland sea reaching north and south-east as far as they could see. Bancroft: the names of the deer hunters can never be known. Ortega returned on the 3rd, unable to cross the inlet, but carrying what he had understood from the people of the peninsula: that at the head of the arm of the sea lay a harbour with a vessel at anchor in it. It was that report, and the hope that the vessel was the San Jose with their supplies, that moved the camp. On 4 November the whole company broke camp, crossed the hills north-eastward and looked down from the summit on the inland sea.
sources: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 159-60, following Crespi's and Costanso's diaries. | Crespi's diary, ed. Brown, A Description of Distant Roads; after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel.

name: The turning-point camp on San Francisquito Creek
summary: The expedition's council on 11 November 1769 under the tall redwood, the palo alto: short of food, with the port still not identified, they turned back south for San Diego.
sources: After the exhibit panel; Crespi diary, ed. Brown.

name: Monterey recognized and occupied
summary: Monterey was identified at last and the presidio and mission of San Carlos founded here on 3 June 1770. No probe north followed under Portola: as soon as a beginning had been made he handed the government of the new establishments to Pedro Fages as military commandant and sailed for San Blas in the San Antonio on 9 July 1770, taking the engineer Costanso with him. The order to explore the port of San Francisco was written in Mexico on 12 November 1770 and reached Fages at Monterey in May 1771; he could not act on it until the spring rains of 1772 had passed.
sources: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 174, 183-84. | Viceroy Croix's measures to establish the Presidio of Monterey and the missions: C-A 1 Doc 23.

name: The Strait of Carquines
summary: Fages left Monterey on 20 March 1772 with Crespi, twelve soldiers, a muleteer and an Indian, under the viceroy's order to find the port of San Francisco. Marching up the eastern bayshore he was stopped here: trying to get round the round bay, which Crespi thought large enough for all the armadas of Spain, the party found the narrows barring the way. They followed the treeless hills along the strait, were received at five large villages whose people came across from the far shore on rafts, and camped on a stream near the shore, probably the Arroyo del Hambre near Martinez.
sources: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 184-86. | Crespi, Diario que se formo en el registro que se hizo del puerto de Nuestro Serafico Padre San Francisco, printed in Palou, Noticias, i. 481-501; trans. in Crespi's diary, ed. Brown, A Description of Distant Roads.

name: The river mouths from the Willow Pass hills
summary: On 30 March the party left the strait, advanced two leagues to the Arroyo de las Nueces near Pacheco, crossed Mount Diablo Creek and climbed a range of low hills near Willow Pass. From the summit they looked down on the two broad rivers and their channels, sloughs and islands, which Crespi described closely, then crossed four or five leagues of plain to camp half a mile from the bank of the great river, which they named the Rio de San Francisco: the San Joaquin, at or near Antioch. It is the farthest inland any Spanish party had yet seen, and the first European sight of the delta.
sources: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 186. | Crespi's diary of the 1772 registro, in Palou, Noticias, i. 481-501, trans. ed. Brown.

name: The cross above the Seal Rocks
summary: From the camp on Lake Merced, Rivera took four soldiers and Palou north-west over the dunes to the beach and followed it until a steep hill stopped them, in sight of the pointed rocks offshore. They climbed it, set up a cross on the summit and were back in camp within four hours. This is the marker Ayala's men had missed the summer before and that later parties found still standing. Rivera had set a first cross a week earlier, on 28 November, on San Francisquito Creek, as a sign that San Francisco was to be founded there; Palou came home from the trip with six sites he thought fit for missions, at Hollister, San Francisquito Creek, two vales between Spanish Town and Pescadero, Santa Cruz on the San Lorenzo, and Watsonville on the Pajaro.
sources: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 233-34. | Palou's diary of the 1774 registro, Noticias, ii. 43-92, trans. Bolton, Historical Memoirs of New California.

name: Into the shore trail of 1769
summary: Exploration of the Rio de San Francisco was put off until after the rains and the party turned for home by the shore route of 1769. Three hours south of Lake Merced on 5 December they struck the old trail, crossed the San Lorenzo and the Pajaro on the 11th and reached the presidio of Monterey on 13 December 1774. This coastal line is the leg they travelled last, not the way they came.
sources: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 234. | Palou's diary of the 1774 registro, Noticias, ii. 43-92.

name: Anza's first overland party reaches Monterey
summary: The Sonora road proved: Alta California can be reached, and colonized, overland.
sources: After the exhibit panel; Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions.

name: The presidio site chosen at the Gate
summary: A table-land commanding the narrows, picked for the presidio on 28 March 1776. Font had written the day before, looking at the port from this side of the water, that it was the harbour of harbours. The white cliff above the Gate became the presidio of San Francisco that autumn.
sources: Font's complete diary, entries of 27 and 28 March 1776, in Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions IV; after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel.

name: The arroyo de los Dolores chosen for the mission
summary: The sheltered creek and lagoon two leagues in from the Gate, named for the Friday of Sorrows: the site of Mission San Francisco de Asis, where these exhibit panels hang today.
sources: After the exhibit panel; Font's complete diary (Bolton IV).

name: To the mouths of the rivers
summary: Anza and Font round the southern bay, run the eastern shore past the strait, and look into the delta before turning for home: the whole future mission-and-presidio geography seen in one circuit.
sources: After the exhibit panel; Font's complete diary (Bolton IV).

name: Mission Santa Ynez
summary: Founded 1804. Zalvidea reached it on the evening of 19 July 1806 and left it on the 20th.

name: Mission San Gabriel
summary: Founded 1771. Zalvidea arrival.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Founded 1797. Moraga departure point.

name: Mission San Fernando
summary: Founded 1797. Moraga arrival.

name: Jonatas
summary: Cook places Jonatas at Las Olivas, the present Los Olivos. Zalvidea found only the remains of the village, three leagues north of Santa Ynez, 20 July 1806.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 1.

name: Saca
summary: On Alamo Pintado Creek. Its people were Christians of Santa Ynez.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 1.

name: Olomosong
summary: Probably on the Sisquoc River near the 120th meridian. Three houses, two old women and four young women with the chief.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 1.

name: Gecp
summary: Apparently on the south slope of the Sierra Madre. Five houses, four men and seven women.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 1.

name: Talihuilimit
summary: Two leagues east of Gecp, on the plains Cook takes for the Cuyama Valley. Perhaps twenty-five people.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 1.

name: Lisahua
summary: Probably in lower Salisbury Canyon, T 9 N, R 26 W. Twenty-eight people.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 2.

name: Cuia
summary: Possibly in lower Santa Barbara Canyon, T 9 N, R 25 W. Nine houses, fourteen men, nineteen women and eight children.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 2.

name: Siguecin
summary: Four leagues south of Cuia by the diary; Cook puts it twelve to fifteen miles up the canyon to the south. Ten men, nineteen women and a few children. The pin follows that bearing and distance and is a guess.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 2.

name: Sgene
summary: In the lower Cuyama Valley, T 10 N, R 25 W. Seven men, sixteen women and three children.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 3.

name: Malapoa (Hoschiu)
summary: Placed by Gifford and Schenck on Bitterwater Creek and identified by them with Hoschiu, of the Yokuts tribe Tulamni. Twenty-nine men, twenty-two women and eight children. The diary puts Malapoa seven leagues east of Sgene, which does not agree with that placement.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 4.

name: Buenavista (Tilamniu)
summary: Identified by Gifford and Schenck with Tilamniu, which Kroeber puts on the western or north-western end of Buena Vista Lake. The Indians gave its numbers as thirty-six men, 144 women and thirty-eight children.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 5.

name: Sisupistu (Pohalin Tinliu)
summary: Considered to be Pohalin Tinliu, at the south-east corner of Kern Lake. Zalvidea counted twenty-eight houses and saw fifty to sixty men; most of the people were away harvesting.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 5.

name: Tupai
summary: The name of Zalvidea's camp. Placed doubtfully by Gifford and Schenck at Tejon Ranch on El Paso Creek.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 6.

name: Tacui (Tecuya)
summary: Undoubtedly Tecuya, on Tecuya Creek. Twenty-three souls.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 7.

name: Yaguelame (Woilo)
summary: The village of the rivers, nine leagues north of Tecuya on the Kern River. Gifford and Schenck proposed either Loasau or Woilo; Cook prefers Woilo, because Loasau was on Kern Lake rather than the river and Woilo is very close to nine leagues from Tecuya. Zalvidea counted ninety-two men aged seven to forty and reckoned the village at 300 souls.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 8.

name: Taslupi
summary: Placed by Gifford and Schenck on Tejon Creek, which fits the distances; Cook thinks Pastoria on Grapevine Creek more likely. Five houses, standing empty in August 1806.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 10.

name: Casteque (Castaic)
summary: At the head of Grapevine Creek. Empty when Zalvidea reached it on 7 August 1806: the people were away at their fields of Guata.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 10.

name: Atongai
summary: A Serrano village of thirty-two men, thirty-six women and fifteen children, with a swamp a league and a half off. Cook does not locate it; the pin follows the diary's four leagues west of Guapiabit and is a guess.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 12.

name: Guapiabit
summary: Nineteen men, sixteen women and eleven children; the expedition rested here on 12 August 1806 and this was its easternmost point. The pin follows the diary's four leagues east of Moscopiabit and is a guess.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 12.

name: Moscopiabit (Muscupian)
summary: Fifteen to eighteen adults and a few children. Cutter identifies the Muscupian of a later expedition with Zalvidea's Moscopiabit, in the vicinity of Cajon Pass; this is the only published fix among the eastern villages.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925). | Cutter's identification of Moscopiabit is reported at Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. IV n. 3.

name: Guapiana
summary: The last village of the journey, by a watering place, where children from San Gabriel were found. Cook does not locate it; the pin follows the diary's leagues and is a guess.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 12.

name: Nupchenche
summary: About 250 souls under a chief called Choley, on the far bank of the San Joaquin among willows. Cook places it on the east bank in T 11 S, R 14 E, far more than the three leagues from camp the diary gives, and counts it among the lower San Joaquin villages effaced so thoroughly that modern informants gave ethnographers no indication they had ever existed. The pin follows the diary's three leagues and is a guess.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 17.

name: Taulamne (Tahualamne)
summary: A village on cliffs the party could not climb, whose people lived in caves. Schenck places Taulamne on an inaccessible rock on the Stanislaus in the foothills, and distinguishes it from Taualames at the ford of the San Joaquin below the mouth of the Tuolumne; Kroeber lists a Lakisamni rancheria at Dent's or Knights Ferry. Cook leaves the people either Miwok or Yokuts, the language boundary running near by, and notes that the villages higher up the river must have been Central Miwok. Tahualamne is the form in the diary's own village list.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 24.

name: Chineguis
summary: The Merced village where an old woman was baptized on 29 September 1806. Near by were Yunate, Chamuasi, Latelate and Lachuo. Cook counts a minimum of six villages in this stretch of the river, averaging about 225 souls.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 19.

name: Pizcache (Pitkachi)
summary: About 200 souls under a chief named Sujoyucomu. The diary places the village farther in the interior of the mountains, on the bank of the San Joaquin; Kroeber has the Pitkachi on the south side of the river at Kohuou near Herndon or Sycamore, at Weshiu on a slough, and at Gewachiu farther downstream, and Cook infers from Gayton that the group moved downstream between 1806 and 1850. The pin follows the diary.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 28.

name: Telame (Telamni)
summary: The large village of the Kaweah delta, about 600 souls, where twenty-two people were baptized in October 1806. These are the Telamni of the ethnographers, repeatedly mentioned by the early explorers. Munoz put the population of the lower Kaweah at 3,000; Cook holds the true figure was probably much higher.
sources: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 33.

name: Santa Barbara
summary: Setting out. The expedition left Santa Barbara on the morning of 19 July 1806 to carry out the Governor's orders, contained in his official letter of the 10th of that month, and reached Mission Santa Ynez the same afternoon. The diary says only Santa Barbara, without distinguishing the presidio from the mission.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Mission Santa Ynez
summary: Departure north. The party left Santa Ynez after Mass on 20 July 1806 and travelled north.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Jonatas (Las Olivas)
summary: The remains of the village of Jonatas, three leagues north of the mission. Cook places it at Las Olivas, the present Los Olivos. His identifications here compress the diary's three-league intervals.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Saca (Alamo Pintado Creek)
summary: Saca, three leagues beyond Jonatas, whose people were Christians of Santa Ynez. Cook places it on Alamo Pintado Creek.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Olomosong (Sisquoc River)
summary: Olomosong, five leagues on, a village of three houses holding two old women and four young women with the chief. Zalvidea baptized the two old women, of eighty and seventy years. Cook: probably on the Sisquoc River near the 120th meridian.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Gecp (south slope, Sierra Madre)
summary: Gecp, four leagues north: five houses, four men and seven women, two old women baptized. The road ran through broken mountains and the party slept in a valley with a small stream. Cook puts it apparently on the south slope of the Sierra Madre, because the next day they climbed a mountain and came out onto plains, which he takes for the Cuyama Valley at about T 10 N, R 28 W.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Talihuilimit
summary: Talihuilimit, two leagues east across the plains, perhaps twenty-five people. Three old women baptized, one with a paralysed leg, one bitten in the hip by a bear, one reckoned over a hundred years old; two had Christian sons at Santa Ynez and La Purisima.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

name: Lisahua (Salisbury Canyon)
summary: Lisahua, six leagues east: twenty-eight people, five baptized. A stream like the one at Mission San Fernando ran near by; the land was arid and saline, without grass or timber. Cook: probably in lower Salisbury Canyon, T 9 N, R 26 W.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 2.

name: Cuia (lower Santa Barbara Canyon)
summary: Cuia, four leagues east: nine houses, fourteen men, nineteen women, eight children, seven baptized. Three small springs near by. Four leagues south lay Siguecin, with ten men, nineteen women and a few children, where two more were baptized; Cook puts Siguecin twelve to fifteen miles up the canyon to the south. The party returned to sleep at Lisahua. Cook: Cuia may have been in lower Santa Barbara Canyon, T 9 N, R 25 W.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 2.

name: Sgene (lower Cuyama Valley)
summary: Sgene, reached after a salt marsh, a cross made of logs and a wild horse: seven men, sixteen women, three children, four baptized. Cook: the party evidently bore more to the north, somewhere in the lower Cuyama Valley, T 10 N, R 25 W.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 3.

name: Malapoa (Bitterwater Creek)
summary: Malapoa, which the diary puts seven leagues east of Sgene: twenty-nine men, twenty-two women, eight children, one old woman baptized. Gifford and Schenck place it on Bitterwater Creek and identify it with Hoschiu, of the Yokuts tribe Tulamni; that placement lies north-west of Sgene rather than seven leagues east of it, and the pin follows Gifford and Schenck. Cook adds that all the preceding villages were Tokya Chumash. That afternoon Zalvidea rode with the Lieutenant to a small settlement of the village of Napolea, which Cook (as Nopalea) places on either Bitterwater or Santiago Creek, and baptized six more.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 4.

name: Buenavista (Tilamniu)
summary: Buenavista, eight leagues north, on the shore of a lake the diary calls eight leagues long and five wide, with rafts on the water and a river that divided into three branches and rejoined to form it. The Indians gave its numbers as thirty-six men, 144 women and thirty-eight children; one old woman of ninety was baptized. The party slept two leagues off. Gifford and Schenck identify the village with Tilamniu, which Kroeber puts on the western or north-western end of the lake.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 5.

name: Sisupistu (Pohalin Tinliu)
summary: Sisupistu, at the end of the lake, reached at dark on 26 July after a day east along the shore and then north. The arrival nearly caused a fight: the villagers fled into a tule swamp and their warriors threw a spear at the chief of the Buenavista party, who were their enemies. Zalvidea talked the two chiefs into peace, collected the Buenavista bows and arrows for the night and returned them in the morning. He counted twenty-eight houses and saw fifty to sixty men. Cook identifies the village with Pohalin Tinliu at the south-east corner of Kern Lake, and the big river as the Kern.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 5.

name: Camp at Tupai (Tejon or El Paso Creek)
summary: The camp, pitched on 27 July at the edge of the foothills with the intention of staying several days to explore, and held for a week. On the way in, an old woman was found dying alone in a hut; Zalvidea baptized her and she died two hours later. The diary gives the place name as Tupai. The reconnaissance of 28 July worked the lower courses of El Paso, Tejon and Pastoria creeks, five streams in all, and Zalvidea judged the surrounding plains, which he thought larger than those of Mission Santa Clara, able to carry twelve thousand head of cattle. Cook: six leagues from Sisupistu would have brought the party to the mouth of either Tejon or El Paso Creek, and Gifford and Schenck place Tupai doubtfully at Tejon Ranch on El Paso Creek.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 6.

name: Tacui (Tecuya Creek)
summary: Tacui, twenty-three souls, two old men baptized, reached on a day ride with the Sergeant, Corporal and seven soldiers past the stream running out of Grapevine Canyon. Cook: the party apparently doubled back west past Grapevine Creek to Tacui, which was undoubtedly Tecuya on Tecuya Creek.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 7.

name: Yaguelame (Woilo), the village of the rivers
summary: The village of the rivers, Yaguelame, reached on 1 August after two days north. Zalvidea counted ninety-two men between seven and forty years old and reckoned the village at 300 souls; he measured the two river branches at sixteen yards by one and seven yards by a third of a yard, and was told of thirteen villages of the Bald Indians two days to the north, all offering themselves for baptism if missions were founded. Some chiefs asked him, in his report, why the missions were not established without delay. Cook puts Yaguelame nine leagues north of Tecuya on the Kern River; Gifford and Schenck proposed either Loasau or Woilo, and Cook prefers Woilo, since Loasau was on Kern Lake rather than the river and Woilo is very close to nine leagues from Tecuya.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 8.

name: Eastern end of Kern Lake
summary: The end of the lake, passed on the afternoon of 3 August on the way south; the party stopped a league beyond. Cook places it at the eastern end of Kern Lake, T 32 S, R 28 E.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 9.

name: Taslupi (Pastoria or Tejon Creek)
summary: Taslupi, a village of five houses standing empty, at the entrance of a canyon where the Indians had killed two soldiers some years before. Gifford and Schenck place Taslupi on Tejon Creek, which fits the distances; Cook thinks Pastoria on Grapevine Creek more likely, since the party reached Castaic at the head of Grapevine Creek on 7 August.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 10.

name: Casteque (Castaic), head of Grapevine Creek
summary: Casteque, visited on 7 August with the Sergeant and seven soldiers. No one was there: the people were all away at their fields of Guata. Cook names the place Castaic, at the head of Grapevine Creek.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 10.

name: Antelope Valley
summary: The wide valley entered on 8 August, which Cook identifies as Antelope Valley. The diary calls it sixteen leagues long with no watering place in the whole expanse; the party crossed it eastward on 9 August, camped by a gully with plenty of water, and spent 10 August in the hills adjacent to the mountains, passing the remains of a village and a few wells.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 11.

name: Atongai
summary: Atongai, reached after seven leagues east on 11 August: thirty-two men, thirty-six women, fifteen children, with a swamp a league and a half off, pine forests in sight and land that would yield grain if watered. Zalvidea baptized two old men and three old women here. Cook does not locate the villages of this eastern leg, noting only that the party saw several Serrano villages well beyond the limits of the San Joaquin Valley; the pin is placed four leagues west of Guapiabit, as the diary gives the interval, and is a guess.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

name: Guapiabit
summary: Guapiabit, four leagues on, where the expedition rested through 12 August: nineteen men, sixteen women, eleven children, with a pine-covered hill two leagues off, a well and ground moist enough for crops. Three old women and two old men were baptized. This was the easternmost point of the journey. The pin is placed four leagues east of Moscopiabit and is a guess; only Moscopiabit in this group carries a published identification.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

name: Moscopiabit (vicinity of Cajon Pass)
summary: Moscopiabit, four leagues west of Guapiabit, where fifteen to eighteen adults and a few children were seen and two old women baptized. Cutter identifies the Muscupian of a later expedition with Zalvidea's Moscopiabit, in the vicinity of Cajon Pass, which is the only published fix on this leg of the route.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III. | Cutter's identification of Moscopiabit is reported at Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. IV n. 3.

name: Camp on a stream running to the Santa Ana
summary: Four leagues west of Moscopiabit the party found a village of five houses standing empty, and two leagues beyond it a big stream which, Zalvidea was told, runs into the Santa Ana River. They camped a short distance from it. The pin follows those leagues west from Cajon Pass and is a guess.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

name: Guapiana
summary: Guapiana, the last village of the journey, by a watering place six leagues on. Children from San Gabriel were there; Zalvidea baptized an old woman and named her Gabriela. Earlier that morning he had baptized a very old man found on the trail who could not name his village. The pin follows the diary's leagues west and is a guess.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

name: Mission San Gabriel
summary: Arrival. The party entered San Gabriel on the night of 14 August 1806, and Zalvidea signed the report there. Cook: the party crossed the mountains and went south-west to the mission, having seen several Serrano villages in country well beyond the limits of the San Joaquin Valley.
sources: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

name: Mission San Juan Bautista
summary: Departure. On the morning of the first day the troops were given a formal address on the purpose of the expedition, and the party left the mission at about two o'clock in the afternoon. Fr. Pedro Munoz went as chaplain and kept the diary; Gabriel Moraga, second lieutenant of the San Francisco company, commanded, under orders from Governor Jose Joaquin de Arrillaga.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

name: Huzaymas, camp on the San Benito River
summary: A league and a half east across a well forage plain to a creek the diary calls that of the Huzaymas, well grown with alders and oaks, dry in summer. Cook: the camp was on the San Benito River, a league and a half from San Juan Bautista, not on Pacheco Creek as Cutter had it.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 13.

name: San Luis Ranch, Pacheco Pass
summary: The second day's camp, made in the discomfort of three showers. Cook: approximately at San Luis Ranch, where Highway 152 crosses San Luis Creek.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 14.

name: Santa Rita camp
summary: The camp at Santa Rita, with black willow along the stream. Cook puts it fifteen to twenty miles east of San Luis Gonzaga and five or six miles west of the main San Joaquin, on Salt Slough or Paso Slough a few miles north-east of Los Banos, and warns that the sloughs and the channels of the San Joaquin are hard to place on a modern map because of a century of drainage and reclamation. On the fourth day a party rode south to a village reported to hold 400 people and found it empty.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 15.

name: Camp on the San Joaquin
summary: The camp moved to the San Joaquin, about two leagues from Santa Rita. Beaver and salmon abounded, by the account of the local Indians. That afternoon forty-two warriors came in, friendly, brought a little fish, were shown an image of Our Lady of Sorrows and stayed the night in camp. Cook: the camp may be assumed to lie in T 8 S, R 11 E.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 16.

name: Nupchenche
summary: Nupchenche, about three leagues off on the far side of the river, hidden among willows: about 250 souls under a chief called Choley. An old woman came out and sprinkled the party with seeds; the chiefs spread mats and deerskins and set out food, including two white loaves of a seed resembling rice. Munoz baptized twenty-three old women and three old men, and told the rest they must wait for a mission. Cook places the village on the east bank of the river in T 11 S, R 14 E, which is far more than three leagues from where he puts the camp; the pin follows the diary's three leagues. Cook adds that this was one of several villages on the lower San Joaquin effaced so thoroughly that modern informants gave ethnographers no indication they had ever existed.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 17.

name: Bear Creek
summary: North across the river and a league of high thick tules to a stream running east to west, with no running water, only pools, about sixty oaks and a few willows. Cutter reads this as Bear Creek rather than Mariposa Creek, since it is about three leagues south of the Merced, and Cook sees no reason to disagree.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 18.

name: Merced River, west of Livingston
summary: The Merced, reached east-north-east after about three leagues. Cook puts the northbound party on the river somewhere west of Livingston in T 6 S, R 11 E, and the other party east of Cressey. The village where the old woman was baptized was Chineguis; near by were Yunate, Chamuasi, Latelate and Lachuo. Cook counts a minimum of six villages in the stretch, averaging about 225 souls, and reckons the population between the San Joaquin and the foothills at fully two thousand.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 19.

name: Tuolumne River (the Dolores)
summary: Seven or eight leagues north-west to a big river, which the party named Our Lady of Sorrows for the day in September on which it had been sighted. Its banks were close together, the pasturage short and the soil saline. No Indians were found, but the signs of several villages and wide, heavily used trails were: word had evidently gone ahead from the Merced. Cook: the Tuolumne, according to the direction, near Modesto.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 20.

name: Dry creek bed
summary: About a league on in the same north-westerly direction, a creek bed full of sand with no water, which the diary judged could be a large river in the rains or the snowmelt. No oaks along its banks and few willows. Cook: undoubtedly Dry Creek, and the description is valid even today. Dry Creek runs north-east of the Tuolumne crossing rather than on the north-westerly line the diary gives, so the pin follows the line of march and the league stated, not the creek's course.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 21.

name: Stanislaus River (the Guadalupe)
summary: Two leagues further the party entered an oak forest about four leagues wide and of undetermined length, and a league and a half into it came on a river narrower than the others, its banks covered with wild grapevines, torote and ash. They named it Our Lady of Guadalupe and pitched a base camp. Cook: the Stanislaus; a party continuing north-west from near Modesto would have reached the river at or east of Ripon, where remnants of the valley oak forest can still be seen, perhaps a mile each side of the river and running unbroken from the San Joaquin junction east beyond Oakdale.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 22.

name: Taulamne, below Knights Ferry
summary: Six leagues east along the river to Taulamne, a village on steep cliffs the party could not climb; the people lived in caves and came down a pole held by one of them. Twelve or fifteen descended to a shelf in the rocks, carrying weapons, and accepted presents and pinole. Their reason for staying up was that soldiers killed and captured people. Cook: six leagues upstream of Ripon or Riverbank barely reaches the limestone bluffs just below Knights Ferry, which are unquestionably precipitous, and no place lower on the river could give the account's physical characteristics; the best guess is the vicinity of Knights Ferry.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 23.

name: Calaveras River (the San Francisco)
summary: About six leagues north-west to the bed of a big stream, dry, heavily overgrown with ash and wild vines, named the San Francisco for the saint's day on which it was found. Cutter identifies it with the Calaveras, and Cook sees little reason to disagree.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 25.

name: Cosumnes River (the Pasion)
summary: Nine leagues further in the same direction, a river of great volume which the party was told had already been found by an expedition looking for a land route to Bodega, and which carried that expedition's name, La Pasion. The people were affectionate and asked for a mission, but their language was wholly different and no interpreter could be had, so none were baptized. The party turned back the same day to the camp on the Stanislaus. Cutter identifies the river with the Cosumnes, and Cook notes that the distances fit and that the Miwok and Maidu language boundary runs along it. But Cook also objects that the diarist never mentions the Mokelumne, an all-year stream, and that a round trip of thirty leagues, about seventy-five miles, is incredible even for horsemen travelling without baggage; his alternative is that the two distances were both measured from the Stanislaus, which would end the day at the Mokelumne.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 25.

name: Base camp on the Stanislaus, the turn south
summary: The party returned to the Guadalupe camp on the evening of its farthest day north and from here worked south, keeping close to the eastern edge of the valley along the Sierra foothills. Whether the far point of 4 October was the Cosumnes or the Mokelumne is unsettled; see the northbound route. On the fifteenth day, still at this camp, about forty armed Indians appeared, firing arrows into the air, with three coming forward as ambassadors carrying a flag made of a black ribbon of feathers with a red stripe down the middle.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

name: Back across the Stanislaus and Tuolumne
summary: On the sixteenth day camp was lifted from the Guadalupe and the party travelled to the Dolores; on the seventeenth it crossed from the Dolores to the Merced, both rivers it had named on the way north.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

name: Mariposa Creek and the Chowchilla
summary: Cutter identifies the diary's Santo Domingo with Mariposa Creek and its Tecolote, named for the owls that abounded there, with the Chowchilla.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 26.

name: Fresno River (the Santa Ana)
summary: Cook: the Santa Ana was the Fresno River. From the Merced to the San Joaquin the party stayed close to the eastern edge of the valley, where the streams are seasonal and permanent settlements were distinctly absent.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 27.

name: Camp on the San Joaquin
summary: The base camp on the San Joaquin, held from the twenty-second day to the twenty-fourth. Cook writes that Moraga probably halted approximately north of Fresno, below Le Grand; those two landmarks are some forty kilometres apart and do not agree, and the pin follows north of Fresno, which is the reading the southward march from the Fresno River supports.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 27.

name: Pizcache (Pitkachi)
summary: Pizcache, about 200 souls under a chief named Sujoyucomu, sighted by the party that scouted up the river on the twenty-third day; two old men and two old women were baptized. From this chief came the expedition's strangest testimony: that soldiers had come from the far side of the mountains about twenty years before, fought the Indians and killed many, that the sea lay ten days to the north beyond the range, and that to the south there was no sea but low hills. The chief said he had been present at the fight and had seen the ocean himself, and Munoz concluded that New Mexico lay very close to the other side of the Sierra. The diary places the village farther in the interior of the mountains, on the bank of the river. Cook's note on the name is a discrepancy: Kroeber has the Pitkachi holding the south side of the San Joaquin, 'living at Kohuou, near Herndon or Sycamore; at Weshiu, on a slough; and at Gewachiu, still farther downstream', and Gayton has Derby reaching Pitkachi country at the bend of the river in 1850, so Cook infers that the group moved downstream between 1806 and 1850. The pin follows the diary's foothills, not the ethnographers' valley floor.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 28.

name: Kings River, near Sanger
summary: Cook: the Kings River was reached near Sanger or Centerville. The village list at the end of the report names Aycayche and four others for the Kings River basin, while the text names Ayquiche and nine more, six upstream and three down, so the list does not include all the villages actually seen.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 30.

name: Kaweah delta and Telame
