summary: On the twenty-eighth day scouts reached the great oak forest along the Kaweah delta at or above Visalia, and the main party moved up on the twenty-ninth. The entry for the twenty-seventh day is missing from the report. The village of about 600 souls at which twenty-two people were baptized was Telame, the Telamni of the ethnographers, repeatedly mentioned by the early explorers. The water was very low, which Cook calls somewhat unusual for the region even in October. Munoz put the population of the lower Kaweah at 3,000; Cook holds that it probably reached a much higher figure.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 33.

name: Tule River, near Porterville
summary: After a winding course of two days the party camped on the Tule River near the foothills, Cook thinks probably not far from Porterville.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 36.

name: Deer Creek
summary: Cook: probably Deer Creek.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 37.

name: White River
summary: Cook: probably White River.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 38.

name: Poso Creek
summary: Cook: no distances are given, but from the description the most likely stream is Poso Creek.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 39.

name: Kern River, above Bakersfield
summary: Cook: the Kern River, probably some miles above Bakersfield.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 40.

name: Kern River, the slough country
summary: Cook: a long trip downstream would have brought the party into the slough country south of Bakersfield. Because Buenavista Lake is never mentioned, farther to the west, he holds it clear that Moraga did not get within sight of it, which is the lake Zalvidea had camped beside three months earlier.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 40.

name: Grapevine Canyon
summary: A sheltered place in the mountains with running water in a little creek and wild grapevines for almost the entire vegetation, reached just before sunset after the worst-worn horses had been sent off by another road. Munoz left the two villages seen that day undescribed, supposing that the Santa Barbara expedition would give a full account of them, and Cook notes that Zalvidea's report for August 1806 indeed did.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 41.

name: Tejon Pass
summary: On 1 November the party found the source of the stream, a grassy marsh, a valley of oaks and a lake of pure salt water, with a village to the east whose people the diary found too cunning in trading, and a second hidden among ravines and badlands whose people were away at a fiesta. Cook: on the last three days the party left the valley by way of Grapevine Canyon, over Tejon Pass, across the Tehachapi Mountains, which Cutter takes for the Santa Susanna Range, to San Fernando.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 42.

name: Mission San Fernando
summary: Arrival. On the last day the party followed the valley through mountains Munoz called indescribably rough, saw a light in the early evening and came upon the ranch of the fathers of San Fernando, reaching the mission itself the following day. Munoz signed the report on 2 November 1806, recording 141 baptisms on the expedition, all in extremis.
sources: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap.
